Department of the Treasury
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
31 CFR Part 1010
AGENCY:
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Treasury.
ACTION:
Order.
SUMMARY:
FinCEN is issuing notice of an order, pursuant to section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act (
Pub. L. 116-283
), as amended by section 6106(b) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (
Pub. L. 117-81
), finding that MEXC Global—including any of its subsidiaries, branches, and offices, as well as any successor entities, operating in any jurisdiction outside of the United States—is a financial institution operating outside of the United States of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance and prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global.
DATES:
This action is effective December 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
FinCEN's Regulatory Support Section by submitting an inquiry at
www.fincen.gov/​contact
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Summary of Order
As set out in this order, MEXC Global has facilitated funds transfers by Russia-affiliated illicit actors and in connection with other Russia-associated illicit activities, including sanctions evasion, and activity facilitated by Russian darknet markets. It has also facilitated billions of dollars in transactions benefitting Iran and its proxies, financial facilitators of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), and other cybercrime actors. Accordingly, this order (1) sets forth FinCEN's determination that MEXC Global, a convertible virtual currency (CVC) exchanger, along with any subsidiaries, branches, and offices of MEXC Global, and any successor entities, operating in any jurisdiction outside of the United States (collectively, MEXC Global)
[
1
]
is a financial institution operating outside of the United States of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance; and (2) prohibits certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global, by any covered financial institution.
II. Background
A. Statutory Provisions
Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act (
Pub. L. 116-283
), as amended by section 6106(b) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (
Pub. L. 117-81
) (section 9714),
[
2
]
provides, in relevant part, that, if the Secretary of the Treasury (Secretary) “determines that reasonable grounds exist for concluding that one or more financial institutions operating outside of the United States . . . is of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance,” the Secretary may, “by order, regulation, or otherwise as permitted by law”: (1) require domestic financial institutions and domestic financial agencies to take one or more of the special measures described in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)
;
[
3
]
or (2) prohibit, or impose conditions upon, certain transmittals of funds (as defined by the Secretary) by any domestic financial institution or domestic financial agency (collectively, covered financial institutions), if such transmittal of funds involves any such financial institution. The authority of the Secretary to administer both section 9714 and the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) has been delegated to FinCEN.
[
4
]
Pursuant to section 9714, the Secretary may impose one or more of six special measures. First, the Secretary may impose any of the five special measures provided for in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)
, commonly known as section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act.
[
5
]
Through special measures one through four, the Secretary may impose additional recordkeeping, information collection, and reporting requirements on covered financial institutions.
[
6
]
Through special measure five, the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, may “prohibit, or impose conditions upon, the opening or maintaining in the United States of a correspondent account or payable-through account” for or on behalf of a foreign banking institution, if such correspondent account or payable-through account involves the financial institution operating outside of the United States found to be of primary money laundering concern.
[
7
]
In addition
(
printed page 72421)
to the special measures set out in
31 U.S.C. 5318A
, section 9714 also provides that the Secretary may impose a special measure prohibiting, or imposing conditions upon, certain transmittals of funds.
[
8
]
B. MEXC Global
MEXC Global is a CVC exchanger founded in 2018 that is incorporated in the Seychelles, without a virtual asset service provider license
[
9
]
and operates in and across over 170 countries
[
10
]
through an array of current or former subsidiaries, branches, and offices, including, but not limited to, MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles; MEXC Estonia OÜ in Estonia; GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland; MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom; and, formerly, Singapore-registered MEXC Global Foundation Ltd and MEXC Singapore Pte Ltd.
[
11
]
As of June 2026, MEXC Global processed more than USD 1 billion in daily transactions, while maintaining approximately USD 5 billion in reserve assets. As such, MEXC Global is among the 20 largest CVC exchangers in the world by trading volume.
[
12
]
As of December 2025, MEXC Global commanded approximately nine percent of the global market share of centralized CVC exchangers by trading volume.
[
13
]
By comparison, the assets of the two largest centralized CVC exchangers together represented 47.4 percent of the global market share.
[
14
]
According to its user agreement, MEXC Global allows customers to open user accounts for exchange between various fiat currencies and CVC, as well as for futures trading and other services.
[
15
]
And, according to non-public information available to FinCEN, as of July 2026, MEXC Global offers the ability to trade in over fifty currencies, including USD and Russian rubles (RUB), as well as access to over 3,000 different CVCs and tokenized assets.
III. Finding That MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution Operating Outside the United States That Is of Primary Money Laundering Concern in Connection With Russian Illicit Finance
Based on public and non-public information available to FinCEN, FinCEN finds that reasonable grounds exist for concluding that MEXC Global is a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance—namely, through its facilitation of funds transfers by Russia-affiliated illicit actors and in connection with other Russia-associated illicit activities, including sanctions evasion, and activity facilitated by Russian darknet markets. Moreover, FinCEN assesses that, in addition to facilitating Russian illicit finance, MEXC Global has, in parallel, facilitated billions of dollars in transactions benefitting Iran and its proxies, financial facilitators of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), and other cybercrime actors.
In making this finding, FinCEN has considered the relevant evidence in light of factors identified in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(c)(2)(B)
, taking into account the specific circumstances of money laundering activities in connection with Russian illicit finance and the protection of U.S. national security and the U.S. financial system. While FinCEN is under no obligation pursuant to section 9714 to consider any particular factor or set of factors when making a finding that a financial institution operating outside of the United States is of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance, it nonetheless finds these factors instructive in guiding the analysis set forth below.
[
16
]
A. MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution Operating Outside the United States
Although section 9714 does not expressly define the term “financial institution,” FinCEN has long defined that term to include “money transmitters,” including persons that accept and transmit value that substitutes for currency, such as CVC.
[
17
]
MEXC Global, in operating as a CVC exchanger, is a “money transmitter” because it is engaged in the transfer of funds or value that substitutes for currency.
[
18
]
By its own account and as described above, MEXC Global operates through affiliates throughout the world—over time maintaining, for instance, subsidiaries, branches, and offices in Seychelles, Hong Kong, Singapore, Estonia, and the United Kingdom—and offers a range of money transmitter services for individual and institutional customers in the CVC sector in over 170 countries.
[
19
]
Considering the services that it provides and its places of registration, FinCEN assesses that MEXC Global is a financial institution operating outside of the United States within the meaning of section 9714.
Notably, to the extent that MEXC Global maintains or otherwise operates through affiliates, subsidiaries, branches, or offices in the United States, this order expressly excludes all such affiliates, subsidiaries, branches, or offices from the definition of “MEXC Global” and, accordingly, such affiliates, subsidiaries, branches, or offices are outside the scope of this order.
B. Finding That MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution of Primary Money Laundering Concern in Connection With Russian Illicit Finance
While MEXC Global's anti-money laundering and countering the financing
(
printed page 72422)
of terrorism (AML/CFT), customer identification and verification (sometimes referred to as “Know Your Customer” or “KYC” information), and other due diligence processes
[
20
]
prohibit, on paper, the opening of accounts by individuals in certain jurisdictions, FinCEN assesses that, based on public and non-public information, MEXC Global has facilitated transactions involving those prohibited jurisdictions. In addition, MEXC Global has facilitated transactions involving Russia-affiliated illicit actors and associated illicit activities, including sanctions evasion, and activity facilitated by Russian darknet markets, as well as transactions involving not only U.S.-, European Union-, and United Kingdom-sanctioned persons working on behalf of Iran and its proxies and the DPRK, but also an array of cybercrime actors.
Notwithstanding MEXC Global's AML/CFT and other due diligence processes, FinCEN found that MEXC Global has skirted compliance with applicable regulatory requirements
[
21
]
—multiple nations' financial regulators have issued notices highlighting that MEXC Global has operated in their jurisdictions without the proper license, and in at least one case added the CVC exchanger to a list of suspicious CVC trading platforms
[
22
]
—and, importantly, that, between May 2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global facilitated the movement of USD 16.7 billion in funds connected to Russian illicit finance and other illicit activities, including sanctions evasion and cybercrime, posing a significant threat to the U.S. financial system. Indeed, within those transactions, FinCEN identified numerous instances in which MEXC Global processed transactions in violation of its own user agreement, including direct transactions between MEXC Global and sanctioned actors, some of whom were operating from MEXC Global's list of prohibited jurisdictions.
[
23
]
1. MEXC Global Is Used in Furtherance of Sanctions Evasion in Connection With Russian Illicit Finance
MEXC Global has a history of processing CVC transfers for multiple key actors that support Russian illicit finance. According to FinCEN analysis of blockchain data, between May 2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global sent or received nearly USD 1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to transactions linked to Russian sanctions evasion and had significant exposure to Russian cyber actors connected to sanctions evasion and/or cybercrime. This includes USD 232 million in direct transactions with entities sanctioned by the United States, the European Union (EU), and/or the United Kingdom (UK).
[
24
]
For example, MEXC Global transacted with the sanctioned, Russia-backed CVC exchangers Garantex and Grinex. Between 2019 and 2025, Garantex facilitated the movement of over USD 100 million for ransomware actors and other cybercriminals.
[
25
]
Garantex's successor entity, Grinex, is itself a vehicle for sanctions evasion, as it was created by Garantex employees to move funds after Garantex was designated by OFAC for operating in Russia's financial services sector.
[
26
]
Following these public designations, MEXC Global directly facilitated approximately USD 129 million in activity with Garantex and USD 4.1 million in activity with Grinex, and MEXC Global continued to transact with both entities as recently as June 2026. Similarly, MEXC Global transacted with components of the Russia-based A7 Network,
[
27
]
a self-described sanctions-resistant payment service provider created by the U.S.-, EU- and UK-designated Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor
[
28
]
and Russia's state-owned defense bank Promsvyazbank Public Joint Stock Company (PSB),
[
29
]
that has evolved into a conduit for illicit activity associated with a wide range of threat actors, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its Quds Force, DPRK-affiliated actors;
(
printed page 72423)
Iran-backed terrorist organizations; and cybercriminals and ransomware actors.
[
30
]
Significantly, OFAC has designated the founders and core components and enablers of the A7 Network, and recently designated the A7 Network, itself, as a significant transnational criminal organization.
[
31
]
Further, FinCEN recently found that transactions involving any company operating outside of the United States that is controlled by the A7 Network belong to a class of transactions of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance.
[
32
]
Based on analysis of blockchain data, FinCEN assesses that MEXC Global facilitated the transmission of at least USD 26 million benefitting the now sanctioned A7 Network and sent or received almost USD 200 million connected to the A7A5 token (a ruble-backed stablecoin that operates on the Tron and Ethereum blockchains
[
33
]
to transfer value across A7 Network-linked actors where banking channels are restricted or less dependable),
[
34
]
including its issuer Old Vector LLC and owner Ilan Shor, both sanctioned by OFAC, as well as the European Union and the United Kingdom.
[
35
]
In addition, MEXC Global has repeatedly transacted with high-risk CVC exchangers that have been sanctioned or that allegedly have no customer identification verification requirements. For example, between May 2018 and July 2026, MEXC Global directly facilitated transactions cumulatively worth over USD 13 billion with at least four high-risk CVC exchangers sanctioned by the UK for facilitating Russian sanctions evasion and funding Russian military operations in Ukraine.
[
36
]
Between May 2021 and May 2026, it also processed approximately USD 2.9 billion in direct transactions with Russian and other CVC exchangers that allegedly do not collect customer identification and verification information, which poses a high risk of transacting with sanctioned entities and individuals and for otherwise engaging in illicit activity. In addition, between September 2020 and July 2026, MEXC Global facilitated USD 8.5 million in transactions involving Russian darknet markets that are known to facilitate the sale of illicit goods and services.
Based on MEXC Global's facilitation of transactions for sanctioned and high-risk Russian CVC exchangers, including the A7 Network, which are widely known to move funds for sanctioned actors, cybercriminals, and ransomware actors, FinCEN assesses that MEXC Global is a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance.
2. MEXC Global Is Used in Furtherance of International Money Laundering
According to public and non-public information, MEXC Global also facilitates activity in furtherance of international money laundering in support of Iran and its proxies, financial facilitators of the DPRK, and cybercrime.
a. MEXC Global Facilitated Transactions Involving Iran and Its Proxies
According to FinCEN analysis of blockchain information, between May 2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global facilitated the transmission of nearly USD 2 billion connected to identified Iranian actors or known or suspected terrorist groups, including approximately USD 1.87 billion in transactions with exposure to Iran, a jurisdiction that is the subject of comprehensive U.S. sanctions
[
37
]
and special measures imposed by FinCEN pursuant to section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act (
31 U.S.C. 5318A
) which prohibit covered financial institutions from opening or maintaining correspondent accounts in the United States for, or on behalf of, Iranian financial institutions.
[
38
]
Despite the fact that MEXC Global's user agreement states that individuals and entities located in Iran are not allowed to use its platform, FinCEN assesses that over USD 1 billion of this exposure took the form of direct transactions between MEXC Global and more than 40 identified Iranian CVC exchangers, some of which are the subject of U.S. and international sanctions. Between May 2021 and May 2026, FinCEN assesses that MEXC Global also facilitated the transmission of approximately USD 22 million in transactions associated with the U.S.- and EU-sanctioned Central Bank of Iran and the U.S.-, EU-, and UK-sanctioned IRGC and its Quds Force.
[
39
]
(
printed page 72424)
MEXC Global has also been exploited by multiple Iran proxy groups. For example, FinCEN identified approximately USD 36 million in transactions that occurred between May 2021 and May 2026 that went to or from MEXC Global related to the Gaza-based U.S.- and UK-sanctioned Al-Qassam Brigades and other Iran linked terrorist groups.
[
40
]
b. MEXC Global Facilitated Transactions Involving Financial Facilitators of the DPRK
MEXC Global has also transmitted funds on behalf of a financial facilitator of the DPRK, a jurisdiction that, like Iran, is the subject of comprehensive U.S. sanctions
[
41
]
and special measures imposed by FinCEN that prohibit covered financial institutions from opening or maintaining correspondent accounts in the United States for, or on behalf of, DPRK financial institutions.
[
42
]
For instance, FinCEN assesses that MEXC Global facilitated U.S.-sanctioned DPRK money launderer Sim Hyon Sop's receipt of approximately USD 350,000 between June and September 2025, more than two years after Sop had been designated by OFAC and even though, as part of his April 2023 designation, OFAC specifically identified and sanctioned his CVC addresses.
[
43
]
c. MEXC Global Facilitated Transactions Connected to Cybercrime
Finally, MEXC Global frequently processes transactions connected to cyber-enabled crimes, ranging from darknet marketplace activity (including the Russian darknet marketplace activity discussed above) and ransomware payments to scam proceeds and stolen funds. Between May 2021 and May 2026, FinCEN assesses that at least USD 1.99 billion in funds originating from or moving to illicit cyber actors moved through MEXC Global, an average of more than USD 1 million per day. Between January 2022 to July 2024, MEXC Global received more than USD 37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments, with exposure to over 125 ransomware variants. MEXC Global also hosts a particularly high-use ransomware-related deposit address, which received over USD 1.17 million during the same period.
C. The Extent to Which MEXC Global Is Used for Legitimate Business Purposes
In reaching its finding that MEXC Global is a financial institution operating outside the United States of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance, FinCEN considered the extent to which MEXC Global is used for legitimate business purposes.
[
44
]
As of June 2026, MEXC Global conducted USD 1 billion in daily transactions, putting it among the top 20 largest CVC exchangers in the world by trading volume. Although FinCEN does not have full insight into the scope of MEXC Global's legitimate activities, for the purposes of this action, FinCEN assumes that a portion of MEXC Global's business activities are legitimate. However, FinCEN assesses that since May 2021, MEXC Global has facilitated at least USD 16.7 billion in likely illicit activity. Accordingly, any legitimate business conducted by MEXC Global is outweighed by the risks posed by MEXC Global's facilitation of illicit activity, including sanctions evasion by Russia and Iran, and the need to protect the U.S. financial sector from the money laundering and terrorist financing risks presented by MEXC Global.
D. The Extent to Which This Action Would Guard Against International Money Laundering and Other Financial Crimes Associated With Russian Illicit Finance
A finding that MEXC Global is of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance establishes—and emphasizes—the significant illicit finance risks posed by MEXC Global's provision of financial services to the Russian illicit finance ecosystem, Russian and other darknet markets and high-risk exchanges. Further, notwithstanding MEXC Global's ties to Russian illicit finance, FinCEN assesses that it has facilitated over USD 1.87 billion in transactions with exposure to Iran, including over USD 1 billion in direct transactions between MEXC Global and Iranian CVC exchangers, as well as transactions benefiting the DPRK and an array of illicit cyber actors, each of which present significant risks to the U.S. financial system. Accordingly, this order will place U.S. and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice to guard against those risks. Moreover, such a finding—in combination with a prohibition on certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global by covered financial institutions—will help safeguard the U.S. financial system by severing MEXC Global's access.
IV. Imposition of a Special Measure Prohibiting Certain Transmittals of Funds Involving MEXC Global
Having found that MEXC Global is a financial institution operating outside of the United States that is of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance, FinCEN has determined that the imposition of a special measure prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global is warranted.
[
45
]
In making this determination and assessing which special measures may be appropriate, FinCEN has considered the relevant evidence in light of factors identified in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(a)(4)(B)
. While FinCEN is under no obligation pursuant to section 9714 to consider any particular factor or set of factors in selecting one or more special measures, it nonetheless finds these factors instructive in guiding the analysis set forth below.
[
46
]
(
printed page 72425)
A. Whether the Prohibition Would Address the Money Laundering Concern in a Manner Consistent With U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy Interests
FinCEN has considered the effect this action will have on U.S. national security and foreign policy, as well as the extent to which multilateral groups or other nations have taken similar actions.
[
47
]
FinCEN has found that, in addition to facilitating Russian illicit financial activity and sanctions evasion schemes and serving as a high-density transactional node for high-risk CVC exchangers, MEXC Global plays a broader role in facilitating transactions for a diverse range of transnational illicit actors. In particular, MEXC Global processes transactions connected to Iranian sanctions evasion, terrorist financing, and the laundering of scam and ransomware proceeds. FinCEN, therefore, assesses that imposing a prohibition on certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global is necessary to safeguard U.S. national security and the U.S. financial system, as well as to serve key U.S. national security objectives.
In light of the quantity and volume of transactions linked to known or suspected illicit activity processed through MEXC Global, prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global would insulate the U.S. financial system from money laundering and other financial crimes. In particular, prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global would further ongoing U.S. efforts to curtail suspected Russia-associated illicit activity and financial transactions. And, targeting illicit proceeds moved by sanctions evasion networks, especially those with a nexus to Iran, is of highest priority for the United States. Consequently, prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global will serve the U.S. national security and foreign policy interests by protecting the U.S. and international financial system from known threat actors.
Moreover, this action reinforces the expectations of AML/CFT compliance in the financial system, highlighting the importance of identifying and reporting suspicious activity by financial institutions around the world. With respect to the illicit finance risks posed by MEXC Global, that is of particular importance, as this order addresses primary money laundering concerns that are still ongoing after multiple jurisdictions' financial regulators have issued notices highlighting that MEXC Global has operated in their jurisdictions without the proper license, and in at least one case added the CVC exchanger to a list of suspicious CVC trading platforms.
[
48
]
B. Whether the Prohibition of Certain Transmittals of Funds Would Impose Undue Burdens on Legitimate Activity of MEXC Global or Third Parties
FinCEN has considered whether prohibiting certain transmittals of funds would create a significant competitive disadvantage, including any undue cost or burden associated with compliance, for financial institutions organized or licensed in the United States, as well as the extent to which the action could have a significant adverse systemic impact on legitimate business activities currently being conducted on the MEXC Global platform.
[
49
]
Indeed, while MEXC Global is used by licit actors, the legitimate business services that it offers are commonly offered by other regulated institutions, meaning that such licit actors could readily find alternatives to facilitate business.
And, FinCEN assesses that prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global will not present a significant competitive disadvantage for or put an undue burden on financial institutions organized or licensed in the United States. Compliance with the prohibition on certain transmittals of funds set out in this order requires no tools or competencies other than those already employed by domestic financial institutions to maintain their current AML/CFT compliance programs. To aid covered U.S. financial institutions with compliance, FinCEN has elected to provide within this order for the rejection of certain transmittals of CVC that are received from or originate at MEXC Global and outline the steps a covered financial institution should take in such circumstances. In providing for the rejection of CVC under certain limited circumstances, FinCEN acknowledges that, at this time, there are technological limitations that may limit or preclude covered financial institutions from declining CVC transfers originating at addresses outside of their control, and compliant institutions may find themselves in receipt of CVC from MEXC Global despite a desire and effort to limit such exposure.
[
50
]
This order therefore allows covered financial institutions the flexibility to act with discretion based on the facts and circumstances of a particular transaction and comply with this order, even where the originating address is no longer accessible, where, for example, (1) CVC transfers originated from MEXC Global, but were held for an extended period of time in an unhosted wallet, or (2) the covered financial institution's risk mitigation procedures would preclude returning funds to MEXC Global. Moreover, by providing for the rejection of CVC, this order ensures that covered financial institutions will not be subject to an undue cost or burden associated with compliance.
C. Whether Any Other Reasonable Alternatives or Special Measures Would Adequately Address the Money Laundering Concern
Before deciding to impose a prohibition on certain transmittals of funds, FinCEN considered other available special measures.
[
51
]
After due
(
printed page 72426)
consideration, FinCEN has determined that a special measure prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global is the appropriate means to adequately address the illicit finance risks posed by MEXC Global.
None of the special measures set out in
31 U.S.C. 5318A
—special measures one through five—would effectively address the illicit finance threat posed by MEXC Global. Any additional recordkeeping, information collection, or reporting requirements, as described in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(1)-(4)
, would be insufficient to guard against the risks posed by covered financial institutions processing transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global. Those special measures would allow such transfers to continue to the benefit of illicit actors connected to Russian illicit finance, as well as Iran-related and other illicit financial activity. Further, merely prohibiting and/or placing conditions upon the opening or maintaining in the United States of correspondent accounts or payable-through accounts for or on behalf of MEXC Global, as described in
31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(5)
, would be similarly inadequate. Neither prohibiting nor imposing conditions on such accounts would safeguard the U.S. financial system to the same degree as prohibiting transmittals of funds, as such a special measure would not address the movement of funds outside of a strict correspondent or payable-through relationship, for example, through the movement of funds outside the traditional banking relationship, which may permit MEXC Global to access USD through indirect correspondent relationships via other foreign financial institutions.
D. Whether the Prohibition Should Be Imposed by Order or Regulation
Pursuant to section 9714, the Secretary may impose one or more special measures, including a prohibition on certain transmittals of funds, “by order, regulation or otherwise as permitted by law.” In determining the appropriate approach in this instance, FinCEN considered imposing the prohibition by order or regulation, taking into account the nature of the underlying threat, and determined that proceeding by an order is the most appropriate course of action given the imminent threats posed by the illicit actors whose transactions and access to funds MEXC Global facilitates, as well as the ongoing transactions associated with suspected activity related to Russian illicit finance that continue to be processed through MEXC Global. Further, FinCEN has assessed that this order will not be unduly burdensome or impose new or unique compliance costs on financial institutions.
A copy of this order will be published in the
Federal Register
. To the extent MEXC Global or other parties have information relevant to this order, they may submit it to FinCEN at
www.fincen.gov/​contact
.
V.
Executive Order 14294
Section 5 of
Executive Order 14294
directs that all future notices of proposed rulemaking (NPRMs) and final rules published in the
Federal Register
, the violation of which may constitute criminal regulatory offenses, should include a statement identifying that the rule or proposed rule is a criminal regulatory offense and the authorizing statute.
[
52
]
Executive Order 14294
directs agencies to draft this statement in consultation with the Department of Justice.
Executive Order 14294
further directs that the regulatory text of all NPRMs and final rules with criminal consequences published in the
Federal Register
after May 9, 2025, should explicitly state a mens rea requirement for each element of a criminal regulatory offense, accompanied by citations to the relevant provisions of the authorizing statute.
Willful violations of any final regulations set forth in this order may be subject to criminal penalties pursuant to
31 U.S.C. 5322
and regulations promulgated in
31 CFR Chapter X
. The statutory authority for criminal liability requires a mens rea of willfulness as an element pursuant to
31 U.S.C. 5322(a)
and
31 U.S.C. 5322(b)
. FinCEN's existing regulation,
31 CFR 1010.840
, that sets out criminal penalties for violations of regulations promulgated in
31 CFR Chapter X
also includes a mens rea of willfulness. In drafting this statement, FinCEN has consulted with the Department of Justice.
VI. Order
A. Definitions
1. MEXC Global
The order defines “MEXC Global,” a Seychelles-based CVC exchanger, to include its branches, subsidiaries, and offices operating as a financial institution in any jurisdiction outside of the United States, and any successor entities. For the purposes of this order, a successor entity means any person that replaces MEXC Global, its branches, subsidiaries, and offices by acquiring its assets, in whole or in part, and/or carrying on the affairs of MEXC Global under a new name. This includes, but is not limited to, any entities referenced in this order as being branches, subsidiaries, or offices of MEXC Global operating as a financial institution in any jurisdiction outside of the United States. Any branches, subsidiaries, and offices of MEXC Global located in the United States are expressly excluded from the definition of “MEXC Global” for the purposes of this order.
2. Convertible Virtual Currency
The order defines “convertible virtual currency” (CVC) as a medium of exchange that either has an equivalent value to currency, or acts as a substitute for currency, but lacks legal tender status. Bitcoin, despite having legal tender status in at least one jurisdiction, is included as a type of CVC for the purpose of this order.
3. Covered Financial Institution
The order defines “covered financial institution” as having the same meaning as “financial institution” in
31 CFR 1010.100(t)
.
4. Transmittals of Funds
The order defines “transmittals of funds” as the sending and receiving of funds, including CVC. For avoidance of doubt, for this section, this definition of transmittal of funds applies rather than the definition of “transmittal of funds” in section 1010.100(ddd).
5. Meaning of Other Terms
All terms used but not otherwise defined herein shall have the meaning set forth in
31 CFR chapter X
and
31 U.S.C. 5312
.
B. Prohibition on Transmittals of Funds Involving MEXC Global
A covered financial institution is prohibited from engaging in any transmittal of funds from or to MEXC Global.
C. Order Period
The terms of this order are effective December 10, 2026, with no cessation date.
D. Reservation of Authority
FinCEN reserves authority to impose conditions on certain transmittals of funds from or to MEXC Global and to grant appropriate exemptions from the requirements of this order.
(
printed page 72427)
E. Other Obligations
Nothing in this order shall be construed to modify, impair, or otherwise affect any requirements or obligations to which a covered financial institution is subject pursuant to the BSA, including, but not limited to, the filing of Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), or other applicable laws or regulations, such as the sanctions administered and enforced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control.
F. Penalties for Noncompliance
The covered financial institution, and any of its officers, directors, employees, and agents, may be liable for civil or criminal penalties under
31 U.S.C. 5321
and
5322
for willfully violating this order.
G. Validity of Order
Any judicial determination that any provision of this order is invalid shall not affect the validity of any other provision of this order, and each other provision shall thereafter remain in full force and effect.
Jimmy L. Kirby,
Deputy Director, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The final rule updates the maintenance inspection requirements for single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft. Aircraft owners and operators now have more inspection program options to choose from and more relaxed mechanical reliability reporting requirements. It also clarifies various maintenance-related regulations. This final rule relieves aircraft owners, operators, maintenance providers, and FAA of certain workload burdens by facilitating a more efficient workload for these individuals without compromising aviation safety.
DATES:
Effective January 11, 2027.

I. Executive Summary
A. Overview of the Final Rule
This final rule revises
14 CFR part 91
to make maintenance requirements for certain aircraft more flexible. To begin, it expands the maintenance inspection program options for owners and operators of single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft. Specifically, single-engine turbine-powered airplane owners and operators can now use an inspection program recommended by the manufacturer, or one created by the registered owner or operator, provided it is approved by the Administrator. Existing inspection options, such as the annual, 100-hour, or progressive inspection programs, remain available as alternatives.
In addition, for unmanned aircraft operating under
14 CFR part 135
, the rule now allows these aircraft owners and operators to follow inspection rules under part 91. This means they can choose either a manufacturer-recommended inspection program or one established by the registered owner or operator, as long as it receives Administrator approval.
Beyond inspection programs, the final rule amends subpart K of part 91 by extending the reporting interval for aircraft mechanical reliability reports from 72 hours to 96 hours. It also provides the option to submit these reports electronically, simplifying the submission process.
Finally, this final rule clarifies and streamlines maintenance-related regulations in various parts of
14 CFR
, including parts 125, 135, 137, 145, and additional subparts of part 91. By addressing confusing or ambiguous language, these updates help aircraft owners, operators, and maintenance providers comply with regulations more easily. Overall, the rule supports FAA's mission of efficiency by enabling greater flexibility for owners, operators, and maintenance providers in meeting maintenance requirements, all while ensuring that aviation safety remains uncompromised.
B. Summary of the Costs and Benefits
This rule's manned aircraft maintenance programs include a 10-year estimate of costs and savings. These estimates are based on the assumption that all manufacturers of single-engine turbine-powered aircraft would develop and make available their manufacturer inspection programs to owners and operators of that aircraft type. Using a seven percent discount rate, the result is an annualized net cost savings of $57.02 million.
II. Authority for This Rulemaking
FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety, such as the rules governing the inspection, maintenance service, and overhauling of aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers, and appliances, as well as the equipment and facilities, the timing of and manner of such activities, is found in title 49 of the United States Code (49 U.S.C.). Subtitle I, section 106 grants the FAA Administrator the authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority, including the authority to issue regulations.
This rulemaking is issued under
49 U.S.C. 44701(a)(2)(A)
and
(B)
, which directs FAA to prescribe regulations and minimum standards in the interest of safety for:
(1) inspecting, servicing, and overhauling aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers, and appliances; and (2) equipment and facilities for, and the timing of and manner of, the inspecting, servicing, and overhauling FAA finds necessary for safety in air commerce. In addition,
49 U.S.C. 44701(a)(5)
charges FAA with promoting the safe flight of civil aircraft by prescribing regulations and minimum standards for other practices, methods, and procedures FAA finds necessary for safety in air commerce and national security.
Finally,
49 U.S.C. 44707
authorizes FAA to examine and rate repair stations and shops that repair, alter, and maintain aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers, and appliances. Specifically, under
49 U.S.C. 44707(2)
, FAA is charged with inspecting and rating repair stations and shops on the adequacy and suitability of the equipment, facilities, and materials for, and methods of, repair and overhaul, and the competency of the individuals doing the work or giving instruction in the work.
III. Background
A. Statement of the Problem
Previously, single-engine turbine-powered airplanes were not authorized to use the inspection options listed in
14 CFR 91.409(f)
as alternatives to the annual or 100-hour inspection requirements. These options listed under § 91.409(f) included a continuous airworthiness inspection program under a part 121 or part 135 operator's Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP), an approved aircraft inspection program under part 135, a manufacturer-recommended inspection program, and a program created by the owner or operator and approved by FAA.
In 1989, FAA updated § 91.409(e), introducing more inspection options for turbine-powered rotorcraft. This allowed operators to schedule inspections in a way that optimized the time between inspections, resulting in more efficient operations. However, single-engine turbine-powered airplanes were excluded from this update because they were less common compared to rotorcraft at the time. Today, that is no longer the case—there are now more than 4,500 single-engine turbine-powered airplanes registered in the U.S. Moreover, the increasing integration of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) into the National Airspace System since 2016 has added further context to the need for regulatory updates. To accommodate and support UAS operations under parts 91 and 135, FAA has granted exemptions and waivers, generally requiring UAS to adhere to the manufacturer's inspection instructions or incorporate those instructions in an operator's approved maintenance inspection program.
Given these developments, FAA sees no safety concerns that justify denying single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and UAS the same regulatory flexibility as turbine-powered rotorcraft when it comes to part 91 inspection options. Manufacturer-recommended inspection programs for turbine-powered rotorcraft have consistently proven to be safe and effective alternatives to annual or 100-hour inspections. FAA anticipates similarly positive outcomes for single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and UAS that use manufacturer recommended programs, or ones established by the owner or operator and approved by the Administrator.
Lastly, there is a pressing need to address ambiguities in part 145 related to maintenance documentation and contract maintenance. FAA has received numerous questions and requests for legal interpretations pertaining to these matters, underscoring the importance of providing clearer regulatory language.
B. Summary of the NPRM
The notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), which published in the
Federal Register
on January 31, 2024, with the comment period closing on May 1, 2024, proposed several amendments. First, it proposed expanding the availability of maintenance inspection program options under
14 CFR 91.409(e)
to
(
printed page 72399)
single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft (excluding part 107 aircraft) operating under parts 91 or 135. This change enables owners and operators to use inspection programs under § 91.409(f), offering greater flexibility. In addition, the NPRM proposed relaxing the mechanical reliability reporting requirements found under § 91.1415(d). The new reporting timeframe, from 72 to 96 hours, would align with §§ 121.703, 125.409, 135.415, and 145.221. It proposed changing the section heading from “Mechanical reliability reports” to “Service difficulty reports” for consistency. The NPRM also proposed clarification of part 145 requirements. Specifically, the proposed changes to § 145.217 would clarify that FAA approval of contract maintenance applies only when a certificated repair station assumes responsibility for outside maintenance and approves it for return to service. In addition, § 145.201(a)(2) would remove “for which the certificated repair station is rated,” allowing repair stations to arrange contract maintenance on articles they are not rated for. Other reorganization changes to part 145 were proposed to reduce administrative burdens and clarify contract maintenance regulations.
Moreover, the NPRM proposed numerous miscellaneous updates to
14 CFR parts 91
,
125
,
135
, and
137
. The proposed amendments aim to clarify and streamline inspection program options and submission processes for aircraft owners and operators. Subtitles “Annual Inspection” and “100-Hour Inspection” were added to § 91.409 at (a) and (b), respectively, to improve consistency in labeling across 14 CFR. Proposed changes to § 91.409(e) included reorganizing it into two subparagraphs: one for large airplanes, multiengine turbine-powered airplanes, and unmanned aircraft, and another for turbine-powered rotorcraft and single-engine turbine-powered airplanes.
Proposed amendments to
14 CFR 91.409(f)
involved simplifying terminology, such as replacing “[a] continuous airworthiness inspection program that is part of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program [CAMP] . . .” with “
an inspection program
that is part of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program . . .” and revising other phrases throughout the subsection for consistency and clarity (emphasis added). The NPRM aimed to reduce administrative burdens by removing the requirement under § 91.409(f)(4) to list the name and address of the person responsible for scheduling inspections. Proposed revisions to § 91.401 (the applicability section for subpart E of part 91) offered to reorganize the section and incorporate certain applicability provisions that are found in other sections of subpart E. Revisions were also proposed to § 91.403(c) to enhance clarity by dividing the alternative compliance options that were located in a single paragraph, into three new paragraphs—(c)(1), (c)(2), and (c)(3).
Finally, the NPRM proposed revisions to
14 CFR 91.405
to clarify maintenance requirements for correcting aircraft discrepancies that are discovered through inspection. Revisions to paragraph (a) proposed to clarify that “repair” of an aircraft discrepancy is not the only maintenance action that owners and operators may take. The revision proposed to list other types of maintenance actions that may be taken, such as inspection, preservation, or replacement of parts. The revision was proposed to add a reference to § 91.213 (“Inoperative instruments and equipment”) in paragraph (a), to inform that deferral of qualifying instruments and equipment under specific conditions and limitations is permitted. The NPRM further proposed to change § 91.405(c) to clarify that there is no time limitation regarding how long the inoperative instrument or equipment item could remain inoperative as long as it is inspected at each required inspection and there is no adverse effect on the aircraft's continued safe operation. Revisions to paragraph (d)'s introductory text were proposed to add the phrase “. . . marking it `Inoperative' ” to enhance clarity and maintain consistency with §§ 43.11(b) and 91.213(d)(3)(ii). Lastly, the NPRM proposed to clarify that all maintenance programs referenced in § 135.411(a)(2) refer to a CAMP, and to reorganize § 137.53(c) (Operation over congested areas: Pilots and aircraft). It proposed to relocate the § 137.53(c)(1)(i) inspection requirement, which mandates a 100-hour or annual inspection or inspection under a progressive system for most aircraft, to § 91.409 to consolidate it with other 100-hour or annual inspections for aircraft operated for hire or flight instruction. In addition, it proposed to remove paragraph (c)(1)(ii) entirely, which specifies inspection requirements for turbine-powered multiengine civil airplanes, since § 91.409(e) already governs inspections for such aircraft. Overall, the NPRM's proposal aimed to ensure consistency and reduce confusion across regulations.
C. General Overview of Comments
FAA received 21 comments in total, including one duplicate and two submitted after the deadline. However, the two late comments were from individuals who were supportive of the rule without any suggested changes. Eight of the comments were from individuals, and the remaining 13 comments were from business entities. Eight commenters supported the rule but suggested additional changes. The commenters' suggested changes are discussed more fully in the `Discussion of Comments and the Final Rule' section below. Two comments were outside the scope of the rule.
IV. Discussion of Comments and the Final Rule
A. Support for Changes to Parts 91, 125, 135, 137, and 145
FAA received only supportive comments regarding the proposed amendments to
14 CFR parts 91
,
125
,
135
, and
137
. There was no opposition or suggested changes to these proposed amendments. Accordingly, FAA is adopting the final rule for these parts as proposed in the NPRM. Though the proposed amendments to part 145 were received well by the public, there were several comments that presented, recommended, or suggested changes to the proposed amendments of this part. As a result of these suggested changes to the proposed amendment regarding part 145, this final rule deletes the word “current” from § 145.211(c)(1)(v) in order to minimize confusion regarding the data that repair stations must maintain. Under § 145.217(a), the final rule inserts the phrase “outside source” in order to clarify the issue of when § 145.217 is applicable. Lastly, part 145 certificated repair stations are included in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) of this final rule.
B. Suggestions for Removal of Current Technical Data Terminology at § 145.211(c)(1)(v)
Section 145.211(c)(1)(v) requires the quality control manual to contain a description of the system and procedures for “[e]stablishing and maintaining current technical data.” The NPRM invited the public to comment on whether to remove the current requirement that a repair station must maintain the specified documents and that the documents be “current” and accessible when the relevant work is being done.
Five commenters wrote and suggested that the term “current” causes confusion, and it would be beneficial if the word “current” were replaced with another word, or completely removed, in the regulation when referring to Instructions for Continued
(
printed page 72400)
Airworthiness (ICA). One individual commenter reasoned that the use of the word “current” is irrelevant to the intent of the rule because repair stations are already required to maintain all technical data regardless of whether it is current or not. The individual further commented that keeping the word would make the requirement confusing because repair stations would think that they only have to maintain current data and not all data, which is not accurate. The individual also suggested amending § 43.13(a) by removing the phrase “Instructions for Continued Airworthiness,” reasoning that the current maintenance manuals are considered instructions for continuous airworthiness, therefore making the term “Instructions for Continuous Airworthiness” redundant.
The other four commenters, likewise, stated that the § 145.211(c)(1)(v) language should be adjusted to accommodate the proposal's requirement that the appropriate technical data be available when the work is performed. They reasoned the NPRM's objective could be achieved by using their recommended language of: “[e]nsuring appropriate technical data is available and used when work is being performed.”
FAA agrees with the suggestion regarding deleting the word “current” from § 145.211(c)(1)(v). However, FAA does not agree with the other changes suggested. Concerning the individual commenter's requested change to § 43.13(a) and assertion that the manufacturer's maintenance manuals are essentially ICA, FAA disagrees because ICA may not always be included in manufacturers' maintenance manuals. Sometimes ICA are found in service bulletins, service letters, and other service documents. Therefore, the current regulatory language is accurate and not redundant. Accordingly, FAA is adopting the rule as proposed, without this suggested omission.
Concerning the four commenters' collective new language at § 145.211(c)(1)(v), FAA believes that the suggested new language creates more ambiguity because that language does not inform or define what “appropriate” technical data means or includes. As such, FAA partially accepts these suggestions and removes the word “current” at § 145.211(c)(1)(v) in the final rule to enhance the clarity of the regulation. Incorporating the suggestions, the text would read as follows: “Establishing and maintaining [deleted] technical data for maintaining articles.”
C. Suggestions for Consistency of Terminology at § 145.217
Two commenters suggested that FAA use the term “outside source” consistently throughout § 145.217. The commenters noted that the term is introduced at § 145.217(a) but then changes to the phrase “non-certificated person” or “outside facility.” For purposes of continuity and because “outside source” may include a noncertificated person, FAA agrees with the two commenters and amends § 145.217 at (a)(1), (a)(2)(i), and (a)(2)(ii) to reflect these suggestions. These suggestions are aligned with the purpose of the rule to streamline and clarify various maintenance regulations, so there is a better understanding of how to comply with them.
In addition, four commenters suggested amending the proposal at § 145.217(a)(1) to make it clear that § 145.217 applies only when the certificated repair station that is contracting for the function will issue an approval for return to service for the work performed by the contractor. To clarify this applicability issue, the commenters suggested removing the phrase “. . . to the outside source” so that subsection (a)(1) can simply read: “[t]he Administrator approves the maintenance function to be contracted.”
FAA agrees with the intent of this suggestion because this change is needed for further clarity, which is the purpose of the proposal. However, instead of accepting the commenters' suggested language, FAA has made the suggested changes at § 145.217(a) for easier readability instead of at § 145.217(a)(1) as the commenters initially suggested. The final rule will read as follows: “[a] certificated repair station may approve the work for return to service following the maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alterations performed on an article by an outside source under contract or other arrangement, in accordance with § 145.201(a)(2), provided all the following conditions are met:.”
D. Suggestions Regarding Clarification of the Work Performed on an Article at § 145.201
Four commenters, collectively, wrote a recommendation in support of the proposed changes to
14 CFR 145.201
. However, they noted that additional changes should be made “[t]o align section 145.201 with § 43.9(a)(4) and make [§ 145.201] more comprehensive . . .” Specifically, they noted that the proposal perpetuated an inconsistency with the § 43.9 privilege of approving work for return to service. When maintenance or alteration is performed, the maintenance provider approves
the work
on the article, rather than the article itself, for return to service. To align § 145.201 with § 43.9(a)(4), the commenters made the following suggestions: (1) add additional text to § 145.201(a)(1) to read as: “[t]he certificated repair station may approve for return to service the work on any article for which the certificated repair station is rated after it has performed maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration in accordance with part 43; (2) replace the phrase “an article” with the phrase “the work” at § 145.201(a)(2); and (3) change subparagraphs § 145.201(c)(1), (2), and (3) to reflect correctly that the repair station only approves for return to service “the work” performed on an article.
Commenters suggested that similar conforming changes should be made to §§ 145.219(c) and 145.223(c), because § 145.219(a) currently requires that records be kept for two years from the date an article was approved for return to service. The commenters also suggested that the paragraph should be changed to two years from the date “the work” was approved for return to service. For the same reason, they suggested that § 145.223(c) should be revised to clarify that a non-certificated source must allow FAA to inspect its work before a certificated repair station may approve for return to service the work performed by the non-certificated source.
FAA partially agrees with the suggestions to amend § 145.201(a)(2) and (c) to replace the term “an article” with the term “the work.” In addition, FAA partially accepts this recommendation and amends the text at § 145.201(c) to include the phrase “the work performed on—”. FAA decided to amend the text at § 145.201(c) introductory paragraph instead of amending at § 145.217(a)(1), (a)(2)(i), and (a)(2)(ii), like the commenters suggested, because this option makes the text more concise and helps with readability. FAA declines the suggested amendment to §§ 145.219(c) and 145.223(c), because these changes exceed the proposed language and interested parties could not have reasonably anticipated the final rule to have such changes.
E. Miscellaneous Issues
1. Comments on the Omission of Part 145 Repair Stations From the NPRM's Regulatory Impact Analysis
Four commenters, collectively, suggested that part 145 repair stations need to be included in the RIA section.
(
printed page 72401)
They stated the removal of the requirement that repair stations must keep “current” data when it may not be needed or used represents potentially millions of dollars in savings for certificated repair stations that comply with the current mandate.
They also state that
14 CFR 145.217
only applies when the certificated repair station approves another person's work for return to service. This amendment clarifies existing regulations, helping both the agency and the industry avoid hours of unnecessary back-and-forth. By reducing continuous changes to repair stations' quality manuals, it minimizes the need for repeated agency reviews, streamlining the process. Furthermore, four commenters, collectively recommended that part 145 repair stations be included in the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) analysis, though it acknowledged that the proposed rule does not impact current reporting and collection requirements for repair stations or certificate holders.

2. Commenter's Request for More Transparency Regarding FAA's Oversight Process for Manufacturer-Recommended and Registered Owner/Operator's Inspection Programs
One commenter suggested that FAA needed to be more transparent regarding the safety data collected and more openly document FAA's acceptance standards for inspection programs with industry stakeholders. Specifically, the commenter requested that FAA share UAS safety data and the process for approval for proposed UAS maintenance inspection programs with industry stakeholders. In addition, the commenter suggested that FAA perform a more complete and thorough oversight and safety review of each manufacturer-recommended inspection program or the program established by the registered owner or operator.
FAA believes the commenter's suggestion is outside the scope of the rule's proposal. The intent of the rule was to lessen the burden on owners, operators, maintenance providers, and FAA without compromising safety. FAA believes it has struck that balance here and that the oversight and review it performs is sufficient to ensure the safety of these inspection programs. Though the commenter is correct that additional disclosure would increase transparency, FAA does not believe, and the commenter has provided no evidence to support, that doing so would increase safety. Further, FAA is concerned that the process outlined by the commenter would likely result in heavily redacted disclosures, reducing even that transparency benefit. Finally, FAA notes that this process only applies to UAS operations under part 135, which comprise a minority of such operations that will only decline in number when the agency's rulemaking to establish a new part 108 for Beyond Visual Line-of-Sight (BVLOS) operations is completed.

14 CFR 145.217(b)
to list the specific maintenance functions that a certificated repair station may contract out to a noncertificated person.
FAA is adopting the final rule as proposed, without adding the requested language, because it is widely understood that the phrase “maintenance functions” also encompasses maintenance, preventative maintenance, and alterations. Accordingly, additional language is not needed.
4. Suggestion To Remove Terminology at §§ 145.201 and 145.217

14 CFR 145.201

145.217

Specifically, they stated 14 CFR provides “vastly different definitions of `contract maintenance' in §§ 121.368, 135.426, and 145.217 . . . .” In the alternative, the commenter suggested adding a second category clarifying that certificated repair stations that perform return to service on articles contracted to them by another certificated repair station are not considered contract maintenance under § 145.217.
FAA notes that the commenter made this suggestion, but did not recommend any viable options for replacing the term. FAA analyzed the issue raised and determined it did not require a change. Accordingly, FAA is adopting the rule as proposed, without the requested omission of the term.

FAA disagrees with this suggestion because the type of certification and rating(s) of an outside source who is performing contract maintenance work is vital information that FAA needs. Accordingly, FAA is adopting the rule as proposed, without the requested omission.

V. Regulatory Notices and Analyses
A. Summary of the Regulatory Impact Analysis
Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and
E.O. 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has determined this rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in section (3)(f)(1) of
E.O. 12866
. Accordingly, FAA has prepared a RIA for this rule, summarized in this section and available in the docket.
E.O. 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity through Deregulation”) issued January 31, 2025, instructs agencies to “alleviate unnecessary regulatory burdens.” FAA has determined this is an
E.O. 14192
deregulatory action.
The final rule will revise the aircraft maintenance rules primarily in the area of manned and unmanned aircraft maintenance and inspections. The most substantial change is the addition of more inspection program options for owners and operators of single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft. Currently, owners and operators of these types of aircraft are limited to annual, 100-hour, or progressive inspection programs. The final rule also amends
14 CFR part 145
to clarify and simplify various maintenance-related regulations in areas with confusing or ambiguous language. These areas include maintenance and inspection requirements for parts 91 and 125 operators and document retention. Furthermore, the rule clarifies part 145 regulations pertaining to repair station maintenance documentation and contract maintenance.
For single-engine turbine-powered airplanes, this final rule will increase these options to include, among others, a manufacturer-recommended inspection program, or an inspection program established by the registered owner or operator and approved by the Administrator. For unmanned aircraft, including unmanned aircraft operating under
14 CFR part 135
that are authorized to use the inspection rules in part 91, this final rule will allow the selection of one of those inspection programs. The added inspection programs will afford aircraft owners more flexibility in performing aircraft inspections as they will have more options and will likely reduce inspection costs incurred by owners and operators. These programs will provide owners and operators of single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft more options for inspecting their aircraft without reducing safety and potentially increasing the current frequency or cycle of inspections.
Repair stations will see cost savings from this final rule by decreasing their cost of maintenance manuals. Currently they must keep “current” data for maintenance manuals they are certificated to repair. With this final rule repair stations will not be required to pay for manuals and maintenance subscriptions for aircraft they are not working on.
This will also enable manufacturers to implement more efficient and effective inspection programs for new and existing fleets of aircraft, which will bolster safety while also controlling associated costs, and will be attractive to new and existing owners. This final rulemaking will not create a burden for owners/operators of single-engine turbine-powered airplanes since the decision to switch aircraft inspection programs is voluntary. Nor will this final rule create a burden for owners/operators of unmanned aircraft because the use of manufacturers' recommended inspection programs is, in general, already required under existing exemptions and will be a less burdensome alternative to FAA-approved inspection programs for part 135 operators.
One manufacturer estimated that inspecting aircraft under a Maintenance Steering Group—3rd Task Force (MSG-3) (used by manufacturers to develop initial scheduled maintenance/inspection requirements) inspection program could save owners/operators approximately $7,974 per aircraft in 2020 US dollars ($9,492 in 2024 US dollars) compared to an annual inspection program.
Manufacturers will incur costs to update inspection programs, but these costs will be voluntary, as the rule will not require manufacturers to develop new inspection programs. However, most manufacturers will likely choose to do so, given the relatively low associated costs compared to potential benefits in terms of safety and customer satisfaction. Furthermore, even if a manufacturer does not choose to create an inspection program for a specific type of aircraft, this rule still provides a benefit to aircraft owners in that it also allows aircraft owners to develop their own inspection program.
Because a manufacturer-developed inspection program or one created by the aircraft owner will be customized to the specific aircraft, improved safety is anticipated to be one of the benefits of this rulemaking. This is due to the utilization of more relevant and appropriate inspection tasks and intervals. A manufacturer-developed program likely will be less invasive compared with the annual or 100-hour inspection. For example, high utilization operators performing a 100-hour inspection frequently generate maintenance issues due to frequent disassembly, inspection, and reassembly of components. Aircraft safety will be improved by having a less invasive scheduled maintenance process. Safety benefits for single-engine turbine-powered airplanes were not quantified; and costs and benefits for unmanned aircraft were not quantified.

This final rule will benefit owners/operators of single-engine turbine-powered airplanes by allowing them the option to choose a program that may be less costly and more effective for inspecting their aircraft. Other changes clarify and simplify the regulations, lengthen the reporting time for mechanical reliability reports for aircraft operating under part 91 fractional ownership rule, and update the language for electronic submissions. B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) of 1980, (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
), as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
) and the Small Business Jobs Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-240
), requires Federal agencies to consider the effects of the regulatory action on small business and other small entities and to minimize any significant economic impact. Agencies must perform a review to determine whether a rule will have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses and not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000.
FAA has determined this rule will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of entities for the following reasons:
The final rule will not impose mandatory costs on small entities or result in any new costs to maintain the manufacturer inspection program.
It is likely to result in cost savings on the order of about $9,255 per aircraft for those small entities who voluntarily choose to use a manufacturer inspection program on their aircraft.
Therefore, for the reasons provided, FAA certifies that this rule will not result in a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
FAA solicited comments regarding this determination and did not receive any comments.
C. International Trade Impact Assessment
The Trade Agreements Act of 1979 (Pub. L. 96-39), as amended by the Uruguay Round Agreements Act (Pub. L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. Pursuant to these Acts, the establishment of standards is not considered an unnecessary obstacle to the foreign commerce of the United States, so long as the standard has a legitimate domestic objective, such as the protection of safety and does not operate in a manner that excludes imports that meet this objective. The statute also requires consideration of international standards and, where appropriate, that they be the basis for the U.S. standards.
FAA has assessed the potential effect of this rule and determined it ensures the safety of the American public and will only have a domestic impact. As a result, FAA does not consider this rule as creating an unnecessary obstacle to foreign commerce.
D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal Government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined that this final rule will not result in the expenditure of $193,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal Governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year.
E. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
) requires that FAA consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. FAA determined this rule will not result in any new information collection requirements.
The final rule will lengthen the reporting interval for mechanical reliability reports, for aircraft operating under part 91 subpart K fractional ownership rules, from 72 to 96 hours, and allow electronic report submissions. This increase in the reporting interval will align the requirement with similar reporting requirements in other regulations, such as
14 CFR 121.703
,
135.415
, and
145.221
.
Currently, the general aviation public, including part 91 subpart K owners and operators, use FAA Form 8010-4, Malfunction and Defect Report, to submit voluntary reporting of occurrences or detection of failure, malfunctions, or defects. Approval to collect such information was previously granted by the OMB under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
) and was assigned OMB Control Number 2120-0663.
The supporting statement submitted to OMB for renewal of the Collection of Information 2120-0663 in October 2020 estimated that 2,000 respondents from the general aviation public each year will use Form 8010-4 by spending 10 minutes each, for an annual 334 total burden hours. This change will simply align the required reporting interval from 72 hours to 96 hours with similar requirements for parts 121, 135, and 145 operators and will neither decrease nor increase the current burden hours on the 2,000 respondents.
Therefore, FAA determined that there will be no new information collection requirements associated with the rule, which will increase the reporting timeframe for mechanical reliability reports under 14 CFR 91.1415 from 72 hours to 96 hours and allow for electronic submissions.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final special conditions; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
These special conditions are issued for the Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation (Gulfstream) Model GVII-G400 airplane. This airplane will have a novel or unusual design feature when compared to the state of technology envisioned in the airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes. This design feature is an envelope protection function to protect the airplane from over- and rapid-rotation on takeoff. The applicable airworthiness regulations do not contain adequate or appropriate safety standards for this design feature. These special conditions contain the additional safety standards that the Administrator considers necessary to establish a level of safety equivalent to that established by the existing airworthiness standards.

This action is effective on Gulfstream on November 10, 2026. Send comments on or before December 28, 2026.
