[A-570-954, C-570-955]
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
In response to a request from the Magnesia Carbon Bricks Fair Trade Committee (the Committee) (the requester), the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is initiating a country-wide circumvention inquiry to determine whether imports of certain refractory bricks containing alumina in an amount greater than zero but less than five percent by weight (bricks with trace alumina) from the People's Republic of China (China) are circumventing the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on certain magnesia carbon bricks (Bricks) from China.
DATES:
Applicable November 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Justin Enck or Cassie Graham, Office of Policy, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-1614 or (202) 482-2159, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 21, 2026, pursuant to section 781(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and
19 CFR 351.226(j)
, the requester
[
1
]
filed a circumvention inquiry request alleging that bricks with trace alumina produced in China and exported to the United States constitute merchandise altered in form or appearance in minor respects that is circumventing the AD and CVD orders on bricks from China
[
2
]
and, accordingly, should be included within the scope of the
Orders.
[
3
]
On October 1, 2026, FRC Global, Inc. (FRC Global) filed comments on the adequacy of the Circumvention Request.
[
4
]
On October 6, 2026, the requester filed rebuttal comments in response to FRC Global's comments.
[
5
]
On October 8, 2026, Commerce officials met with counsel to the requester to discuss the Circumvention Request.
[
6
]
On October 9, 2026, Commerce issued a supplemental questionnaire to the requester.
[
7
]
On October 15, 2026, the requester filed its response to Commerce's requests for additional information.
[
8
]
On October 19, 2026, Commerce extended the initiation deadline by 15 days, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.226(d)(1)
.
[
9
]
Scope of the Orders
The scope of the
Orders
includes certain chemically-bonded (resin or pitch), magnesia carbon bricks with a magnesia component of at least 70 percent magnesia (MgO) by weight, regardless of the source of raw materials for the MgO, with carbon levels ranging from trace amounts to 30 percent by weight, regardless of enhancements (for example, magnesia carbon bricks can be enhanced with coating, grinding, tar impregnation or coking, high temperature heat treatments, anti-slip treatments or metal casing) and regardless of whether or not antioxidants are present (for example, antioxidants can be added to the mix from trace amounts to 15 percent by weight as various metals, metal alloys, and metal carbides). For a full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Circumvention Initiation Checklist.
[
10
]
Merchandise Subject to the Circumvention Inquiry
The circumvention inquiry covers certain chemically bonded (resin or pitch) refractory bricks having a magnesia component of at least 70 percent magnesia (MgO) by weight and carbon levels ranging from trace amounts to 30 percent by weight, and containing alumina (Al
2
O
3
) in an amount greater than zero but less than five percent by weight upon importation, produced in China and exported to the United States. X-ray diffraction should be used to determine the amount of aluminum oxide under such condition that aluminum oxide would not be created from aluminum during the analysis.
Initiation of Circumvention Inquiry
Section 351.226(d)(1)(iii) of Commerce's regulations states that if Commerce determines that a request for a circumvention inquiry satisfies the requirements of
19 CFR 351.226(c)
, then Commerce “will accept the request and initiate a circumvention inquiry.” Section 351.226(c)(1) of Commerce's regulations, in turn, requires that each circumvention inquiry request allege “that the elements necessary for a circumvention determination under section 781 of the Act exist” and be “accompanied by information reasonably available to the interested party supporting these allegations.” The requester alleged circumvention pursuant to section 781(c) of the Act (merchandise altered in form or appearance in minor respects).
(
printed page 72530)
Section 781(c)(1) of the Act provides that the class or kind of merchandise subject to an AD or CVD order shall include articles that have been “altered in form or appearance in minor respects . . . whether or not included in the same tariff classification.” Section 781(c)(2) of the Act provides an exception that section 781(c)(1) of the Act “shall not apply with respect to altered merchandise if the administering authority determines that it would be unnecessary to consider the altered merchandise within the scope of the {order}.” Concerning the allegation of minor alterations under section 781(c) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(j)
, Commerce may consider criteria including, but not limited to: (1) the overall physical characteristics of the merchandise; (2) the expectations of the ultimate users; (3) the use of the merchandise; (4) the channels of marketing; and (5) the cost of any modification relative to the total value of the imported products.
In accordance with
19 CFR 351.226(m)(2)
, for companion AD and CVD proceedings, “the Secretary will initiate and conduct a single inquiry with respect to the product at issue for both orders only on the record of the antidumping proceeding.” Further, once “the Secretary issues a final circumvention determination on the record of the AD proceeding, the Secretary will include a copy of that determination on the record of the CVD.” Accordingly, once Commerce concludes this circumvention inquiry, Commerce intends to place its final circumvention determination on the record of the companion CVD proceeding.
Analysis
Based on our analysis of the requester's circumvention inquiry request and supplemental response, we determine that it has satisfied the criteria under
19 CFR 351.226(c)
, and thus, pursuant to
19 CFR 351.226(d)(1)(iii)
, we are initiating the requested circumvention inquiry. For a full discussion of the basis for our decision to initiate the circumvention inquiry,
see
the Circumvention Initiation Checklist. As explained in the Circumvention Initiation Checklist, the information provided by the requester warrants initiating the circumvention inquiry on a country-wide basis. Commerce has taken this approach in prior circumvention inquiries, where the facts warranted initiation on a country-wide basis.
[
11
]
Consistent with the approach in the prior circumvention inquiries that were initiated on a country-wide basis, Commerce intends to solicit information from certain companies in China concerning their production of bricks with trace alumina and their shipments thereof to the United States.
Suspension of Liquidation
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.226(l)(1)
, Commerce will notify U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) of this initiation and direct CBP to continue the suspension of liquidation of entries of products subject to the circumvention inquiry that were already subject to the suspension of liquidation under the
Orders
and to apply the cash deposit rates that would be applicable if the products were determined to be covered by the scope of the
Orders.
Should Commerce issue an affirmative preliminary or final circumvention determination, Commerce will follow the suspension of liquidation rules under
19 CFR 351.226(l)(2)-(4)
. In the event that Commerce issues an affirmative preliminary or final circumvention determination that the products are circumventing the
Orders,
Commerce will instruct CBP to continue the suspension of liquidation of previously suspended entries and to apply the applicable cash deposit rate. Commerce will also instruct CBP to begin the suspension of liquidation and application of cash deposits for any unliquidated entries not yet suspended, entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption, on or after the date of publication of the notice of initiation of the circumvention inquiry pursuant to
19 CFR 351.226(l)(2)(ii)
and
(l)(3)(ii)
. In addition, pursuant to
19 CFR 351.226(l)(2)(iii)(A)
and
(l)(3)(iii)(A)
, Commerce may instruct CBP to begin the suspension of liquidation and application of cash deposits for any unliquidated entries not yet suspended, entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption, prior to the date of initiation of the circumvention inquiry, but not for such entries prior to November 4, 2021, the effective date of these provisions in the
Final Rule.
[
12
]
These rules will not affect CBP's authority to take any additional action with respect to the suspension of liquidation or related measures for these entries, as stated in
19 CFR 351.226(l)(5)
.
Notification to Interested Parties
In accordance with
19 CFR 351.226(d)
and section 781(c) of the Act, Commerce determines that the requester's request for a circumvention inquiry satisfies the requirements of
19 CFR 351.226(c)
. Accordingly, Commerce is notifying all interested parties of the initiation of the circumvention inquiry to determine whether bricks with trace alumina are circumventing the
Orders.
In addition, we have included a description of the products that are subject to this inquiry, and an explanation of Commerce's decision to initiate the inquiry is provided in the accompanying Circumvention Initiation Checklist.
[
13
]
In accordance with
19 CFR 351.226(e)(1)
, unless the circumvention inquiry is rescinded, in whole or in part, or extended, Commerce intends to issue its preliminary circumvention determination no later than 150 days from the date of publication of the notice of initiation of this circumvention inquiry in the
Federal Register
. Furthermore, in accordance with section 781(f) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(e)(2)
, unless the circumvention inquiry is rescinded, in whole or in part, or extended, Commerce intends to issue its final determination within 300 days from the date of publication of the notice of initiation of the circumvention inquiry in the
Federal Register
.
This notice is published in accordance with section 781(c) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(d)(1)(iii)
.

Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The merchandise covered by the investigation is polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), which is a polymer consisting of linear diols (
i.e.,
organic chemical compound that has two hydroxyl  (-OH) functional groups) with a molecular backbone of repeating tetramethylene units  (-CH2CH2CH2CH2-) interconnected through ether bonds (
i.e.,
a single oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms), with a chemical formula HO{(CH2)4} nOH. PTMEG is also referred to as Polytetrahydrofuran, PTHF, Polytetramethylene ether glycol, PTMG, and Polybutylene glycol. PTMEG is typically blended with butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) or another stabilizer such as higher molecular weight hindered phenols or phosphoric acid. In addition to a stabilizer, PTMEG is sometimes blended with a modifier or additive, such as phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid. The scope includes all blends consisting of PTMEG and stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, where the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively account for no more than two percent of the total weight of the PTMEG blend. PTMEG is normally associated with Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) registry number 25190-06-1.
The scope includes all forms of PTMEG, regardless of physical form, purity, molecular weight, number of hydroxyls, number of acids, color, density, softening point, glass transition point, flash point, water content, viscosity, and packaging. PTMEG that has been blended with other products is included within this scope when such blends include constituent parts that have been intermingled but that have not been chemically reacted with each other to produce a different product. For such blends, only the PTMEG component of the mixture, inclusive of any stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively accounting for no more than two percent of the combined weight of the PTMEG component and the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, is covered by the scope of the investigation.
The scope includes merchandise matching the above description that has been processed in a third country, including by commingling, diluting, introducing, or removing stabilizers, modifiers, or additives, or performing any other processing that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the investigation if performed in the subject country. The scope also includes PTMEG that is commingled or blended with PTMEG from sources not subject to the investigation. Only the subject component of such commingled products is covered by the scope of the investigation. The subject merchandise is classifiable in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) under subheading 3907.29.0000. Subject merchandise may also be imported under
(
printed page 72522)
HTSUS subheadings 2932.11.0000 and 3404.91.5150. Although the HTSUS subheading and CAS registry number are provided for convenience and customs purposes, the written description of the scope is dispositive.

Sections 733(d)(1)(ii) and 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act provide that in the preliminary determination, Commerce shall determine an estimated all-others rate for all exporters and producers not individually examined. Section 735(a)(2) of the Act provides that a final determination may be postponed until not later than 135 days after the date of the publication of the preliminary determination if, in the event of an affirmative preliminary determination, a request for such postponement is made by exporters who account for a significant proportion of exports of the subject merchandise, or in the event of a negative preliminary determination, a request for such postponement is made by the petitioner. Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The merchandise covered by the investigation is polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), which is a polymer consisting of linear diols (
i.e.,
organic chemical compound that has two hydroxyl (- OH) functional groups) with a molecular backbone of repeating tetramethylene units (- CH2CH2CH2CH2-) interconnected through ether bonds (
i.e.,
a single oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms), with a chemical formula HO{(CH2)4}nOH. PTMEG is also referred to as Polytetrahydrofuran, PTHF, Polytetramethylene ether glycol, PTMG, and Polybutylene glycol. PTMEG is typically blended with butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) or another stabilizer such as higher molecular weight hindered phenols or phosphoric acid. In addition to a stabilizer, PTMEG is sometimes blended with a modifier or additive, such as phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid. The scope includes all blends consisting of PTMEG and stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, where the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively account for no more than two percent of the total weight of the PTMEG blend. PTMEG is normally associated with Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) registry number 25190-06-1.
The scope includes all forms of PTMEG, regardless of physical form, purity, molecular weight, number of hydroxyls, number of acids, color, density, softening point, glass transition point, flash point, water content, viscosity, and packaging. PTMEG that has been blended with other products is included within this scope when such blends include constituent parts that have been intermingled but that have not been chemically reacted with each other to produce a different product. For such blends, only the PTMEG component of the mixture, inclusive of any stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively accounting for no more than two percent of the combined weight of the PTMEG component and the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, is covered by the scope of the investigation.
The scope includes merchandise matching the above description that has been processed in a third country, including by commingling, diluting, introducing, or removing stabilizers, modifiers, or additives, or performing any other processing that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the investigation if performed in the subject country. The scope also includes PTMEG that is commingled or blended with PTMEG from sources not subject to the investigation. Only the subject component of such commingled products is covered by the scope of the investigation.
The subject merchandise is classifiable in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) under subheading 3907.29.0000. Subject merchandise may also be imported under HTSUS subheadings 2932.11.0000 and 3404.90.5150. Although the HTSUS subheading and CAS registry number are provided for convenience and customs purposes, the written description of the scope is dispositive.

Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The merchandise covered by the investigation is polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), which is a polymer consisting of linear diols (
i.e.,
organic chemical compound that has two hydroxyl  (-OH) functional groups) with a molecular backbone of repeating tetramethylene units  (-CH
2
CH
2
CH
2
CH
2
-) interconnected through ether bonds (
i.e.,
a single oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms), with a chemical formula HO{(CH
2
)
4
}nOH. PTMEG is also referred to as Polytetrahydrofuran, PTHF, Polytetramethylene ether glycol, PTMG, and Polybutylene glycol. PTMEG is typically blended with butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) or another stabilizer such as higher molecular weight hindered phenols or phosphoric acid. In addition to a stabilizer, PTMEG is sometimes blended with a modifier or additive, such as phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid. The scope includes all blends consisting of PTMEG and stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, where the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively account for no more than two percent of the total weight of the PTMEG blend. PTMEG is normally associated with Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) registry number 25190-06-1.
The scope includes all forms of PTMEG, regardless of physical form, purity, molecular weight, number of hydroxyls, number of acids, color, density, softening point, glass transition point, flash point, water content, viscosity, and packaging. PTMEG that has been blended with other products is included within this scope when such blends include constituent parts that have been intermingled but that have not been chemically reacted with each other to produce a different product. For such blends, only the PTMEG component of the mixture, inclusive of any stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives collectively accounting for no more than two percent of the combined weight of the PTMEG component and the stabilizers, modifiers, and/or additives, is covered by the scope of the investigation.
The scope includes merchandise matching the above description that has been processed in a third country, including by commingling, diluting, introducing, or removing stabilizers, modifiers, or additives, or performing any other processing that
(
printed page 72529)
would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the investigation if performed in the subject country. The scope also includes PTMEG that is commingled or blended with PTMEG from sources not subject to the investigation. Only the subject component of such commingled products is covered by the scope of the investigation.
The subject merchandise is classifiable in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) under subheading 3907.29.0000. Subject merchandise may also be imported under HTSUS subheadings 2932.11.0000 and 3404.90.5150. Although the HTSUS subheading and CAS registry number are provided for convenience and customs purposes, the written description of the scope is dispositive.

Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The products within the scope of this investigation are tin mill flat-rolled products that are coated or plated with tin, chromium, or chromium oxides. Flat-rolled steel products coated with tin are known as tinplate. Flat-rolled steel products coated with chromium or chromium oxides are known as tin-free steel or electrolytic chromium-coated steel. The scope includes all the noted tin mill products regardless of thickness, width, form (in coils or cut sheets), coating type (electrolytic or otherwise), edge (trimmed, untrimmed or further processed, such as scroll cut), coating thickness, surface finish, temper, coating metal (tin, chromium, chromium oxide), reduction (single- or double-reduced), and whether or not coated with a plastic material.
Excluded from the scope of this investigation is certain single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel tape for use as an armoring and shielding layer for fiber optic and telecommunications cables (commonly known in the industry as “copolymer coated steel tape”). Such excluded certain single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel tape is excluded only if it meets all seven (7) of the below requirements:
(1) Single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel,
(2) Actual thickness of 0.160 mm or less (55-pound base box weight),
(3) Type MR steel,
(4) T2-T3 temper,
(5) With a tensile range of 45-57 KSI or 310.20-393.00 Mpa,
(6) 15% minimum elongation, and
(7) 0.06-012 g/m2 chromium coating.
The merchandise subject to this investigation is currently classified in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), under HTSUS subheadings 7210.11.0000, 7210.12.0000, 7210.50.0020, 7210.50.0090, 7212.10.0000, 7212.50.0000, if of non-alloy steel and under HTSUS subheadings 7225.99.0090, and 7226.99.0180 if of alloy steel. Suspension of Liquidation and Cash Deposit Requirements
In accordance with section 733(d)(2) of the Act, Commerce will direct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to suspend liquidation of entries of subject merchandise, as described in Appendix I, entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. Further, pursuant to section 733(d)(1)(B) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.205(d)
, Commerce will instruct CBP to require a cash deposit as follows: (1) for subject merchandise exported by one of the companies listed above, the cash deposit rate will be equal to the company-specific estimated weighted-average dumping margins determined in this preliminary determination; (2) if the exporter is not a respondent identified above, but the producer is, then the cash deposit rate will be equal to the company-specific estimated weighted-average dumping margin established for that producer of the subject merchandise; and (3) the cash deposit rate for all other producers and exporters will be equal to the all-others estimated weighted-average dumping margin.
Section 733(e)(2) of the Act provides that, given an affirmative determination of critical circumstances, any suspension of liquidation shall apply to unliquidated entries of subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the later of: (a) the date which is 90 days before the date on which the suspension of liquidation was first ordered; or (b) the date on which notice of initiation of the investigation was published. Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The products within the scope of this investigation are tin mill flat-rolled products that are coated or plated with tin, chromium, or chromium oxides. Flat-rolled steel products coated with tin are known as tinplate. Flat-rolled steel products coated with chromium or chromium oxides are known as tin-free steel or electrolytic chromium-coated steel. The scope includes all the noted tin mill products regardless of thickness, width, form (in coils or cut sheets), coating type (electrolytic or otherwise), edge (trimmed, untrimmed or further processed, such as scroll cut), coating thickness, surface finish, temper, coating metal (tin, chromium, chromium oxide), reduction (single- or double-reduced), and whether or not coated with a plastic material.
Excluded from the scope of this investigation is certain single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel tape for use as an armoring and shielding layer for fiber optic and telecommunications cables (commonly known in the industry as “copolymer coated steel tape”). Such excluded certain single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel tape is excluded only if it meets all seven (7) of the below requirements:
(1) Single-reduced electrolytically chromium-coated steel,
(2) Actual thickness of 0.160 mm or less (55-pound base box weight),
(3) Type MR steel,
(4) T2-T3 temper,
(5) With a tensile range of 45-57 KSI or 310.20-393.00 Mpa,
(6) 15% minimum elongation, and
(7) 0.06-012 g/m2 chromium coating.
The merchandise subject to this investigation is currently classified in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), under HTSUS subheadings 7210.11.0000, 7210.12.0000, 7210.50.0020, 7210.50.0090, 7212.10.0000, 7212.50.0000, if of non-alloy steel and under HTSUS subheadings 7225.99.0090, and 7226.99.0180 if of alloy steel. Although the subheadings are provided for convenience and customs purposes, the written description of the scope of the investigation is dispositive.

7 CFR Part 273
[FNA-2026-0661]
RIN 0584-AF10
AGENCY:
Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA), USDA.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
Under section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are categorically eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at
45 CFR 260.31
. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of simplifying program administration.
A 100-word summary of this rule has been posted to
www.regulations.gov
and can be found here.
DATES:
Written comments must be received on or before December 10, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
ADDRESSES:
The Food and Nutrition Administration, USDA, invites interested persons to submit written comments on this proposed rule. Comments may be submitted in writing by one of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
Send comments to SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705.
Website:
Go to
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Email:
Send comments to:
sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov
.
Include Docket ID Number [FNA-2026-0661], “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility” in the subject line of the message.
(
printed page 72455)
All written comments submitted in response to this proposed rule will be included in the record and will be made available to the public. Please be advised that the substance of the comments and the identity of the individuals or entities submitting the comments will be subject to public disclosure. FNA will make the written comments publicly available on the internet via
http://www.regulations.gov
.
The Department believes that this proposal to limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at
45 CFR 260.31
, aligns with SNAP's statutory eligibility requirements. However, the Department invites comments on whether there are alternative approaches to limit categorical eligibility with TANF that achieve the same policy goals.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705, Phone: (703) 305-2022.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Prior Rulemaking
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA or the Department) previously proposed changes to categorical eligibility on July 24, 2019. The proposed rule, titled “Revision of Categorical Eligibility in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP),” would have limited the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) benefits that may be used to confer categorical eligibility for SNAP to those that were ongoing and substantial (
84 FR 35570
). Categorical eligibility allows households that have been determined eligible for TANF or certain other means-tested programs to also be eligible for SNAP. The Biden Administration withdrew the proposed rule on June 10, 2021 (
86 FR 30795
). The Department is now proposing revised changes to categorical eligibility rules to limit categorical eligibility only to households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at
45 CFR 260.31
. As explained in the Regulatory Impact Analysis accompanying this rule, the Department acknowledges these revisions may result in some level of increased administrative burden on States, a reduction in SNAP benefit spending, and associated effects on school meals eligibility.
Background
SNAP provides nutrition assistance to eligible, low-income households who apply for participation and meet nationwide income and resource standards created by Congress.
[
1
]
The Food Stamp Act of 1977 (Pub. L. 93-86) established eligibility for SNAP, then known as food stamps, based on household income and resources. The Omnibus Reconciliation Act of 1982 (Pub. L. 97-759) revised those income eligibility standards to create the Federal standards SNAP uses today. Currently, the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (
7 U.S.C. 2011
et seq.
) (the Act) requires that households without elderly or disabled members have a monthly gross income equal to or lower than 130 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) and a net income equal to or lower than 100 percent of the FPG to be SNAP eligible. Households with an elderly or disabled member need only meet the net income limit. The Act also specifies resource limits for SNAP households.
To simplify the eligibility determination process for households that qualify for a variety of benefit programs in addition to SNAP, the Food Security Act of 1985 (Pub. L. 99-198) amended Section 5(a) of the Act to create a categorical eligibility pilot project which eliminated the need for State workers to repeat an eligibility determination for SNAP if a household had already been determined eligible for another means-tested assistance program with financial criteria equal to or more restrictive than SNAP. The Food Security Act of 1985 temporarily established SNAP categorical eligibility for households in which all members received Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits or cash benefits from the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program.
The Hunger Prevention Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-435) made categorical eligibility permanent. In describing the purpose of categorical eligibility, the Senate report on the Hunger Prevention Act of 1988 noted that “relying on eligibility determinations made under other programs can greatly reduce the paperwork burden on both applicants and eligibility workers while assuring that food stamps go only to very needy individuals.”
[
2
]
SNAP certification starts with an eligibility determination, followed by a benefit calculation. Categorical eligibility impacts the eligibility determination by allowing State SNAP agencies to “deem,” or accept, specified eligibility factors from another means-tested program's eligibility determination for the purpose of determining SNAP eligibility. These factors are limited to resources, gross and net income limits, residency, social security number, and sponsored alien information, as described in
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(v)
. Individuals who are not eligible for SNAP based on certain nonfinancial factors, including alien ineligibility, student ineligibility, and failure to comply with work requirements, cannot become eligible via categorical eligibility. Current SNAP regulations do not require State agencies to verify categorically eligible households' incomes to determine their
eligibility,
but they must verify all households' incomes to determine their
benefit calculation.
At the time Congress created categorical eligibility, AFDC and SNAP had similar eligibility requirements and served a similar population. AFDC provided cash assistance to needy families with children. While States had flexibility under AFDC to define need, set benefit levels, and establish resource limits, the income and resource limits had to fall within Federal limitations, which in most cases aligned with or were more stringent than those of SNAP.
[
3
]
Almost all AFDC families were income-eligible for SNAP, and about 85 percent of AFDC families also received SNAP.
[
4
]
Therefore, Congress authorized categorical eligibility permanently based on similarities between the programs at the time.
The close alignment between the programs began to shift with the passage of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA). PRWORA replaced AFDC with the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grant program. This represented a fundamental change in the program, transitioning from primarily cash assistance to cash assistance and other non-cash services.
[
5
]
States gained
(
printed page 72456)
significant control over TANF eligibility criteria, and the Federal parameters for income and resource limits under AFDC were eliminated. While States continued to offer cash assistance, many States began to use TANF funds on non-cash benefits, such as programs and benefits without the income and resource limits that had defined AFDC. TANF allows States to fund a wide range of services, including childcare, work, education and training activities, pre-K and Head Start, nonrecurrent short-term benefits, child welfare services, and a variety of other family support services.
[
6
]
Resource limits are set by States, and not Federally required, for TANF-funded benefits, and States' income criteria for non-cash assistance vary greatly and can sometimes far exceed SNAP limits. The proliferation of programs with eligibility criteria significantly different from SNAP standards has created a challenge for the Department in preserving categorical eligibility as originally intended.
In the wake of PRWORA, the Department acknowledged the complexity introduced by the change from AFDC to TANF but reaffirmed categorical eligibility's original purpose of supporting program administration. A July 14, 1999, policy memo noted that the intent of categorical eligibility was “to deem eligibility for food stamp families already subjected to an income and resource test” under TANF.
[
7
]
Therefore, the memo affirmed, States have discretion over whether to confer categorical eligibility to recipients of TANF-funded benefits that are not limited to needy families.
[
8
]
Less than two years later, with the publication of a final rule codifying PRWORA changes to SNAP,
[
9
]
the Department acknowledged the degree of State discretion allowed by the 1999 memo had “allowed State agencies to use categorical eligibility beyond the scope of what was originally intended.” The rule attempted to place bounds, that were still beyond the scope of what was originally intended, on categorical eligibility by establishing a 200 percent FPG gross income limit for TANF- or state maintenance of effort (MOE)-funded programs not designed to target “needy families.” In doing so, the rule acknowledged that the changes made by PRWORA allowed States to fund in-kind and non-cash TANF benefits, including some benefits (under TANF purposes three and four) without income eligibility criteria. However, the rule reiterated the Department's understanding that the purpose of categorical eligibility was to eliminate superfluous eligibility tests, not to increase income eligibility criteria, or eliminate eligibility criteria entirely.
Despite the guardrails the rule attempted to establish, the practice of using non-cash TANF-funded programs to confer categorical eligibility continued and, in fact, expanded. Initially, these non-cash programs included benefits, such as work supports, kinship care resources, and transitional benefits. Beginning in 2009, States began implementing particularly expansive categorical eligibility policies, known as “broad-based categorical eligibility” or BBCE.
[
10
]
At the time, data indicated many eligible low-income households were not accessing SNAP benefits. SNAP participation had dropped after the passage of PRWORA
[
11
]
and BBCE was seen as a way to increase participation among eligible households. From FY 2008 to FY 2011 the number of States implementing BBCE policies grew from 18 to 43. This widescale adoption of the policy was not organic but was encouraged formally by USDA under the Obama administration explicitly “to increase SNAP participation”.
[
12
]
There was a corresponding rise in the number of SNAP participants overall reaching a record of nearly 45 million participants,
[
13
]
and also an increase in households that exceeded SNAP's Federal income and resource limits for SNAP, reflecting their eligibility only due to BBCE. In recent years, the share of participants in households with income and/or resources exceeding the Federal limits for SNAP has increased to 17.6 percent (as shown in the Regulatory Impact Analysis).
[
14
]
States were encouraged specifically by USDA to use benefits of nominal value, such as “an informational pamphlet or an 800-number to call to locate TANF-funded services,” as the “benefit” to confer categorical eligibility.
[
15
]
BBCE has enabled States to use non-cash TANF program eligibility criteria to create a de facto and significant increase in the SNAP gross income and significant increases and even total elimination of resource statutory limits. Such an expansion has compromised the statutory underpinnings of categorical eligibility, as it goes beyond flexibility to reduce administrative burdens and increases eligibility for households who would not otherwise qualify based on the income and resource limits established in law. The Department believes the proposed changes would ensure States implement categorical eligibility in accordance with its original intent and would address concerns that States used BBCE to expand SNAP eligibility beyond congressionally approved limits intended to preserve benefits for the truly needy.
Over time, BBCE has created a varied “patchwork” of eligibility criteria across States. Many States now use income and resource limits for their non-cash TANF benefits that are higher than the statutory standards for SNAP
(
printed page 72457)
eligibility.
[
16
]
As of December 2025, forty-six States are currently using BBCE to expand eligibility to households that receive non-cash TANF benefits of nominal value.
[
17
]
Of those, thirty-seven States have gross income limits higher than the SNAP gross income limit and forty-one States have no resource limit at all.
The expansion of SNAP eligibility under BBCE policies may threaten the integrity of the program by eroding public trust that SNAP benefits are available only to those who meet the eligibility limits set in law. For example, in States with no resource limit, a household with a million dollars or more in available resources but no regular income could apply for and be eligible to receive SNAP benefits. “Resources” in SNAP include liquid or near liquid assets, with many exclusions including a home and retirement and pensions. The Department is aware of instances where millionaires have received SNAP benefits.
[
18
]
It is irresponsible to Congress and the taxpayer to support regulations that permit this practice.
Federal audits have also raised concerns about BBCE's implications for the integrity of the SNAP eligibility determination process. A 2012 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report exposed weaknesses of categorical eligibility policies, describing them as having “a potentially negative effect on SNAP program integrity” and suggested that BBCE may contribute to more payment errors.
[
19
]
In particular, there were payment errors for 17.2 percent of SNAP households eligible under BBCE that had incomes over the Federal limits in Fiscal Year (FY) 2010, compared to just 6.7 percent of other SNAP households. Findings from a 2015 USDA Office of Inspector General (OIG) audit identified similar vulnerabilities with BBCE. The audit took issue with the way BBCE essentially deferred SNAP eligibility determinations to TANF and seemed to solidify the perception of those outside of SNAP that BBCE lacks rigor.
[
20
]
Together, these findings demonstrate a policy out of sync with the directive of Congress to ensure that SNAP benefits are reserved for the most vulnerable households.
[
21
]
The Department is also strongly committed to responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars and ensuring SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households. In contrast, many State BBCE policies expand SNAP to households that would otherwise not qualify under the SNAP income and resource limits established in law, adding unnecessary program costs. In FY 2010, only about four percent of SNAP participants were in households with income and/or resources exceeding the Federal limits,
[
22
]
indicating that they were only eligible due to BBCE. The share doubled to eight percent by FY 2013 and remained relatively constant reaching a peak of 10 percent in FY 2018.
[
23 24
]
More recent 2019 U.S. Census Bureau data suggests that the proportion of participating households exceeding the resource limit has grown substantially since that time. The Department estimates that 11.5 percent of participating SNAP households in FY2024 (2.5 million households containing 5.4 million individuals) had resources above the SNAP limit and 5.4 percent of households (1.2 million households containing 2.0 million individuals) had incomes above the Federal SNAP gross or net income limits.
[
25 26
]
BBCE households, like other SNAP households, with three members or more must have net incomes low enough to receive a SNAP benefit. The SNAP benefit is calculated after eligibility is established, so some households determined eligible for SNAP through BBCE may receive zero SNAP benefits. However, all SNAP-eligible households with one or two members get at least the minimum SNAP benefit regardless of their income or deductions.
[
27
]
The Department estimates in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) that more than 840,000 one- and two-person households received the minimum SNAP benefit in 2024 only because they were determined to be categorically eligible for SNAP through BBCE. Most of these households (94 percent) would have been ineligible for SNAP under the SNAP income and resource limits and thus receive no SNAP benefit in the absence of BBCE. This represents nearly $214 million to households whose incomes or resources exceeded SNAP's statutory limits in 2024, but still received a minimum benefit. This spending does not align with Congress' intent or the Secretary's guiding principle to support policy options that protect both truly needy recipients and the American taxpayer.
[
28
]
A rule change is necessary to avoid the continuation of SNAP regulations that allow a categorical eligibility policy that expands SNAP to households without demonstrated needs and reaches far beyond the congressional intent to simplify eligibility determinations for needy households.
Therefore, the Department proposes aligning categorical eligibility more closely to the policy originally implemented in 1985 based on Federal law, under which categorical eligibility was conferred only to those households receiving cash assistance payments, rather than those receiving non-assistance benefits, such as childcare, training, or other services. Specifically, the proposed rule would revise regulations at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)
to align with the definition of TANF assistance
(
printed page 72458)
in
45 CFR 260.31(a)
. Under
45 CFR 260.31(a)
, TANF “assistance” includes cash, payments, vouchers, and other forms of benefits designed to meet a family's ongoing basic needs, which includes certain non-cash supportive services, such as child care and transportation assistance for parents who are unemployed.
[
29
]
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) uses the term “non-assistance” to refer to the variety of other TANF-funded services, as described at
45 CFR 260.31(b)
, which includes the types of benefits used in BBCE policies. Current SNAP regulations do not distinguish between TANF “assistance” and “non-assistance,” but rather between “cash” and “non-cash or in-kind benefits or services.” In this rule, “TANF assistance” refers to the cash and non-cash supportive services referred to in
45 CFR 260.31(a)
, while “non-cash or in-kind benefits or services” means the TANF “non-assistance” described in
45 CFR 260.31(b)
.
[
30
]
This proposed change would limit categorical eligibility conferred through TANF to those households receiving TANF assistance, rather than the non-cash or in-kind services from TANF-funded programs that also currently confer categorical eligibility.
Like AFDC before it, TANF assistance as defined at
45 CFR 260.31(a)
is largely a cash payment benefit designed to meet the basic needs of families with incomes and resources below the SNAP statutory requirements. The definition of TANF assistance includes cash, payments, vouchers, and other forms of benefits designed to meet a family's ongoing basic needs. Additionally, TANF assistance programs have a robust eligibility determination that thoroughly reviews household income and resources. Income standards used to determine TANF assistance eligibility vary by State but are typically lower than SNAP standards.
[
31
]
Summary of Proposed Approach
The proposed rule would change SNAP categorical eligibility regulations at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)
by limiting the TANF benefits that a State agency can use to confer categorical eligibility to only TANF assistance, defined at
45 CFR 260.31(a)
. To conform with this change, the proposed rule would also eliminate the use of “non-cash or in-kind benefits or services” to confer categorical eligibility for SNAP. Finally, the Department proposes several conforming amendments.
Categorical Eligibility From TANF Assistance
Current regulations at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(i)(A)
require States to confer categorical eligibility to households in which all members receive or are authorized to receive “cash” through a TANF program. The Department proposes to amend
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(i)(A)
to replace “cash” with “assistance as defined at
45 CFR 260.31(a)
.” The vast majority of TANF assistance is cash or cash equivalents, intended to meet families' basic needs.
[
32
]
Aligning the terminology in SNAP regulations with that used in TANF regulations promotes consistency between the programs. Additionally, such a change would close the loophole that has allowed for 17.6 percent of the SNAP participant caseload to be eligible solely due to receiving TANF non-assistance,
i.e.,
non-cash benefits with eligibility criteria that far exceed Federal SNAP limits.
Eliminating Categorical Eligibility From Non-Cash or In-Kind Benefits or Services
Current SNAP regulations provide two ways in which non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from a TANF-funded program may confer categorical eligibility: a mandatory requirement, described at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(i)(B)
and
(C)
, and a State option, described at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(ii)
. These various provisions are based on the proportion of the program funded by TANF or State MOE funding, the TANF purposes that the program furthers, and the gross income limit of the program.
The proposed rule would remove
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(i)(B)
,
(2)(i)(C)
, and
(2)(ii)
, meaning States would no longer be permitted to confer categorical eligibility for SNAP to households that receive non-cash or in-kind TANF- or State MOE-funded benefits or services, other than TANF assistance. This would eliminate the practice of States using nominal TANF benefits from programs with a variety of weaker gross income and resource limits to confer categorical eligibility. The proposed change would help ensure closer alignment with congressional intent.
Authorized To Receive
Current regulations throughout
7 CFR 273.2(j)
apply categorical eligibility for SNAP to households in which all members receive or are “authorized to receive” specified TANF, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or general assistance (GA) benefits. The “authorized to receive” language does not align with Congress's intent for categorical eligibility and creates a loophole that could make households categorically eligible for SNAP based on their eligibility for a TANF benefit, even if they do not actually receive it.
[
33
]
The Department wants to strike the right balance between administrative streamlining and ensuring that households actually receive the benefit that confers categorical eligibility. Therefore, the Department is removing the “authorized to receive” language throughout
7 CFR 273.2
.
Conforming Amendments
The Department proposes to amend the regulations at
7 CFR 273.2(j)(2)(iv)
,
273.2(j)(4)(vi)
, and
273.8(e)(17)
to update or remove the citations to conform with the regulations redesignated or removed by this rule.
Alternate Approach for Consideration
The Department also considered an alternative approach, which is the “ongoing and substantial” framework proposed in the 2019 proposed rule (described below). The Department believes the current proposal to align SNAP categorical eligibility with receipt of TANF assistance is the best solution because it eliminates discrepancies between SNAP and TANF regulations and is easier to operationalize than the two alternatives; however, the Department is seeking public comment on how this alternate approach would compare to the proposed approach.
Alternative Approach
The Department considered returning to the categorical eligibility framework originally proposed in the July 24, 2019, proposed rule, “Revision of Categorical
(
printed page 72459)
Eligibility in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)”.
24
Under the “ongoing and substantial” framework of the 2019 proposed rule, both cash and non-cash TANF benefits could confer categorical eligibility but only if those benefits were “ongoing and substantial”. To be considered “ongoing,” the benefits would be those a household receives for a period of at least six months. To be considered “substantial,” the benefits would be valued at a minimum of $50 per month or, should HHS develop a minimum threshold amount for TANF cash benefits, the higher of the two standards.
In addition, non-cash categorical eligibility would be limited to specific types of TANF benefits—subsidized employment, work supports, and/or childcare—that support family self-sufficiency and involve meaningful eligibility determinations. The Alternative approach would remove mention of TANF purposes from 7 CFR 273.2(j)(2), since the Department understands from HHS that these distinctions are not necessarily meaningful in conferring non-cash categorical eligibility because different States may consider similar benefits to be furthering different TANF purposes. Instead, the Alternative approach would link categorical eligibility to specific types of TANF
benefits
rather than to TANF block grant
purposes.
Finally, the Alternative approach would also simplify the terminology used at 7 CFR 273.2(j)(2) from “non-cash or in-kind benefits or services” to “non-cash benefits.” For oversight purposes, the proposal would also require State agencies to inform FNA of all non-cash TANF benefits conferring categorical eligibility.
With the introduction in the Alternative of the “ongoing” and “substantial” requirements, the Department would seek to eliminate the practice of conferring categorical eligibility based on receipt of nominal, one-time benefits. Categorical eligibility based on the receipt of benefits that are nominal in value encourages cursory or nonexistent eligibility determinations because the value of those TANF benefits do not warrant the cost of staff time and resources to conduct robust eligibility determinations. Requiring the benefits to be substantial limits categorical eligibility to only those TANF benefits for which a State is more likely to establish a meaningful eligibility determination.
In addition, the types of benefits conferring categorical eligibility under the Alternative approach would be limited to those that provide opportunities for households to obtain employment and financial stability. The emphasis on TANF benefits that directly encourage self-sufficiency aligns with the amendments to the Act made by Sec. 313 of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA,
Pub. L. 118-5
). In June 2023, the FRA expanded SNAP's purpose to include assisting low-income adults in obtaining employment and increasing their earnings. The Department believes this reaffirms efforts to reduce dependency on public assistance programs and increase self-sufficiency. The framework of the Alternative approach would align categorical eligibility with the new statutory purpose of the program, which is explicitly tailored to support work.
In withdrawing the 2019 proposed rule, the Department determined the proposed revisions did not sufficiently justify the impact on SNAP households or the costs to State agencies to implement the change. However, the Department believes that the Alternative approach merits reconsideration at this time. Unlike the proposal in this NPRM, it acknowledges that some TANF non-assistance, non-cash benefits may comport with SNAP's standards for eligibility requirements and SNAP's mission to support participants' self-sufficiency through employment. Ultimately, the Department chose the proposal in this NPRM because implementation of categorical eligibility based on alignment with TANF assistance would be less administratively burdensome for State agencies than the “ongoing and substantial” standard.

Abstract:
Section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, as amended, (the Act), provides that households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded under Part A of Title IV of the Social Security Act (SSA) (also known as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grants) shall be categorically eligible for SNAP. Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at
45 CFR 260.31
. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to households that have sufficiently demonstrated need by qualifying for TANF assistance while aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of streamlining program administration.
Congress established categorical eligibility to reduce administrative burden, not to increase eligibility in the program. However, States have used the flexibility of the TANF program to implement particularly expansive categorical eligibility policies, known as “broad-based categorical eligibility” or BBCE. BBCE has enabled States to use non-cash TANF program eligibility criteria to create a de facto increase in the SNAP gross income and resource statutory limits. Under the Act's regular program rules, households without an elderly or disabled member must have a gross income of no more than 130 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) to qualify for SNAP; under BBCE, States can increase such limits to as much as 200 percent FPG. The Act also specifies resource limits for SNAP households, but under BBCE policies, States can increase or entirely eliminate resource limits. Such an expansion has compromised the statutory underpinnings of categorical eligibility, as it goes beyond flexibility to reduce administrative burdens and increases eligibility for households who would not otherwise qualify.
The proposed rule would provide more uniform SNAP eligibility across the country by limiting categorical eligibility through TANF to households that qualify for TANF assistance, rather than the non-cash or in-kind services from TANF-funded programs that also currently confer categorical eligibility. Section 5(j) of the Act indicates that households who are categorically eligible are considered to have met the SNAP resource limit and therefore these households do not undergo another resource determination. The proposed rule would reduce the number of households who would be categorically eligible. Therefore, States would have to apply regular SNAP income and resource tests to determine SNAP eligibility for more households. The Department estimates that 11.5 percent of currently participating SNAP households (2.5 million households or 5.4 million individuals) have resources above the SNAP limit and 5.4 percent (1.2 million households or 2.0 million individuals) have incomes above the Federal SNAP gross income limit of 130 percent FPG and/or net income limit of 100 percent FPG. While States do not verify categorically eligible households' incomes to determine their
eligibility,
they must verify all households' incomes to determine their
benefit calculation.
However, as noted earlier, some States have BBCE policies that entirely eliminate resource limits. Under this rule, those States would need to add resource assessments to their SNAP eligibility determination process for an increased number of non-categorically eligible households.
FNA is requesting to revise OMB Control Number 0584-0621 for the requirements in this proposed rule, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility. Because State agencies do
(
printed page 72462)
not verify resources for applicants that are categorically eligible per 5(j) of the Act, they would be required to make changes to their application process to assess the resources of those households' that would no longer be categorically eligible. As of December 2025, 46 out of the 53 State agencies have adopted BBCE, and 41 States are not currently assessing resource information as part of the SNAP eligibility determination process.

Description of Costs and Assumptions:
This proposed rule would limit categorical eligibility through TANF only to households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at
45 CFR 260.31(a)
. The proposed restriction of categorical eligibility would reduce the number of households who would be categorically eligible for SNAP and require States to assess more households' resources to determine if they are eligible for SNAP. Under the rule, the 45 State agencies that have expanded categorical eligibility would now be required to assess resource information from more households. For example, States and households would need to contact financial institutions, Departments of Motor Vehicles, or other entities to obtain documentation of household resources. The proposed rule may require the States that do not currently assess resources to modify their eligibility systems to both collect and verify household resource information as needed. System costs include the cost of requirements gathering, design, development, testing, implementation, and operations and maintenance.
Reporting Burden Activities:
Currently, all applicant households are required to meet the SNAP resource limits at
7 CFR 273.8
(Resource eligibility standards); applicants who are categorically eligible are considered to have met the SNAP resource limit (Section 5(j) of the Act). Under this rulemaking, fewer SNAP households would be categorically eligible through their receipt of non-cash TANF benefits. As fewer SNAP households would be categorically eligible, more households would therefore need to have their resources assessed by SNAP eligibility workers to determine whether the households meet the SNAP resource limit. Resources are one of several factors used to determine SNAP eligibility and are subject to verification if questionable (
7 CFR 273.2 (f)(2)
).
State Agency Burden Assessment Feedback
FNA used the estimates in OMB Control Number 0584-0621 (expiration date: 1/31/2029) to estimate the amount of time that resource verification would take for the additional 45 State agencies that have expanded categorical eligibility. FNA estimates that 11 States would verify resources for households at all times (“Always” States), 10 States would verify resources only when deemed questionable (“Self-Attestation States”), and 24 States would adopt a policy to verify a household's resources if close to the resource limit (“High Limit States”).
Using the estimates in OMB Control Number 0584-0621 (expiration date: 1/31/2029), FNA estimates that State agency staff in “Always” States would on average spend 32.5 minutes (.534 hours) per case at initial certification and 19.16 minutes (.321 hours) per case at recertification. FNA estimates that State agency staff in “Self-Attestation” States would on average spend 12.4 minutes (.201 hours) per case at initial certification and 8.8 minutes (0.135 hours) per case at recertification. FNA estimates that State agency staff in “High Limit” States would on average spend 33.15 minutes (0.554 hours) per case at initial certification and 33.2 minutes (0.550 hours) per case at recertification to verify resources.
FNA then needed to estimate the percentage of a State's caseload that would be subject to these resource verification requirements to calculate the State agency burden. In the estimated 11 “Always” States, the entire caseload would be subject to verification. In “Self-Attestation” and “High Limit” States, only a certain percent of SNAP applicants would meet the criteria (
e.g.,
substantial resources or questionable information) that would necessitate the caseworker undertaking resource verification.
Using caseload data, FNA estimates that “High Limit” States would have to verify household resources about 27 percent of the time; FNA rounded up to 30 percent to take into account caseworker discretion to verify when questionable. FNA estimates that “Self-Attestation States” States would have to verify household resources 10 percent of the time. Accordingly, the estimated number of households whose resources would be verified by a caseworker are adjusted to 30 percent of the caseload in the estimated 24 “High Limit” States and 10 percent of the caseload in the estimated 10 “Self-Attestation” States. The estimated number of households for the 11 “Always” States would be 100 percent of the SNAP applicant households in those States.
In addition, the Department anticipates one-time costs related to changes to application forms, staff training, and modifications to State systems. The Department has limited data on the potential costs of these changes, particularly the system changes. System costs include the cost of requirements gathering, design, development, testing, and implementation. For the purpose of calculating the burden for this proposed rule, FNA assumes that all 45 State agencies that confer expanded categorical eligibility collect, but do not currently verify, resource information from households. The Department seeks additional comment on whether this assumption is correct, and if not, how long it would take States to make changes to their systems to gather, review, and verify this information beyond the efforts described above.

On February 18, 2026, the Port of Olympia, grantee of FTZ 216, submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board on behalf of Essex Laboratories, within FTZ 216, in Chehalis, Washington.
The notification was processed in accordance with the regulations of the FTZ Board (
15 CFR part 400
), including notice in the
Federal Register
inviting public comment (
91 FR 8406
, February 23, 2026). On November 5, 2026, the applicant was notified of the FTZ Board's decision that no further review of the activity is warranted at this time. The production activity described in the notification was authorized on a limited basis, subject to the FTZ Act and the FTZ Board's regulations, including section 400.14, and further subject to quantitative limits on the admission of foreign status Mentha Piperita Oil, Mentha Spearmint Oil, and Mentha Arvensis Oil. The annual quantitative limit for foreign status Mentha Piperita Oil will be equal to one-fifth the number of U.S.-origin sourced Mentha Piperita Oil. The annual quantitative limit for foreign status Mentha Spearmint Oil and Mentha Arvensis will be 45,000 kgs, and 4,000 kgs respectively. Essex must provide a single report within one year of approval documenting its foreign and domestic sourcing of these components. If Essex fails to provide this report, the FTZ Board should review the authorization for the importation of the components.

ACTION:
Notice of availability and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
This document provides the public with notice that, on October 26, 2026, the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (Amtrak) submitted a request for amendment (RFA) to one of its FRA-approved Positive Train Control Safety Plans (PTCSP). As this RFA may involve a request for FRA's approval of proposed material modifications to an FRA-certified positive train control (PTC) system, FRA is publishing this notice and inviting public comment on the railroad's RFA to its PTCSP.
DATES:
FRA will consider comments received by November 30, 2026. FRA may consider comments received after that date to the extent practicable and without delaying implementation of valuable or necessary modifications to a PTC system.
ADDRESSES:
Comments:
Comments may be submitted by going to
https://www.regulations.gov
and following the online instructions for submitting comments.
Instructions:
All submissions must include the agency name and the applicable docket number. The relevant PTC docket number for this host railroad is Docket No. FRA-2010-0029. For convenience, all active PTC dockets are hyperlinked on FRA's website at
https://railroads.dot.gov/​research-development/​program-areas/​train-control/​ptc/​railroads-ptc-dockets
.
All comments received will be posted without change to
https://www.regulations.gov
;
this includes any personal information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Gabe Neal, Staff Director, Signal, Train Control, and Crossings Division, telephone: 816-516-7168, email:
Gabe.Neal@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In general,
49 U.S.C. 20157(h)
requires FRA to certify that a host railroad's PTC system complies with
49 CFR part 236, subpart I
, before the technology may be operated in revenue service. Before making certain changes to an FRA-certified PTC system or the associated FRA-approved PTCSP, a host railroad must submit, and obtain FRA's approval of, an RFA to its PTCSP under
49 CFR 236.1021
.
Under
49 CFR 236.1021(e)
, FRA's regulations provide that FRA will publish a notice in the
Federal Register
and invite public comment in accordance with
49 CFR part 211
, if an RFA includes a request for approval of a material modification of a signal or train control system. Accordingly, this notice informs the public that, on October 26, 2026, Amtrak submitted an RFA to its PTCSP for its Interoperable Electronic Train Management System, which seeks FRA's approval for updates associated with previously approved system enhancements, revised Amtrak and MARC high-speed operations safety analyses, updated risk assessment information, operational and functional clarifications, and associated supporting documentation. That RFA is available in Docket No. FRA-2010-0029.
Interested parties are invited to comment on Amtrak's RFA to its PTCSP by submitting written comments or data. During FRA's review of this railroad's RFA, FRA will consider any comments or data submitted within the timeline specified in this notice and, to the extent practicable, without delaying implementation of valuable or necessary modifications to a PTC system.
See
49 CFR 236.1021
;
see also
49 CFR 236.1011(e)
. Under
49 CFR 236.1021
, FRA maintains the authority to approve, approve with conditions, or deny a railroad's RFA to its PTCSP at FRA's sole discretion.
Privacy Act Notice
In accordance with
49 CFR 211.3
, FRA solicits comments from the public to inform its decisions. DOT posts these comments, without edit, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
https://www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14 FDMS), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/​privacy
.
See
https://www.regulations.gov/​privacy-notice
for the privacy notice of
regulations.gov
. To facilitate comment tracking, we encourage commenters to provide their name, or the name of their organization; however, submission of names is optional. If you wish to provide comments containing proprietary or confidential information, please contact FRA for alternate submission instructions.
Issued in Washington, DC.
John Karl Alexy,
Associate Administrator for Railroad Safety, Chief Safety Officer.

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Susquehanna River Basin Commission will conduct its regular business meeting on December 10, 2026 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Details concerning the matters to be addressed at the business meeting are contained in the Supplementary Information section of this notice. Also, the Commission published a document in the
Federal Register
October 5, 2026 concerning its public hearing on October 28th, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.
DATES:
The meeting will be held on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 9 a.m.
ADDRESSES:
This public meeting will be conducted in person and digitally from the Susquehanna River Basin Commission at 4423 North Front Street, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jason E. Oyler, General Counsel and Secretary to the Commission, telephone: 717-238-0423; fax: 717-238-2436.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The business meeting will include actions or presentations on the following items: (1) Adoption of the Access to Records Policy; (2) Adoption of the 2027 Regulatory Program Fee Schedule; (3) Approval of contract and grants; and (4) 19 actions on 11 regulatory program projects.
This agenda is complete at the time of issuance, but other items may be added, and some stricken without further notice. The listing of an item on the agenda does not necessarily mean that the Commission will take final action on it at this meeting. When the Commission does take final action, notice of these actions will be published in the
Federal Register
after the meeting. Any actions specific to projects will also be provided in writing directly to project sponsors.
The meeting will be conducted both in person and digitally at the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, 4423 North Front Street, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. The public is invited to attend the Commission's business meeting. The public may access the Business Meeting remotely via TEAMS:
https://teams.microsoft.com/​meet/​24332537930182?​p=​jurKh2mlnwH1bS3k7r;​
Meeting ID: 243 325 379 301 82; Passcode: G5EM2V9d or via telephone: #1-929-777-2488, Phone Conf ID: 517 701 386#.
A public hearing and written comment period was provided for the actions on the 11 projects, the Proposed Access to Records Policy and the Proposed 2027 Regulatory Program Fee Schedule and the comment period on those proposed actions is closed. Written comments pertaining to all other items on the agenda at the business meeting may be mailed to the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, 4423 North Front Street, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania 17110, or submitted electronically at the link Business Meeting Comments. Comments are due to the Commission for all items on the business meeting agenda on or before December 7, 2026. Comments will not be accepted at the business meeting noticed herein.

SUMMARY:
This document provides the public notice that the Central Florida Rail Corridor (CFRC) petitioned FRA for an extension of relief from certain regulations concerning periodic testing requirements on vital microprocessor-based signal systems.
DATES:
FRA must receive comments on the petition by January 11, 2027. FRA will consider comments received after that date to the extent practicable.
ADDRESSES:

https://www.regulations.gov
and following the online instructions for submitting comments.

All submissions must include the agency name and docket number. All comments received will be posted without change to
https://www.regulations.gov
;
this includes any personal information. Please see the Privacy Act heading in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document for Privacy Act information related to any submitted comments or materials.
Docket:
For access to the docket to read background documents or comments received, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and follow the online instructions for accessing the docket.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Scott Johnson, Railroad Safety Specialist, FRA Signal, Train Control, and Crossings Division, telephone: 406-657-6642, email:
scott.j.johnson@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under
part 211 of title 49 Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR), this document provides the public notice that by letter dated June 1, 2026, CSXT petitioned FRA for an extension of a waiver of compliance from certain provisions of the Federal railroad safety regulations contained at
49 CFR part 236
(Rules, Standards, and Instructions Governing the Installation, Inspection, Maintenance, and Repair of Signal and Train Control Systems, Devices, and Appliances). The relevant Docket Number is FRA-2009-0120.
Specifically, CFRC seeks an extension of relief from the 2-year periodic testing requirements in §§ 236.377,
Approach locking;
236.378,
Time locking;
236.379,
Route locking;
236.380,
Indication locking;
and 236.381,
Traffic locking,
related to vital microprocessor-based systems. The existing relief extends the testing requirements in these sections from “at least once every 2 years” to every 4 years, after initial testing is completed. In its petition, CFRC states that it has “updated and submitted the listings of all signal[ ] locations being periodically testing in accordance” with the waiver and that “all new locations have been thoroughly tested prior to being placed in service.”
A copy of the petition, as well as any written communications concerning the petition, is available for review online at
www.regulations.gov
.
Interested parties are invited to participate in these proceedings by submitting written views, data, or comments. FRA does not anticipate scheduling a public hearing in connection with these proceedings since the facts do not appear to warrant a hearing. If any interested party desires an opportunity for oral comment and a public hearing, they should notify FRA, in writing, before the end of the comment period and specify the basis for their request.
Communications received by January 11, 2027 will be considered by FRA before final action is taken. Comments received after that date will be considered if practicable.
Privacy Act
Anyone can search the electronic form of any written communications and comments received into any of FRA's dockets by the name of the individual submitting the comment (or signing the document, if submitted on behalf of an association, business, labor union, etc.). Under
5 U.S.C. 553(c)
, DOT solicits comments from the public to inform its processes. DOT posts these comments, without edit, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14 FDMS), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/​privacy
.
See also
https://www.regulations.gov/​privacy-notice
for the privacy notice of
regulations.gov
.

Associate Administrator for Railroad Safety, Chief Safety Officer.
