AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-05-07, which applies to all Leonardo S.p.a. Model AW189 helicopters. AD 2024-05-07 requires revising the airworthiness limitations section (ALS) of the existing helicopter maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA) and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-05-07, it was determined that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations are necessary. This proposed AD would require revising the ALS of the existing maintenance manual or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this NPRM by December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
regulations.gov.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Mail:
U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13796; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this NPRM, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI) any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.
Material Incorporated by Reference:
For Air vehicle maintenance planning information material identified in this proposed AD, contact Leonardo Helicopters, Via Giovanni Agusta 520, 21017 Cascina Costa di Samarate (Va) Italy; phone: (+39) 0331-229111; email:
helicoptersinfo@leonardo.com
.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call (817) 222-5110.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
George Weir, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (817) 222-4045; email:
george.a.weir@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13796; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00015-R” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend the proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial
(
printed page 72471)
information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to George Weir Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2024-05-07, Amendment 39-22698 (
89 FR 24686
, April 9, 2024) (AD 2024-05-07), for all Leonardo S.p.a. Model AW189 helicopters. AD 2024-05-07 was prompted by an MCAI originated by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2023-0161, dated August 16, 2023 (EASA AD 2023-0161), to correct an unsafe condition identified as fatigue cracking, damage, and corrosion in principal structural elements.
AD 2024-05-07 requires revising the ALS of the existing helicopter maintenance manual or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable. The FAA issued AD 2024-05-07 to address fatigue cracking, damage, and corrosion in principal structural elements.
Actions Since AD 2024-05-07 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2024-05-07, EASA superseded EASA AD 2023-0161 and issued EASA AD 2025-0090, dated April 23, 2025, which was superseded by EASA AD 2026-0004, dated January 13, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0004) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations have been developed.

These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

Office of the United States Trade Representative
AGENCY:
Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In prior notices, the U.S. Trade Representative (Trade Representative) modified the actions in the Section 301 investigation of China's acts, policies, and practices related to technology transfer, intellectual property, and innovation by excluding from additional duties certain products of China. While most exclusions have expired in prior years, certain exclusions remain in force. This notice announces the Trade Representative's determination to further extend all 178 current exclusions.
DATES:
The modifications announced in the annexes to this notice further extend the exclusions through 11:59 p.m. eastern time on January 9, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For general questions about this notice, contact Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Monitoring & Enforcement Philip Butler at (202) 395-5725. For specific questions on customs classification or implementation of the product exclusions, contact
traderemedy@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
A. Background
In the course of this investigation, the Trade Representative has imposed additional duties on products of China in four tranches.
See
83 FR 28719
(June 20, 2018);
83 FR 40823
(August 16, 2018);
83 FR 47974
(September 21, 2018), as modified by
83 FR 49153
(September 28, 2018); and
84 FR 43304
(August 20, 2019), as modified by
84 FR 69447
(December 18, 2019) and
85 FR 3741
(January 22, 2020). Additionally, the Trade Representative has established certain processes by which U.S. stakeholders could request the temporary exclusion of particular products subject to the actions. With few exceptions, most of these exclusions expired in 2019 and 2020.
On December 29, 2023, USTR invited the public to submit comments on whether to extend 352 previously reinstated exclusions and 77 COVID-related exclusions.
See
88 FR 90225
(December 29, 2023). On May 30, 2024, USTR announced the extension of 164 of these exclusions through May 31, 2025.
See
89 FR 46948
(May 30, 2024) (the May 30, 2024 FRN). In connection with the four-year review of the actions taken in this investigation, on September 18, 2024, USTR announced fourteen exclusions covering certain solar manufacturing equipment.
See
89 FR 76581
(September 18, 2024) (the September 18, 2024 FRN). The fourteen exclusions were effective from January 1, 2024, through May 31, 2025. On May 31, 2025, USTR announced the further extension of the 164 exclusions extended in May 2024 and the fourteen exclusions granted in September 2024, through August 31, 2025.
See
90 FR 23987
(June 5, 2025). USTR announced a further extension for these 178 exclusions for 90 days, through November 29, 2025.
See
90 FR 42500
(September 2, 2025).
On September 16, 2025, USTR invited the public to submit comments on whether any of the 178 current exclusions warrant further extension beyond November 29, 2025.
See
90 FR 44749
(the September 16, 2025 FRN). Among the factors considered, the September 16, 2025 FRN provided that USTR would consider whether further extending an exclusion is consistent with the Administration's priorities and how further extending an exclusion would impact U.S. interests, including the overall impact of the exclusion on the goal of obtaining the elimination of China's acts, policies, and practices covered in the Section 301 investigation.
On November 1, 2025, the White House announced a historic trade and economic deal reached between President Trump and President Xi Jinping of China.
[
1
]
Pursuant to this deal, the United States would further extend the 178 exclusions scheduled to expire on November 29, 2025, until November 10, 2026. Among other actions, China would continue its exclusion process and further extend existing exclusions through December 31, 2026, which would facilitate China's purchases of U.S. goods.
On November 26, 2025, USTR announced the extension of all 178 current exclusions through November 9, 2026, and that USTR might consider further extensions or additional modifications as appropriate.
See
90 FR 55232
(December 1, 2025).
B. Determination To Extend Exclusions
The Section 301 statute, which is set out in Sections 301 to 308 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 2411-2418
), provides authority for the Trade Representative to modify the action being taken in an investigation. In particular, Section 307(a)(1) authorizes the Trade Representative to modify or terminate any action taken under Section 301, subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President, if the burden or restriction on U.S. commerce of the acts, policies, and practices that are the subject of the action has increased or decreased, or the action is being taken under Section 301(b) and is no longer appropriate.
In light of ongoing discussions with China, the Trade Representative has determined that it is appropriate to further extend all 178 current exclusions until January 10, 2027.
The Trade Representative's decision to further extend the 178 current exclusions takes into consideration the public comments received in response to the September 16, 2025 FRN. The Trade Representative's decision to extend these exclusions also takes into consideration public comments previously provided, the advice of the advisory committees, and the advice of the interagency Section 301 Committee.
As indicated in the May 30, 2024 FRN and the September 18, 2024 FRN, the exclusion extensions in the annexes to this notice are available for any product that meets the description in the product exclusion. Further, the scope of each exclusion is governed by the scope of the ten-digit Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) statistical reporting numbers and product descriptions set forth in U.S. notes 20(vvv)(i), 20(vvv)(ii), 20(vvv)(iii), and 20(vvv)(iv) and 20(www) to subchapter III of chapter 99 of the HTSUS.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection will issue instructions on entry guidance and implementation.
The Trade Representative may continue to consider further extensions or additional modifications as appropriate.
(
printed page 72611)
Annex A
The Trade Representative has determined to extend all exclusions under heading 9903.88.69 and U.S. notes 20(vvv)(i), 20(vvv)(ii), 20(vvv)(iii), and 20(vvv)(iv) to subchapter III of chapter 99 of the HTSUS.
See
89 FR 46948
(May 30, 2024),
90 FR 23987
(June 5, 2025),
90 FR 42500
(September 2, 2025), and
90 FR 55232
(December 1, 2025). The extension is effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on November 10, 2026, and before 11:59 p.m. eastern time on January 9, 2027. Effective on November 10, 2026, the article description of heading 9903.88.69 of the HTSUS is modified by deleting “November 9, 2026,” and by inserting “January 9, 2027,” in lieu thereof.
Annex B

Title:

Abstract:
This collection of information is required by the Trademark Act (Act),
15 U.S.C. 1051
et seq.,
which provides for the registration of trademarks, service marks, collective trademark and service marks, collective membership marks, and certification marks. Individuals and businesses that use or intend to use such marks in commerce may file an application to register their marks with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). This information collection generally contains information that is not submitted with the initial trademark application but is associated with, or required for, the USPTO review of applications for registration.
In some instances, the USPTO issues Office actions to applicants who have applied to register a mark, or to request information that was not provided with the initial submission but is required before the issuance of a registration. Also, the USPTO may determine that a mark is not entitled to registration, pursuant to one or more provisions of the Act. In such cases, the USPTO will issue an Office action advising the applicant of the refusal to register the mark. Applicants respond to these Office actions by providing the required information and/or by advancing legal arguments as to why the refusal of registration should be withdrawn.
The USPTO administers the Act through
Title 37 of the Code of Federal Regulations
. These rules allow the USPTO to request and receive information required to process applications. These rules also allow applicants to submit certain amendments to their applications.
Applicants may also supplement their applications and provide additional information by filing a Voluntary Amendment Not in Response to USPTO Office Action/Letter, a Request for Reconsideration after Final Action, a Post-Approval/Publication/Post-Notice of Allowance (NOA) Amendment, a Response to Suspension Inquiry or Letter of Suspension, or a Request for Extension of Time to File a Response.
Since the publication of the 60-day notice, the USPTO has updated the number of responses associated with

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2021-13-20, which applies to certain Airbus Canada Limited Partnership Model BD-500-1A10 and BD-500-1A11 airplanes. AD 2021-13-20 requires inspecting the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door for corrosion, and doing applicable on-condition actions. Since the FAA issued AD 2021-13-20, the FAA has determined that a full secondary fuel vapor barrier must be applied. This proposed AD would retain all requirements of AD 2021-13-20 and would also require, for certain airplanes, an additional inspection of the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door for corrosion, and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this proposed AD by December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:

regulations.gov.

202-493-2251.

U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13807; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this NPRM, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.

For Transport Canada material identified in this proposed AD, contact Transport Canada, Transport Canada National Aircraft Certification, 159 Cleopatra Drive, Nepean, Ontario K1A 0N5, Canada; telephone 888-663-3639; email

.

Camille Seay, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 817-222-5149; email:
Camille.L.Seay@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the
ADDRESSES
section. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13807; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00620-T” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to regulations.gov, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Camille Seay, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 817-222-5149; email:
Camille.L.Seay@faa.gov
.
Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2021-13-20, Amendment 39-21625 (
86 FR 38223
, July 20, 2021) (AD 2021-13-20), for certain Airbus Canada Limited Partnership Model BD-500-1A10 and BD-500-1A11 airplanes. AD 2021-13-20 was prompted by an MCAI originated by Transport Canada, which is the aviation authority for Canada. Transport Canada issued AD CF-2020-42, dated October 16, 2020 (Transport Canada AD CF-2020-42), to correct an unsafe condition.
AD 2021-13-20 requires inspecting the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door for corrosion, and doing applicable on-condition actions. The FAA issued AD 2021-13-20 to address this corrosion, which could lead to cracking or holes in the waste box or airplane skin, and consequent cabin pressure leakage and catastrophic structural damage of the airplane.
(
printed page 72466)
Actions Since AD 2021-13-20 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2021-13-20, Transport Canada superseded Transport Canada AD CF-2020-42 and issued Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26, dated June 19, 2026 (Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for certain Model BD-500-1A10 and BD-500-1A11 airplanes.
The MCAI states that corrosion, caused by leakage of wastewater from the waste service panel ball valve, has been reported on the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door at the rear fuselage, and that some corrosion findings have been severe enough to require structural repairs or replacement of the affected parts. Since Transport Canada AD CF-2020-42 was issued, the manufacturer revised the service information, designating the existing instructions as Part A and introducing a new Part B applicable to certain airplanes; Part A improves the prior instructions (
i.e.,
Part A ensures a full application of secondary fuel vapor barrier to the entire waste box), and Part B adds repairs to the waste access doubler, replacement of fillet sealant, removal of corrosion-inhibiting compound, and application of secondary fuel vapor barrier (to the Part B inspection of the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door for corrosion, and applicable on-condition actions).
The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13807.
Explanation of Retained Requirements
Although this proposed AD does not explicitly restate the requirements of AD 2021-13-20, this proposed AD would retain all of the requirements of AD 2021-13-20. Those requirements are referenced in Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26, which, in turn, is referenced in paragraph (g) of this proposed AD.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26 specifies procedures for a general visual inspection of the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door for corrosion, applying secondary fuel barrier sealant (for certain airplanes), and applicable on-condition actions. On-condition actions include repairing any corrosion found, applying secondary fuel barrier to the entire waste box, and applying corrosion protection.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would retain all of the requirements of AD 2021-13-20. This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26 described previously, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some civil aviation authority (CAA) ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Material required by Transport Canada AD CF-2026-26 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
by searching for and locating Docket No. FAA-2026-13807 after the FAA final rule is published.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

This AD was prompted by reports of corrosion on the waste box, waste access doubler, and waste service door at the aft waste service port, caused by leakage of wastewater from the waste service panel ball valve. 19 U.S.C. 1337
) in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain electronic control units and products containing the same. The complaint names as respondents: Lucid Group, Inc. of Newark, CA; Lucid USA, Inc. of Casa Grande, AZ; Lucid Group USA, Inc. of Newark, CA; Rivian Automotive, Inc. of Irvine, CA; and Rivian Automotive, LLC of Wittman, AZ. The complainant requests that the Commission issue a limited exclusion order, cease and desist orders and impose a bond upon respondents' alleged infringing articles during the 60-day Presidential review period pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1337(j)
.
Proposed respondents, other interested parties, members of the public, and interested government agencies are invited to file comments on any public interest issues raised by the complaint or § 210.8(b) filing. Comments should address whether issuance of the relief specifically requested by the complainant in this investigation would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) explain how the articles potentially subject to the requested remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the requested remedial orders;
(
printed page 72559)
(iii) identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the requested exclusion order and/or a cease and desist order within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) explain how the requested remedial orders would impact United States consumers.
Written submissions on the public interest must be filed no later than by close of business, eight calendar days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. There will be further opportunities for comment on the public interest after the issuance of any final initial determination in this investigation. Any written submissions on other issues must also be filed by no later than the close of business (5:15 p.m.),
[
1
]
eight calendar days after publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. Complainant(s) may file replies to any written submissions no later than three calendar days after the date on which the written submissions were due. Notwithstanding § 201.14(a) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, the deadlines for written submissions and replies shall be counted by calendar days starting with the first calendar day following the
Federal Register
publication date or the due date for written submissions, respectively. The provisions of § 201.14(a) regarding the last day of the period still apply concerning the due date of any filings. No other submissions will be accepted, unless requested by the Commission. Any submissions and replies filed in response to this Notice are limited to five (5) pages in length, inclusive of attachments.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above. Submissions should refer to the docket number (“Docket No. 3947”) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (

Any person desiring to submit a document to the Commission in confidence must request confidential treatment. All such requests should be directed to the Secretary to the Commission and must include a full statement of the reasons why the Commission should grant such treatment.

. Documents for which confidential treatment by the Commission is properly sought will be treated accordingly. Appendix 3; or (ii) by U.S. government employees and contract personnel,

solely for cybersecurity purposes. All nonconfidential written submissions will be available for public inspection at the Office of the Secretary and on EDIS.
[

19 U.S.C. 1337
), and of §§ 201.10 and 210.8(c) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (

printed page 72393)
ACTION:
Final rule; correction.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is correcting an airworthiness directive (AD) that was published in the
Federal Register
. That AD applies to all Airbus SAS Model A330-243, A330-243F, A330-341, A330-342, A330-343, A330-841, and A330-941 airplanes; and Model A340-211, A340-212, A340-213, A340-311, A340-312, A340-313, A340-541, and A340-642 airplanes. As published, a paragraph reference specified in the regulatory text is incorrect. This document corrects that error. In all other respects, the original document remains the same.
DATES:
This correction is effective November 23, 2026. The effective date of AD 2026-21-03 remains November 23, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of November 23, 2026 (
91 FR 65952
, October 19, 2026).
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-8780; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule; correction, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Material Incorporated by Reference:
For European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) material identified in this AD, contact EASA, Konrad-Adenauer-Ufer 3, 50668 Cologne, Germany; telephone +49 221 8999 000; email
ADs@easa.europa.eu
.
You may find this material on the EASA website at
ad.easa.europa.eu.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call 206-231-3195. It is also available in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-8780.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Anthony D. Decaro, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 562-627-5374; email:
Anthony.D.Decaro@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
AD 2026-21-03, Amendment 39-23492 (
91 FR 65952
, October 19, 2026) (AD 2026-21-03), requires repetitive leak checks of certain fuel low pressure shut-off valves (LPSOVs) and replacement of an affected part if any discrepancy is detected. AD 2026-21-03 also allows the installation of an affected part under certain conditions. That AD applies to all Airbus SAS Model A330-243, A330-243F, A330-341, A330-342, A330-343, A330-841, and A330-941 airplanes; and Model A340-211, A340-212, A340-213, A340-311, A340-312, A340-313, A340-541, and A340-642 airplanes.
Need for the Correction
As published, a paragraph reference specified in the regulatory text of AD 2026-21-03 is incorrect. Paragraph (h)(4) of AD 2026-21-03 inadvertently references paragraph (4) of EASA AD 2026-0060R1 instead of paragraph (2) of EASA AD 2026-0060R1.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies procedures for repetitive leak checks of the fuel LPSOVs to confirm that the LPSOV isolates the fuel supply to the associated engine, and replacement of an affected part if any discrepancy is detected (
e.g.,
any leak is found). EASA AD 2026-0060R1 also allows the installation of an affected part under certain conditions. EASA AD 2026-0060R1 also provides acceptable methods of compliance for the actions.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Correction of Publication
This document corrects an error and correctly adds the AD as an amendment to
14 CFR 39.13
. Although no other part of the preamble or regulatory information has been corrected, the FAA is publishing the entire rule in the
Federal Register
.
The effective date of this AD remains November 23, 2026.
Since this action only corrects a paragraph reference, it has no adverse economic impact and imposes no additional burden on any person. Therefore, the FAA has determined that notice and public comment procedures are unnecessary.

14 CFR Part 39
Air transportation

Aviation safety

Adoption of the Amendment
Accordingly, pursuant to the authority delegated to me by the Administrator, the FAA amends part 39 of the Federal Aviation Regulations (
14 CFR part 39
) as follows:
PART 39—AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVES
1.
The authority citation for part 39 continues to read as follows:
Authority:
49 U.S.C. 106(g)
,
40113
,
44701
.
§ 39.13
[Corrected]
2.
The FAA amends § 39.13 by adding the following new airworthiness directive:
2026-21-03 Airbus SAS:
Amendment 39-23492; Docket No. FAA-2026-8780; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00262-T.
(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective November 23, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all Airbus SAS airplanes specified in paragraphs (c)(1) and (2) of this AD, certificated in any category.
(1) Model A330-243, A330-243F, A330-341, A330-342, A330-343, A330-841, and A330-941 airplanes.
(2) Model A340-211, A340-212, A340-213, A340-311, A340-312, A340-313, A340-541, and A340-642 airplanes.
(d) Subject
Air Transport Association (ATA) of America Code 28, Fuel.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports of leaks on closed fuel low pressure shut-off valves (LPSOVs) due to the LPSOV failing to seal. The FAA is issuing this AD to address such leaks, which, depending on the amount of the leak, could sustain a fire. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could lead to the inability to extinguish a fire and result in significant damage to airplane structure or systems.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2026-0060R1, dated June 9, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0060R1).
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2026-0060R1
(1) Where Table 1 of EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies a compliance time of between November 12, 2025, and March 3,
(
printed page 72394)
2029, this AD requires accomplishing the initial leak check within 35 months after the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where EASA AD 2026-0060R1 refers to April 3, 2026 (the effective date of the original issue of EASA AD 2026-0060), this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(3) Where EASA AD 2026-0060R1 defines a serviceable part as “Any fuel LPSOV eligible for installation in accordance with Airbus instructions”, for this AD, replace that text with “Any fuel LPSOV eligible for installation”.
(4) Where paragraph (2) of EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies “any discrepancy of an affected part, as specified in the SB, is detected”, for this AD, replace that text with “any discrepancy of an affected part is detected”.
(5) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2026-0060R1.
(i) No Reporting and No Return of Parts
Although the material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0060R1 specifies to submit certain information to the manufacturer and to send removed parts to the manufacturer, this AD does not include those requirements.
(j) Additional AD Provisions
The following provisions also apply to this AD:
(1)
Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs):
The Manager, AIR-520, Continued Operational Safety Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the Continued Operational Safety Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (k) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
.
Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office.
(2)
Contacting the Manufacturer:
For any requirement in this AD to obtain instructions from a manufacturer, the instructions must be accomplished using a method approved by the Manager, AIR-520, Continued Operational Safety Branch, FAA; or EASA; or Airbus SAS's EASA Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(3)
Required for Compliance (RC):
Except as required by paragraph (j)(2) of this AD, if any material contains procedures or tests that are identified as RC, those procedures and tests must be done to comply with this AD; any procedures or tests that are not identified as RC are recommended. Those procedures and tests that are not identified as RC may be deviated from using accepted methods in accordance with the operator's maintenance or inspection program without obtaining approval of an AMOC, provided the procedures and tests identified as RC can be done and the airplane can be put back in an airworthy condition. Any substitutions or changes to procedures or tests identified as RC require approval of an AMOC.
(k) Additional Information
For more information about this AD, contact Anthony D. Decaro, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 562-627-5374; email:
Anthony.D.Decaro@faa.gov
.
(l) Material Incorporated by Reference
(1) The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference (IBR) of the material listed in this paragraph under
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
and
1 CFR part 51
.
(2) You must use this material as applicable to do the actions required by this AD, unless this AD specifies otherwise.
(3) The following material was approved for IBR on November 23, 2026 (
91 FR 65952
, October 19, 2026).
(i) European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2026-0060R1, dated June 9, 2026.

.
You may find this material on the EASA website at
ad.easa.europa.eu.
(5) You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call 206-231-3195.
(6) You may view this material at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). For information on the availability of this material at NARA, visit
www.archives.gov/​federal-register/​cfr/​ibr-locations
or email
fr.inspection@nara.gov
.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Labor (Department), through the Employment and Training Administration (ETA), is proposing to amend
20 CFR part 604
both to reflect a 2012 update in Federal law in which Congress, by amending section 303(a) of the Social Security Act (SSA), established a Federal work search requirement; and to establish a national minimum weekly work search requirement standard for the Federal-State unemployment compensation (UC) program. This proposed rule would mandate, among other things, that States require individuals claiming UC to complete at least five qualifying work search activities or, where applicable, meet State-adopted points-based system requirements amounting to five qualifying activities or satisfy equivalent labor force attachment criteria, each week for which UC is claimed; that individuals report their work search activities as part of their certification process prior to payment being issued; and that State law allow for certain qualifying work search activities beyond simply employer contacts. This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work. The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering a UC program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market.

II. Executive Summary
Purpose of the Rule and Summary of the Rule's Major Provisions
In 2012, Congress amended the SSA at section 303(a) to require that an individual must be actively seeking work to be eligible for UC. However, implementation across States of the requirement to actively seek work has demonstrated inconsistencies in expectations for individuals receiving UC. This rule will operationalize the statutory requirement at section 303(a)(12) of the SSA that States require that, to be eligible for UC, individuals are able to work, available to work, and are actively seeking work for each week that benefits are claimed.
To implement the statutory changes, the Department is proposing this rule, which would establish a national minimum weekly work search standard for the UC program. This proposed regulation would establish that:
State law must require individuals to complete a minimum of five qualifying work search activities or, where applicable as defined later in this preamble, meet State-adopted points-based system requirements amounting to five qualifying activities or satisfy equivalent labor force attachment criteria, each week for which UC is claimed. Circumstances under which individuals may be deemed to have met the minimum work search requirement are when work search activities would not serve to promote labor force attachment, when the timing of an initial claim does not provide time to complete the minimum number of work search activities, or when there are other limited extenuating circumstances that would preclude an individual from meeting the minimum number of work search activities in a week.
State law must require individuals to report work search activity as part of the continued claim certification process prior to payment being released.
State law must allow for certain qualifying work search activities beyond simply employer contacts, to include registration and ongoing contact with placement agencies or unions for the purposes of seeking employment. States may designate additional activities as satisfying the requirement as enumerated in the proposed text. These
(
printed page 72474)
examples are illustrative, non-exhaustive, and include qualifying activities that are reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment.
These standards codify and provide consistency across the UC system for best practices and standards that the Department has previously placed in subregulatory guidance. The proposed rule also would:
Require States to provide notice to individuals regarding the applicable work search requirements; and
Prohibit States from giving formal or informal warnings to individuals who fail to complete the required work search activities for each benefit week claimed, in lieu of determining their ineligibility.
Under the proposed framework, States would have latitude to adapt the work search requirement to labor market conditions by adopting a points-based system for satisfying the minimum weekly work search requirement. Under such a system, States may assign point values to qualifying work search activities and require individuals to accumulate a minimum of five points per benefit week.
The proposed rule would not require a specific reporting method, form, or questions. States could continue to accept work search activity reporting using existing reporting methods within their systems, provided the work search activities are reported for each benefit week claimed and before payment is issued. States will continue to follow their existing UC record retention policies, as required in
20 CFR part 604
, with respect to work search activity reported data. Additionally, the proposed rule does not mandate how States verify reported work search activities, the frequency or scope of audits, or the adjudication procedures applied when an individual fails to complete or report the required work search activities or fails to demonstrate equivalent labor force attachment. These operational and enforcement decisions would remain within the discretion of States, consistent with applicable Federal law.
The Department acknowledges that these proposed provisions could temporarily increase the UC program's estimated improper payment rate as States and individuals adapt to the new requirements and asserts that such risk is necessary to ensure the UC system is effectively meeting its mission of providing temporary assistance to eligible individuals while they become reemployed.
III. Background
To qualify for UC, an individual must have demonstrated recent attachment to the labor market and be unemployed through no fault of their own. As such, they have also demonstrated skills that enabled them to maintain employment, though such skills may be dated or no longer relevant to the labor market within which they are seeking work. The UC system plays a critical role in connecting these recently unemployed individuals with tools and resources and jobs to become reemployed. State work search requirements must recognize the individual within this context and allow for a broad array of activities to connect the individual with the broader workforce system.
Eligibility for UC is determined on a week-to-week basis. Once an individual files their initial claim for UC, they are required to submit continued claim certifications for confirmation of their continued eligibility. Most States require such certification on a weekly basis and some States provide for submission on a biweekly basis, though this still requires that the individual confirm their continued eligibility for each separate week within the biweekly period.
States currently implement the Federal “actively seeking work” requirement under section 303(a)(12) of the SSA using a wide range of inconsistent work search standards. A comparative compilation of State UC laws shows that minimum required weekly work search activities vary substantially across States, including numeric requirements, qualitative standards (
e.g.,
“quality not quantity”), and circumstances in which the number of required activities is unspecified or varies based on labor market, individual circumstances, or policy preferences.
[
1
]
Policy preferences also vary by State in whether they are set by the State UC agency, Governor's office, or State legislature.
Across States, acceptable work search activities are typically defined broadly and may include, among other actions: direct employer contacts and employment applications; resume creation or updates; use of online job search tools and job matching systems; participation in American Job Center services and workshops; job fairs and recruitment events attendance; and other activities reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment. In many States, contact with an individual's union is also an acceptable work search activity.
States monitor compliance with work search requirements through multiple channels, including program integrity sampling (
e.g.,
Benefit Accuracy Measurement (BAM)) and reemployment engagement processes (
e.g.,
Reemployment Services and Eligibility Assessment (RESEA)). Many States also conduct eligibility reviews, random or targeted audits, interviews, or other State-defined checks.
The proposed rule would not require a specific reporting method. States could continue to accept work search activity reporting using existing reporting methods within their systems, provided the work search activities are reported for each benefit week claimed and before payment is issued. Additionally, the proposed rule does not mandate how States verify reported work search activities, the frequency or scope of audits, or the adjudication procedures applied when an individual fails to meet a work search requirement. These operational and enforcement decisions would remain within the discretion of States, consistent with applicable Federal law.
A. Need for Rulemaking
Federal law requires individuals receiving UC to be able to work, available to work, and actively seeking work as a condition of eligibility. Section 303(a)(12) of the SSA (
42 U.S.C. 503(a)(12)
). States have developed differing standards to enforce this requirement that speak to both the number and type of required activities, as well as the frequency and methods of reporting them. States range from simply requiring an affirmative statement of conducting work search activities to requiring upwards of five activities in any given week. States also vary in what they consider to be a qualifying activity.
As of January 1, 2025, a few States already generally require five work search activities per week, a few States generally require four work search activities per week, nearly one-half of States generally require three work search activities per week, some States generally require two work search activities per week, and the remaining States generally require one work search activity per week.
These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear. Additionally,
(
printed page 72475)
variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules.
Despite the issuance of guidance and model legislation, work search errors continue to be one of the primary drivers of improper payment rates across the UC system and the UC improper payment rate remains above the 10-percent performance target established by the Payment Integrity Information Act (
31 U.S.C. 3351-3358
). Significant improvement was made in addressing work search errors in the year leading up to the March 2020 start of the pandemic. However, Congress enacted legislation to temporarily waive the work search requirement during the pandemic; once reinstated, work search errors again increased significantly. This proposed rule would specifically increase program integrity by requiring individuals claiming UC to report their work search activities prior to the payment of benefits, and by establishing consistency in the way that States apply equivalent labor force attachment.
Given these challenges, this proposed rule would establish a national minimum weekly work search standard that provides a clear and consistent expectation for individuals to be “actively seeking work” across the Federal-State UC program. The proposed approach supports meaningful engagement with the labor market and reflects modern job search practices, which can involve multi-day or clustered activities such as interviews, job fairs, or assessments. By requiring individuals to complete at least five weekly work search activities—with limited and specified exceptions—and to report such activities prior to issuing payment, the proposed rule would improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment. The proposed rule also supports an assurance that individuals are informed of the requirements and have access to a broader set of qualifying activities.
In drafting this proposed regulation, the Department is also addressing the risk of prolonged unemployment due to an insufficient search for work, a risk that may arise from a potential moral hazard
[
2
]
associated with UC. UC provides temporary partial wage replacement and, by replacing a portion of lost wages, reduces some of the immediate financial cost of continued unemployment, which may marginally reduce the financial incentive to search for or accept suitable work.
The proposed rule would help address this risk by establishing a clear national minimum weekly work search requirement and requiring individuals to report qualifying work search activities as part of the continued claim certification process before payment is issued. Requiring activities that are specific, identifiable, and reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment would help unemployed individuals find work more quickly. Conditioning eligibility for a claimed week on satisfaction of the applicable work search requirement would also strengthen the incentive for individuals claiming UC to remain meaningfully engaged with the labor market, thus helping them return to work faster. The reporting requirements in the proposed regulation would provide States with contemporaneous information regarding compliance and a record that States can use for eligibility reviews, audits, and other program integrity activities.
The Department expects that establishing a national minimum weekly work search standard as proposed would also result in a reduction in the duration of unemployment because individuals would obtain reemployment more quickly. A randomized controlled trial by Lachowska, Meral, and Woodbury (2016) examined the long-term effects of more stringent work search requirements on individuals claiming UC in Washington State over a 9-year follow-up period. The study found that individuals subject to more intensive work search requirements exited the UC program sooner and experienced higher employment rates in the year following their claims. Specifically, individuals with standard or modified work tests received approximately $429-$484 (1986 and 1987 nominal dollars) less in UC and experienced roughly 3 fewer weeks of benefit receipt compared with individuals who were not subject to work test requirements.
[
3
]
B. Statutory and Regulatory History and Authority
Statutory and Regulatory History
Section 303 of the SSA (
42 U.S.C. 503
) provides that specific conditions must be included under State UC law for the State to be certified by the U.S. Secretary of Labor (Secretary) to receive Federal administrative grants (
42 U.S.C. 502(a)
), including requirements related to eligibility conditions and methods of administration. Under
42 U.S.C. 1302(a)
the Secretary has authority to promulgate regulations that are “necessary to the efficient administration of the functions” the Secretary is responsible for under chapter 7 of the SSA, which includes title III (
