).
The Department and its predecessors have consistently interpreted provisions of Federal UC law to require that individuals be able and available (A&A) for work. This longstanding interpretation was codified on January 16, 2007, when the Department issued a final rule, set forth at
20 CFR part 604
(
72 FR 1890
) (Part 604 Final Rule). Based on the Federal statutory authority in place at that time, the Part 604 Final Rule provided that an active work search provision was not required, although a State could require an individual to actively seek work as part of the requirement to be available for work or could impose a separate State law requirement that the individual must actively seek work as a condition of weekly eligibility.
The Department's July 22, 2005, proposed rule (
70 FR 42474
) preceding the Part 604 Final Rule also noted that almost every State had an active work search requirement (
70 FR 42479
). In the Part 604 Final Rule, when addressing public comments submitted regarding work search, the Department expressed agreement as a policy matter that States should require an active work search but explained that a Federal “work search requirement would need to be legislated by Congress” (
72 FR 1891
).
On February 22, 2012, the Middle Class Tax Relief and Job Creation Act of 2012 (2012 Act),
Public Law 112-96
, was signed into law. Title II of the 2012 Act amended section 303(a) of the SSA to add a new paragraph (12), which specifies that a State must require, as a condition of eligibility for regular compensation, that “a claimant must be able to work, available to work, and actively seeking work,” thereby establishing a Federal work search requirement.
Passage of the 2012 Act both established the Federal mandate that States require individuals to actively search for work as a condition of UC eligibility and directly set out the Federal A&A requirement that previously had been implicit.
(
printed page 72476)
Subregulatory Guidance and Agency Policy
Following enactment of the 2012 Act specifying that “actively seeking work” was a required condition of eligibility for UC, ETA played an active role in creating best practices and facilitating State implementation of the work search requirement, including publishing subregulatory guidance, conducting webinars with States, and providing model legislative language.
Soon after Congress enacted the 2012 Act, the Department published Unemployment Insurance Program Letter (UIPL) No. 05-13, “Work Search and Overpayment Offset Provisions Added to Permanent Federal Unemployment Compensation Law by Title II, Subtitle A of the Middle Class Tax Relief and Job Creation Act of 2012” (issued Jan. 10, 2013). This subregulatory guidance informed States of the codified work search requirement and advised that “States will exercise their discretion consistent with the strong expectation that UC beneficiaries will be engaged in concerted and effective efforts calculated to find a suitable job in the shortest period of time that is practicable. . . . Any requirements established by [States] on the type or number of work search contacts must be closely tied to an expectation that the claimant will be quickly reemployed.” However, the regulation promulgated to address the A&A requirement has not been updated to reflect this statutory change to incorporate the work search requirement.
Since this time, ETA has issued several advisories to States regarding work search requirements for individuals claiming UC. The guidance issued included: Training and Employment Notice (TEN) No. 18-16, “Pathways to Reemployment Tools and Resources” (issued Nov. 21, 2016); TEN No. 02-17, “Enhanced My Reemployment Plan Tools and Resources” (issued July 14, 2017); and TEN No. 17-19, “Model Unemployment Insurance State Work Search Legislation” (issued Feb. 10, 2020).
TEN No. 18-16 announced the Pathways to Reemployment framework and introduced the My Reemployment Plan as a resource for job seekers and workforce professionals. The framework “re-envisions” work search requirements for individuals claiming UC to support their successful reemployment in the 21st-century labor market. The guidance encouraged States to modernize work search policies and expand the scope of activities that meet the work search requirement but did not mandate any changes. States were “encouraged to access, review and use” the tools, and to “assess current reemployment policies and procedures to identify areas in need of modernization.”
TEN No. 02-17 announced enhanced tools the Department developed to implement the My Reemployment Plan, including a companion video series for job seekers and a reference guide for workforce professionals in American Job Centers. The notice “encouraged” State workforce agencies to use these resources but did not require compliance.
TEN No. 17-19 announced the availability of Model Unemployment Insurance State Work Search Legislation and “strongly encouraged” States to adopt the model language and framework. The notice requested State administrators to “consider working with the [State's] legislature and [UC] stakeholders to adopt the model legislative language,” but specified that States “may implement” the model legislation, which was “developed to assist [States].” ETA provided this model legislation as technical assistance and “encourage[d] [States] to review their work search laws, regulations, and policies, and to consider adopting the approach.” Attachment I to TEN No. 17-19 provided detailed model statutory language for work search requirements, including definitions of acceptable work search activities and documentation requirements. The language was presented as a model for States to consider, not as a Federal mandate.
The advisories provided suggestions for States to improve work search models, including expanding the scope of acceptable work search activities, encouraging the use of individualized reemployment plans, promoting integration of workforce services and technology, providing tools and resources for job seekers and workforce professionals, and offering model legislative language for States to adopt. However, States were not required to comply with the guidance, and adoption of the suggestions remained voluntary.
Additionally, the RESEA program includes a review of each individual's work search activities for purposes of assessing UC eligibility and providing reemployment support as part of the individualized RESEA engagement. The Department has regularly published annual guidance specifically applicable to grants available for States to administer their RESEA programs and not the broader UC program. This operating guidance is generally published as a joint UIPL and Training and Employment Guidance Letter (TEGL) to ensure awareness across the UC and workforce systems, most recently including: UIPL No. 02-23/TEGL No. 08-22 for Fiscal Year (FY) 2023 (issued Feb. 23, 2023); UIPL No. 08-24/TEGL No. 11-23 for FY 2024 (issued Feb. 21, 2024); and UIPL No. 12-25/TEGL No. 14-24 for FY 2025 (June 10, 2025). Within this scope, States are advised to ensure communication feedback loops between their UC and workforce operations to ensure support for swift reemployment and to use evidence-based strategies for helping individuals return to work.
The Department views the publication of this proposed regulation as the next step in effectuating the requirements of the 2012 Act. The Department is proposing to amend
20 CFR part 604
to reflect the Federal work search requirement created by the 2012 Act, which is set out in section 303(a)(12) of the SSA.
IV. Section-by-Section Discussion of the Proposed Changes
Section IV of this NPRM's preamble describes how the proposed rule would operationalize the statutory requirement at section 303(a)(12) of the SSA that individuals must actively seek work to be eligible for UC. This proposed rule also includes a definition of the term “employer contact” and sets forth a national minimum weekly work search standard.
The Department recognizes that certain provisions of the proposed rule would require States to amend their laws. In recognition of varying State legislature schedules, the Department proposes a compliance date of 1 year from the effective date of the final rule for States to comply with the requirements of the final rule. To facilitate a smooth transition, the Department expects States to discontinue both formal and informal warnings to individuals who fail to complete the required work search activities upon publication of this final rule, or as soon as possible if State law must be amended, as such warnings are inconsistent with Federal law.
A. Proposed Changes to §§ 604.1, 604.2, and 604.5
Section 604.1 Purpose and Scope
The Department is proposing a revision to § 604.1 from the current requirement that individuals are “able to work and available for work” to add the phrase “and actively seeking work.” This would codify the existing requirement in section 303(a)(12) of the SSA that, as a condition of eligibility,
(
printed page 72477)
States require that individuals are able to work, available to work, and are actively seeking work each week. The existing regulation applies to all State UC programs. To the extent that Federal UC programs, such as Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees or Unemployment Compensation for Ex-Servicemembers, defer to State requirements with respect to A&A and work search, this regulation would also be applicable.
Section 604.2 Definitions
Section 604.2 provides definitions for this part. The Department is proposing to add a new definition of the term “employer contact.” As proposed, employer contacts are communications between an individual and an individual employer by various means. The Department is proposing to define employer contact broadly to encompass the various ways in which individuals may contact employers and not solely limited to in person contact.
Section 604.5 Application—Availability for Work
The Department is proposing to remove paragraph (h), which addresses work search, from § 604.5. When paragraph (h) was adopted, there was no Federal work search requirement explicitly in statute and so it provides that States may include a work search requirement, which would be included either as an element of satisfying the available for work requirement or as a separate State requirement. As noted earlier in this NPRM's preamble, the 2012 Act amended section 303(a) of the SSA to require that an individual claiming UC be able to work, available to work, and actively seeking work. With this NPRM, the Department is proposing to align the Federal regulatory requirements with the statutory requirement by removing existing paragraph (h).
B. Section 604.6 Work Search Requirement
Proposed § 604.6 would establish a national minimum framework for work search standards applicable to all States as a condition of certification of its State UC law under title III of the SSA. Paragraphs (a) through (i) would define the minimum weekly work search activity requirement, identify permissible methods of satisfying that requirement, explain reporting expectations, provide guardrails designed to promote consistency across States, and require clear communication of work search expectations to individuals.
C. Paragraph 604.6(a) In General
Paragraph (a) would establish a requirement that States implement and administer a work search requirement for individuals consistent with § 604.6 to qualify for certification under title III of the SSA. This proposed paragraph would introduce the framework for the specific requirements, which are set forth in proposed paragraphs (b) through (i).
Paragraph (a) would also make clear that this new work search requirement would defer to existing work search requirements under
20 CFR part 615
that apply to the Federal-State Extended Benefits program. The Department is not seeking to contravene the work search regime that States implement under section 202(a)(3)(A)(ii) of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970 (EUCA). To the extent that the proposed provisions would conflict with the regulations at
20 CFR part 615
as they apply to the Extended Benefits program,
20 CFR part 604
would not apply. Conversely, to the extent that
20 CFR part 615
defers to State law, then State law must, at a minimum, align with the proposed revisions to
20 CFR part 604
.
Under this paragraph, a State would not be permitted to pay UC for a claimed week of unemployment unless the individual completes the work search requirement under § 604.6 or demonstrates an equivalent labor force attachment as provided in State law, consistent with paragraph (g).
The Department is proposing this paragraph to establish a clear national baseline, consistent with section 303(a)(12) of the SSA. Section 303(a)(12) requires State law to condition the payment of UC on an individual actively seeking work. This proposed paragraph is intended to clarify that the obligation to implement and enforce work search requirements rests with the State. This approach is consistent with the Department's authority to regulate State law for conformity and compliance under the Federal-State UC program.
D. Paragraph 604.6(b) Work Search Requirement
Paragraph (b) would establish that States must condition individual eligibility to receive UC only if the individual satisfies the applicable work search requirement for that week under proposed paragraphs (c) and (d) or demonstrates equivalent labor force attachment under proposed paragraph (g), in addition to meeting the other eligibility requirements set forth in State and Federal law.
E. Paragraph 604.6(c) Minimum Number of Work Search Activities
Paragraph (c) would establish the minimum number of weekly work search activities required for individuals to demonstrate that they are actively seeking work, as required under section 303(a)(12) of the SSA. Under this proposed paragraph, an individual must complete at least five qualifying work search activities during each week of unemployment for which UC is claimed, unless the individual satisfies the requirement through a State-adopted points-based system under paragraph (f) or meets the requirements under paragraph (g).
In determining the minimum number of work search activities in this proposed rule, the Department reviewed State work search requirements nationwide. While there is variability in the number of work search activities required in States, there are a few States that already require five work search activities per week. Therefore, the Department has concluded that proposing a minimum of five work search activities per week is a reasonable and implementable requirement. The Department believes that establishing a clear minimum of five work search activities per week, with consideration for alternative demonstrations of sufficient labor force attachment described in paragraphs (f) and (g), provides a consistent and understandable baseline for active work search while remaining reasonable, achievable, and administratively feasible. The proposed requirement reflects a reasonable minimum demonstration of active labor market engagement.
F. Paragraph 604.6(d) Work Search Activity Reporting
Paragraph (d) would add a requirement that State law must require individuals to report the details of each completed work search activity, or the details of the individual's equivalent labor force attachment under paragraph (g) of this section, as part of the certification process prior to the payment of UC for a claimed week.
Some States already include this reporting requirement at the time of continued claim certification. All States currently require reporting work search activities when a claim is selected for a BAM audit, with the exception of one territory that does not operate a BAM program. Some States may also request work search information, or equivalent labor force attachment information, after payment through randomized audits, targeted reviews, or post-payment
(
printed page 72478)
verification processes. Requesting work search activities, or equivalent labor force attachment information, post-payment creates challenges for individuals, States, and employers to accurately recall, document, and verify such activities weeks or months after the activities, or equivalent labor force attachment, occurred. This delayed reporting contributes to improper payments and administrative inefficiencies.
States would retain flexibility in how they implement this proposed requirement, provided that such reporting is required for each week of claimed UC before payment is released. States would also retain discretion to determine what specific information individuals must report to the State, consistent with State law and administrative practices. The proposed provision would allow States to determine the information that individuals would be required to report with respect to their work search activities, or equivalent labor force attachment, as part of the continued claim certification process. States should only collect information that is necessary for the proper administration of the UC program. The Department recommends States collect enough information to facilitate any future audit of work search activity, or equivalent labor force attachment. The proposed provision does not prescribe specific information that must be reported to the State. The Department anticipates that most States would implement this requirement through existing certification systems and processes.
For States that administer the continued claim certification on a biweekly basis, this proposed paragraph clarifies that the work search requirement must be satisfied separately for each week of unemployment for which UC is claimed. However, States with continued claim certifications administered biweekly may satisfy the proposed requirements in § 604.6 by obtaining weekly work search activity, or equivalent labor force attachment, information from individuals on a biweekly basis and before a biweekly payment is made.
G. Paragraph 604.6(e) Work Search Activity
Paragraph (e) would establish the general requirements governing what constitutes a qualifying work search activity for purposes of satisfying the work search requirement under § 604.6. Under this proposed paragraph, State law would be required to include only those work search activities that allow individuals to meet the requirement by completing specified work search activities that are specific, identifiable and reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment. States must provide for certain activities, including employer contacts, as well as registration and ongoing contact with placement agencies or unions for the purposes of seeking employment. States would retain discretion to define additional qualifying work search activities consistent with § 604.6.
The Department is proposing the work search activity provisions in paragraph (e) to reflect modern job search behavior, which generally comprises many types of activities, not only employer contacts, and to provide room for such activities to evolve over time. The Department considers these types of activities, when specific, identifiable, and reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment, to be legitimate work search activities.
The Department intends for this provision to provide States with flexibility to tailor work search requirements to local labor market conditions, individual populations, and administrative capacity, while ensuring that individuals are able to understand and comply with the requirement. The Department further intends to reduce procedural denials that may occur when work search requirements are vague, inconsistently applied, or difficult for individuals to understand.
The Department expects that an individual may perform multiple activities of the same type in a given week. Some examples of how this requirement might be applied include:
An individual makes five discrete employer contacts for the purpose of seeking work in a given week; or
An individual does two job interviews, attends a job fair, takes a professional assessment, and submits an employment application in a given week.
Paragraph (e)(1)
As proposed, paragraph (e)(1) would provide that State law must not limit qualifying work search activities solely to employer contacts. The Department recognizes that modern work search behavior includes a broader range of activities as described in subsequent paragraphs.
Paragraph (e)(2)
Paragraph (e)(2) is a proposed list of work search activities that States would be required to recognize as work search activities in State law for purposes of the work search requirement set out in paragraph (b): employer contacts (as defined in § 604.2) for the purpose of seeking employment, specifically including employment application submissions, job interviews, and skill, aptitude, or competency assessments with a specific employer; registration and ongoing contact with placement agencies for the purpose of seeking employment; and contact with the individual's union for a job referral. The Department has determined that these work search activities are integral to the reemployment process and thus individuals should always be given credit toward the work search requirement for completing them in a given week.
Employer contacts are an important and effective component of active work search and are reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment. The Department believes requiring States to recognize employer contacts as qualifying work search activities would promote more rapid reemployment and ensure that direct employer engagement remains a core component of the work search requirement.
The Department's intent in requiring that skill, aptitude, or competency assessments with a specific employer be recognized as qualifying work search activities in State law is that such activities are important evaluation tools used to assess individuals for employment. Skills assessments measure an individual's technical or functional ability to perform tasks related to a specific job. Aptitude assessments are intended to measure an individual's potential to succeed in a given job. Competency assessments are intended to evaluate an individual's skills and knowledge, generally, for a particular role within an organization. The Department proposes to include registration and ongoing contact with placement agencies because such contacts are important routes to obtaining employment. Much like contacting an individual employer for work, contacting a placement agency is a useful way to obtain a job.
Additionally, contact with the individual's union for a job referral would be a qualifying work search activity for the purpose of the work search requirement in paragraph (b). Contact with a union would be recognized in State law as a qualifying work search activity regardless of whether the union offers a hiring hall. Therefore, the Department proposes that a union member contacting their union for a job referral must also be considered a valid work search activity.
The Department recognizes that for an individual who is a member of a union that prohibits members from taking non-union work, accepting non-union work
(
printed page 72479)
may result in the individual violating the terms of their union membership agreement. Under such circumstances, an individual who otherwise does not meet the requirement in accordance with paragraph (g)(2) may meet the minimum work search requirement by making contact with their union for job referrals and completing any other work search activities described in paragraph (e)(2), such as skill and competency assessments, as well as work search activities that may be recognized by the State consistent with paragraph (e)(3), such as training, that do not require contacting non-union employers for the purpose of obtaining work.
The Department is considering including a requirement that at least one of the individual's work search activities each week be an activity from the list in paragraph (e)(2) and welcomes comment on this approach.
Paragraph (e)(3)
The Department strongly encourages States to allow a wide variety of work search activities to satisfy the work search requirement. Paragraph (e)(3) proposes a non-exhaustive list of additional activities that States may include as qualifying work search activities. These include:
Attending job fairs or hiring events (proposed paragraph (e)(3)(i));
Utilizing career center or employment services (proposed paragraph (e)(3)(ii));
Attending workshops, training, or skill-building educational events (proposed paragraph (e)(3)(iii));
Taking professional assessments or certification examinations (proposed paragraph (e)(3)(iv)); and
Other activities reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment, as determined by the State (proposed paragraph (e)(3)(v)).
All of these activities may be considered to be reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment. An individual taking a professional assessment may more easily obtain employment in a specific industry and the assessment may contain aspects of skill, aptitude, or competency assessments. The Department believes professional assessments and certifications are valuable work search activities and can lead an individual to reemployment. However, because professional assessments and certificate exams can vary widely from industry to industry and State to State, the Department does not propose to make these activities mandatory for inclusion in State law. This optional category is distinct from the skill, aptitude, or competency assessments related to employment that States must recognize under proposed paragraph (e)(2)(i)(C).
The Department proposes including the illustrative list in paragraph (e)(3) to preserve State flexibility to account for differences in labor markets, industries, geography, and administrative systems. This approach allows States to define additional qualifying activities as appropriate and also provides room for such activities to evolve over time, based on economic conditions within the State, changes in technology, or other factors that would require the State to add or delete acceptable work search activities.
The Department recognizes that there may be other government programs that involve work search requirements. For example, the Department notes that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services issued an interim final rule on June 3, 2026, regarding the requirement for certain Medicaid applicants and beneficiaries to demonstrate community engagement through specific qualifying activities as a condition of their Medicaid eligibility (
91 FR 33348
). Accordingly, the Department encourages States to work with their State Medicaid agency to align, to the extent appropriate, their work search requirements so that the work search activities that individuals applying for UC may complete align with the mandatory community engagement activities required by their State Medicaid agency.
H. Paragraph 604.6(f) Points-Based System
The Department included proposed regulatory text under paragraph (f) to solicit comments on a proposed points-based system. The Department is considering whether such a system aligns with the goals of this proposed rule and, if included in the final rule, how it might be implemented. Paragraph (f) would permit a State to adopt a points-based system as a method for satisfying the weekly work search requirement proposed in paragraph (b). Proposed paragraph (f) offers States flexibility to establish a points-based system to accomplish the requirement in proposed paragraph (c). Under a points-based system, qualifying work search activities would be assigned point values, as determined by the State, and an individual would satisfy the weekly work search requirement when the total point value of completed and reported activities equals or exceeds the minimum threshold of five points established by this paragraph. Nothing would preclude an individual from completing five one-point work search activities in a claimed week—the adoption of a points-based system simply encourages an individual to do certain activities over others by providing those activities a greater weight in completing the work search requirement.
The option for States to adopt a points-based system is intended to provide a tool for prioritizing activities that connect individuals to sectors and localities with greater job openings—the specific application of which can change over time. A carefully developed points-based system may act as an incentive for individuals to engage in activities that are more likely to result in rapid reemployment, especially employment in occupations that are experiencing worker shortages. It also may incentivize individuals to broaden their work search to geographical areas that may have more or better reemployment opportunities and mitigate work search difficulties when work where the individual resides may be limited.
The Department intends this provision to preserve flexibility for States while ensuring that any points-based system remains substantially equivalent to the minimum weekly work search requirement established in paragraph (c).
Paragraph (f)(1)
Paragraph (f)(1) would establish the minimum requirements for a State points-based system. Under this proposed paragraph:
Qualifying work search activities would be assigned point values by the State (proposed paragraph (f)(1)(i)) and must be consistent with the qualifying work search activities described in paragraph (e);
The weekly work search requirement would be satisfied only when the total number of points assigned to qualifying work search activities an individual has completed for the benefit week claimed equals at least five points (proposed paragraph (f)(1)(ii)); and
Each work search activity is assigned a value of one, two, or three points (proposed paragraph (f)(1)(iii)).
The Department believes these minimum requirements for a State points-based system are necessary to ensure consistency, transparency, and equivalency across States. Establishing a points-based system provides States flexibility in structuring and incentivizing work search activities while maintaining a consistent baseline nationwide.
The limitation that each work search activity must be assigned a value of one,
(
printed page 72480)
two, or three points is intended to establish guardrails that prevent States from assigning disproportionately high or low values to individual activities in ways that could undermine the consistency or integrity of the work search requirement.
The Department believes a one-to-three-point range appropriately balances flexibility and consistency by allowing States to differentiate among activities based on their relative value while ensuring that no single activity alone satisfies the weekly requirement.
Paragraph (f)(2)
Paragraph (f)(2) would provide that, when assigning more than one point to a qualifying work search activity, States must determine that the activity either:
Connects individuals to specific industries and geographic locations that need workers; or
Has strong evidence for directly leading to reemployment.
These mandatory criteria ensure that activities receiving more than one point meaningfully promote reemployment and reflect current labor market needs. For instance, the State may incentivize job search activities in growth sectors with more plentiful employment options by assigning additional points to such activities. This approach encourages individuals to broaden their search and focus job search efforts on occupations where their skills are most needed.
The Department is particularly interested in comments from States, industry leaders, and other relevant stakeholders on the points-based system option proposed in paragraph (f). The Department recognizes that some States currently include flexibility in how they implement their work search requirement (
i.e.,
requiring a different number of work search activities based upon geographic factors such as whether the individual claiming UC is in an urban or rural area). The Department welcomes comments on the factors that should be used to allow greater weighting of activities.
The Department is considering the points-based approach as a potential flexibility for States and welcomes comments about additional considerations for ensuring that such a points-based system does not circumvent the underlying intent of the proposed rule (
i.e.,
a permanent workaround to avoid requiring five work search activities in any given week) and whether such a system should be included in the final rule.
I. Paragraph 604.6(g) Equivalent Labor Force Attachment
Paragraph (g) proposes to establish circumstances under which an individual may be considered to have an equivalent attachment to the labor force and therefore is deemed by the State to have satisfied the State's minimum work search requirement for a week.
The Department recognizes that certain individuals remain sufficiently attached to the labor force through participation in approved programs or because of specific employment-related circumstances such that requiring completion of the minimum weekly work search requirement may be unnecessary or duplicative. The Department also recognizes that there may be extenuating circumstances that would prevent an individual from conducting the required minimum weekly work search activities while the individual should otherwise be eligible for UC. This paragraph is intended to preserve consistency with other Federal UC requirements and maintain existing State practices where they align with the goal of this proposed rule in facilitating reemployment. The Department also seeks comments on other circumstances that are not represented in the draft text but might be in place under current State law and align with the goals of this proposed regulation.
Paragraph (g)(1)
Paragraph (g)(1) identifies circumstances in which an individual would be deemed to have met the minimum number of work search activities required under paragraph (c). The following equivalent labor force attachment circumstances would meet the minimum work search requirement under proposed paragraph (c) when the individual is:
Enrolled in, and making satisfactory progress in, State-approved training under
26 U.S.C. 3304(a)(8)
(proposed paragraph (g)(1)(i));
Participating in the Self-Employment Assistance (SEA) program under
26 U.S.C. 3306(t)
(proposed paragraph (g)(1)(ii));
Participating in the Short-Time Compensation (STC) (also known as “Workshare” or “Shared Work”) program under
26 U.S.C. 3306(v)
by being available for their workweek (proposed paragraph (g)(1)(iii)); or
Participating in a Registered Apprenticeship program (proposed paragraph (g)(1)(iv)).

]
The circumstances referenced in proposed paragraphs (g)(1)(i) through (iii) are determined by other provisions of Federal law that provide that the individual cannot be denied for failure to complete work search when they are participating in State-approved training or the SEA program or when they are deemed to have met the minimum work search requirement by being available for their workweek under the STC program.
The Department further proposes that individuals participating in a Registered Apprenticeship program, under
29 U.S.C. 50
, also be deemed to have satisfied the minimum work search requirement. Individuals engaged in a Registered Apprenticeship program are engaged in activities specifically designed to prepare them for employment in a particular field. These programs combine on-the-job learning with related instruction, equipping participants with new skills that will lead to employment in occupations offering higher wages.
Additionally, at the conclusion of the Registered Apprenticeship program, individuals may be hired by the company where they completed their apprenticeship. An individual earning wages during the Registered Apprenticeship program must, in accordance with State law, report such wages, which could impact the amount of UC available in the week. Separate from this monetary impact, requiring apprentices to seek additional work while participating in the program would interfere with the intended purpose and goals of the Registered Apprenticeship program and with the workforce attachment the program fosters. The reasoning for this exception aligns with similar provisions for individuals enrolled in State-approved training programs.
Paragraph (g)(2)
Paragraph (g)(2) identifies a specific category of individuals who would be deemed to have met the minimum work search requirement under paragraph (c). This provision would apply when an individual is a member in good standing with their union, that union utilizes a hiring hall for job referrals, and the individual follows the requirements of their union regarding contact with the union's hiring hall, provided the individual must contact their hiring hall at least once a week. The Department recognizes that for an individual who is
(
printed page 72481)
a member of a union that utilizes a hiring hall for job referrals, looking for work outside of the hiring hall may result in the individual violating the terms of their union membership agreement.
For individuals who otherwise contact their union for work but do not meet the parameters described in paragraph (g)(2), such contact would qualify as an acceptable work search activity under paragraph (e)(2), though it would only be sufficient for satisfying one of the minimum five activities in any given week.
Paragraph (g)(3)
The Department proposes in paragraph (g)(3) to specify limited circumstances in which a State may deem an individual to have met the weekly work search requirement because the individual either maintains clear attachment to the labor force or faces specific conditions that make conducting work search activities unreasonable or impractical. By outlining these circumstances directly in the regulation, the Department aims to ensure national consistency, provide clarity for States administering UC programs, and appropriately recognize situations in which individuals should be deemed to have satisfied the weekly work search requirement for the applicable week.
Paragraph (g)(3) would permit a State to deem an individual to have met the work search requirement for a week if one of these limited circumstances applies.
The individual has a definite return-to-work date with their separating employer within 8 weeks of the separation date (proposed paragraph (g)(3)(i)).
If an individual is on a short-term layoff with a definite return-to-work date from their separating employer, requiring that individual to nonetheless conduct a work search may harm the employer by risking the loss of a skilled member of their workforce if the individual receives and accepts a different offer of employment. This may result in the individual being required to accept a less desirable job or risk being found ineligible to receive UC.
The individual is a Federal employee, is unemployed due to a lapse in Federal appropriations, and is expected to return to work when the lapse ends (proposed paragraph (g)(3)(ii)).
A similar argument for short-term layoffs applies to Federal employees who are unemployed due to a lapse in appropriations. In this situation, the employee does not have a definite return-to-work date—pending congressional action—but is still considered job-attached and is expected to be recalled to work after the lapse in appropriations ends.
The individual files an initial claim less than 72 hours prior to the end of the week (proposed paragraph (g)(3)(iii)) and therefore has insufficient time to both receive notification of the work search requirement and conduct the associated activities before filing their first continued claim certification.
Generally, an individual may file an initial claim at any point during a week. If there is insufficient time for the State to advise the individual of the work search requirement and for the individual to complete the work search activities for the week claimed, it creates an unreasonable burden for the individual. For example, if the individual files their initial claim with less than three full days remaining in the benefit week, it may not be reasonable to expect the individual to complete the minimum work search activities before the end of the week. Likewise, if the State backdates the individual's initial claim, the individual may be precluded from meeting the State's minimum work search requirement for that week.
The individual is serving on jury duty (proposed paragraph (g)(3)(iv)), and the individual's jury duty service precludes the individual from completing the minimum number of work search activities.
The Department recognizes that under section 202(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of EUCA, individuals who are lawfully issued summons to appear for jury duty may be exempted from seeking work if State law provides this exception under the Federal-State UC program. Therefore, a State may deem an individual to have met the State's minimum work search requirement for a claimed week, if the individual's jury duty service precludes the individual from meeting the minimum number of work search activities under proposed paragraph (c). For example, if the individual is only called for one day of jury duty, the jury duty might not preclude them from completing the minimum number of work search activities. States must determine if the jury duty service precluded the individual from completing the minimum number of work search activities. The individual must continue to meet all other eligibility requirements for the week, including being able to work and available for work under State law.
The individual is hospitalized for treatment of an emergency or life-threatening condition (proposed paragraph (g)(3)(v)), and the hospitalization precludes the individual from completing the minimum number of work search activities.
Similarly, the Department recognizes that under section 202(a)(3)(A)(ii)(II) of EUCA, individuals who are hospitalized for treatment of an emergency or life-threatening condition may be excepted from work search if the Federal-State UC program provides for an exception. This rule would implement this exception where the hospitalization precludes the individual from completing the minimum number of required work search activities under proposed paragraph (c) for a claimed week. In these circumstances, the minimum work search requirement may only be deemed to have been met if the State determines the hospitalization precludes them from meeting the requirement. For example, if the individual is hospitalized for one day and then is discharged and was fully able to look for work either before or after the hospitalization, the hospitalization might not preclude them from meeting the minimum number of work search activities and thus the individual would need to meet the work search requirement in paragraph (c). The individual must continue to meet all other eligibility requirements for the week, including being able to work and available for work under State law.
These proposed provisions are intended to provide employers, individuals, and States some flexibility while preserving the overall integrity of the weekly work search requirement. Individuals who are determined to meet one of the circumstances in paragraph (g)(3) must continue to meet other applicable State and Federal eligibility requirements to receive UC for a claimed week. The Department welcomes public comment on these and other possible circumstances from stakeholders.
Paragraph (g)(4)(i)
This proposed provision would allow States the flexibility to deem individuals to have met the work search requirement in this section for a claimed week when there is a federally declared major disaster as defined under the Stafford Act,
42 U.S.C. 5122(2)
. This provision is only applicable where States have laws that allow them to modify an individual's work search requirements during major disasters. This provision is meant to grant States the flexibility to make modifications to work search requirements based on the circumstances surrounding disasters. The Department understands that during disasters work search activities may be difficult or impossible for
(
printed page 72482)
individuals to complete and that businesses in affected areas may be temporarily closed or unable to accept new employment applications or new hires. Further, resources that individuals could use to complete work search activities, such as training providers, placement agencies, and workforce development organizations, may be impacted as well.
Paragraph (g)(4)(ii)
This proposed provision would cap the amount of time that paragraph (g)(4)(i) may apply. The proposed rule would cap the period during which individuals may suspend their work search to no more than 26 weeks following the week in which the disaster period commences to align the regulation with existing Disaster Unemployment Assistance program requirements and practices. The Department intentionally uses the term “incident period” in the proposed regulatory text because that term is defined in the Federal Emergency Management Agency's regulations at
44 CFR 206.32(f)
. The Department intends this term to have the meaning assigned to it in
44 CFR 206.32(f)
because federally declared disasters involve both the State and several Federal agencies. The Department proposes this duration limitation to provide individuals affected by federally declared major disasters with appropriate flexibilities while balancing the goal of the work search requirement, which is to require active labor market participation for individuals seeking benefits.
Paragraph (g)(5)
The purpose of requiring an active search for work is to facilitate reemployment. Proposed paragraph (g)(5) recognizes that an individual who has accepted a bona fide offer of employment with a definite start date in the near future is demonstrating that purpose. Once an individual has accepted such an offer, requiring that individual to continue searching for other work during the short period before the new job begins may be unnecessary and create avoidable complications. For example, if the individual receives and is required to accept another offer or lose UC eligibility, that may result in the individual being forced to accept a less desirable job with lower wages and forces the employer offering the position to search for other candidates. Furthermore, if the individual receives and refuses an additional offer of employment, the State may need to adjudicate whether the refusal affects eligibility, despite the fact that the individual has already secured employment.
The proposed provision is limited and would apply on a week-by-week basis. A State may deem an individual to have met the minimum work search requirement under paragraph (c) for a claimed week only if the individual has accepted a bona fide offer of employment and the start date of such employment is within 4 weeks of the week being claimed. For any claimed week that falls outside of that 4-week period, the individual would be required to continue to satisfy the applicable minimum work search requirement under paragraph (c). When the conditions of paragraph (g)(5) are met for a claimed week, the State may deem the individual to have met the minimum work search requirement for the entire week. The State need not impose a separate, partial-week work search requirement under this paragraph.
For those weeks before the individual qualifies under paragraph (g)(5), the individual must satisfy the work search requirement through any qualifying work search activities permitted by the State under paragraph (e). The Department is setting a timeframe because an extended period during which an individual is not seeking work is inconsistent with the principles of the Federal work search requirement. This provision is intended to provide employers, individuals, and States a limited level of flexibility while preserving the overall integrity of the weekly work search requirement.
J. Paragraph 604.6(h) Notification Requirements
Proposed paragraphs (a) and (b) would establish that a State may not pay UC for a week claimed unless the individual satisfies the applicable work search requirement under § 604.6 or has an equivalent labor force attachment as provided in State law, consistent with paragraph (g). Proposed paragraph (h) sets out the proposed requirement that States notify individuals of the work search requirement at certain points during the continued claim certification process.
Paragraph (h)(1)
Paragraph (h)(1) would require States to provide clear notice to individuals regarding the pertinent aspects of the work search requirement for their continued eligibility for UC. Clear communication about work search requirements is essential to ensuring compliance, reducing inadvertent eligibility violations, and supporting program integrity.
Under section 303(a)(1) of the SSA, a State's UC law must provide for methods of administration that are reasonably calculated to ensure full payment of UC when due. The Department has determined that section 303(a)(1) of the SSA requires that individuals claiming UC are able to obtain, complete, and submit information related to their initial and continued claims, appeals, reemployment services, and any other available program functions or services. All individuals must have the opportunity to be informed of and take appropriate action(s) to apply for UC, maintain their entitlement to UC, and access services without undue burdens or barriers.
Appendix A to 20 CFR part 602 (Standard for Claim Determination—Separation Information) requires State laws to include provisions that will ensure that “[i]ndividuals who may be entitled to [UC] are furnished such information as will reasonably afford them an opportunity to know, establish, and protect their rights under the [UC] law of such State.” The Department is proposing to add this work search notification provision to the existing notifications the State sends individuals as part of the requirement that States provide individuals with sufficient information “to know, establish, and protect their rights” to UC. The goal of this provision is to support individual reemployment, program integrity, transparency, and accountability.
Under this proposed paragraph, States would be required to provide enough information to individuals to ensure they are aware of the work search requirements that apply to the individual's claim. Such notice would be required to be provided in writing at the time the initial claim is filed and at any time during the benefit year that such requirements applicable to the individual substantially change.
The Department recognizes that many States already provide benefit rights and responsibilities information to individuals through handbooks, online portals, continued claim certification systems, and other communications. This provision is intended to ensure that work search requirements are clearly and consistently communicated through existing channels or other communication methods reasonably calculated to ensure awareness.
At a minimum, the notice provided under this paragraph (h) would be required to include the following information:
The acceptable types of work search activities (proposed paragraph (h)(1)(i));
(
printed page 72483)
That a minimum of five qualifying work search activities are required during each week of unemployment for which UC is claimed (proposed paragraph (h)(1)(ii));
If the State has adopted a points-based system under paragraph (f), an explanation of that system in plain language (proposed paragraph (h)(1)(iii));
That the individual must report work search activities each time the individual files a continued claim certification and be prepared to provide additional documentation of their work search activities upon request (proposed paragraph (h)(1)(iv)); and
That UC will not be paid for any week if the individual does not complete and report the required work search activities or demonstrate an equivalent labor force attachment under paragraph (g) (proposed paragraph (h)(1)(v)).
Paragraph (h)(2)
Paragraph (h)(2) would require the State to notify individuals: (1) when the State determines that the circumstances under paragraph (g) apply (
i.e.,
the individual meets an equivalent labor force attachment provision); and (2) when the individual's circumstances have substantially changed and different work search requirements now apply. This individualized notification requirement would only be applicable when the State has enough information to determine that paragraph (g) applies to an individual. As such, the Department expects States would put in place methods of obtaining enough information from individuals to ascertain whether proposed paragraph (g) applies to the individuals.
The Department proposes this provision to ensure that States make individuals aware of their situation-specific requirements so that they may provide the information necessary for the State to accurately apply paragraph (g), to ensure that individuals understand what is required of them, and to ensure that individuals are notified when their work search requirements change.
The Department believes this provision would improve the individuals' understanding of the State's work search requirements and reduce procedural denials caused when individuals fail to complete the required work search activities or fail to keep a record of their weekly work search activities.
K. Paragraph 604.6(i) Prohibition on Formal and Informal Warnings
Some States have used formal or informal warnings in lieu of holding an individual accountable for weeks in which the individual failed to actively seek work, with States oftentimes advising the Department that this rationale is based on the premise that the individual was not properly aware of the work search requirement. Paragraph (i) would state that individuals who do not complete the minimum number of required work search activities are ineligible for UC for that week. Under this proposed paragraph, States may not issue formal or informal warnings in lieu of determining ineligibility when an individual fails to complete and report the minimum required work search activities or does not meet the requirements in paragraph (g).
The Department proposes this paragraph to codify its longstanding legal interpretation that the SSA does not permit States to give individuals claiming UC a warning—whether formal or informal—when they fail to meet the statutory requirement to actively seek work for a claimed week. Section 303(a)(12) of the SSA provides that State law must require an individual to actively seek work as a condition of eligibility for each week claimed.
The Department is aware that some States have historically issued warnings to individuals upon identifying a potential work search eligibility issue. A State law or policy that permits such warnings, whether formal or informal, would be inconsistent with this proposed regulation and would, under this paragraph, be out of conformity with the SSA and the Federal Unemployment Tax Act. These laws and policies would need to be changed to conform with this proposed regulation. When a State determines that an individual did not complete and report the required work search activities and did not qualify under paragraph (g) for a claimed week, the State would be required to find the individual ineligible for that week and establish an overpayment when appropriate.
Recognizing the policy rationale often cited by States to the Department that individuals are not aware of the work search requirement, the proposed rule seeks to mitigate such occurrences by facilitating regular reporting of work search activities before UC is paid. Additionally, the Department is proposing that States may include certain circumstances under paragraph (g) allowing for equivalent labor force attachment such as when an individual files their initial claim less than 72 hours prior to the benefit week ending date. The proposed rule also requires that the State provide notification to individuals when the expectation for their work search activity changes, as described in paragraph (h).
L. Section 604.7 Conformity and Substantial Compliance
The Department is proposing to redesignate § 604.6 to § 604.7. The Department is proposing to place the work search requirement in § 604.6 because it would be in addition to the requirements in § 604.4 (Application—ability to work) and § 604.5 (Application—availability for work). The Department is not proposing any change to this section; it is simply proposing to redesignate it.

1. Need for Regulation
Federal law requires individuals receiving UC to be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work as a condition of eligibility.
42 U.S.C. 503(a)(12)
. States have developed differing standards to enforce this requirement that speak to both the number and type of required activities, frequency and methods of reporting them. States range from simply requiring an affirmative statement of conducting work search activities to requiring only one work search activity; as well as requiring upwards of five activities in any given week. States also vary in what they consider to be a qualifying activity. These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear. Additionally, variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules.
Given these challenges, this proposed rule would establish a national minimum weekly work search standard that provides a clear and consistent expectation for individuals to be “actively seeking work” across the Federal—State UC program. The proposed approach supports meaningful engagement with the labor market and reflects modern job search practices, which can involve multi-day or clustered activities such as interviews, job fairs, or assessments. By requiring individuals to complete at least five weekly work search activities—with limited and specified exceptions—and to report such activities prior to issuing payment, the proposed rule would improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment. The proposed rule also supports an assurance that individuals are informed of the requirements and have access to a broader set of qualifying activities.
2. Subject-by-Subject Analysis
In this section, the Department describes all anticipated costs, transfers, and benefits of the proposed rule, including both quantified and unquantified impacts. The proposed rule would directly regulate States by requiring them to revise their UC work search requirements as a condition of conformity with Federal UC law, and the Department expects every State operating UC programs to implement the required changes. Accordingly, this analysis treats resulting downstream effects on individuals claiming UC, State UC agencies, employers, and other affected parties as impacts of the proposed rule. Each impact is described, and quantifiable impacts are estimated while nonquantifiable impacts are discussed qualitatively.
Unemployed individuals eligible for UC in their State face the same choices under this proposed rule as they currently do, though some parameters would change. Such individuals select among: performing more extensive work search and reporting activities (with the associated opportunity cost of time and effort) to be eligible for UC; not engaging in work search and reporting activities and being found ineligible for UC; or foregoing filing for UC and accepting the best immediately available job.

The quantified costs include costs to State UC agencies for familiarizing themselves with the regulatory change. The nonquantifiable costs include the cost to individuals for complying with the proposed rule; cost to job support structures and organizations; costs for revising State UC law and the associated implementation activities; increased administrative activities for some States; and costs for State IT system changes and annual maintenance.

b. Nonquantifiable Costs
In this section, the Department describes various nonquantifiable costs of the proposed rule, including cost to individuals for complying with the proposed rule; cost to job support structures and organizations; costs for revising State UC law and the associated implementation activities; increased administrative activities for some States; and costs for State IT system changes and annual maintenance.
1. Cost of Conducting Additional Work Search Activities
The proposed rule is expected to increase the amount of time that some individuals claiming UC spend on work search activities per benefit week claimed. The magnitude of the increase would depend on the work search requirements in place by the State in which an individual is filing and the types of activities individuals are completing already. Because of variation across States, the Department cannot directly observe the number of work search activities individuals claiming UC actually complete at baseline (current practice). While States set minimum work search requirements, States differ in how requirements are defined (for example, numeric thresholds versus qualitative standards), whether requirements vary by category of the individuals claiming UC (for example, those subject to union hiring hall provisions), and how activities are reported and tracked.
Moreover, actual search behavior may exceed the minimum required and may vary from week to week. When subject to a weekly minimum requirement, some individuals who would otherwise have concentrated more work search activities in one week and fewer in another may redistribute activities across weeks to satisfy the requirement each week. To the extent this occurs, the rule could affect the timing of some work search activities. However, the Department expects this effect to be limited because many application opportunities are time-sensitive, and individuals claiming UC generally have incentives to pursue suitable opportunities when they arise. Deferring such activities could result in lost job opportunities or delayed reemployment. For these reasons, creation of a national minimum weekly work search requirement may not result in a quantifiable increase in actual activities performed per individual. The Department also lacks data sufficient to quantify the extent of any shifting across weeks or any resulting effect on reemployment timing.
In general, the Department assumes that most individuals would experience an increase in the number of work search activities performed each week. Such activities take time, and there is an opportunity cost associated with that time. Opportunity cost refers to the value of the next best alternative use of a person's time. In this context, it represents the value of the time that individuals claiming UC would spend completing additional work search activities instead of using that time for other purposes. The Department is not able to estimate the net opportunity cost. A reliable estimate would require assumptions about baseline work search behavior, the number and type of additional activities performed, the time required for each activity, the value of individuals' time, and the extent to which additional work search activities accelerate reemployment. Because these factors are not directly observed and may vary substantially across individuals, States, and labor market conditions, the Department cannot quantify the net opportunity cost accurately. The Department is seeking public comments and input on ways to monetize the cost to the individual of conducting additional work search activities.
The Department developed an illustrative example based on an assumed average of 30 minutes per additional work search activity, reflecting variation in the time associated with different types of activities. Some work search activities like updating a resume may be completed quickly, while other activities like filling in an employment application or participating in an interview (including travel and preparation time) may take significantly longer.
For purposes of these illustrative estimates, the Department assumes approximately 100 million continued weeks claimed annually, based on 2025 continued weeks claimed data.
[

Because individuals may complete more work search activities than the minimum required by their State and data on the number of activities actually completed are not available, the Department uses State work search requirements as a proxy for baseline work search activity. The Department grouped States into five categories based on requirements of one to five work search activities per week. For States that require work search activities but do not specify a minimum number, the Department assigned a baseline of one activity per week. For States in which the requirement varies based on geography or other factors, the Department used the lower applicable number of activities. The Department allocates continued weeks claimed across the five scenarios based on baseline work search activity derived from State requirements and rounds the resulting estimates to the nearest million.
For this purpose, Exhibit 2 estimates the annual additional time spent on work search activities to be approximately 133.5 million hours.

2. Impacts on Existing Job Search Support Structures and Organizations
The proposed rule is expected to increase work search activities of individuals claiming UC, which in turn would affect organizations that provide reemployment assistance, job search support, career counseling, training, workshops, or job placement services to unemployed workers, including individuals claiming UC. Many such organizations focus primarily on helping individuals obtain employment rather than advising individuals on UC eligibility requirements, and so the primary impact of this proposed rule for job search support organizations would be the increase in work search activities causing increased service utilization. However, some organizations may also serve individuals claiming UC by providing support in navigating State requirements. These organizations may therefore need to review, revise, or supplement materials, workshop content, staff guidance, websites, referral resources, or other support materials to reflect the updated State laws that would result from the proposed rule.
There are distinct challenges in monetizing this impact because of the variability in organizations, support services offered by these organizations, and work search activities. The Department, therefore, does not quantify the impact on existing job search support structures and organization and is seeking public comments on this cost impact from stakeholders.
3. Revision of State UC Law and Associated Implementation Activities
The Department anticipates that the proposed rule would require all States to amend State law (inclusive of statutes, regulations, policies, or administrative procedures). According to unpublished internal data, as of January 1, 2025, a vast majority of States (85%) used some type of numerical work search standard, but those standards varied widely, ranging from one to five activities per week, hybrid formulations, urban-rural distinctions, and requirements tied to applications rather than activities. And as of January 1, 2025, nearly all States defined the work search requirement in statute, as opposed to only in regulation and/or UC agency policy or procedure. Following any rule changes, State UC agencies may need to undertake a range of implementation activities to administer the revised requirements. These activities could include updating forms, notices, handbooks, websites, FAQs, slide decks, call center scripts, and other guidance materials; revising internal procedures and staff instructions; and training personnel involved in individual assistance and eligibility adjudication. State UC agencies also may need to revise outreach and educational materials related to work search obligations and reporting requirements to help individuals understand and comply with the revised standards.
The scope, timing, and resource needs associated with this one-time cost are expected to vary across States depending on existing State law, administrative structure, communication systems, and the extent to which current policies already align with the proposed requirements. Because these implementation activities may occur through a variety of State legislative, regulatory, and administrative processes and may be conducted alongside broader system or policy updates, the Department does not quantify these costs.
4. Increased Administrative Activities for Some States
The Department expects increased administrative activities arising from States' implementation of the proposed rule applicable to individuals claiming UC, specifically with respect to assessing whether a circumstance described under paragraph (g) might apply to the individual, adjudicating eligibility when an individual fails to report work search activity (with a downstream potential of also impacting appeals workload), and monitoring reports of weekly work search activities to address anomalies or trends in the data that might be indicative of improper payments. The Department acknowledges that administrative activities also may increase under the proposed rule for States that are not currently requiring individuals to report work search activities as part of the continued claim certification before releasing payment or for States that are not currently using such information to combat improper payments. This impact is not readily quantifiable based on the information available to the Department.
5. State IT System Changes and Annual Maintenance
To implement the proposed rule, some State UC agencies may need to modify their IT systems to capture, store, and use additional data elements related to individuals' work search activities. This includes modifications to continued claim certification channels for individuals claiming UC (online portals, interactive voice
(
printed page 72487)
response systems, and paper workflows), as well as changes to back-end eligibility determination and case management systems that support data validation, adjudication, and audit functions. Depending on the State's current practices and the flexibility of its existing platform, these changes could include adding new data fields, updating user interfaces and scripts, adjusting data retention and retrieval processes, and enhancing reporting outputs used for program management and oversight. States that currently collect details only “upon request” or rely on manual processes likely would incur greater development and implementation effort than States that already collect structured work search activity information as part of the continued claim certification.
States making IT changes would also incur costs associated with testing, deployment, and change management. These activities may include quality assurance testing across multiple claim types (
e.g.,
intrastate, interstate, Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees, Unemployment Compensation for Ex-Servicemembers); regression testing to ensure timely payment and payment accuracy are not adversely affected; updates to interfaces with other State systems or vendor products; and training for staff who support individuals claiming UC and conduct eligibility reviews—both within the State UC agency and as part of its RESEA program.
In addition, States may face incremental storage needs and cybersecurity and privacy compliance activities (
e.g.,
updating access controls, audit logs, and security monitoring) commensurate with the sensitivity of individual data handled by UC systems. The magnitude and timing of these costs would vary substantially across States based on the age and architecture of their UC platforms (including whether the State operates a modernized integrated benefits system or a legacy mainframe), the degree of customization required, and whether changes can be incorporated into planned modernization releases.
Because of the complexity and diversity across State IT systems and lack of existing cost estimates for these modifications, this cost category is not quantified. The Department is seeking public comments about the approximate scale of these costs.
ii. Transfers
Transfer payments are monetary payments from one group to another that do not affect the total resources available to society (or, if they do affect total resources, the mechanism is incentives that would require more extensive inputs to analyze). Transfers are reported separately from benefits and costs. This proposed rule is expected to reduce UC outlays. Because decreased payments to individuals are offset by increases in State UC trust fund balances, these monetary changes are considered transfers. Due to data limitations, the Department is not able to develop a definitive estimate of the transfers that would be attributable to the proposed rule. Instead, the Department provides an illustrative range based on estimates from existing research. The Department invites public comments and data that could inform a more precise estimate of these transfers at the final rule stage.
Research consistently finds that UC recipients who are subject to work search requirements, or to more stringent requirements, return to work more quickly than similar unemployed individuals.

Evidence from State program evaluations shows that both work search requirements and reemployment services shorten the duration of insured unemployment spells by accelerating individuals' return to work. These interventions have proven cost effective due to their low administrative costs combined with measurable reductions in unemployment duration.
