Because shorter durations of insured unemployment generally result in lower UC payments, this research provides a basis for developing illustrative estimates of the transfers associated with the proposed rule.
For this purpose, the Department relies on estimates from Lachowska et al. (2016), who analyzed long-term outcomes from a randomized controlled trial of work search requirements for individuals claiming UC in Washington State over a 9-year follow-up period.
[
10
]
The study found that, relative to a no-work-test group, individuals subject to a standard work test received $429 less in UI benefits, while individuals subject to a modified work test received $484 less. Because the Washington Alternative Work Search (WAWS) experiment was conducted in 1986-1987, the Department converted these estimates to 2025 dollars using the consumer price index.
[
11
]
The resulting estimates are $1,216 and $1,372 per individual in 2025 dollars.
To provide illustrative estimates of the transfers associated with the proposed rule, the Department applied these estimates to the 5.3 million Regular UI beneficiaries in 2025,
[
12
]
resulting in an illustrative annual reduction in UC payments of $6.445 billion to $7.272 billion. This reduction in UC payments would represent a transfer: individuals who return to work sooner would receive less in UC benefits, resulting in a corresponding increase in State UC trust fund balances rather than a reduction in total resources available to society.
These illustrative estimates should be interpreted with caution. The WAWS experiment compared individuals subject to a work test with individuals assigned to an “honor system,” under which they were encouraged to search for work but were not required to report their search efforts. In contrast, individuals claiming UC are currently required to conduct at least one work search activity per week, and the proposed rule would increase the required number of work search activities rather than establish a minimum number of required work search activities where none previously existed. Therefore, it may not be reasonable to assume that increasing the number of required work search activities would produce the full reduction in UI benefits estimated by Lachowska et al. (2016). Accordingly, the estimates above are intended to illustrate the potential magnitude of transfers and should not be interpreted as estimates of the actual transfers that would result from the proposed rule.
iii. Benefits
In the following sections, the Department describes the expected benefits of the proposed rule, including both direct and indirect impacts on individuals claiming UC, State UC agencies, employers, and the broader economy. These benefits are primarily
(
printed page 72488)
driven by increased employment and faster reemployment resulting from enhanced work search activity, as well as improvements in program accountability, administrative consistency, and labor market functioning. All of these benefits are not readily monetized due to data limitations and uncertainty regarding behavioral responses. Consistent with OMB Circular A-4, the Department describes these benefits qualitatively where robust quantification or monetization is not feasible.
a. Benefits to Individuals From Increased Employment and Accelerated Reemployment
As discussed in section V.A.2.ii, the proposed rule is expected to increase employment and accelerate reemployment among individuals claiming UC by encouraging more consistent and structured work search activity. As evidenced in the Lachowska, Meral, and Woodbury (2016) study discussed earlier, additional work search requirements result in individuals finding and returning to work sooner.
[
13
]
By shortening the duration of unemployment spells, the rule may improve labor force attachment and lead to improved employment outcomes for affected individuals. Earlier reemployment may provide meaningful benefits to individuals claiming UC beyond the immediate resumption of earnings. Individuals who return to work sooner spend less time out of the labor force and begin receiving wages and any associated employment benefits earlier than they otherwise would. Reduced time out of work also may help individuals maintain a more continuous employment history, preserve workforce skills and professional connections, and accumulate additional experience that could contribute to future advancement opportunities and long-term earnings growth.
Research suggests that permanent job gains can generate broad benefits. Bartik (2015) notes that reducing involuntary unemployment can improve workers' health, well-being, and future earnings, and that job gains can generate broader economic effects through suppliers and retailers. Based on estimates of how permanent job gains affect unemployment and labor force participation, Bartik finds that such gains can generate additional value equivalent to approximately 10 to 25 percent of the earnings associated with jobs added in the manner examined in Bartik's study.
Earlier reemployment can generate direct benefits for employers as well, including filling vacancies faster, and reduced vacancy duration where increased job search activity expands the pool of available and engaged applicants. To the extent that employers can fill positions more quickly or identify better matched candidates, firms may experience modest productivity gains and reduced disruption associated with prolonged vacancies. The magnitude of these benefits would depend in part on labor market conditions. In tighter labor markets, or where employers would otherwise face difficulty filling positions, the benefits of faster reemployment and improved labor market matching may be more pronounced. In weaker labor markets or where vacancies are already filled quickly, the incremental employer-side benefits of the rule may be smaller.
While the literature generally finds that more intensive work search requirements increase reemployment and reduce unemployment duration, the available evidence is less conclusive regarding the quality of subsequent employment outcomes. To the extent that more intensive work search requirements accelerate reemployment, some individuals may accept employment sooner than they otherwise would have, which could affect subsequent wages, benefits, job match quality, or employment stability. In addition, Kuminoff et al. (2015) found that effects on household well-being vary with the duration of unemployment and do not have a simple fixed multiplier relationship with changes in earnings; rather, these effects depend on factors such as the desirability of available housing, commuting, and job options.
[
14
]
The Department lacks sufficient evidence to quantify these potential effects and therefore does not monetize them. Accordingly, the benefits discussed in this section should not be interpreted as capturing all potential dimensions of claimant economic security.
The proposed rule includes an allowance for certain qualifying work search activities beyond simply employer contacts, to include registration and ongoing contact with placement agencies or unions for the purposes of seeking reemployment. States may also designate additional activities as satisfying the requirement, such as “[a]ttending workshops, training, or skill-building educational events” (see proposed § 604.6(e)(3)(iii)). Workers engaged in skill development during periods of unemployment may enter the workforce with improved qualifications that better align with employers' needs. Improved alignment between worker skills and job requirements may contribute to improved hiring outcomes and reduced employee turnover. Lower turnover may reduce recruitment and training costs for employers and support greater workforce stability.
b. Improved Accountability
Clear work search requirements, including required reporting prior to release of payment, also enable States to monitor individual eligibility for UC and reduce improper payments. Failure to meet work search requirements is one of the leading causes of UC overpayments.
[
15
]
Work search errors often occur because individuals do not provide enough information about their work search efforts for past weeks as part of audits conducted by States to verify such activities. This issue underscores the need for reliable reporting systems. Strengthening work search requirements, including contemporaneous information submission, helps ensure that individuals claiming UC are actively seeking employment, thereby improving resource stewardship, reducing improper payments, and maintaining program integrity.
c. Benefits to Broader Economy From Increased Employment and Accelerated Reemployment
Securing employment sooner (or avoiding unemployment outcomes before they occur
[
16
]
) generates substantial social benefits that extend well beyond the direct earnings gained
(
printed page 72489)
by workers. When individuals find jobs more quickly, they may reduce their reliance on UC and public assistance programs, such as food assistance and housing subsidies, potentially lowering public expenditures. Earlier returns to work may also generate positive spillover effects for local economies as increased earnings support additional consumer spending and economic activity.
In addition to these broader benefits from accelerated reemployment, employed individuals contribute to tax revenues through income taxes, payroll taxes, and consumer spending that generates sales tax revenue. Together, these effects can produce positive feedback loops that extend beyond individual employment outcomes and contribute to broader economic activity. Accordingly, the Department considers below a potential effect of earlier reemployment: additional tax revenues associated with increased earnings.
The Department developed illustrative estimates of these potential tax revenue benefits using a rate of 17 percent of those earnings.
[
17
]
The Department applied this rate to the illustrative range of annual reductions in UC payments calculated in section V.A.2.ii ($6.445 billion to $7.272 billion), which the Department uses as a proxy for increased earnings, resulting in illustrative estimates of annual tax revenue benefits ranging from $1.096 billion to $1.236 billion. These figures are intended to illustrate the potential magnitude of the benefits rather than estimate the amount of additional tax revenue that would actually be realized.
d. Improved Clarity and Consistency
The proposed rule would establish a more consistent framework for work search requirements. Harmonizing these expectations would simplify understanding among individuals claiming UC, reduce confusion regarding allowable activities, and streamline administrative oversight and performance monitoring across State systems. Clearer definitions of qualifying activities would also support more uniform enforcement and reduce the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear. Additionally, adopting a standardized framework would facilitate better data collection and analysis, enabling State UC agencies, the Department, and other policymakers to identify trends and address systemic issues more effectively.
e. Health Benefits of Securing Employment Sooner
Upon receiving the financial benefits of working, individuals who return to work could experience positive health benefits. Employment is recognized as an important factor in individuals' long-term health and well-being. Existing research indicates obtaining and maintaining stable employment provides individuals with reliable income and financial stability, which in turn supports access to safe housing, nutritious food, and other resources.
[
18
,
19
]
A literature review conducted by Rueda et al. (2012) looked at 18 studies of working-aged adults who were returning to work after a period of unemployment. Overall, these studies found that returning to work had a positive effect on the workers' health and well-being. The literature review found beneficial effects of returning to work in a variety of populations, times, and settings.

3. Summary of the Analysis
i. Costs
The Department's monetized cost estimates include one-time rule familiarization costs for State UC agencies to review and understand the regulatory changes. The estimated cost to State UC agencies for time spent on rule familiarization is approximately $23,799 in labor costs, undiscounted. Annualized over 10 years, rule familiarization costs are estimated at $2,709 with 3-percent discounting and $3,167 with 7-percent discounting.
The Department also discusses additional cost categories that are not quantified (
e.g.,
cost to individuals for complying with the proposed rule; cost to job support structures and organizations; costs for revising State UC law and the associated implementation activities; increased administrative activities for some States; and costs for State IT system changes and annual maintenance) elsewhere in section V.A.2.i.b. For the cost to individuals, the Department provides illustrative estimates of the additional hours spent on work search activities.
ii. Transfers
The proposed rule is expected to result in unquantified transfer payments through reduced UC outlays, for which the Department provides illustrative estimates of potential magnitude. Strengthened work search requirements will shorten the duration of UC receipts through increased work search participation by UC recipients resulting in recipients returning to employment more quickly, or through UC recipients being found ineligible for receipt of benefits due to not completing the required number of work search activities in a week claimed. Payments to individuals claiming UC would decrease, with corresponding increases in State UC trust fund balances. Overall, the time-reallocation effects of this rule may reduce annual government deficits. Because these monetary changes represent a redistribution between affected individuals and State UC trust funds rather than a change in total societal resources, the Department treats them as transfers and is seeking public comment to support quantification at the final rule stage.
iii. Benefits
As discussed in section V.A.2.iii, the proposed rule is expected to generate several categories of nonquantified benefits primarily through increased employment and faster reemployment among individuals claiming UC. By encouraging more consistent and structured work search activity, the rule is anticipated to shorten the duration of unemployment spells, resulting in improved labor force attachment and enhanced employment outcomes. Earlier reemployment may produce broader economic benefits, including reduced reliance on public assistance programs, increased tax revenues, and positive spillover effects for local economies. The rule is also expected to improve program accountability and integrity by strengthening work search reporting and enabling State agencies to better monitor eligibility, thereby reducing improper payments. In addition, establishing a more consistent framework for work search requirements would improve clarity for individuals. Increased job search engagement and expanded recognition of skill-building activities may also improve the efficiency of labor market matching, benefiting both workers and employers.
(
printed page 72490)
Finally, earlier returns to work are associated with improved individual health and well-being, including positive mental health outcomes and increased financial stability.
4. Regulatory Alternatives
The Department considered three alternatives as part of determining whether to issue this NPRM. These alternatives included: (1) issuing additional subregulatory guidance to improve work search quality and providing suggested methods to reduce improper payments due to work search errors; (2) issuing regulations that mandate universal pre-payment verification of work search activities that would require individuals to report work search activities for each benefit week claimed, and also require the State to independently verify that each reported activity actually occurred before issuing payment for the week; and (3) maintaining the status quo.
Alternative One: Issuing Additional Subregulatory Guidance
Despite the issuance of guidance and model legislation, as explained in detail in Section III.B of this preamble, work search errors continue to be one of the primary drivers of improper payment rates across the UC system and the UC improper payment rate remains above the 10-percent performance target established by the Payment Integrity Information Act. Significant improvement was made in addressing work search errors in the year leading up to the March 2020 start of the pandemic. However, Congress enacted legislation to temporarily waive the work search requirement during the pandemic; once reinstated, work search errors again increased significantly.
Based on this evidence and the need to update the regulation setting forth an A&A requirement to reflect subsequent statutory changes that incorporate a work search requirement, the Department determined that voluntary guidance and technical assistance were insufficient to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level standards for individuals to actively seek work.
Therefore, the Department determined that it was necessary to promulgate a regulation that requires States to take specific actions to increase participation in the labor market by individuals collecting UC, including requiring States to include a broader array of acceptable work search activities in their laws and require the reporting of such activities prior to releasing payment. This regulatory approach is necessary to ensure greater consistency, accountability, and effectiveness in promoting rapid reemployment and maintaining UC program integrity.
Alternative Two: Issuing Regulations That Require Verification of Work Search Prior to Payment of UC
The Department considered an alternative approach that would have required States to verify all individual work search activities prior to the payment of UC. Under this alternative, States would have been required to collect, review, and validate documentation associated with each qualifying work search activity before issuing UC for the week claimed.
The Department recognizes that verification of work search activities is an important program integrity tool. However, the Department determined that a universal, pre-payment verification framework would be administratively difficult for many States and could compromise the statutory requirement in section 303(a)(1) of the SSA that UC be paid “when due.” States vary considerably in staffing levels, system modernization, governance structures, and adjudication capacity. Many State UC systems are not designed to validate documentation at scale or distinguish eligibility verification from quality-control sampling. Universal, pre-payment verification of work search would require significant IT reprogramming; substantially increase adjudication workloads and call-center inquiries; and heighten the risk of delayed UC payments. These issues raise compliance concerns under section 303(a)(1) of the SSA, which requires that States use methods of administration reasonably calculated to ensure the full payment of UC when due.
In evaluating this alternative, the Department also considered the operational experience of the BAM program. The existing BAM program requires detailed validation of work search activities through statistically valid sampling. These investigations often require States to perform exhaustive fact-finding, contact individuals and employers, review documents, and verify reemployment activity. BAM investigations can take several weeks to complete, depending on case complexity. BAM is intentionally designed as a post-payment quality-control function, not as an eligibility determination mechanism. Requiring a similar level of documentation and verification prior to each weekly payment would effectively duplicate and interfere with the BAM program's established role, undermine its audit integrity, and impose an additional administrative layer that States are not equipped to manage at scale.
The Department further analyzed the tradeoffs between accuracy and timeliness. Universal, pre-payment verification could increase accuracy marginally but would significantly impair timeliness. Individuals would face increased procedural hurdles, and States would experience higher rates of pending issues, greater numbers of nonmonetary determinations, increased appeals queues, and delays in benefit delivery. Delayed UC benefit payments frustrate the program's core statutory purpose of providing income support to individuals who are unemployed through no fault of their own. Additionally, employers are not mandated to keep proof of employment applications, resumes, or outreach from individuals seeking work with their company, and these verification attempts may not have the intended effect.
For these reasons, the Department determined that the second alternative would not provide net benefits. States are required to have a robust internal quality control program for assessing risk, evaluating outcomes, and adapting mitigation activities to improve improper payment risk management strategies—including work search verifications. Doing this for all work search activities across all weeks claimed would impose substantial administrative burdens on States and employers, undermine the timeliness of UC benefit payments, and create procedural obstacles that are not sufficiently justified by the integrity gains. Instead, the Department concluded that a weekly minimum work search requirement, paired with mandating that States require individuals to report their work search activities each week, best balances timeliness, integrity, and administrative feasibility.
Alternative Three: Maintaining the Status Quo
Under this no-action alternative, the Department would not issue the proposed rule, and existing State practices regarding work search requirements and qualifying activities would remain in place. This alternative would avoid any implementation or administrative costs associated with the proposed rule. However, it would also forgo the anticipated benefits of the proposed rule, including greater clarity for individuals claiming UC, more consistency across State systems, improved accountability, and expected
(
printed page 72491)
gains from facilitating reemployment. Because this alternative would not address the concerns identified in this proposed rule, the Department has decided against maintaining the status quo.
The Department invites comments on these or other possible alternatives with the goal of ensuring thorough consideration and discussion at the final rule stage.

E.O. 13132
aims to guarantee the division of governmental responsibilities between the Federal Government and the States and to further the policies of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA). Accordingly,
E.O. 13132
requires executive departments and agencies to ensure that the principles of federalism guide them in the formulation and implementation of policies. Further, agencies must adhere to constitutional principles, examine the constitutional and statutory authority supporting a regulation that would limit the policymaking discretion of the States, and assess the need for such a regulation. To the extent practicable, agencies must consult State and local officials before implementing any such regulation.
E.O. 13132
further provides that agencies must implement a regulation that limits the policymaking discretion of the States only where there is constitutional and statutory authority for the regulation and it addresses a problem of national significance. For a regulation administered by the States, the Federal Government must grant the States the maximum administrative discretion possible to avoid intrusive Federal oversight of State administration, and agencies must adhere to special requirements for a regulation that preempts State law.
E.O. 13132
also sets forth the procedures that agencies must follow for certain regulations with federalism implications, such as preparation of a summary impact statement.
The Department reviewed this proposed rule in accordance with
E.O. 13132
and determined that the rule may have federalism implications. However, the Department's unique relationship with the States requires regular consultation and collaboration with State partners, including on matters pertaining to the work search requirement in section 303(a)(12) of the SSA. Such engagement with State partners often relates to their conformity with the existing statute at
42 U.S.C. 503(a)(12)
and regulations at

UMRA (

, codified at

et seq.

Title II of UMRA directs agencies to prepare a written statement assessing the effects of a regulation that includes any Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in a year. A Federal mandate is any provision in a regulation that imposes an enforceable duty upon State, local, or tribal governments or upon the private sector, except as a condition of Federal assistance or a duty arising from participation in a voluntary Federal program.

§ 604.6
Work search requirement.
(a)
In general.
States must implement a work search requirement in accordance with this section, except where implementation would conflict with the work search requirements in part 615 of this chapter. States may not pay UC for a week during which the individual does not complete the work search requirement.
(b)
Work search requirement.
A State may not determine that an individual is eligible to receive UC for a claimed week unless the individual completes the required work search activities in accordance with this section or demonstrates an equivalent labor force attachment under paragraph (g) of this section for the week for which UC is claimed.
(c)
Minimum number of work search activities.
An individual meets the work search requirement and may receive UC for a claimed week, provided they are otherwise eligible for UC, only if, for the week in question:
(1) The individual completes a minimum of five qualifying work search activities;
(2) In States with a points-based system that meets the criteria in paragraph (f) of this section, the individual completes qualifying work search activities with a combined total point value that equals or exceeds five; or
(3) The individual meets the criteria in paragraph (g) of this section.
(d)
Work search activity reporting.
State law must require individuals to report the details of each work search activity, or the details of the individual's equivalent labor force attachment under paragraph (g) of this section, as part of the UC certification process prior to the payment of UC for the week claimed. States may obtain this information on a weekly or biweekly basis through their certification process.
(e)
Work search activity.
State law must include only those work search activities that are specific, identifiable, and reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment, and that are defined by the State consistent with this paragraph.
(1) State law must not limit what constitutes a qualifying work search activity to only employer contacts for the purpose of seeking employment.
(2) State law must include the following work search activities for the purposes of satisfying the work search requirement in paragraph (b) of this section:
(i) Employer contacts for the purpose of seeking employment, including:
(A) Employment application submission;
(B) Job interviews; and
(C) Skill, aptitude, or competency assessments related to employment with a specific employer, an American Job Center or One Stop;
(ii) Registration with placement agencies for the purpose of seeking employment;
(iii) Ongoing contact with placement agencies for the purpose of seeking employment; and
(iv) Contact with the individual's union for a job referral regardless of whether the individual satisfies the criteria in paragraph (g)(2) of this section.
(3) Additional work search activities that a State may designate as satisfying the work search requirement include:
(i) Attending job fairs or hiring events;
(ii) Utilizing career center or employment services;
(iii) Attending workshops, training, or skill-building educational events;
(iv) Taking professional assessments or certification exams; and
(v) Other activities that are reasonably calculated to lead to reemployment, as determined by the State.
(f)
Points-based system.
(1) A State may adopt a points-based system to implement the State's work search requirement provided by paragraph (b) of this section, under which:
(i) Qualifying work search activities, in accordance with paragraph (e) of this section, are assigned point values by the State;
(ii) The weekly work search requirement is satisfied when the total number of points assigned to the qualifying work search activities an individual has completed for the benefit week claimed equals or exceeds five points; and
(iii) Each work search activity is assigned a value of one, two, or three points.
(2) When providing that a work search activity will be assigned more than one point, States must determine that such work search activity either:
(i) Connects individuals to specific industries and locations that need workers; or
(ii) Has strong evidence for directly leading to reemployment.
(g)
Equivalent labor force attachment.
(1) An individual is deemed to have met the minimum number of work search activities as described in paragraph (c) of this section when one of the following circumstances applies:
(i) The individual is enrolled in and making satisfactory progress in State-approved training under
26 U.S.C. 3304(a)(8)
;
(ii) The individual is participating in the Self-Employment Assistance Program under
26 U.S.C. 3306(t)
;
(iii) The individual is participating in the Short-Time Compensation Program under
26 U.S.C. 3306(v)
by being available for their workweek; or
(iv) The individual is enrolled in a Registered Apprenticeship program under
29 U.S.C. 50
.
(2) An individual is deemed to have met the minimum number of work search activities as described in paragraph (c) of this section if they are a union member who satisfies the following conditions:
(i) The individual is a member in good standing of a union;
(ii) The union the individual is a member of utilizes a hiring hall for job referrals; and
(iii) The individual follows the requirements of their union regarding contact with the union's hiring hall, provided the individual contacts their hiring hall at least once a week.
(3) A State may deem an individual to have met the minimum number of work
(
printed page 72493)
search activities as described in paragraph (c) of this section for a benefit week if any of the following circumstances are met:
(i) The individual has a definite return-to-work date with their separating employer within 8 weeks of the separation date.
(ii) The individual is a Federal employee, is unemployed due to a lapse in Federal appropriations, and is expected to return to work when the lapse ends.
(iii) The individual files an initial claim for UC less than 72 hours prior to the benefit week ending date.
(iv) The individual is serving on jury duty, and the individual's jury duty service precludes the individual from completing the minimum number of work search activities.
(v) The individual is hospitalized for treatment of an emergency or life-threatening condition, and the hospitalization precludes the individual from completing the minimum number of work search activities.
(4)(i) A State may deem an individual to have met the minimum work search requirement in paragraph (c) of this section for a claimed week when the area in which the individual resides or is searching for work is covered by a federally declared major disaster as defined under
42 U.S.C. 5122(2)
and State law provides the authority to modify an individual's work search requirements during a federally declared major disaster.
(ii) An individual may only be deemed to have met the work search requirement under paragraph (g)(4)(i) of this section where the week is within 26 weeks of the commencement of the incident period.
(5)(i) A State may deem an individual to have met the minimum work search requirement in paragraph (c) of this section for a week if the individual accepted a bona fide offer of employment and the start date for the new employment is within 4 weeks of the week being claimed.
(ii) The individual must meet the work search requirement in paragraph (b) of this section for each week prior to satisfying the circumstance in paragraph (g)(5)(i) of this section.
(h)
Notification requirements.
(1) At the time the initial claim is filed, and at any other time during the benefit year if the State's work search requirements substantially change for an individual, States must provide written notice in a manner reasonably calculated to ensure awareness of the following:
(i) The acceptable types of work search activities;
(ii) That the individual must complete a minimum of five work search activities, in accordance with State law, for each claimed week of UC;
(iii) If the State has a points-based system in place, an explanation of the system in plain language;
(iv) That the individual must report work search activities each time they file a continued claim and be prepared to provide documentation of their work search activities upon request; and
(v) That payment of UC will not be made if the individual does not complete the work search requirements for the week claimed.
(2) When the State determines that paragraph (g) of this section applies to an individual or that an individual's circumstances with respect to paragraph (g) of this section have substantially changed, the State must notify the individual in writing of the following:
(i) The specific work search requirements that apply to the individual if paragraph (g) of this section applies; and
(ii) The duration of the applicable circumstance in paragraph (g) of this section.
(i)
Prohibition on formal and informal warnings.
Individuals who do not complete the work search requirement under this section in a claimed week are ineligible for UC for that week. States may not give formal or informal warnings to individuals in lieu of determining that the individual is ineligible for UC for a week for which the individual has not met the requirements of this section.

A. Overview of Information Collection
Title of Information Collection:
Section 202 Supportive Housing for the Elderly Application Submission Requirements.
OMB Approval Number:
2502-0267.

Extension of currently approved collection.
Form Number:
HUD-92041, HUD-92042, HUD-92015-CA, HUD-2530, HUD-2880, HUD-2993, SF-424, SF-LLL.
Description of the need for the information and proposed use:
HUD collects this information to review applications for Section 202 Capital Advance and PRAC funding under Section 202 of the Housing Act of 1959, as amended (
12 U.S.C. 1701q
). Applicants submit Form HUD-92015-CA, narrative exhibits, and required standard and HUD forms and certifications. HUD uses the submission to determine whether the applicant and the proposed project are eligible, and to rate and score each application. This
(
printed page 72556)
covers whether the project meets the need for supportive housing for very-low-income elderly households, whether the development plan, budget, and operating pro forma are feasible, and whether the project satisfies site control, environmental, site and neighborhood, and relocation requirements. It also covers whether the supportive services planned for residents are adequate.
Without this information, HUD could not judge the merit of the applications, confirm that projects and services meet statutory and regulatory requirements, or assess the risk to the Government. The collection helps protect federal funds against fraud, waste, and mismanagement.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
(
printed page 72468)
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Bombardier, Inc., Model CL-600-2B16 (604 Variants) airplanes. This proposed AD was prompted by reports of cracks being found on the lower wing plank at the rear spar wing station (WS) 59 to WS 65 web and/or flange. This proposed AD would require inspecting the lower wing plank rear spar web and lower flange, the forward surface of the pressure bulkhead frame under the stiffeners, and the vertical stabilizer front spar to frame attachment fitting lower legs for cracks, and repair or rectification if applicable. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this proposed AD by December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Fax:
202-493-2251.
Mail:
U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations,M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13808; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this NPRM, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.
Material Incorporated by Reference
For Transport Canada material identified in this proposed AD, contact Transport Canada, Transport Canada National Aircraft Certification, 159 Cleopatra Drive, Nepean, Ontario K1A 0N5, Canada; telephone 888-663-3639; email
TC.AirworthinessDirectives-Consignesdenavigabilite.TC@tc.gc.ca
. You may find this material on the Transport Canada website at
tc.canada.ca/en/aviation.
It is also available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13808.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call 206-231-3195.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christopher Spencer, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: 516-228-7300; email:
9-avs-nyaco-cos@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the
ADDRESSES
section. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13808; Project Identifier MCAI-2024-00785-T” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov,
including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Christopher Spencer, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: 516-228-7300; email:
9-avs-nyaco-cos@faa.gov
.
Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
Transport Canada, which is the aviation authority for Canada, has issued Transport Canada AD CF-2024-47, dated December 23, 2024 (Transport Canada AD CF-2024-47) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for certain Bombardier, Inc. Model CL-600-2B16 (604 Variants) airplanes. The MCAI states that there were reports of cracks being found on the lower wing plank at the rear spar WS 59 to WS 65 web and/or flange. Further investigation revealed that six non-destructive testing manual procedures associated with airworthiness limitations tasks could lead to undetected cracks, which could lead to structural failure of the airplane.
The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13808.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
Transport Canada AD CF-2024-47 specifies procedures for eddy current and ultrasonic inspections for cracks of the lower wing plank at the rear spar web WS 59 to WS 65 and lower flange, the forward surface of the pressure bulkhead frame under the stiffeners between left buttock line 9.00 and right buttock line 9.00 at fuselage station 409.00, and the vertical stabilizer front spar to frame attachment fitting lower legs at fuselage station 755.00; it also specifies procedures for repair or rectification of cracks.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain Airbus SAS Model A350-941 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on March 30, 2026 (
91 FR 15569
). The NPRM was prompted by EASA AD 2025-0150, dated July 14, 2025 (EASA AD 2025-0150) (also referred to as the
(
printed page 72395)
MCAI), issued by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. The MCAI states an occurrence was reported of a missing MLG brake rod center pin nut sub-assembly detected during an inspection. Further investigation revealed severe corrosion on the threads and splines of the MLG brake rod center pin and nut sub-assemblies that could have led to the detachment of the MLG brake rod center pin nut sub-assembly. This condition, if not addressed, could prevent the extension of the MLG, possibly resulting in damage to the airplane and injury to occupants.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require, depending on airplane configuration, inspection of the MLG brake rod center pin nut, lock ring, and end plate, inspection of the MLG brake rod center pin and nut, and applicable corrective actions, as specified in EASA AD 2025-0150. The proposed AD also required additional work for certain airplanes, as specified in EASA AD 2025-0150. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-2729.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive Comments
The FAA received a comment from the Air Line Pilots Association, International (ALPA) who supported the NPRM without change.
The FAA received additional comments from Delta Air Lines (Delta). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Allow Alternative Subtasks
Delta requested the FAA add an exception in paragraph (h) of the proposed AD to allow use of the applicable subtasks to Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) Task A350-A-32-11-62-01001-720A-A, instead of requiring only Subtask 321162-40100060004 to Task A350-A-32-11-62-01001-720A-A. Delta stated the referenced subtask is not applicable to all affected Airbus SAS Model A350-941 airplanes. Delta also stated that the referenced steps to Subtask 321162-40100060004 are correct, so using only the step references will allow operators to use the applicable subtask.
The FAA agrees and has added a new exception in paragraph (h)(4) of this AD accordingly.
Request To Allow Other Paint Repair Procedures
Delta requested the FAA add an exception in paragraph (h) of the proposed AD to specify that the note in Airbus Alert Operators Transmission (AOT) A32P034-24, Revision 01, dated May 27, 2025 (the AOT), for repairing any paint damage, provides an accepted procedure, not a required procedure. Delta stated the procedure in that note requires using paint and primer products that are not available to Delta, and that Airbus clarified that the note directing the operator to use certain vendor service information for repairing any paint damage is a general repair instruction and is intended only to guide operators in restoring paint damage. Delta also stated that Airbus confirmed operators may follow standard repair processes via other documentation and that they have no objections to Delta's approved external paint repair process.
The FAA disagrees with this request. The FAA reviewed Airbus's response to Delta and determined that an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) is required to repair paint damage using other methods not specified in the vendor service information referenced in the AOT. Although Airbus has no objection to Delta restoring the paint damage using its approved repair process, the note in the AOT resides under a paragraph designated as Required for Compliance (RC), and that note specifies to repair any damage to paint “in accordance with” certain vendor service information. Additionally, the FAA does not consider it appropriate to include provisions in an AD applicable only to a single operator's unique maintenance practices. However, under the provisions of paragraph (i)(1) of this AD, an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) may be requested for a deviation to any procedures identified as required for compliance in the service information. The FAA has not changed the AD in this regard.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, and any other changes described previously, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.

Corrective actions include replacement of the brake rod pin sub-assembly.
EASA AD 2025-0150 introduces additional work for airplanes with any MLG brake rod pin sub-assembly that has been reinstalled without reinstalling lockwire and applying sealant. HUD is seeking approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the information collection described below. This notice informs the public that HUD is seeking approval from OMB for the information collection described in Section A.

Title of Information Collection:
Comprehensive Transactional Forms Supporting FHA's Section 242 Mortgage Insurance Program for Hospitals.

Description of the need for the information and proposed use:
This collection of information is required specifically for the application and administration of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, Federal Housing Administration Section 242 Hospital Mortgage Insurance Program pursuant to
24 CFR 242
,
241
,
223(f)
, and
223(a)(7)
. The collection is a comprehensive set of HUD documents that are critically needed for processing applications and loan endorsements for FHA mortgage insurance under the Section 242 Hospital Mortgage Insurance Program, for ongoing asset management of such facilities, and other information related to these facilities for loan modifications, construction projects, and physical and environmental reviews. This
(
printed page 72550)
information is requested and is used by the Office of Healthcare Facilities (OHF) and Office of Architecture and Engineering (OAE) within FHA's Office of Healthcare Programs (OHP).
The purpose for which the information is being collected by HUD is to review Section 242 applications to determine the eligibility of applicant hospitals for FHA mortgage insurance, underwrite insured hospital loans, ensure that the collateral securing each loan is adequate, capture administrative data, process initial/final endorsement, and manage FHA's hospital portfolio. Additional information related to loan modifications, construction projects, and physical and environmental reviews is collected if applicable.
The information being collected consists of various HUD forms that program participants complete with project specifications, technical descriptions, details, and/or signatures that are utilized by HUD during various stages of the application, underwriting, commitment, closing, and asset management processes involved with the administration of FHA's Section 242 mortgage insurance program.
The information is used by HUD staff for internal review of applications to determine if projects qualify for Section 242 hospital mortgage insurance and to manage and monitor the application, commitment, initial/final endorsement, asset management, and administration processes needed to support hospital projects insured by FHA. Agreements and legal documents are used by HUD staff, lenders, borrowers, construction managers, and depository institutions, when applicable, to process initial/final endorsement of loans. Information reported for ongoing asset management of FHA-insured facilities will be used by HUD staff to monitor and manage risk within the FHA portfolio and ensure ongoing compliance with HUD Program Obligations. Information is also used by HUD staff to determine whether the Program meets its stated goals and management objectives. The information is collected from lenders/mortgage bankers, borrowers/hospital management officials, attorneys, general contractors/construction managers, architects/engineers, agents and others involved in hospital projects, which may, at times include local government entities and other third parties, as well as HUD staff to allow OHF to manage and monitor the application, commitment, initial/final endorsement, asset management, and administration processes needed to support hospital projects insured by FHA.
This collection is needed to update and renew the current collection that was approved for a 36-month period by OMB on April 18, 2023, with an expiration date of April 30, 2026.
The warning language has been updated on all forms. Twelve documents within the collection are being renewed with only changes to the revised Public Burden Statement and the Warning. The remaining twenty-nine of the forty-one forms within the collection are being renewed with changes. Revisions include edits that were made to clarify current policies and definitions, reflect updated generally accepted accounting standards, or to address inconsistencies across documents.

Title:

Abstract:
Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 1441 (Withholding of tax on nonresident aliens), states any nonresident alien individual or of any foreign partnership shall deduct and withhold from such items a tax equal to 30 percent or 14 percent depending on circumstances. The collection of information pursuant to this rule,

Title:
Gross Collection of Exchange-Set Margins for Omnibus Accounts (OMB Control Number 3038-0026). This is a request for extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
Commission Regulation 1.58 requires that FCMs margin omnibus accounts on a gross, rather than a net, basis. The regulation provides that the carrying FCM need not collect margin for positions traded by a person through an omnibus account in excess of the amount that would be required if the same person, instead of trading through an omnibus account, maintained its own account with the carrying FCM. To prevent abuse of this exception to the regulation, a carrying FCM must maintain a written representation from the originating FCM or foreign broker that the particular positions held in the omnibus account are part of a hedge or spread transaction. This rule is promulgated pursuant to the Commission's rulemaking authority contained in Sections 4c, 4d, 4f, 4g and 8a of the Commodity Exchange Act,

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
EPA is amending significant new use rules (SNURs) issued under section 5(a)(2) of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) for certain chemical substances identified herein, which were the subject of premanufacture notices (PMNs) and significant new use notices (SNUNs). This action amends the SNURs by allowing certain new uses reported in the SNUNs or PMNs without additional notification requirements, modifying the significant new use notification requirements based on the actions and determinations for the SNUN or PMN submissions or based on the examination of new test data or other information, and making technical
(
printed page 72434)
amendments to several SNURs. EPA is issuing these amendments based on review of new and existing data for the chemical substances.
DATES:
This rule is effective on January 11, 2027. For purposes of judicial review, this rule shall be promulgated at 1 p.m. (EST) on November 24, 2026.

or in person at the Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics Docket (OPPT Docket) in the Environmental Protection Agency Docket Center (EPA/DC). Please review the visitor instructions and additional information about the docket available at

.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary
A. What is the Agency's authority for taking this action?
TSCA section 5(a)(2) (
15 U.S.C. 2604(a)(2)
) authorizes EPA to determine that a use of a chemical substance is a “significant new use.” EPA must make this determination by rule after considering all relevant factors, including the factors in TSCA section 5(a)(2). Procedures and criteria for modifying or revoking SNUR requirements appear at
40 CFR 721.185
or
725.984
(for microorganisms).
B. What action is the Agency taking?
EPA is finalizing amendments to the SNURs for certain chemical substances in
40 CFR part 721, subpart E
and
part
725, Subpart M (for microorganisms). A SNUR for a chemical substance designates certain activities as significant new uses. Persons who intend to manufacture or process a chemical substance for a significant new use must notify EPA at least 90 days before commencing that activity. The required notification (
i.e.,
a SNUN) initiates EPA's evaluation of the intended use. Manufacture and processing for the significant new use may not commence until EPA has conducted a review of the notice, made an appropriate determination on the notice, and taken such actions as are required in association with that determination.
Previously, EPA proposed amendments to the SNURs for these chemical substances in the
Federal Register
of October 28, 2025, (
90 FR 48717
(FRL-12967-01-OCSPP)). The docket includes information considered by the Agency in developing the proposed and final rules, including public comments and EPA's responses to the comments received as discussed in Unit II.D.
C. Does this action apply to me?
1. General Applicability
This action applies to you if you manufacture, process, or use the chemical substances identified in this document. The following list of North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes is not intended to be exhaustive, but rather provides a guide to help readers determine whether this document applies to them. Potentially affected entities may include:
Manufacturers or processors of one or more subject chemical substances (NAICS codes 325 and 324110),
e.g.,
chemical manufacturing and petroleum refineries.
2. Applicability to Importers and Exporters
This action may also apply to certain entities through pre-existing import certification and export notification requirements under TSCA (
https://www.epa.gov/​tsca-import-export-requirements
).
Chemical importers are subject to TSCA section 13 (
15 U.S.C. 2612
), the requirements in
19 CFR 12.118
through
12.127
,
19 CFR 127.28
, and
40 CFR part 707, subpart B
. Importers of chemical substances in bulk form, as part of a mixture, or as part of an article (if required by rule) must certify that the shipment of the chemical substance complies with all applicable rules and Orders under TSCA, including regulations issued under TSCA sections 5, 6, 7 and Title IV.
Pursuant to
40 CFR 721.20
or
40 CFR 725.920
(for microorganisms), any persons who export or intend to export a chemical substance identified in this document are subject to the export notification provisions of TSCA section 12(b) (
15 U.S.C. 2611(b)
) and must comply with the export notification requirements in
40 CFR part 707, subpart D
.
D. What are the incremental economic impacts of this action?
EPA has evaluated the potential costs of establishing SNUN reporting requirements for potential manufacturers and processors of the chemical substances identified in this document. This analysis, which is available in the docket, is briefly summarized here.
1. Estimated Costs for SNUN Submissions
A SNUR requires that any person who intends to engage in such activity in the future must first notify EPA by submitting a SNUN. If a SNUN is submitted, costs are an estimated $45,000 per SNUN submission for large business submitters and $14,500 for small business submitters. These estimates include the cost to prepare and submit the SNUN (including registration for EPA's Central Data Exchange (CDX)), and the payment of a user fee. Businesses that submit a SNUN would be subject to either a $37,000 user fee required by
40 CFR 700.45(c)(2)(ii)
and
(d)
, or, if they are a small business as defined at
13 CFR 121.201
, a reduced user fee of $6,480 (
40 CFR 700.45(c)(1)(ii)
and
(d)
). These estimates reflect the costs and fees as they are known at the time of this rulemaking.
2. Estimated Costs for Export Notifications
EPA has also evaluated the potential costs associated with the pre-existing export notification requirements under TSCA section 12(b) and the implementing regulations at
40 CFR part 707, subpart D
. For persons exporting a substance that is the subject of a SNUR, a one-time notice to EPA must be provided for the first export or intended export to a particular country. The total costs of export notification will vary by chemical, depending on the number of required notifications (
i.e.,
the number of countries to which the chemical is exported). While EPA is unable to make any estimate of the likely number of export notifications for the chemical substances covered by these SNURs, as stated in the accompanying economic analysis, the estimated cost of the export
(
printed page 72435)
notification requirement on a per unit basis is approximately $106.
II. Background
A. General Information About SNURs
Unit II. of the proposed rule provides general information about SNURs, and additional information about EPA's new chemical program is available at
https://www.epa.gov/​reviewing-new-chemicals-under-toxic-substances-control-act-tsca
.
B. Applicability of the Significant New Use Designation
To establish a significant new use, EPA must determine that the use is not ongoing. As discussed in Unit II.E. of the proposed rule, for one of the SNURs addressed in this rule, EPA proposed to designate as a “significant new use” several additional uses that were not previously specifically designated as significant new uses under the existing SNURs, but which would be designated as significant new uses requiring notification if the proposed rule were finalized. EPA concluded that these proposed significant new uses were not ongoing. EPA also stated that if EPA subsequently determined that such a use was ongoing as of the date of publication of the proposed rule and did not cease prior to issuance of the final rule, EPA would not designate that use as a significant new use in the final rule. EPA has no information to suggest that any of the significant new uses identified in this rule meet this criterion.
As discussed in the
Federal Register
of April 24, 1990 (
55 FR 17376
(FRL-3658-5)), EPA believes that the intent of TSCA section 5(a)(1)(B) is best served by designating a use as a significant new use as of the date of publication of the proposed rule rather than as of the effective date of the final rule. The objective of EPA's approach is to ensure that a person cannot impede finalization of a SNUR by initiating a significant new use after publication of the proposed rule but before the effective date of the final rule. Uses arising after the publication of the proposed rule are distinguished from uses that are identified in the final rule as having been ongoing on the date of publication of the proposed rule. The former would be new uses, the latter ongoing uses, except that uses that are identified as ongoing as of the publication of the proposed rule would not be considered ongoing uses if they have ceased by the date of issuance of a final rule.
In the unlikely event that before a final rule becomes effective a person begins commercial manufacturing (including importing) or processing of the chemical substances for a use that is designated as a significant new use in that final rule, such a person would have to cease any such activity upon the effective date of the final rule. To resume their activities, these persons would have to first comply with all applicable SNUR notification requirements and wait until all TSCA prerequisites for the commencement of manufacture or processing have been satisfied.
Issuance of a SNUR for a chemical substance does not signify that the chemical substance is listed on the TSCA Chemical Substance Inventory (TSCA Inventory). Guidance on how to determine if a chemical substance is on the TSCA Inventory is available on the internet at
https://www.epa.gov/​tsca-inventory
.
C. Important Information About SNUN Submissions
1. SNUN Submissions
SNUNs must be submitted on EPA Form No. 7710-25, generated using e-PMN software, and submitted to the Agency in accordance with the procedures set forth in
40 CFR 720.40
and
721.25
. E-PMN software is available electronically at
https://www.epa.gov/​reviewing-new-chemicals-under-toxic-substances-control-act-tsca
.
2. Development and Submission of Information
EPA recognizes that TSCA section 5 does not require development of any particular new information (
e.g.,
generating test data) before submission of a SNUN. There is an exception: If a person is required to submit information for a chemical substance pursuant to a rule, Order or consent agreement under TSCA section 4, then TSCA section 5(b)(1)(A) requires such information to be submitted to EPA at the time of submission of the SNUN.
In the absence of a rule, TSCA Order, or consent agreement under TSCA section 4 covering the chemical substance, persons are required only to submit information in their possession or control and to describe any other information known to or reasonably ascertainable by them (see
40 CFR 720.50
or
40 CFR 725.160
(for microorganisms)). However, upon review of PMNs, SNUNs, and MCANS, the Agency has the authority to require appropriate testing. To assist with EPA's analysis of the SNUN, submitters are encouraged, but not required, to provide the potentially useful information as identified for the chemical substance in Unit III.C. of the proposed rule.
EPA strongly encourages persons, before performing any testing, to consult with the Agency pertaining to protocol selection. Furthermore, pursuant to TSCA section 4(h), which pertains to reduction of testing in vertebrate animals, EPA encourages consultation with the Agency on the use of alternative test methods and strategies (also called New Approach Methodologies, or NAMs), if available, to generate the recommended test data. EPA encourages dialog with Agency representatives to help determine how best the submitter can meet both the data needs and the objective of TSCA section 4(h). For more information on alternative test methods and strategies to reduce vertebrate animal testing, visit
https://www.epa.gov/​assessing-and-managing-chemicals-under-tsca/​alternative-test-methods-and-strategies-reduce
.
The potentially useful information described in Unit III. of the proposed rule may not be the only means of providing information to evaluate the chemical substance associated with the significant new uses. However, submitting a SNUN without any test data may increase the likelihood that EPA will take action under TSCA sections 5(e) or 5(f). EPA recommends that potential SNUN submitters contact EPA early enough so that they will be able to conduct the appropriate tests.
SNUN submitters should be aware that EPA will be better able to evaluate SNUNs which provide detailed information about human exposure and environmental release that may result from the significant new use of the chemical substances.
D. Public Comments on Proposed Rule and EPA Responses
EPA received public comments on the proposed amendments to the SNURs and prepared a Response to Comment document that provides the Agency responses. The comments and the Response to Comment document are available in the docket. 40 CFR 721.10966

(

For J-9-1 (
40 CFR 725.1080

A. What is the designated cutoff date for ongoing uses?
EPA designates the date of publication of the proposed rule as the cutoff date for determining whether the significant new uses are ongoing,
i.e.,
October 28, 2025 (
90 FR 48717

https://www.epa.gov/​laws-regulations-and-executive-orders

C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
According to the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information that requires OMB approval under PRA, unless it has been approved by OMB and displays a currently valid OMB control number. The OMB control numbers for EPA's regulations in
title 40 of the CFR

Federal Register

40 CFR part 9

The information collection requirements related to SNURs have already been approved by OMB pursuant to PRA under OMB control number 2070-0038 (EPA ICR No. 1188). This action does not impose any burden requiring additional OMB approval. If an entity were to submit a SNUN to the Agency, the annual burden is estimated to average between 30 and 170 hours per submission. This burden estimate includes the time needed to review instructions, search existing data sources, gather and maintain the data needed, and complete, review, and submit the required SNUN.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
I certify that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). The requirement to submit a SNUN applies to any person (including small or large entities) who intends to engage in any activity described in the final rule as a “significant new use.” Because these uses are “new,” based on all information currently available to EPA, EPA has concluded that no small or large entities presently engage in such activities.
A SNUR requires that any person who intends to engage in such activity in the future must first notify EPA by submitting a SNUN. Although some small entities may decide to pursue a significant new use in the future, EPA cannot presently determine how many, if any, there may be. However, EPA's experience to date is that, in response to the promulgation of SNURs covering over 1,000 chemicals, the Agency receives only a small number of notices per year. For example, the number of SNUNs received was 7 in Federal fiscal year (FY) 2020, 9 in FY2021, 9 in FY2022, 23 in FY2023, 7 in FY2024, and 10 in FY 2025 and only a fraction of these submissions were from small businesses.
In addition, the Agency currently offers relief to qualifying small businesses by reducing the SNUN submission fee from $37,000 to $6,480. This lower fee reduces the total reporting and recordkeeping cost of submitting a SNUN to about $14,500 per SNUN submission for qualifying small firms. Therefore, the potential economic impacts of complying with these proposed SNURs are not expected to be significant or adversely impact a substantial number of small entities. In a SNUR that published in the
Federal Register
of June 2, 1997 (
62 FR 29684
(FRL-5597-1)), the Agency presented its general determination that SNURs are not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, which was provided to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration.

This action does not contain an unfunded mandate of $100 million or more (in 1995 dollars) in any one year as described in UMRA,

, and does not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Based on EPA's experience with proposing and finalizing SNURs, State, local, and Tribal governments have not been impacted by SNURs, and EPA does not have any reasons to believe that any State, local, or Tribal government will be impacted by these SNURs. In addition, the estimated costs of this action to the private sector do not exceed $183 million or more in any one year (the 1995 dollars are adjusted to 2023 dollars for inflation using the GDP implicit price deflator). AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is determining under the Clean Air Act (CAA) that the Detroit, Michigan Moderate nonattainment area (“Detroit area” or “area”) attained the 2015 ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) by the applicable attainment date. This determination relies on the EPA's concurrence on an exceptional events request submitted by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) on February 19, 2026, and concurred on by the EPA on March 24, 2026. Therefore, the EPA is taking final agency action on Michigan's exceptional events request. This action fulfills the EPA's statutory obligation to determine whether the Detroit area attained the 2015 ozone NAAQS by the Moderate attainment date of August 3, 2024.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on November 10, 2026.
