AGENCY:
Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) has determined to extend for three months the ongoing Section 301 investigation of certain acts, policies, and practices of the Government of Vietnam related to intellectual property (IP) protection and enforcement.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Questions regarding this notice should be directed to Philip Butler, Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Monitoring & Enforcement, or Christina Olson, Senior Associate General Counsel, at (202) 395-5725.
DATES:
This notice is effective as of
Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 12:01 a.m. EDT.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On May 29, 2026, the Trade Representative initiated a Section 301 investigation into certain acts, policies, and practices of the Government of Vietnam related to IP protection and enforcement under Section 302(b)(2) of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act).
See
91 FR 33285
(June 3, 2026). For investigations initiated under that section that do not involve a trade agreement, Section 304(a)(3)(A) directs the Trade Representative to make findings on actionability and what action, if any, to take within six months of the date of initiation. Section 304(a)(3)(B) provides that, if the Trade Representative determines that the investigation involves complex or complicated issues that require additional time, the foreign country involved in the investigation is making substantial progress in drafting or implementing legislative or administrative measures that will provide adequate and effective protection of IP rights, or the foreign country involved in the investigation is undertaking enforcement measures to provide adequate and effective protection of IP rights, then the Trade Representative shall make findings on actionability and what action, if any, to take within nine months of the date of initiation. Pursuant to this provision, the Trade Representative has
(
printed page 72610)
determined that the investigation involves complex or complicated issues that require additional time. Accordingly, the determinations in the investigation will be made by no later than February 28, 2027.

Office of the United States Trade Representative
AGENCY:
Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
To allow for further discussion with China regarding the acts, policies, and practices at issue in this investigation, the U.S. Trade Representative (Trade Representative) is modifying the action taken in this investigation to further suspend that action for two months, until January 10, 2027.
DATES:
November 9, 2026:
The actions taken in this investigation are further suspended through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Philip Butler, Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Monitoring and Enforcement; Thomas Au, Senior Counsel for Industrial Policy; or David Salkeld, Associate General Counsel at (202) 395-5725.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
For background on the proceedings in this investigation, please see the prior notices issued in this investigation, including
89 FR 29424
(April 22, 2024),
90 FR 8089
(January 23, 2025),
90 FR 10843
(February 27, 2025),
90 FR 17114
(April 23, 2025) (April 23, 2025 FRN),
90 FR 24856
(June 12, 2025),
90 FR 48320
(October 16, 2025) (October 16, 2025 FRN);
90 FR 50762
(November 10, 2025) (November 10, 2025 FRN),
90 FR 50947
(November 13, 2025) (November 13, 2025 FRN), and
91 FR 67388
(October 26, 2026) (October 26, 2026 FRN).
On April 17, 2025, pursuant to sections 301(b), 301(c), and 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act) (
19 U.S.C. 2411(b)
,
2411(c)
, and
2414(a)
), and subsequently on October 16, 2025, pursuant to section 307(a) (
19 U.S.C. 2417(a)
), following consideration of public comments, as well as consultations with advisory committees and the Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative determined to take action in this investigation, including fees on certain maritime transport services and duties on ship-to-shore (STS) cranes and other cargo handling equipment of China.
See
April 23, 2025 FRN; October 16, 2025 FRN (modifying certain aspects of the actions in the investigation).
On November 1, 2025, the White House announced a historic trade and economic deal reached between President Trump and President Xi of China. The White House, Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Strikes Deal on Economic and Trade Relations with China (Nov. 1, 2025),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/​fact-sheets/​2025/​11/​fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-strikes-deal-on-economic-and-trade-relations-with-china/​
.
Pursuant to this deal, the United States would suspend for one year, beginning on November 10, 2025, the responsive actions taken in this investigation. This period would allow the United States to negotiate with China pursuant to Section 301 regarding the issues raised in this investigation as well as to continue U.S. domestic efforts and discussions with key allies and partners on revitalizing American shipbuilding.
Following consideration of public comments and advice from the Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative, at the specific direction of the President, suspended the actions in this investigation from November 10, 2025 through November 9, 2026.
See
November 13, 2025 FRN.
Discussions with China regarding the acts, policies, and practices at issue in this investigation are ongoing. In this light, and in accordance with Section 307(a)(2) of the Trade Act, on October 23, 2026, the Trade Representative proposed to further suspend the action in this investigation for two months, until January 10, 2027. The Trade Representative requested comments from any interested person regarding the proposal to further suspend the responsive actions.
See
October 26, 2026 FRN.
II. Determination To Modify the Action
Section 307(a)(1) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative to modify any action being taken under Section 301, subject to the specific direction of the President, including if such action being taken under Section 301(b) is no longer appropriate.
The circumstances that warranted the initial suspension continue to exist, and to allow for further discussion with China regarding the issues in this investigation, and at the direction of the President, the Trade Representative has determined that the action taken on
(
printed page 72609)
April 17, 2025, as modified, is no longer appropriate and will be further suspended for two months, until January 10, 2027.
Therefore, effective on November 9, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative is further suspending the responsive actions taken in this investigation in the April 23, 2025 FRN, as modified by the October 16, 2025 FRN and as further modified by the November 13, 2025 FRN, until January 10, 2027. Accordingly, effective on November 9, 2026, headings 9903.91.12, 9903.91.13, 9903.91.14, 9903.91.15, and 9903.91.16 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States are each amended by deleting “November 10, 2026,” and by inserting “January 10, 2027,” in lieu thereof.
During the suspension period, no party will accrue liability for or be required to pay the fees on maritime transport services under Annexes I, II, or III of the April 23, 2025 FRN, as modified by the October 16, 2025 FRN and as further modified by the November 13, 2025 FRN. Further, during the suspension period, no party will accrue liability for or be required to pay the duties provided in Annex V.A of the October 16, 2025 FRN, as further modified by the November 13, 2025 FRN.
III. Responses to Significant Comments
In response to the October 26, 2026 FRN, USTR received approximately 60 unique comments. Some comments supported the proposal to further suspend the action. Some comments noted that further suspension of the action would avoid increased shipping costs and prevent commercial disruptions. Some comments also recommended further suspension of the actions to provide time for continued negotiation with China on the issues raised in this investigation.
Comments opposing the further suspension asserted that the responsive action is needed to address China's acts, policies, and practices by creating incentives to invest in U.S. shipbuilding and related industries, such as containers. These comments argue that, without the action, China's dominance across the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors will increase.
Some comments recommended permanent suspension of one or all of the maritime service fees provided for in Annex III of the April 23, 2025 FRN, as modified by the October 16, 2025 FRN. These comments generally asserted that if the suspension is not continued, there may be commercial disruptions that negatively impact U.S. exports.
Some comments addressing the suspension of restrictions of Annex IV of the April 23, 2025 FRN, as modified by the October 16, 2025 FRN, generally supported further suspension and recommended permanently lifting the restrictions provided in Annex IV.
Some comments addressing the suspension of the additional tariffs on STS cranes and other cargo handling equipment in Annex V.A of the October 16, 2025 FRN, as well as the proposed tariffs on additional cargo handling equipment in Annex V.B of the October 16, 2025 FRN, generally supported ending the suspension and addressing tariffs separately from the maritime service fees.
Considering the comments, the Trade Representative has determined that the action taken on April 17, 2025, as modified, is no longer appropriate and will be further suspended for two months, until January 10, 2027. During this further suspension, the United States will continue discussions with China to address the acts, policies, and practices at issue in this investigation and take actions to expand domestic commercial shipbuilding capacity, build a resilient workforce, and continue to partner with key allies to increase U.S. shipbuilding capacity.
See
The White House, America's Maritime Action Plan (Feb. 2026),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​2026/​02/​Restoring-Americas-Maritime-Dominance.pdf
.
IV. Ongoing Monitoring
The Trade Representative will continue to monitor the issues raised in this investigation pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act and will consider whether it is appropriate to continue the suspension period or whether further action is appropriate in advance of the January 10, 2027, suspension deadline. If modification to the action may be appropriate pursuant to Section 307 of the Trade Act, the Trade Representative may consider the comments received in response to previously proposed responsive actions.
Jennifer Thornton,
General Counsel, Office of the United States Trade Representative.

AGENCY:
Food and Drug Administration, HHS.
ACTION:
Final amendment; order; notification of partial denial of petition.
SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by the International Association of Color Manufacturers (IACM or petitioner), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of abandonment, to remove the authorized uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin. The petitioner provided data demonstrating that these uses have been permanently abandoned. FDA is denying as moot the portion of the petition proposing that the color additive regulations be amended, on the basis of abandonment, to no longer authorize the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This request is moot because the authorization for this use has been removed, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, in response to a separate petition.
DATES:
This order is effective January 11, 2027. If any provisions are delayed or stayed by the filing of proper objections, FDA will publish such notification in the
Federal Register
. Submit either electronic or written objections and requests for a hearing on the order by December 10, 2026. See section IX for further information on the filing of objections.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit objections and requests for a hearing as follows. Please note that late, untimely filed objections will not be considered. The
https://www.regulations.gov
electronic filing system will accept objections until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time at the end of December 10, 2026. Objections received by mail/hand delivery/courier (for written/paper submissions) will be considered timely if they are received on or before that date.
Electronic Submissions
Submit electronic objections in the following way:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments. Objections submitted electronically, including attachments, to
https://www.regulations.gov
will be posted to the docket unchanged. Because your objection will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your objection does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your objection, that information will be posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
If you want to submit an objection with confidential information that you do not wish to be made available to the public, submit the objection as a written/paper submission and in the manner detailed (see “Written/Paper Submissions” and “Instructions”).
Written/Paper Submissions
Submit written/paper instructions as follows:
Mail/Hand Delivery/Courier (for written/paper submissions):
Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.
For written/paper objections submitted to the Dockets Management Staff, FDA will post your objection, as well as any attachments, except for information submitted, marked and identified, as confidential, if submitted as detailed in “Instructions.”
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the Docket No. FDA-2026-C-3071 for “Color Additive Petition from the International Association of Color Manufacturers; Request to Amend the Color Additive Regulations to Remove the Solvents Methylene Chloride, Trichloroethylene, and Ethylene Dichloride.” Received objections, those filed in a timely manner (see
ADDRESSES
), will be placed in the docket and, except for those submitted as “Confidential Submissions,” publicly viewable at
https://www.regulations.gov
or at the Dockets Management Staff between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, 240-402-7500.
Confidential Submissions—To submit an objection with confidential information that you do not wish to be made publicly available, submit your objection only as a written/paper submission. You should submit two copies total. One copy will include the information you claim to be confidential with a heading or cover note that states “THIS DOCUMENT CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION.” We will review this copy, including the claimed confidential information, in our consideration of objections. The second copy, which will have the claimed confidential information redacted/blacked out, will be available for public viewing and posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Submit both copies to the Dockets Management Staff. If you do not wish your name and contact information to be made publicly available, you can provide this information on the cover sheet and not in the body of your objections and you must identify this information as “confidential.” Any information marked as “confidential” will not be disclosed except in accordance with
21 CFR 10.20
and other applicable disclosure law. For more information about FDA's posting
(
printed page 72411)
of comments to public dockets, see

I. Introduction
In the
Federal Register
of April 1, 2026 (
91 FR 16169
), we announced that we filed a color additive petition (CAP 5C0340) submitted by IACM, 1101 17th St. NW, Suite 700, Washington, DC 20036.
The petition proposed that we amend §§ 73.30 (
21 CFR 73.30
, “Annatto extract”), 73.345 (
21 CFR 73.345
, “Paprika oleoresin”), and 73.615 (
21 CFR 73.615
, “Turmeric oleoresin”) to remove methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride as permitted extraction solvents for the manufacture of annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin for use as exempt color additives in food. The petition further proposed that we amend § 73.1 (
21 CFR 73.1
, “Diluents in color additive mixtures for food use exempt from certification”) to remove methylene chloride as a permitted diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petition identified §§ 73.1030 (
21 CFR 73.1030
, “Annatto extract”) and 73.2030 (
21 CFR 73.2030
, “Annatto”) as also being impacted by this petition. Although the regulations in §§ 73.1030 and 73.2030 do not directly refer to methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, or ethylene dichloride, the regulations authorize their use by cross-referencing § 73.30(a)(1). The petition requested that we make these amendments on the basis that these uses of the solvents have been permanently abandoned.
The substances that were the subject of this petition and their corresponding Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) numbers are:
1. Methylene chloride (CAS No. 75-09-2);
2. Trichloroethylene (CAS No. 79-01-6); and
3. Ethylene dichloride (CAS No. 107-06-2).
The notification of petition gave interested parties until June 1, 2026, to submit comments on the filed color additive petition, which was made available in the docket.
II. Background
The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) authorizes us to regulate “color additives” (see section 721(b) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 379e(b)
)). The FD&C Act defines “color additive” as a material which is a dye, pigment, or other substance made by a process of synthesis or similar artifice, or extracted, isolated, or otherwise derived, with or without intermediate or final change of identity, from a vegetable, animal, mineral, or other source, and that when added or applied to a food, drug, or cosmetic, or to the human body or any part thereof, is capable (alone or through reaction with another substance) of imparting color (“color” includes black, white, and intermediate grays) thereto (see section 201(t) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 321(t)
)). Color additives used in or on a food, drug, certain medical devices, or cosmetics are deemed unsafe and prohibited except to the extent that we approve their use (see section 721(a) of the FD&C Act).
The FD&C Act provides a process through which any person who wishes to use a color additive in or on food, drugs, certain medical devices, or cosmetics may submit a petition proposing the issuance of a color additive regulation listing such use with supporting information. A color additive petition may also be submitted to propose the amendment or repeal of an existing color additive regulation (see section 721(b)(5)(C) and (d) of the FD&C Act). In response to a color additive petition, FDA may issue a regulation listing a color additive for use in or on food, drugs, certain medical devices, or cosmetics only if it determines that the additive is suitable and safe for such use (see section 721(b)(2)(A) of the FD&C Act).
Section 701(e) through (g) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 371(e)
through
(g)
) applies to the issuance, amendment, or repeal of color additive regulations (see section 721(d) of the FD&C Act). Section 701(e) of the FD&C Act provides that any action for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a color additive regulation may be initiated by a proposal made by the Secretary or by a petition of any interested persons showing reasonable grounds. It further requires that FDA publish such a proposal, provide an opportunity for all interested persons to present their views, and then by order act upon such proposal.
III. Evaluation of Abandonment
A.
21 CFR 73.30
“Annatto Extract,”
21 CFR 73.345
“Paprika Oleoresin,” and
21 CFR 73.615
“Turmeric Oleoresin”
As support for the assertion that the uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride in the manufacture of annatto extract and annatto, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin have been abandoned, the petition includes a summary of the results of a survey that IACM sent to its members and other non-member firms. The petitioner describes IACM members as comprising a meaningful proportion of the current global color industry representing manufacturers and users of color additives. The other non-member firms that IACM surveyed included members of the American Spice Trade Association, the Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association, and the Natural Food Colors Association, and independent firms, to cover the total U.S. market and support their conclusion that the uses of these substances have been permanently abandoned.
The petitioner asked recipients of the survey to verify that they do not:
Currently manufacture, purchase, use, or import annatto extract (§ 73.30), paprika oleoresin (§ 73.345), and/or turmeric oleoresin (§ 73.615) for color additive use using methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and/or ethylene dichloride as extraction solvents whether individually or in combination;
Intend to manufacture or import for use in food in the United States the color additives annatto extract (§ 73.30), paprika oleoresin (§ 73.345), or turmeric oleoresin (§ 73.615) using methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, or ethylene dichloride whether individually or in combination as extraction solvents; and
(
printed page 72412)
Currently maintain any inventory of the color additives annatto extract (§ 73.30), paprika oleoresin (§ 73.345), or turmeric oleoresin (§ 73.615) that were manufactured using methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, or ethylene dichloride whether individually or in combination as extraction solvents which will be used in food in the United States.
In its summary of the survey results, the petitioner stated that the survey included 44 unique companies and 3 trade associations that collectively represent an additional 375 companies. All the companies that participated in the survey confirmed that they have abandoned methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride for use in the manufacture of annatto extract (§ 73.30), paprika oleoresin (§ 73.345), and turmeric oleoresin (§ 73.615).
With respect to § 73.30, while the petitioner's survey focused on the use of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and/or ethylene dichloride as extraction solvents to manufacture annatto extract as specified in § 73.30, the petitioner asserts that the color industry manufactures the colors according to the specifications in FDA's color additive regulations, without consideration of end use. Therefore, the petitioner asserts that since the survey confirmed that methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride have been abandoned in the United States for the manufacturing, purchasing, use, or import of annatto extract as specified in § 73.30, the abandonment of the use of these solvents to manufacture annatto extract applies not only to use of the solvents to manufacture annatto extract used in coloring foods (§ 73.30), but also to the use of the solvents to manufacture annatto extract used in coloring drugs (§ 73.1030) and annatto used in coloring cosmetics (§ 73.2030).
In addition, when we published the notification of filing of CAP 5C0340, stakeholders had an opportunity to provide information regarding whether any of the three solvents were still being used in the manufacture of the subject color additives. We received no comments that demonstrated current use, which is further evidence supporting the petitioner's claim that these uses are abandoned.
In light of the evidence submitted in the petition, as well as the absence of any evidence demonstrating lack of abandonment, we are granting the petition's requests with respect to §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. We conclude that methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride have been abandoned with respect to their use in the manufacture of color additives. Accordingly, FDA is removing the authorizations for the use of these substances in §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615.
B.
21 CFR 73.1
“Diluents in Color Additive Mixtures for Food Use Exempt From Certification”
As support for the assertion that the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables has been abandoned, the petitioner engaged in discussions with both the International Fresh Produce Association (IFPA), which represents the full fresh produce supply chain, and the National Association of Printing Ink Manufacturers (NAPIM), which represents 85 percent of domestic ink manufacturing. The petitioner found that the use of inks for marking fruit and vegetables is limited and that no chlorinated organics are used in production ink systems or the manufacturing process. IACM received confirmation from NAPIM that NAPIM's members do not manufacture nor market their products for marking fruits and vegetables. IACM also confirmed with IFPA that IFPA's members do not:
Currently manufacture for use in food in the United States inks for marking fruit and vegetables (§ 73.1(b)(1)(ii)) using methylene chloride as a diluent;
Currently import for use in food in the United States inks for marking fruit and vegetables (§ 73.1(b)(1)(ii)) using methylene chloride as a diluent;
Intend to manufacture or import for use in food in the United States inks for marking fruit and vegetables (§ 73.1(b)(1)(ii)) using methylene chloride as a diluent; and
Currently maintain any inventory of inks for marking fruit and vegetables (§ 73.1(b)(ii)) using methylene chloride as a diluent which will be used in food in the United States.
Related to CAP 5C0340, elsewhere in this issue of the
Federal Register
, we published a final order in response to CAP 4C0327 granting that petition, in part, and amending § 73.1 to no longer provide for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures for use in inks for marking fruit and vegetables on the basis of the Delaney Clause (section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act). Because the final order issued in response to CAP 4C0327 removes methylene chloride from § 73.1, the petitioner's request based on abandonment is moot.
IV. Comments Related to the Petition
We provided 60 days for comments on the petition. We received one comment, which supported the petitioner's conclusion that the uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride as described in the petition have been abandoned. We received no other comments in response to the notification of petition.
V. Conclusion
FDA reviewed the data and other information in the petition and other available relevant material to evaluate whether the uses of these extraction solvents in the manufacture of color additives have been abandoned. Based on the available information, we have determined that these uses have been abandoned. Therefore, we are amending §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615 of the color additive regulations to no longer provide for the uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, or ethylene dichloride in the manufacture of color additives because these uses have been abandoned. Although the regulatory text in §§ 73.1030 and 73.2030 will not be amended, these regulations are also affected because they authorize the use of these substances by cross-referencing § 73.30. Therefore, in removing the authorization of the use of these substances from § 73.30, their use is no longer authorized under §§ 73.1030 and 73.2030.
We are denying as moot the request to remove methylene chloride from § 73.1 because elsewhere in this issue of the
Federal Register
, FDA has revoked the authorization for methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables on the basis of the Delaney Clause.

Specifically, the petitioners state these substances have been found to induce cancer in animals and, therefore, are not safe pursuant to section 721(b)(5)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (
21 U.S.C. 379e(b)(5)(B)

The notification of petition gave interested parties until March 11, 2024, to submit comments on the filed color additive petition. The petition was made available in the docket. In the

of May 28, 2026 (

This order grants the petition's request to amend the regulations to no longer provide for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This order denies the petition's remaining requests. However, as noted in section VI of this document, FDA is taking action on these remaining requests in response to a separate petition based on industry's abandonment of these uses.
(

II. Background
A. Statutory and Regulatory Background of Color Additive Regulation
The FD&C Act authorizes us to regulate “color additives” (see section 721(b) of the FD&C Act). The FD&C Act defines “color additive” as a material which is a dye, pigment, or other substance made by a process of synthesis or similar artifice, or extracted, isolated, or otherwise derived, with or without intermediate or final change of identity, from a vegetable, animal, mineral, or other source, and that when added or applied to a food, drug, or cosmetic, or to the human body or any part thereof, is capable (alone or through reaction with another substance) of imparting color (“color” includes black, white, and intermediate grays) thereto (see section 201(t) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 321(t)
)). Color additives used in or on a food, drug, cosmetic, or certain medical devices are deemed unsafe and prohibited except to the extent that we approve their use (see section 721(a) of the FD&C Act). Certain color additives must be certified by FDA (see section 721(c) of the FD&C Act).
The FD&C Act provides a process through which any person who wishes to use a color additive in or on food, drugs, certain devices, or cosmetics may submit a petition proposing the issuance of a color additive regulation listing such use with supporting information. A color additive petition may also be submitted to propose the amendment or repeal of any existing color additive regulation (see section 721(b)(5)(C) and (d) of the FD&C Act). In response to a color additive petition, FDA may issue a regulation listing a color additive for use in or on food, drugs, devices, or cosmetics only if it determines that the additive is suitable and safe for such use (see section 721(b)(1) of the FD&C Act).
Under section 721(b) of the FD&C Act, we will not establish a regulation for the use of a color additive if a fair evaluation of the data fails to establish that the proposed use of the color additive, under the conditions of use to be specified in the regulation, will be safe. To determine whether a color additive is safe, the FD&C Act requires FDA to consider, among other relevant factors: (1) probable consumption of, or other relevant exposure from, the additive and of any substance formed in or on food, drugs or devices, or cosmetics because of the use of the additive; (2) cumulative effect, if any, of such additive “in the diet of man or animals,” taking into account the same or any chemically or pharmacologically related substance or substances in such diet; and (3) safety factors recognized by experts “as appropriate for the use of animal experimentation data” (see section 721(b)(5)(A) of the FD&C Act) (referred to as the “general safety clause”). FDA's determination that a color additive is safe means that there is convincing evidence that establishes with reasonable certainty that no harm will result from the intended condition of use of the color additive (§ 70.3(i) (
21 CFR 70.3(i)
)). We refer to this safety standard as “a reasonable certainty of no harm.”
In addition, section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act, often referred to as the Delaney Clause, deems a color additive unsafe under certain circumstances. The Delaney Clause for color additives consists of two parts. The first part (section 721(b)(5)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act) pertains specifically to ingested color additives. The second part (section 721(b)(5)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act) applies to non-ingested color additives. For purposes of our review of this petition, we reviewed these uses of the solvents ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene under the first part because these uses result in ingestion. Section 721(b)(5)(B)(i) of the FD&C Act states that a color additive shall be deemed unsafe for any use which will or may result in ingestion of all or part of such additive if the additive is found by the Secretary to induce cancer when ingested by man or animal, or if it is found by the Secretary, after tests which are appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of additives for use in food, to induce cancer in man or animal. Courts have concluded that the Delaney Clause is to be interpreted very rigidly. In
Public Citizen
v.
Young,
831 F.2d 1108, 1122 (D.C. Cir. 1987), the court held that Congress intended for the Delaney Clause to be “extraordinarily rigid,” to protect the public from cancer-causing substances without exception, rejecting FDA's argument that a particular color additive should be approved because it did not pose more than a de minimis cancer risk; see also
Les
v.
Reilly,
968 F.2d 985, 986 (9th Cir. 1992) (holding that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) refusal to revoke regulations permitting the use of certain pesticides, which were regulated as food additives at the time of the court decision and subject to a similarly worded Delaney Clause for food additives, on the grounds that they pose a de minimis cancer risk, is contrary to the provisions of the Delaney Clause). Importantly, however, the Delaney Clause applies to the additive itself and not to constituents (such as nonfunctional chemicals present in the additive) or impurities in the additive. That is, where an additive itself has not been shown to cause cancer but contains a carcinogenic constituent or impurity, the additive is properly evaluated under the general safety clause using risk assessment procedures to determine whether there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from the intended use of the additive (
Scott
v.
FDA,
728 F.2d 322 (6th Cir. 1984)).
There is a similar Delaney Clause provision for food additives under section 409(c)(3) of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 348(c)(3)
), which states that no food additive shall be deemed safe if it is found to induce cancer when ingested by man or animal, or if it is found, after tests which are appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of food additives, to induce cancer in man or animal. In revoking certain authorizations for food additives under the Delaney Clause, FDA stated that the Delaney Clause limits FDA's discretion to determine the safety of food additives. FDA stated that the Delaney Clause prevents FDA from finding a food additive to be safe if it has been found to induce cancer when ingested by humans or animals, “regardless of the probability, or risk, of cancer associated with exposure to the additive or of the extent to which the experimental conditions of the animal study or the carcinogenic mode of action provide insight into the health effects of human consumption and use of the additive in question” (
83 FR 50490
at 50492, October 9, 2018).
Section 721(d) of the FD&C Act provides for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of regulations authorizing the use of a color additive, and, among other things, it specifies that the safety provisions of section 721(b)(5) of the FD&C Act apply to such actions. For FDA to grant a petition that seeks repeal of a color additive regulation based upon new data concerning the safety of the color additive, such data must be adequate for FDA to conclude that there is no longer a reasonable certainty of no harm for the intended use of the color additive or that it must be deemed unsafe under the Delaney Clause.
B. History of the Color Additive Regulations Where Amendments Are Requested
In the
Federal Register
of June 20, 1963 (
28 FR 6351
), FDA established
21 CFR 8.305
for the listing of annatto extract in food use exempt from certification, now codified in § 73.30. Ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are allowed as food-grade extractants in the
(
printed page 72416)
preparation of annatto extract (§ 73.30(a)(1)(ii)). In the
Federal Register
of October 8, 1964 (
29 FR 13893
), FDA established
21 CFR 8.390
for the listing of diluents in color additive mixtures for food use exempt from certification, including methylene chloride (with a restriction of no residues) for the special use in inks for marking fruit and vegetables, now codified in § 73.1.
In the
Federal Register
of January 27, 1966 (
31 FR 1063
), FDA established, among other things,
21 CFR 8.308
and
8.310
for the listing of paprika oleoresin and turmeric oleoresin, now codified in §§ 73.345 and 73.615, respectively. Ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are allowed as solvents in the preparation of both paprika oleoresin and turmeric oleoresin (§§ 73.345(a)(1) and 73.615(a)(1)).
III. Summary and Context of Determination
We have evaluated the data and other information submitted in the petition, as well as other relevant data. FDA finds that ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene induce cancer in animals. We must revoke the authorizations providing for any color additive use of these substances on the basis of the Delaney Clause. As described further in section IV of this document, we conclude that methylene chloride is a color additive in § 73.1. Therefore, we are amending the regulations to remove the use of this color additive under section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act as a matter of law.
We are denying the petition's remaining requests. As described further in section IV of this document, we conclude that ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are not color additives in §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. Therefore, the Delaney Clause does not apply to these uses.
IV. Evaluation of Petition
The petitioners assert that the Delaney Clause applies to ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene in §§ 73.1, 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. The petitioners state that ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene have been shown to induce cancer in animals. The petitioners cite to studies sponsored by the Department of Health and Human Services' National Toxicology Program (NTP) (Refs. 1-3).
For ethylene dichloride, in the National Cancer Institute Technical Report No. 55 (1978) on 1, 2—dichloroethane, the authors reported that the test material caused significantly increased incidence of squamous cell carcinomas of the forestomach and hemangiosarcomas of the circulatory system in male rats and adenocarcinomas of the mammary gland in female rats (Ref. 1). FDA previously evaluated these data and found that ethylene dichloride induced cancer in animals (Refs. 4 and 5).
For methylene chloride, in the NTP Report No. 306 (January 1986) on inhalation studies in F344/N rats and B6C3F
1
mice, the authors reported that the test material (Dichloromethane (Methylene Chloride) (CAS Reg. No. 75-09-2)) caused an increased incidence of liver cell neoplasms and lung neoplasms in both male and female B6C3F
1
mice (Ref. 2). FDA previously evaluated these data and found that methylene chloride induced cancer in animals (Ref. 6).
For trichloroethylene, the National Cancer Institute Technical Report No. 2 presents a synopsis of the results of a carcinogenesis bioassay of trichloroethylene using mice and rats and concludes that trichloroethylene induces liver cancer in mice (Ref. 3). FDA previously evaluated these data and found that trichloroethylene induced cancer in animals (Ref. 7).
Based on these studies, we conclude that ethylene dichloride and trichloroethylene have been “found by the Secretary to induce cancer when ingested by . . . animal[s]” (Refs. 1 and 3).
We also conclude that methylene chloride is an animal carcinogen based on an NTP-sponsored two-year inhalation study in mice (NTP inhalation mouse study) and that this study is appropriate for evaluating the safety of this additive for its intended use. Previously, FDA concluded that data from the NTP inhalation mouse study were appropriate for the safety evaluation of methylene chloride as a food additive (
50 FR 51551
and Refs. 8 and 9).
In the NTP inhalation mouse study with methylene chloride, carcinogenic incidences were reported in lungs and also in liver, an organ removed from the site of administration (Ref. 8). These effects occurred independent of each other (id.). Further, FDA compared data from the NTP inhalation mouse study with those from a National Coffee Association-sponsored two-year drinking water study conducted with the same strain of mice but at lower dose levels (Ref. 8). While the drinking water studies did not demonstrate any carcinogenic effects in the liver or lungs, increased incidences of non-neoplastic proliferative lesions were observed in the liver (Ref. 6), and FDA concluded that mice receiving methylene chloride in the drinking water study may not have been tested at levels comparable to the NTP inhalation study (Ref. 6). Making an assumption that methylene chloride induced cancer just below the detection limit of the doses tested in the drinking water studies, FDA concluded that the upper-bound cancer risk of methylene chloride from the drinking water studies was approximately the same as its upper-bound cancer risk from the NTP inhalation study (Ref. 9).
On a case-by-case basis, data from non-oral animal toxicity studies, such as studies based on inhalation exposure route, can be used in place of oral animal toxicity studies to evaluate the safety of substances after oral exposure (Refs. 10 and 11). This assessment involves examining and comparing chemical and toxicological profiles of the substance between oral and inhalation exposure routes (id.). In general, substances that have a high vapor pressure and are therefore considered volatile can enter the blood after inhalation exposure and potentially induce toxic effects in internal organs away from the site of administration (id.). For such substances, data from non-oral exposure studies (
e.g.,
inhalation studies) are considered relevant to evaluate their safety after oral exposure (Ref. 10). Methylene chloride is a volatile substance with a high vapor pressure (see
29 CFR 1910.1052
Appendix A). Further, in the NTP inhalation mouse study, methylene chloride induced carcinogenic effects in the liver—an organ removed from the site of administration.
Therefore, data from the NTP inhalation mouse study of methylene chloride is applicable to its evaluation of safety after oral exposure, and this study is appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of this additive for color additive use. Thus, the reported results from the NTP inhalation mouse study are appropriate when considering the applicability of the Delaney Clause for methylene chloride, and based on this study, we conclude that methylene chloride has been found “to induce cancer in . . . animal.” We also conclude that the NTP inhalation mouse study (Ref. 2) for methylene chloride is “appropriate for the evaluation of the safety of additives for such use.”
Because these solvents (ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene) have been “found to induce cancer in . . . animal[s],” the Delaney Clause applies to their use as a color additive. The Delaney Clause prevents FDA from finding the color
(
printed page 72417)
additive uses of these solvents to be safe if the solvents have been found to induce cancer in animals, regardless of the probability, or risk, of cancer associated with exposure from the color additive uses.
Finally, we evaluated the uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene in these color additive regulations to determine whether, based on the specific authorized uses, these substances are color additives (which are subject to the Delaney Clause) or are constituents or impurities in a color additive (which are not subject to the Delaney Clause).
The discussion that follows describes FDA's evaluation of whether ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene, as they appear in §§ 73.1, 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615, are considered color additives or constituents or impurities in the color additive. For uses of substances that we determine to be color additives, the Delaney Clause applies, and the authorization for such uses must be revoked. For uses of substances that we determine to be constituents or impurities in a color additive, the Delaney Clause does not apply. As the petition's request is based on the Delaney Clause, we are denying its request to revoke the applicable authorizations on the basis of the Delaney Clause for uses that we determine result in these solvents being constituents or impurities in a color additive rather than the color additive itself.
A.
21 CFR 73.1
“Diluents in Color Additive Mixtures for Food Use Exempt From Certification”
Under § 73.1(b)(1)(ii), methylene chloride is allowed as a diluent in color additive mixtures for use in inks for marking fruit and vegetables with the restriction of no residue. A color additive mixture is a color additive that is made, in relevant part, by mixing “one or more straight colors and one or more diluents” (§ 70.3(k)). While such diluents do not impart color and are not by themselves a color additive (§ 70.3(m)), they are regulated as color additives when they are intentionally mixed with a color to make a color additive mixture. Because of a diluent's functional purpose in the color additive mixture, we consider the authorized use of methylene chloride in § 73.1(b)(1)(ii), as a diluent in color additive mixtures for use in inks for marking fruit and vegetables, to be a color additive that is subject to the Delaney Clause. Therefore, we are amending the regulation to no longer provide for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures for use in inks for marking fruit and vegetables in § 73.1(b)(1)(ii) under section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act as a matter of law.
B.
21 CFR 73.30
“Annatto Extract”
Under § 73.30(a)(1)(ii), ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are each allowed as a food-grade extractant to manufacture the color additive “annatto extract.” Annatto extract must contain no more solvent residue than is allowed of the corresponding solvents in spice oleoresins under applicable food additive regulations in parts 170 through 189 (
21 CFR parts 170
through
189
) (see § 73.30(b)). Total chlorinated solvents residues are limited to 30 parts per million (ppm) (milligram per kilogram (mg/kg)) (see §§ 173.230 (
21 CFR 173.230
), 173.255 (
21 CFR 173.255
), and 173.290 (
21 CFR 173.290
)). Through the extraction process, ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene may end up as a residue of, and therefore an impurity in, the color additive “annatto extract.” While these extractants may end up as impurities in the color additive “annatto extract,” they are not color additives themselves in § 73.30. Therefore, we are denying the petition's request to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of approved food-grade extractants in § 73.30 under section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act. As discussed in section II.A of this document, the Delaney Clause is applicable to color additives but not to impurities in a color additive.
C.
21 CFR 73.345
“Paprika Oleoresin”
Under § 73.345(a), ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are each allowed as a solvent for the extraction of paprika to obtain the color additive “paprika oleoresin.” Paprika oleoresin must contain no more solvent residue than is allowed of the corresponding solvents in spice oleoresins under applicable food additive regulations in parts 170 through 189 (see § 73.345(b)). Total chlorinated solvents are limited to 30 ppm (mg/kg) (see §§ 173.230, 173.255, and 173.290). Through the extraction process, ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene may end up as a residue of, and therefore an impurity in, the color additive “paprika oleoresin.” While these solvents may end up as impurities in the color additive “paprika oleoresin,” they are not color additives themselves in § 73.345. Therefore, we are denying the petition's request to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of approved solvents in § 73.345 under section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act. As discussed in section II.A of this document, the Delaney Clause is applicable to color additives but not to impurities in a color additive.
D.
21 CFR 73.615
“Turmeric Oleoresin”
Under § 73.615(a), ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are each allowed as a solvent for extraction of turmeric to obtain the color additive “turmeric oleoresin.” Turmeric oleoresin must contain no more solvent residue than is allowed of the corresponding solvents in spice oleoresins under applicable food additive regulations in parts 170 through 189 (see § 73.615(b)). Total chlorinated solvents are limited to 30 ppm (mg/kg) (see §§ 173.230, 173.255, and 173.290). Through the extraction process, ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene may end up as a residue of, and therefore an impurity in, the color additive “turmeric oleoresin.” While these solvents may end up as an impurity in the color additive “turmeric oleoresin,” they are not color additives themselves in § 73.615. Therefore, we are denying the petition's request to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of approved extractants in § 73.615 under section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act. As discussed in section II.A of this document, the Delaney Clause is applicable to color additives but not to impurities in a color additive.
V. Comments Related to the Petition
FDA received several comments in response to the notification of petition and the reopening of the comment period. Most comments expressed general support for the petition's requested revocation of the provisions allowing for the use of these solvents in foods. Some comments addressed matters outside the scope of this petition, and some comments were duplicate submissions.
We summarize and respond to relevant portions of comments in this final order. We have numbered each comment to help distinguish between different comments. We have grouped similar comments together under the same number, and, in some cases, we have separated different issues discussed in the same comment and designated them as distinct comments for purposes of our responses. The number assigned to each comment is for organizational purposes only and does not signify the comment's value,
(
printed page 72418)
importance, or the order in which it was submitted.
(Comment 1) One comment stated that chlorinated solvents are no longer used for the manufacture of color additives. The comment further encouraged FDA to take this opportunity to consider removing ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene as extraction solvents, as well as methylene chloride as a diluent in inks for marking fruits and vegetables based on the abandonment of these authorized uses.
(Response 1) We did not consider abandonment for the approved uses of these solvents as part of our evaluation of this petition because the petition is based on the Delaney Clause. We note, however, that elsewhere in this issue of the
Federal Register
, we have published a final order in response to CAP 5C0340, submitted by the International Association of Color Manufacturers, partially granting that petition and amending the color additive regulations to no longer provide for the extraction solvent uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene which are covered by this petition because these uses have been abandoned.
(Comment 2) Some comments raised EPA's proposed actions to eliminate or restrict the use of trichloroethylene and methylene chloride under the Toxic Substances Control Act or otherwise noted uses(s) of a chlorinated solvent that would be under EPA's jurisdiction.
(Response 2) While FDA and EPA may both regulate a particular substance, each agency regulates the uses of substances under its own applicable legal authority.
(Comment 3) Several comments expressed support for the removal of the authorizations for the use of these solvents from our color additive regulations. Some comments stated that these authorizations should be removed because there are alternatives.
(Response 3) We are taking this action to revoke the authorization for the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables, because the color additive use of this solvent is deemed unsafe under the Delaney Clause. The existence of alternatives is not a factor in determining whether a color additive is safe under either the Delaney Clause or the general safety clause (see section 721(b)(5)(B) of the FD&C Act).
(Comment 4) Some comments mentioned other substances that FDA should also review for removal from our color additive regulations.
(Response 4) This color additive petition requests the removal of the three specified solvents from §§ 73.1, 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. Therefore, these comments are outside the scope of this order.
(Comment 5) Some comments discussed the regulatory status of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene in other countries and questioned how FDA could continue to allow these substances in the U.S. food supply.
(Response 5) FDA's regulatory decisions are based on its own assessments of the available scientific information supporting the safety of color additives and on the statutory and regulatory framework in the United States.
(Comment 6) One comment expressed support for the petition and discussed evidence related to the use of these solvents and potential negative health impacts to humans. The comment cited certain studies to support their claims.
(Response 6) The petition's request is based on the Delaney Clause, and therefore our review of these solvents is based on the Delaney Clause. If the Delaney Clause applies, regardless of the safety of this use under the general safety clause, such an additive may not “be deemed to be safe” as a matter of law. Therefore, under the Delany Clause, FDA must revoke the authorization for the color additive use of methylene chloride. By contrast, ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene are not color additives in §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615, but rather they are impurities in those color additives. Therefore, we are denying the petition's request to revoke these authorizations, and any further review is outside the scope of this order responding to the petition.
VI. Conclusion
Ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene have been shown to cause cancer in laboratory animals. Under the Delaney Clause, this finding of carcinogenicity renders a color additive “unsafe” as a matter of law. Therefore, FDA is revoking the authorization for methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. We are amending § 73.1 as set forth in this document.
Our revocation of this authorization is based on a finding under the Delaney Clause that methylene chloride can induce cancer in animals. It is not based on a finding that the intended use is no longer safe under the general safety clause. Upon the effective date of this order (see
DATES
), the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables is no longer authorized. FDA is revoking this authorization in a manner consistent with its international obligations. This decision is consistent with the United States' long-standing Appropriate Level of Protection regarding carcinogenic additives in food, which seeks to eliminate exposure to additives that have been found to induce cancer in man or animals.
The Delaney Clause is applicable to the color additive itself but not to constituents or impurities in the additive. Residues of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene, when used as an extractant for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, may end up as an impurity in the color additive and would be considered an impurity in the color additive, not a color additive itself. The Delaney Clause applies to color additives, and not to impurities in a color additive. Because the Delaney Clause does not provide a basis for removing these authorizations, FDA is denying the petition's request to remove the authorized uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene in §§ 73.30, 73.345, and 73.615. We note, however, that elsewhere in this issue of the
Federal Register
, we have published a final order amending the color additive regulations to no longer provide for these uses of ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene because these uses have been abandoned. Therefore, FDA is taking all of the actions requested by the petitioners.
VII. Public Disclosure
In accordance with § 71.15 (
21 CFR 71.15
), the petition and the documents that we considered and relied upon in reaching our decision to approve the petition in part and to deny the petition in part will be made available for public disclosure (see
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
). As provided in § 71.15, we will delete from the documents any materials that are not available for public disclosure. As stated in the notification of filing for CAP 4C0327, the petition is available in the docket.
VIII. Analysis of Environmental Impacts
As stated in the January 11, 2024,
Federal Register
notification of petition for CAP 4C0327 (
89 FR 1856
), the petitioner claimed that this action is categorically excluded under § 25.32(m) (
21 CFR 25.32(m)
) because it constitutes an action to prohibit or otherwise
(
printed page 72419)
restrict or reduce the use of a substance in food, food packaging, or cosmetics. We further stated that, if FDA determines a categorical exclusion applies, neither an environmental assessment nor an environmental impact statement is required. We did not receive any new information or comments regarding this claim of categorical exclusion. We considered the petitioner's claim of categorical exclusion and determined that this action is categorically excluded under § 25.32(m) (Ref. 12). Therefore, neither an environmental assessment nor an environmental impact statement is required.
IX. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995
This order contains no collection of information. Therefore, clearance by the Office of Management and Budget under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 is not required.
X. Objections
This order is effective as shown in the
DATES
section, except as to any provisions that may be stayed by the filing of proper objections. If you will be adversely affected by one or more provisions of this regulation, you may file with the Dockets Management Staff (see
ADDRESSES
) either electronic or written objections. You must separately number each objection, and within each numbered objection you must specify with particularity the provision(s) to which you object and the grounds for your objection. Within each numbered objection, you must specifically state whether you are requesting a hearing on the particular provision that you specify in that numbered objection. If you do not request a hearing for any particular objection, you waive the right to a hearing on that objection. If you request a hearing, your objection must include a detailed description and analysis of the specific factual information you intend to present in support of the objection in the event that a hearing is held. If you do not include such a description and analysis for any particular objection, you waive the right to a hearing on the objection.
Any objections received in response to the regulation may be seen in the Dockets Management Staff office between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, and will be posted to the docket at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
We will publish notice of the objections that we have received or lack thereof in the
Federal Register
.

Office of Foreign Assets Control
AGENCY:
Office of Foreign Assets Control, Treasury.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is publishing the names of one or more persons and vessels that have been placed on OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) based on OFAC's determination that one or more applicable legal criteria were satisfied. All property and interests in property subject to U.S. jurisdiction of these persons are blocked, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with them. The vessels placed on the SDN List have been identified as property in which a blocked person has an interest.
DATES:
This action was issued on April 15, 2026. See
Supplementary Information
for relevant dates.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission
17 CFR Part 38
AGENCY:
Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
ACTION:
Interpretation.
SUMMARY:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“Commission” or “CFTC”) is issuing an interpretation of the requirement that designated contract markets (“DCMs”) provide competitive, open, fair, and impartial access to their members and persons with trading privileges under Commission Regulation 38.151(b) (“Impartial Access Requirements”). Specifically, this final interpretive guidance is being issued to inform the public of the Commission's views on the Impartial Access Requirements that should be guiding exchanges' selections of access criteria. The Commission issues this interpretive guidance after a significant amount of time and effort overseeing the listing and trading of event contracts and other financial assets, as well as monitoring DCM access requirements.
DATES:
Effective November 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Tyler S. Badgley, General Counsel, Office of the General Counsel, and Aaron M. Levine, Deputy General Counsel for Regulation,
rulemaking@cftc.gov
,
(202) 418-5000, Office of the General Counsel, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette
(
printed page 72408)
Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581; Cameron Sinsheimer, Counselor, Office of the General Counsel, Commodity Futures Trading Commission,
rulemaking@cftc.gov
,
(646) 746-3928, 290 Broadway, 6th Floor, New York, NY 10007; and Roger Smith, Associate Chief Counsel,
rsmith@cftc.gov
,
(202) 418-5344, Division of Market Oversight, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, 77 West Jackson Blvd., Suite 800, Chicago, IL 60604.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A core component of the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”)
[
1
]
is the requirement that DCMs provide competitive, open, fair, and impartial access to their members and persons with trading privileges. This measure prevents the inappropriate use of discriminatory access as a competitive tool against market participants. Moreover, it benefits DCMs and national markets by increasing overall liquidity and by maximizing risk management opportunities and price- and information-discovery functions.
The Commission is issuing this interpretive guidance to share with DCMs and their affiliates and partners certain views based on staff's experience overseeing the listing and trading of event contracts and other financial assets as well as monitoring DCMs' access requirements.
This final interpretive guidance is being issued to inform the public of the Commission's views on the Impartial Access Requirements that should be guiding exchanges' selections of access criteria.
II. Regulatory Framework Requiring Impartial Access
DCMs must comply with 23 statutory Core Principles set forth in the CEA,
[
2
]
as well as applicable CFTC rules and regulations.
[
3
]
The Core Principles for DCMs reflect the important role that these exchanges play in promoting the integrity of derivatives markets by, among other things, establishing and enforcing rules for trading on the DCM—including setting open and impartial access criteria—and monitoring trading activity.
Core Principle 2 of the CEA provides that a DCM “shall establish, monitor, and enforce compliance with the rules of the [DCM], including . . . access requirements.”
[
4
]
Core Principle 9 requires a DCM to “provide a competitive, open, and efficient market and mechanism for executing transactions that protects the price discovery process of trading in the centralized market of the board of trade.”
[
5
]
Specifically, a DCM “must provide its members, persons with trading privileges, and independent software vendors with impartial access to its markets and services, including . . . [a]ccess criteria that are impartial, transparent, and applied in a non-discriminatory manner.”
[
6
]
A DCM “must establish and impartially enforce rules governing denials, suspensions, and revocations of a member's and a person with trading privileges' access privileges to the designated contract market, including when such actions are part of a disciplinary or emergency action by the designated contract market.”
[
7
]
III. General Impartial Access Principles
In 2012, the Commission explained that “impartial access rules are necessary in order to prevent the use of discriminatory access requirements as a competitive tool against certain participants.”
[
8
]
To achieve this goal, the Commission has set forth basic principles that should guide regulated entities in developing access criteria. “In particular, access to a DCM should be based on the financial and operational soundness of a participant, not on factors that could bar access and result in discriminatory access or act as a barrier to entry.”
[
9
]
Adopting fair and evenhanded access standards benefits both DCMs and their members. For example, “granting impartial access to participants that satisfy a DCM's access requirements will likely enhance the DCM's liquidity and the overall transparency of the swaps and futures markets.”
[
10
]
A guiding principle is that “DCMs may establish different categories of market participants, but may not discriminate within a particular category.”
[
11
]
As a general matter, the Commission believes that discriminatory limitations on participation affects the overall health and efficiency of a market. When a DCM restricts access or disincentivizes participation for broad categories of otherwise financially or operationally sound participants, market liquidity may be diminished. Reduced liquidity, in turn, may result in less robust price discovery. This degradation of pricing and market efficiency may then lead to increased volatility, as fewer participants are available in the ordinary course to absorb and respond to market shocks. Ultimately, these effects could undermine a DCM's ability to function as an effective marketplace for trading and risk management.
As such, the Commission believes that market participants seeking to access a DCM must be evaluated against criteria that are clearly defined, published in advance, and applied uniformly. These standards should ensure that every participant is aware of the requirements and can prepare accordingly, fostering a fair environment for access to the DCM. Access criteria that are opaque, arbitrary, or unrelated to the financial and operational soundness of a participant undermine the principles of impartial access under Commission Regulation 38.151. Therefore, the Commission believes that when objective and transparent financial and operational eligibility requirements are met, DCMs have an obligation to grant access without bias. This approach supports a competitive and robust derivatives market that allows a wide range of participants to contribute to market liquidity.
Previously, when market trends and behavior have implicated impartial access concerns, the Commission has responded by releasing guidance to regulated entities. For example, in 2011, the Commission proposed placing significant requirements on swap execution facilities (“SEFs”) to ensure impartial access, resulting in a final rule promulgated in 2013.
[
12
]
Also in 2013, Division of Market Oversight, the Division of Clearing and Risk, and the Division of Swap Dealer and Intermediary Oversight (now the Market Participants Division) published a guidance document addressing certain trading restraints or “enablement mechanisms” implemented by certain SEFs.
[
13
]
Earlier this year, the Commission released a staff letter
(
printed page 72409)
setting forth guidelines for DCMs in setting comparable fee structures in incentive programs.
[
14
]
IV. Access Criteria Based On Geographic Location
The Commission is aware that some DCMs have adopted access criteria that restrict access to certain event contract markets based on prospective traders' location or residence.
The CEA and Commission Regulations generally do not permit a DCM to limit access based on the location of an otherwise eligible market participant within the United States.
[
15
]
In enacting the CEA, Congress specifically identified a “national public interest” in federal regulation of derivatives markets because those markets “provid[e] a means for managing and assuming price risks, discovering prices, or disseminating pricing information through trading in liquid, fair and financially secure trading facilities.”
[
16
]
Derivatives markets must operate on a uniform basis at a national scale in order to achieve the CEA's purpose.
As noted above, DCMs may not implement access criteria that intentionally exclude or discourage participation from market participants who otherwise meet eligibility requirements. When a DCM restricts access based on domestic geographic location—permitting participants from one region or State within the United States while barring those from another—it excludes otherwise eligible individuals. Such selective restrictions undermine the principle of impartial access, as they do not uniformly apply to all similarly situated (in terms of financial or operational soundness) eligible market participants and arbitrarily differentiate between such market participants based solely on their location.
Limiting access by geographic location raises significant concerns for both financial integrity and risk management within derivatives markets. For instance, if a market participant establishes a position in a region where access is allowed but subsequently travels to a location where access is restricted, that participant would be unable to manage their position. That participant may not be able to adequately manage their position, respond to market events, or meet margin calls. When participants are unable to manage their positions or meet margin calls due to geographic restrictions, forced liquidations may occur. This process can generate losses for both the futures commission merchants and clearing organizations involved, ultimately heightening systemic risk across the derivatives and broader financial markets. As such, the resulting disruption may affect not only individual participants, but also the relevant market as a whole, undermining its integrity and efficiency.
Limiting access based on location also detracts from a DCM's price-discovery function and overall efficiency. In certain markets, barring residents of certain States or regions from participating may cause distortions because States and regions have differently composed economies. Restricting access in States or regions that are home to large concentrations of high-volume traders (
e.g.,
where market making entities are located) is likely to introduce liquidity concerns, and such consequences may disproportionately affect particular contracts. This, in turn, would reduce overall volume and lead to wider bid-ask spreads, raising the cost of trading for all participants.
Location-based restrictions may also fragment a national pool of liquidity. Fragmentation may impede arbitrage between related contracts or between derivatives and their underlying cash markets when relevant participants cannot access all markets from their location. Under those circumstances, temporary price discrepancies could persist for longer, and participants may face greater basis risk if available hedges track their exposures less closely.
Further, location-based restrictions may concentrate trading activity among a smaller or less diverse set of participants. A broader participant base can supply different time horizons, risk tolerances, information, and trading strategies, which may make liquidity more resilient when conditions change. Removing an entire jurisdiction could increase dependence on a more limited group of market participants, particularly when the excluded jurisdiction accounts for meaningful activity. Sports-related contracts illustrate the point. Insomuch as particular contracts attract disproportionately regional interest (
e.g.,
whether a home team advances to its playoffs), excluding such regions could decrease the contracts' overall liquidity.
Moreover, location-based access restrictions undermine hedging opportunities and DCMs' price and information-discovery functions in additional ways when the excluded jurisdiction contains participants with relevant commercial experience, localized exposure or knowledge, or significant trading activity. For example, the exclusion of a region prone to extreme weather events from weather-related contracts would deprive that region's traders of a mechanism to hedge their exposures to such weather events. Likewise, to the extent a restriction excludes energy producers, merchants, or traders located in a region with substantial energy production and infrastructure, it could limit their ability to hedge production, shipping, and storage-related exposures, and could remove price signals from such hedging, arbitrages, or speculative activity. Similar effects may arise in other economically specialized areas, at least to some extent, including for example areas with concentrations of financial, agricultural, cultural, and technological expertise.
Election markets may be particularly sensitive to harms stemming from geographic access restrictions. Some statewide and more localized election markets may generate the most volume and/or knowledge from residents of the State or locality where the election takes place. Accordingly, restricting access to a particular State's residents could severely undercut volume and/or the information-discovery function of any market concerning an election in that State. This is especially problematic given election contract markets' uniquely valuable information-discovery role, with benefits accruing nationwide even while the most informed trading may be sourced on a State or local basis. Such effects may
(
printed page 72410)
extend beyond the immediate trading population because third parties, including media organizations and other observers, may use election-contract prices as one source of information about expected outcomes.
For these reasons, the Commission believes that geographic access restrictions are inconsistent with the CEA and Commission rules and regulations. The Commission expects DCMs to evaluate their access criteria, exchange rules, and intermediary access arrangements to ensure compliance.
The Office of Management and Budget has determined that this action is not a significant regulatory action as defined in
Executive Order 12866
, as amended, and therefore it was not subject to
Executive Order 12866
review.
Issued in Washington, DC, on November 5, 2026, by the Commission.
Christopher Kirkpatrick,
Secretary of the Commission.

AGENCY:
Office of Foreign Assets Control, Treasury.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is publishing the name of one or more persons that have been placed on OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) based on OFAC's determination that one or more applicable legal criteria were satisfied. All property and interests in property subject to U.S. jurisdiction of these persons are blocked, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with them.
DATES:
This action was issued on November 5, 2026. See
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
for relevant dates.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
OFAC: Associate Director for Global Targeting, 202-622-2420; Assistant Director for Licensing, 202-622-2480; Assistant Director for Sanctions Compliance, 202-622-2490; or
https://ofac.treasury.gov/​contact-ofac
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

https://ofac.treasury.gov
.
