43 CFR Part 1600
[A2407-014-004-065516, #O2509-014-004-125222.1]
RIN 1004-AF53
AGENCY:
Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The BLM proposes to amend existing regulations that establish the procedures to prepare, revise, or amend land use plans pursuant to the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, as amended (FLPMA). We solicit comment on all aspects of this proposed rule.
DATES:
Send your comments on this proposed rule to the BLM on or before January 11, 2027. The BLM is not obligated to consider any comments received after this date in making its decision on the final rule.
If you wish to comment on the information-collection requirements in this proposed rule, please note that the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) is required to make a decision concerning the information-collections contained in this proposed rule between 30 and 60 days after publication of this
(
printed page 72496)
proposed rule in the
Federal Register
. Therefore, comments should be submitted to OMB by December 10, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by one of the following methods:
Mail, personal, or messenger delivery:
U.S. Department of the Interior, Director (630), Bureau of Land Management, 1849 C St. NW, Room 5646, Washington, DC 20240, Attention: 1004-AF53.
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
In the Search box, enter “BLM-2026-0298” and click the “Search” button. Follow the instructions at this website. Pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act at
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of the proposed rule is also available on the Federal eRulemaking Portal.
Comments on Information-Collection Requirements:
Written comments and recommendations for the information-collection requirements should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
Find this information-collection by selecting “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stacie McIntosh, Deputy Assistant Director of Resources and Planning, The BLM Directorate of Resources and Planning, Division of Decision Support, Planning, and NEPA, by phone at (208) 373-3818, or by email at
blm_hq_planningrule@blm.gov
for information relating to the BLM planning program and information about the proposed rule. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The BLM manages more than 245 million acres of land, the most of any Federal agency. This land, known as the National System of Public Lands, is primarily located in 12 Western states, including Alaska. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation.
FLPMA is the BLM's “organic act” that directs management of the public lands on the basis of multiple-use and sustained yield, unless otherwise specified by law (
43 U.S.C. 1732(a)
). Multiple use as defined in FLPMA “means the management of the public lands and their various resource values so that they are utilized in the combination that will best meet the present and future needs of the American people; making the most judicious use of the land for some or all of these resources or related services over areas large enough to provide sufficient latitude for periodic adjustments in use to conform to changing needs and conditions; the use of some land for less than all of the resources; a combination of balanced and diverse resource uses that takes into account the long-term needs of future generations for renewable and nonrenewable resources, including, but not limited to, recreation, range, timber, minerals, watershed, wildlife and fish, and natural scenic, scientific and historical values; and harmonious and coordinated management of the various resources without permanent impairment of the productivity of the land and the quality of the environment with consideration being given to the relative values of the resources and not necessarily to the combination of uses that will give the greatest economic return or the greatest unit output” (
43 U.S.C. 1702(c)
). FLPMA defines “public lands” as “any land and interest in land owned by the United States within the several States and administered by the Secretary of the Interior through the Bureau of Land Management, without regard to how the United States acquired ownership” (
43 U.S.C. 1702(e)
). FLPMA defines “sustained yield” to mean “the achievement and maintenance in perpetuity of a high-level annual or regular periodic output of the various renewable resources of the public lands consistent with multiple use” (
43 U.S.C. 1702(h)
).
Section 202 of FLPMA (
43 U.S.C. 1712
) directs the Secretary of the Interior to “develop, maintain, and, when appropriate, revise land use plans which provide by tracts or areas for the use of the public lands” (
43 U.S.C. 1712(a)
) and outlines requirements for developing and revising land use plans. Section 202(f) (
43 U.S.C. 1712(f)
) directs the Secretary of the Interior, by regulation, to “establish procedures . . . to give Federal, State, and local governments and the public, adequate notice and opportunity to comment upon and participate in the formulation of plans and programs relating to the management of the public lands.”
The BLM administers its planning program under the regulations at
Title 43 Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) part 1600,
Planning, Programming, Budgeting.
The BLM first developed land use planning regulations in 1979 (
44 FR 46386
, August 7, 1979). These regulations established the term “resource management plan” for the land use plans directed by FLPMA, to replace the then-existing “management framework plans.” The BLM made significant revisions to the regulations in 1983 to clarify the planning process and “eliminate burdensome, outdated, and unneeded provisions” (
48 FR 20364
, May 5, 1983) and revised them again in 2005 to make clear the role of cooperating agencies in the land use planning process and to emphasize the importance of working with Federal and State agencies and local and tribal governments through cooperating agency relationships in developing, amending, and revising the BLM's resource management plans (
70 FR 14561
, March 23, 2005). The BLM conducted a substantial revision to the land use planning regulations in 2016 (
70 FR 89580
, December 12, 2016) which was subsequently disapproved under the Congressional Review Act (
82 FR 60554
, December 21, 2017). In 2024, the BLM revised the portion of the planning regulations governing the designation and management of areas of critical environmental concern,
43 CFR 1610.7-2
(
89 FR 40308
, May 9, 2024). In 2026, the BLM completed a deregulatory rulemaking process regarding the designation and management of areas of critical environmental concern, issuing a final rule that returned the BLM to the previous text of this regulation (
91 FR 25787
, May 12, 2026).
This proposed rule is intended to streamline, modernize, and better align the BLM's land use planning process with section 202 of FLPMA (
43 U.S.C. 1712
). The proposed rule would eliminate procedures not required by statute that impose delays and roadblocks and remove unnecessary program-specific procedures that could be better addressed in other parts of the regulations while improving the BLM's coordination with Federal, State, and local governments, and tribes. The proposed rule would also improve the readability of the planning regulations.
II. Section-by-Section Discussion
The proposed rule would revise part 1600, including subparts 1601 (Planning) and 1610 (Resource Management Planning), and establish a new subpart at 1611 (Amending Land Use Plans to Address Emergencies). The BLM is proposing a number of minor changes to modernize language, clarify ambiguities, and eliminate redundancies.
(
printed page 72497)
The proposed rule includes revisions to section designations and organization of the provisions to bring the proposed regulations into compliance with the Office of the Federal Register's Document Drafting Handbook requirements. This includes the removal of hyphens in the existing section designations and adding structural symmetry in which we insert some [Reserved] sections to fill in gaps in the CFR numbering.
The BLM also proposes the following substantive changes to individual sections of Part 1600.
Part 1600—Planning, Programming, Budgeting
The BLM is proposing to remove “programming” and “budgeting” from the title of this part to accurately reflect that the existing and proposed regulations do not address agency programming or budgeting.
Subpart 1601—Planning
Section 1601.0-1 Purpose
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.10 and revise it to clarify land use planning terminology consistent with BLM practice and to include specific direction from FLPMA for the establishment of land use plans.
In § 1601.10 and throughout these proposed regulatory changes, the BLM is proposing revisions to use consistent terminology concerning the “development, revision, amendment, and maintenance” of land use plans. The “development” of a land use plan occurs when BLM first establishes a land use plan for an area of public lands or first establishes a land use plan under new authority, such as for lands within the boundaries of a new area designated for special management by Congress. The “revision” of a land use plan occurs when the BLM makes substantial changes to the scope of the decisions for public lands currently managed under a land use plan. The “amendment” of a land use plan occurs when the BLM makes limited changes to a land use plan. The BLM is proposing to clarify that “maintenance” of a land use plan occurs when the BLM corrects errors and is limited to further refining the documentation of a decision of the approved plan. These corrections and refinement of documentation must not result in an expansion in the scope of resource uses or restrictions or change the decisions. Maintenance of land use plans is also being proposed to document land use or restrictions of uses on the public lands established by law or Presidential Proclamation.
The BLM is also proposing to remove the phrase “use of existing plans” to clarify that the purpose of these regulations is to provide the process for approving or changing land use plans, not the procedures for implementing land use plans.
Section 1601.0-2 Objective
Section 1601.0-2 establishes the objective of land use planning. The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.20 and edit it to clarify that land use plans “provide by tracts or areas for the use of the public lands” (
43 U.S.C. 1712
) and to remove clauses not necessary in regulation. The BLM is also proposing to relocate the last sentence in existing § 1601.0-2 that explains that “resource management plans are designed to guide and control future management actions and the development of subsequent, more detailed and limited scope plans for resources and uses” to a new proposed § 1610.10, “Land use plans.” The intent of this section is to state the objective of these regulations not the resource management plans themselves.
Section 1601.0-3 Authority
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.30 and make minor changes to include all sections of FLPMA that authorize establishing these land use planning regulations and to remove the reference to the Public Rangelands Improvement Act of 1978 because it does not provide authority for land use planning procedures. With this proposed regulatory revision, the BLM is removing all references to non-planning requirements from the part 1600 regulations and has removed all regulations specific to coal and mining from this part. With these proposed changes, the Federal Coal Leasing Amendments Act of 1976 and the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 are not specific authority for this Part of the regulations. While these other statutes provide authority relevant to the BLM's management of the public lands, they are not necessary in this section. Moreover, as described in more detail in the associated sections below, the BLM is proposing to relocate portions of existing §§ 1610.5-7(c) and 1610.2(j) and (k) to
43 CFR 3420
. These changes also reduce barriers to efficiently completing land use plans by eliminating unnecessary references.
Section 1601.0-4 Responsibilities
The BLM is proposing to remove § 1601.0-4 because it provides internal BLM procedures and delegations that are more appropriate in the BLM's delegation manual and policy and are not required by statute. Removal of this section reduces the regulatory burden on the BLM and allows State Directors to manage internal work for land use planning as appropriate for their State.
Section 1601.0-5 Definitions
The BLM is proposing to remove § 1601.0-5 to remove definitions in this section that are already provided in statute (
e.g.,
repetition of FLPMA's definition of `multiple use'); to remove terminology no longer used in these proposed regulations due to other changes the BLM is proposing (
e.g.,
`resource area or field office'); and, where relevant, to relocate regulatory requirements in the existing `definitions' section (
e.g.,
`conformity or conformance') that the BLM wants to retain to other sections of the regulations. Removal of this section substantially streamlines the planning regulations and reduces redundancies that add length and not clarity to the existing regulatory procedures.
Section 1601.0-6 Environmental Impact Statement
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.40, retitle it to “Environmental compliance,” and to remove the existing language in this section that requires the BLM to prepare an environmental impact statement every time the BLM develops or revises a plan. Instead, the BLM would be guided by the Department of the Interior's NEPA procedures,
91 FR 8738
(February 24, 2026) to ensure that it complies with NEPA when completing land use planning. This proposed change is deregulatory and it would not prevent the BLM from preparing an environmental impact statement for a plan revision; rather, it would allow the BLM to determine how best to comply with NEPA during land use planning, consistent with applicable law and agency NEPA procedures and the specific facts of the individual planning process the BLM is undertaking consistent with the procedures in these regulations.
Section 1601.0-7 Scope
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.50 and edit it for clarity, including changes to reflect the terminology the BLM has historically used for land use planning work. The BLM is specifically proposing to add language to paragraph (a) to clarify that these regulations apply only to BLM-administered lands that are subject to section 202 of FLPMA. Thus, for example, these regulations do not apply to public lands on the north slope of Alaska within the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska because those lands are
(
printed page 72498)
exempt from section 202 of FLPMA per the Naval Petroleum Reserves Production Act of 1976.
Section 1601.0-8 Principles
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1601.60 and edit it for clarity, including changes to incorporate terminology for planning work to align more consistently with language in sections 103 and 202 of FLPMA. The BLM proposes removing the statement regarding the scope of impacts because the scope of impacts is driven by the BLM's determination of what is necessary to understand significance and make an informed decision for compliance with NEPA.
Section 1601.70 Administrative Remedy
The BLM is proposing a new § 1601.70 to relocate and clarify existing regulatory direction in existing § 1610.5-2(b) that a land use plan decision is the final decision of the Department of the Interior and not subject to appeal or review to the Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA), including the Interior Board of Land Appeals. The proposed language adding “and is not reviewable by the Office of Hearings and Appeals” is not a substantive change but merely clarifies the existing scope of OHA's jurisdiction.
Subpart 1610—Resource Management Planning
The BLM is proposing an editorial change to the title of this subpart to restore use of the term “land use planning” as it appears in FLPMA rather than continuing to refer to new terminology in the regulations of “resource management planning.”
Section 1610.1 Resource Management Planning Guidance
The BLM is proposing to remove existing § 1610.1 because it provides internal BLM procedures and delegations that are more appropriate in the BLM's delegation manual and policy and are not required by statute. For example, the current regulations instruct
how
the State Director would communicate instructions to a Field Manager regarding the planning effort and describe the permissive scope of an interdisciplinary team. This internal process is not required by law or necessary or appropriate for inclusion in the regulations. The early identification of key information during the planning process, such as information needed for analysis, is also duplicative of proposed § 1610.41, which would require the BLM to assemble resource, environmental, social, economic, and institutional data when preparing for planning. The BLM would still require early identification of key information, but this change eliminates internal workload procedures that are more appropriate for policy.
Removing this section also removes the existing regulatory direction that a resource management plan be prepared and maintained on a resource or field office areas basis, unless the State Director authorizes a more appropriate area. While under the current regulations the State Director may determine the appropriate planning area, this change removes internal delegations that are more appropriate for policy and provides more flexibility for the BLM to determine a planning area boundary that is appropriate for the particular planning effort.
Additionally, the BLM is proposing a new section to be located at 1610.10 called “Land use plans” which would incorporate language from FLPMA's definition of land use plans and clarify the role and content of those plans. To clarify and ensure consistency across the BLM, paragraph (a) of this proposed section provides that land use plans consist of: (1) desired resource use and condition objectives, (2) designations identified by statute, regulation, or national policy of land areas for exclusive purposes or uses (
e.g.,
establishment of areas of critical environmental concern under FLPMA; establishment of herd management areas under BLM regulations for Protection, Management, and Control of Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros at
43 CFR 4710.1
; or establishment of corridor designations for BLM scenic and backcountry byways, consistent with BLM's Byways Handbook 8357-1), (3) lands allocated for allowable uses, and (4) management direction for the general management practices or program constraints needed to achieve the resource use and condition objectives. Language in existing § 1601.0-5(n)(8) providing that the BLM will establish intervals and standards for monitoring and evaluating the plan to determine the effectiveness of the plan and the need for amendment or revision is proposed for relocation to paragraph (b) of this proposed section. Most of the concepts in this section are currently scattered across the existing planning regulations, including the definition section. This proposed section would also clarify that BLM does not generally make implementation-level decisions through the land use planning process, which is consistent with the BLM's practice. Direction in the existing regulations that approval of land use plans is the responsibility of State Directors would be clarified and added to paragraph (c) of this proposed section. Finally, paragraph (d) would clarify that land use plans are titled as resource management plans to reduce any confusion about these two terms and to ensure consistent use of these terms across the BLM.
Section 1610.2 Public Participation
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.20 and edit it to outline procedures for meaningful participation opportunities consistent with FLPMA section 202(a), which requires the BLM to develop and revise land use plans “with public involvement” and section 309(e) which requires the BLM by regulation, to establish “procedures, including public hearings where appropriate, to give the Federal, State and local governments and the public adequate notice and an opportunity to comment upon the formulation of standards and criteria for, and to participate in, the preparation and execution of plans and programs for, and the management of, the public lands” while greatly reducing internal administrative workflows and overburdensome procedures that were not providing meaningful benefits to the process.
The BLM is proposing to remove references to NEPA in this section and throughout the proposed rule to allow the BLM to comply with NEPA as appropriate for the individual planning effort. The BLM is also proposing to remove the requirement to publish notice in the
Federal Register
at the initiation of the planning process and the existing requirement for public review of the proposed planning criteria and a 30-day public comment period on any significant changes made to a proposed plan or amendment prior to issuing a decision. The 90-day public comment period requirement for all draft land use plans, revisions and amendments supported by environmental impact statements in existing § 1610.2(e) is also proposed for removal. A 90-day comment period is not required by statute and will make it more difficult for the BLM to meet the statutory deadlines set by NEPA, as amended (
42 U.S.C. 4336a(g)
), including the direction to complete an environmental assessment in one year and an environmental impact statement in two years, unless the deadlines are extended in accordance with that Act.
Consistent with direction in section 202 of FLPMA and 309(e), the BLM would continue to provide opportunities for public involvement, but the proposed rule would allow greater flexibility to determine public
(
printed page 72499)
participation that is appropriate to the areas and people involved in the specific planning process. The BLM is proposing that opportunity for public participation, at a minimum, must be provided at the outset of the planning process (consistent with proposed § 1610.42) and the BLM would provide a public involvement opportunity through the protest process upon publication of a proposed plan, revision, or amendment (consistent with proposed § 1610.51). The BLM proposes to retain a minimum 30-calendar-day comment period when a public comment period is required (consistent with proposed § 1610.20(a)(1)) or the BLM elects to provide one, and an ability to extend the comment period. Under proposed paragraph (b)(1), an extension may not exceed an additional 30-calendar-days to help ensure BLM can meet the deadlines established in NEPA. The current regulations require a greater number of minimum required public comment periods and can result in delays to the planning process that also do not benefit informed decision-making. For example, the current regulations require planning efforts, including amendments, that are supported by environmental impact statements to hold a minimum of a 90-day public comment period on the draft plan. A 90-day minimum public comment period is more than double the public comment period formerly required under Council on Environmental Quality's regulations for implementing the procedural requirements of NEPA, which the Council on Environmental Quality rescinded (
91 FR 618
, January 8, 2026), and there is no corresponding requirement in either NEPA (
42 U.S.C. 4321-4347
) or the Department of the Interior's 2026 NEPA procedures (
91 FR 8
,
738
, February. 24, 2026). With the requirement to complete environmental impact statements in two years absent an extension (
42 U.S.C. 4336a(g)(1)
), a 90-day public comment period is burdensome to BLM's ability to comply with NEPA. Furthermore, use of a long comment period as reliance for quality public engagement is not always the right approach for each planning effort. The proposed procedures introduce flexibility to the process so that the BLM can formulate public involvement in a manner that appropriately supports the planning effort. The proposed text would allow the BLM the flexibility to determine for each planning effort if the minimum required public engagement would be adequate or what public engagement beyond the minimum required would best support the planning effort while also ensuring the BLM can meet our statutory requirements under NEPA for timely completion of analysis.
The BLM recognizes that its approach to providing opportunities for public involvement in the proposed rule represents a change from the approach in the existing rule. While both approaches are consistent with the requirements of FLPMA, based on its experience the BLM believes that its proposed approach is likely to provide greater flexibility to tailor the public participation process to each planning effort, reduce regulatory burdens, and allow the BLM to more efficiently meet other statutory requirements. The BLM specifically seeks public comment on these proposed changes and how the BLM can structure opportunities for public involvement, including public comment in a manner that meets BLM's statutory obligations, reduces regulatory burden and allows for completion of the planning process in an efficient manner consistent with all applicable laws.
The BLM is also proposing an option in paragraph (b)(2) of this section for a public meeting in lieu of a public comment period when permissible under other authorities—such as NEPA—and when adequate notice to the public is provided. This proposed paragraph does not prevent the BLM from offering both a public meeting and public comment period when deemed appropriate. This proposed paragraph provides flexibility for the BLM to streamline planning efforts when appropriate. For example, the BLM may need to conduct amendments to consider changes to land tenure decisions to allow small parcels of public lands to be made available for disposal, sometimes as small as a half-acre, to address unintentional trespass or sales to communities. A plan amendment of this nature is generally only of interest to the highly localized community, and a public meeting may provide for more engaging public involvement than a 30-day written comment period and allow the process to progress more quickly. The proposed paragraph opens flexibility to the BLM to avoid delays to planning efforts, particularly where there is only localized interest in the decision BLM is considering.
In order to focus these regulations on planning procedures, the BLM is proposing to remove paragraphs (j) and (k) of this section, which relate specifically to coal resources. The BLM planning regulations are not an appropriate location for this program-specific regulation, and it would decrease confusion by moving these coal related provisions to the program specific regulations. Specifically, the BLM proposes relocating the last three sentences of paragraph (j) to appear verbatim at the end of the current paragraph at
43 CFR 3420.1-4(e)(4)(i)
. The BLM also proposes relocating the second and third sentences in paragraph (k) and the three subsequent parts to
43 CFR 3420.1-5
verbatim, excepting the removal of the internal reference “§ 3420.1-5 of” from the relocated sentence as the cross-reference is no longer necessary. The BLM is proposing to remove the first sentences of paragraphs (j) and (k) because they are duplicative of existing regulations in part 3420. These proposed changes are not substantive and would not change existing practice.
Section 1610.3 Coordination With Other Federal Agencies, State and Local Governments, and Indian Tribes
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.30 and edit it to introduce the following subsections that clarify differences between coordination and consistency as required by FLPMA, and to make clear that these FLPMA responsibilities are separate from responsibilities of other authorities, such as involving government entities through NEPA's cooperating agency status.
Section 1610.3-1 Coordination of Planning Efforts
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.31 and make changes to better align this provision's description of the BLM's responsibilities for coordination during the land use planning process with the BLM's obligations under FLPMA section 202(c)(9). The proposed regulations provide a clear definition of coordination with other Federal agencies, State and local governments, and Tribes that is distinct to the BLM's land use planning process and is based on Congress's recognition that state, local, and tribal government entities play a unique and necessary role in land use planning. As stated by the Public Land Law Review Commission
[
1
]
in the 1970 Report to Congress:
[
2
]
“First, these
(
printed page 72500)
governments represent the people and institutions that will be most directly affected by Federal programs growing out of land use planning” (page 61). This intent is reflected in the proposed paragraph (a)(1), which explains that coordination in the planning process means inviting the participation of governmental entities regarding the general approach of the planning effort as representatives of people and institutions that are impacted by the BLM's management of public lands.
The BLM is also proposing to clarify the direction to consider plans of State and local governments and Indian tribes in this section. The BLM believes that the consideration of these plans is part of the coordination process that occurs during land use planning. The BLM would also clarify that the definition of “approved resource-related plans” in paragraph (b)(1) of this section includes approved resource-related “policies.” These proposed regulations also use the term “approved resource-related plans” or “plans” when referring to plans or policies adopted by State, local, and tribal governments in discussions at § 1610.41 “Preparing for planning”, § 1610.52 “Governor's consistency review”, and § 1610.53 “Local governments' consistency review.”
The BLM also proposes a terminology change from “officially approved and adopted resource related plans” to just “approved resource-related plans” based on changes in paragraph (b)(1) of this section that a plan must be “prepared and approved pursuant to and in accordance with authorization provided by State, local, or Tribal constitutions, legislation, or charters for the relevant governmental entity” and, as such, believes the qualifiers of “officially” and “adopted” as unnecessary. This change occurs throughout the regulatory text.
FLPMA's coordination requirements ensure the BLM coordinates its planning with the planning and management programs of other federal agencies, state and local governments, and tribes. While this coordination may inform consistency, FLPMA has a separate requirement that BLM land use plans be consistent with State and local plans to the maximum extent the Secretary finds consistent with Federal law and the purposes of FLPMA, as discussed in further detail below.
Section 1610.3-2 Consistency Requirements
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.32 and make general revisions to focus this section on consistency and complement changes proposed to other sections. The BLM is proposing specific changes to clarify that FLPMA's consistency requirements are distinct from the BLM's coordination responsibilities contained in proposed § 1610.31. To clarify that this section outlines procedures for how the BLM should seek consistency with State and local plans, the BLM is proposing to change the section title to “Seeking consistency with State and local plans.” The BLM has also made editorial revisions to the existing regulatory text to include the terms “to the maximum extent consistent with Federal law and the purposes of [the Federal Land Policy and Management Act]” when describing consistency with approved state and local resource related plans. This language more closely tracks section 202(c)(9) of FLPMA, which states, “[l]and use plans of the Secretary under this section shall be consistent with the State and local plans to the maximum extent [the Secretary] finds consistent with Federal law and the purposes of this Act.” The BLM is also clarifying in paragraph (a)(1) that BLM should seek consistency with plans of state and local governments “that are germane in the development of land use plans for public lands” (
43 U.S.C. 1712(c)(9)
).
The current regulations at § 1610.3-1(d)(1) direct the BLM to determine consistency with “other Federal agencies, State agencies, Indian tribes and local governments that may be affected.” The BLM proposes to remove consistency requirements from both other Federal agency plans and tribal plans because § 202(c)(9) of FLPMA provides that, to the maximum extent the Secretary finds consistent with Federal law and the purposes of FLPMA, land use plans “shall be consistent with State and local plans.”
43 U.S.C. 1712(c)(9)
. The BLM specifically requests comment on these proposed changes and the appropriate scope of consistency in these regulations, including those entities that should be included in the consistency review.
In clarifying that consistency obligations are distinct from coordination, the BLM is proposing to incorporate the definition of “consistency,” a principle identified in the 1970 Public Land Law Review Commission Report to Congress, which informed the development and passage of FLPMA. The Report stated, “As a general rule, no use of public land should be permitted which is prohibited by state or local zoning. There may be exceptions, however, and the federal agency should be authorized to allow such a use, but only when the agency makes a finding that overriding national interest requires the use.” (Public Land Law Review Commission,
One Third of the Nation's Land,
63 (1970)). The proposed changes to the definition of “consistency” clarify that the BLM would not allow uses on the public lands that would be prohibited under State or local laws or that would otherwise conflict with an approved resource-related plan of a State or local government, except when required by Federal law or it is in the national interest to do so. This clarification would not change the BLM's practice of continuing to work with State and local governments to manage the impacts of management on public lands, but the proposed rule clarifies how this consistency process would occur. The BLM also seeks to clarify that the definition of approved resource-related plans are plans and policies approved in accordance with State and local constitutions, legislation or charters.
The BLM is also proposing to relocate and revise the Governor's consistency review procedures in existing § 1610.3-2 to new proposed § 1610.52, which is described in more detail below. The BLM is also proposing a new § 1610.53 described below, which would establish a local government consistency review process.
Section 1610.4 Resource Management Planning Process
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.40, retitle it “Land use planning process,” and edit it to simplify the required steps of the land use planning process by removing unnecessary procedures for compliance with NEPA, emphasizing the importance of preparing for planning and outlining steps required to meet FLPMA's requirements. The BLM is also proposing to remove overly prescriptive procedures that present barriers to efficient completion of land use planning and regulatory requirements not directed by FLPMA. The BLM proposes as the new subsections of § 1610.40 a more streamlined planning process responsive to FLPMA's requirements that allows the BLM greater flexibility to conduct a land use planning process that is tailored to the scope of and specific issues presented in an individual planning effort.
Section 1610.4-1 Identification of Issues.
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.41, retitle it “Preparing for planning,” and to revise it to address three steps the BLM must
(
printed page 72501)
take to prepare for planning to provide a more informed and efficient planning process.
First, as described in proposed paragraph (a)(1), the BLM must gather and review its existing resource, environmental, social, and other relevant data and information. These edits remove the reference to collecting data at this point in the process, consistent with direction in section 202(c)(4) of FLPMA to “rely, to the extent it is available, on the inventory of the public lands, their resources, and other values on the existing inventories of public lands.”
Second, as described in proposed paragraph (a)(2), the BLM must request all relevant approved State and local government and Tribal plans. If any such government would like its plans to be considered during the BLM planning process, it must, within 45 days of the BLM's request, provide all relevant approved plans and a summary of the uses that the State, local, or Tribal government generally prohibits or restricts within its jurisdiction. The BLM should seek this information before the State Director identifies guidelines for the plan or revision and prior to the development of alternatives. This early outreach and information collection would engage these government entities earlier in the process and facilitate a stronger working relationship throughout the planning process, which would lead to a more efficient process. It would also provide more information early in the process where it is most useful to inform the planning process and associated environmental review.
Third, as described in proposed paragraph (a)(3) of this section, the BLM must document a planning area profile and analysis framework when developing or revising a land use plan. This profile and analysis framework would include information about current conditions, trends, forecasts for resources, resource uses, existing uses, social and economic uses, and other information about the area to inform the approach for the planning effort. The BLM would make this document publicly available for transparency.
Section 1610.4-2 Development of Planning Criteria
The BLM is proposing to remove this section from the regulations, eliminating the development of planning criteria as a distinct step in the planning process. The development of planning criteria adds additional time to the planning process and is overly prescriptive. The new direction in proposed § 1610.41(a)(3) to document and make publicly available a framework for analysis as part of preparing for planning would provide information that is more relevant and useful to the planning process earlier in the process.
Section 1610.42 Public Notice of Planning
The BLM is proposing a new § 1610.42, titled “Public notice of planning.” This new section requires the BLM to provide public notice when it initiates the development, revision or amendment of a land use plan and request public participation. This proposed new section and the proposed changes in public participation in § 1610.20 would remove extraneous requirements for multiple
Federal Register
notifications, allow for a more efficient planning process, ensure public participation early in the planning process where it is most helpful to the BLM, and allow the BLM to manage public notification and additional public involvement in a manner consistent with the scope of a planning effort.
Section 1610.4-3 Inventory Data and Information Collection
The BLM is proposing to relocate the direction in this section to proposed § 1610.41(a)(1) to clarify that the BLM assembles data to support a planning effort when preparing for planning.
Section 1610.4-4 Analysis of the Management Situation
The BLM is proposing to remove this subsection from the regulations because it is unnecessarily prescriptive and imposes procedure not required by FLPMA, and its removal will provide the BLM with more flexibility to compile this information for a particular planning effort. For example, subparts (a) through (i) identify a list of “factors to be considered” in identifying the issues and opportunities for a planning area that are more appropriate for policy to provide guidance on rather than a regulatorily established list. Additionally, the current regulations state that “the analysis of the management situation shall provide . . . the basis for formulating reasonable alternatives.” FLPMA provides no instruction for the formulation of alternatives and this procedure complicates the authorities under NEPA for the development of alternatives (
42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C)(iii)
). Proposed § 1610.41(a)(3) includes a requirement to document and make publicly available a planning area profile as part of preparing for planning, which the BLM believes would better inform the BLM's decision-making.
Section 1610.4-5 Formulation of Alternatives
The BLM is proposing to remove this section from the regulations, consistent with the overall intent of this deregulatory effort to remove procedures of other programs from the planning regulations and to reduce duplication, redundancy, confusion, and unnecessary regulation. The formulation of alternatives is governed by NEPA procedures and this section is duplicative of those procedures and unnecessary to repeat in the planning regulations since it does not establish any additional or planning-specific procedures. This direction for NEPA compliance in the planning regulations was developed based on the BLM's interpretation of its obligations under the Council on Environmental Quality's regulations in effect at the time. Since then, the Council on Environmental Quality has amended and, most recently, rescinded its regulations. Similarly, the Department of the Interior has updated its NEPA procedures, including by amending its own NEPA regulations. To avoid duplication and inconsistency, and to reduce confusion and ensure compliance with statutory requirements and Department of the Interior NEPA procedures, the BLM proposes to remove sections addressing NEPA compliance from these regulations. The BLM is required to comply with NEPA when developing, revising, or amending land use plans.
Section 1610.4-6 Estimation of Effects of Alternatives
The BLM is proposing to remove this section consistent with the overall intent of this deregulatory effort to remove procedures of other programs from the planning regulations and to reduce duplication, confusion, and unnecessary regulation. The estimation of effects of alternatives is governed by NEPA procedures. The existing regulations do not establish any additional or planning-specific procedures but instead repeat how the BLM will generally consider alternatives in an environmental impact statement or environmental assessment. Removing this section would eliminate duplication, create consistency with NEPA requirements, and reduce confusion.
Section 1610.4-7 Selection of Preferred Alternatives
The BLM is proposing to remove this section, consistent with the overall intent of this deregulatory effort to remove procedures for other BLM programs from the planning regulations
(
printed page 72502)
and to reduce duplication, confusion, and unnecessary regulation. The BLM's current planning regulations at this section direct the identification of a preferred alternative in a draft environmental impact statement. This is not required by NEPA or the Department's NEPA procedures and removing this provision would eliminate confusion caused by these discrepancies.
Section 1610.4-8 Selection of Resource Management Plan
The BLM is proposing to retain this section, redesignate in the revised sequence as 1610.43, and retitle this section as “Proposed land use plan, revision, or amendment.” The BLM is proposing to remove internal administrative workflows in the existing regulation and focus this section on the requirement to prepare and release a proposed land use plan, revision, or amendment that is subject to protest. The existing regulations require a protest process for proposed land use plans and amendments, and the BLM is also proposing to clarify that proposed land use plans and amendments must establish intervals and standards as appropriate for future monitoring and evaluation of the plan. These changes would clarify and better organize the existing regulations and are not substantive.
Section 1610.4-9 Monitoring and Evaluation
The BLM is proposing to remove this subsection and has incorporated the relevant text for development of a monitoring plan for the proposed land use plan, revision, or amendment into proposed § 1610.43.
Section 1610.5 Resource Management Plan Approval, Use and Modification
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.50, insert “pre-decisional review” into the section heading, and organize pre-decisional review procedures that are currently scattered throughout the existing regulations in this section. This reorganization would clarify the procedures at this end-stage of the planning process prior to the BLM issuing a decision.
Section 1610.5-1 Resource Management Plan Approval and Administrative Review
The BLM is proposing to relocate the provisions for land use plan approval to proposed § 1610.54, “Land use plan approval,” to have the procedures occur sequentially in the regulation.
In the relocated text in proposed § 1610.54, the BLM proposes removing the internal administrative workflows contained in these regulations and NEPA procedures which were developed under the Council on Environmental Quality's NEPA now-rescinded regulations. The BLM is proposing to retain the language that clarifies approval must be withheld on any portion of a plan, revision, or amendment being protested until the protest is resolved through issuance of a response.
Section 1610.5-2 Protest Procedures
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.51 to appear sequentially to the land use planning process and to update its existing protest procedures to make them less burdensome to the public and the BLM. The changes proposed acknowledge technological and other changes since 1985 when these regulations were first promulgated and remove requirements that the Office of the BLM Director respond to protests via certified letter. Instead, the BLM's response to a protest would be made available to the public, generally through the
BLM.gov
website. The BLM is proposing to modify the current regulations, which permit protests to be submitted in hard copy or electronically, to require that all protests be submitted electronically through the BLM's NEPA register and be received by the BLM by the end of the 30-calendar-day protest period. These changes would create a clear and efficient method for the public to submit protests and would allow the BLM to manage the land use planning process more efficiently by eliminating the time the BLM currently has to wait to receive protests that are postmarked by the close of the protest period, but not received until after the period has closed. Under the current regulations, the BLM has experienced delays of 10 business days or more closing out protest periods where few or no protests were received by the close of the period, while it awaited the possible receipt of a timely postmarked protest letter. The BLM welcomes comments on moving protest filings to an electronic-only format.
The BLM is also proposing to reduce the paperwork the public must provide in a protest. Rather than requiring protesting parties to provide redundant copies of “all documents addressing the issue or issues submitted during the planning process by the protesting party” as currently required under § 1610.5-2(a)(2)(iv), the BLM would require that protestors submit only that information necessary to address the protest. Specifically, the proposed regulations would require a protest to contain the name and interest of the person filing a protest, a statement of the issue or issues being protested, and a concise statement explaining why the proposed decision is believed to be inconsistent with relevant law, regulation, or policy. These proposed changes would retain the meaningful opportunity for involvement in the land use planning process, make it less burdensome to the BLM and the public, and build efficiencies by allowing the planning process to keep moving with better understanding of timeframes.
Section 1610.52 Governor's Consistency Review Procedures
The BLM is proposing for § 1610.52 to sequentially insert the procedures for the Governor's consistency review from existing § 1610.3-2(e) and to make changes addressing Governor's consistency review as part of general proposed changes to address FLPMA's direction in section 202(c)(9). The new proposed process to obtain information from States outlined in § 1610.41 would provide an opportunity for States to provide information early where it is most helpful to consider and address in the BLM's planning process. Because the BLM would be able to consider and resolve issues earlier in the planning process, the BLM is proposing to shorten the Governor's consistency review period at the end of the planning process from 60 days to 30 days and is proposing to eliminate the appeal opportunity to the BLM Director and associated procedures, including publication of the response by the Office of the BLM Director in the
Federal Register
. Under the proposed regulations, the BLM would coordinate earlier in the planning process with Governors to identify concerns and gain information than it does under the present regulations. This advanced coordination would better inform the BLM's development of management alternatives that address the issues and concerns raised by the Governor. The establishment of this early engagement process is expected to result in the BLM identifying and addressing concerns early in the planning process, leading to more informed decision-making and reduce the need for a separate Governor's appeal process at the end of the planning process.
The BLM is also proposing to remove the existing requirement in § 1610.3-2(e) for the State Director to provide the public with an opportunity to comment on any recommendations of the Governor that were not raised during the public participation process. The
(
printed page 72503)
BLM is proposing to remove this requirement to improve predictability in the duration of the land use planning process. Notably, since the establishment of this procedure in 1983, the BLM has only two recorded instances of initiating a public comment period due to receiving recommendations from the Governor's review that were not previously raised during the land use planning process. Further, the proposed changes that provide for enhanced early coordination create another opportunity for the Governor to raise recommendations that the BLM can address earlier in the process.
The BLM is also proposing to remove the direction for the Governor to provide recommendations related to inconsistencies of local plans. Instead, a new procedure for local government officials to provide inconsistencies with local plans is proposed as described below.
Section 1610.53 Local Governments' Consistency Review Procedures
The BLM is proposing a new section of § 1610.53, titled “Local governments' consistency review procedures.” This new section establishes a new opportunity for local government officials to submit recommendations to resolve inconsistencies directly to the BLM prior to the BLM's approval of the plan, revision, or amendment. This process is separate from the Governor's consistency review process but would run concurrently with that process. Under the current regulations at § 1610.3-2(e), the BLM submits inconsistencies with local plans to the State Governor for resolution. The proposed change would provide local government officials the opportunity to directly present recommendations to the BLM to resolve inconsistencies without going through the Governor's office. The BLM welcomes comments on this new process for consistency review, including whether and how to define a local government official.
Section 1610.5-3 Conformity and Implementation
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as § 1610.55 and revise it to remove redundancy and non-planning program procedure in the existing regulation and to clarify the meaning of plan conformance. The BLM would retain the requirement in paragraph (a) that all future authorizations and actions must conform to the approved plan, which is consistent with direction in FLPMA. This requirement applies to all BLM implementation decisions, regardless of the BLM program making the decision. The BLM proposes to move language in existing § 1601.0-5(b) that defines conformity and conformance to this section to integrate the definition and requirements for plan conformance in one section. If a proposed action is not in conformance with the approved plan, and warrants further consideration, the BLM should consider the action through a plan revision or amendment. This provision is retained in paragraph (b). The BLM is proposing in paragraph (c) to relocate direction in existing § 1610.4-9 to monitor and evaluate land use plans in accordance with established intervals and standards and at other appropriate times and to add language to clarify the BLM may initiate an amendment or revision based on new data, new or revised policy, or a change in circumstances.
The BLM is proposing to remove existing paragraphs (b) and (d) of this section because they are duplicative of the requirement in proposed paragraph (a) that all future BLM decisions and authorizations for all programs must conform to the approved plan. Existing direction relating to an appeal of future implementation decisions in paragraph (b) of this section is not a planning procedure and the appeal procedures for implementation decisions are duplicative of existing regulations in
43 CFR 4.400
that set forth the rules applicable to appeals before the Office of Hearings and Appeals, Interior Board of Land Appeals. Finally, the references to detailed plans for coal, oil shale, and tar sands resources in paragraph (b) are duplicative of the specific regulations for those resources and outside of the scope for these regulations; they would be removed in this proposed rule.
Section 1610.5-4 Maintenance
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this as § 1610.56 and revise it to clarify the scope of plan maintenance. Under the existing regulations, maintenance must not result in an expansion in the scope of resource uses or restrictions, or change the terms, conditions and decisions of the approved plan. The BLM is proposing to remove the terminology of “terms” and “conditions” because land use plans typically do not include terms and conditions and the use of this term has caused confusion. The BLM is also proposing changes to this section to clarify that the BLM may maintain a plan to document management changes made for an area by a law or Presidential Proclamation. The BLM would maintain other features of this regulation, including that maintenance does not require public involvement, interagency coordination, or preparation of an environmental assessment, environmental impact statement, or any other environmental review.
Section 1610.5-5 Amendment
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this as § 1610.57 and revise the section to clarify land use plan amendments. NEPA terms and NEPA compliance procedures in the existing regulations are also proposed for removal consistent with the need to remove duplicative regulations and to allow the BLM to comply with NEPA as appropriate for a plan amendment. The terminology of “terms” and “conditions” would also be removed because they are not typically included in land use plans and the use of this term has caused confusion.
Section 1610.5-6 Revision
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this as § 1610.58 and revise the section to clarify when the BLM would undertake a land use plan revision and remove unnecessary statements from the text. The language would clarify that a revision is appropriate when the BLM contemplates substantial changes to the scope of planning decisions providing for the management of public lands. These changes address confusion about when a land use plan revision (as opposed to an amendment) is appropriate.
Section 1610.5-7 Situations Where Action Can Be Taken Based on Another Agency's Plan, or a Land Use Analysis
The BLM is proposing to remove this section because the current procedures are either duplicative of NEPA or its implementing procedures or not required by law. These changes would allow the BLM to take appropriate steps to comply with NEPA and NEPA procedures.
The BLM is proposing to remove subpart (c) of this section from the planning regulations to focus these regulations on planning procedures. The BLM planning regulations are not an appropriate location for this program-specific regulation. The BLM proposes relocating the last two sentences of (c) to appear verbatim at the end of the current paragraph at
43 CFR 3420.1-4(a)
. The BLM proposes to remove from regulation the first two sentences of paragraph (c) as duplicative of existing
43 CFR subpart 3420
, which addresses coal resources. This change is not substantive and would not result in changes in the BLM's current program or practice; instead, it would reduce confusion by locating requirements specific to the coal program in the regulations governing that program.
(
printed page 72504)
Section 1610.6 Management Decision Review by Congress
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.60 and make a minor change in terminology to revise the existing term “resource management plan” to “land use plan” consistent with the changes to these terms throughout the regulations. The BLM is also proposing to add the term “contiguous” to clarify that contiguous tracts of 100,000 acres or more are subject to the reporting requirements if a planning decision totally eliminates one or more principal or major uses in the area. This is consistent with BLM's current practice.
Section 1610.7 Designation of Areas
The BLM is proposing to remove this section as an organizational matter because this proposed rulemaking only addresses areas of critical environmental concern, which is the designation specifically defined in FLPMA.
Section 1610.7-1 Designation of Areas Unsuitable for Surface Mining
The BLM is proposing to remove this subpart of these planning regulations as part of the intent of this revision is to focus these regulations on planning procedures. The BLM planning regulations are not an appropriate location for this program-specific instruction and are duplicative of procedures already established within the surface mining programs.
Section 1610.7-2 Designation of Areas of Critical Environmental Concern
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.70 and remove burdensome requirements in the existing regulations for areas of critical environmental concern. Specifically, the BLM is proposing to eliminate the requirement in the existing regulations at § 1610.7-2(b) for the identification of areas of critical environmental concern in a draft land use plan, the associated 60-day comment period, and the existing requirement for a
Federal Register
notice publication. This 60-day public comment period is redundant because there are other opportunities for public involvement in the planning process. The public would continue to be able to comment on areas of critical environmental concern during any public comment opportunity. To align with the statutory direction in FLPMA, the BLM is proposing language to clarify that special management attention is required to prevent or protect against irreparable damage in those areas designated as an area of critical environmental concern.
The BLM is also proposing changes that would clarify when the BLM would consider areas of critical environmental concern in an amendment process, considerations for boundaries, and the agency's discretion to modify or un-designate an area previously designated as an area of critical environmental concern. Other edits to this section clarify terms for consistency with FLPMA. The BLM is also considering addressing public nominations received during the planning process and specifically seeks public comment on what a valid public nomination should include and when the public should submit nominations in the planning process to inform the consideration and designation of areas of critical environmental concern.
Section 1610.8 Transition Period
The BLM is proposing to redesignate this section as 1610.80 and edit it to remove NEPA procedures and Environmental Protection Agency requirements that no longer apply. Some areas of the public lands are still managed under management framework plans (the predecessor to resource management plans) and some areas have no governing land use plan. The BLM is proposing changes to consolidate and clarify the sections of the regulations that provide procedures for areas managed under a management framework plan and where there is no governing land use plan.
Subpart 1611 Amending Land Use Plans To Address Emergencies
The BLM is proposing to add a new subpart to address emergency procedures for land use planning.
Section 1611.10 Emergency Procedures
The BLM is proposing a new section that would address emergency procedures to expedite the planning process for certain amendments necessary to review applications for projects that are submitted to address emergency circumstances. In emergency circumstances an officer in the Office of the Secretary that has been confirmed by the Senate could authorize modifications to otherwise-applicable procedural requirements in this Part to facilitate preparation of a land use plan amendment for the review of a proposed implementation action to address emergency circumstances. Modified procedures described in paragraphs (a)(1)-(3) could include: (1) reducing timeframes for public participation, or waiving the requirement for public participation at notice or protest, but not waiving both; (2) waiving some coordination procedures, as long as some remain; (3) reducing timeframes to respond to the BLM's request for approved plans at the outset of planning and consistency review timeframes for governor and local government consistency reviews, or (4) waiving the requirement to request plans or hold a governor or local government consistency review, but not both. Pursuant to paragraph (b), these procedures only apply for the duration of the emergency circumstances. If modified procedures under this section would be used, the BLM would be required to publish these procedures to inform the public and other agencies, State and local governments, and tribes how the requirements for public involvement, coordination, and consistency during planning would be met for the amendment. These new proposed procedures outline opportunities for officials to approve modified procedures to address emergency circumstances while still meeting the obligations for planning under FLPMA.

§ 1601.10
Purpose.
The purpose of this subpart is to establish in regulations a process for the approval of the development, revision, amendment, and maintenance of land use plans, as provided for by the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976, for public lands administered by the Bureau of Land Management.

Objective.
The objective of land use planning by the Bureau of Land Management is to provide by tracts or areas for the use of public lands through procedures that promote multiple use and sustained yield management and ensure participation by the public, state and local governments, Indian tribes, and appropriate Federal agencies.
