November 5, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 27, 2026, Texas Stock Exchange LLC (“Exchange” or “TXSE”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) a proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) a proposal to amend Rule 17.180 to permit an issuer to elect a higher listing tier for an exchange traded product at any time during a calendar year and to provide for the related incremental listing fee. The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
) at the Exchange's website (
https://www.txse.com/​regulations/​rules-filings
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 17.180 to allow an issuer to move an exchange traded product (“ETP”) to a higher listing tier during a calendar year.
[
3
]
The proposal would enable an issuer to elect the liquidity support associated with a higher tier without waiting until the following year. The proposed rule change would not alter the annual fee for any tier or require any issuer to upgrade an ETP.
Background
Rule 17.180 establishes three annual listing fee tiers for ETPs: the Signature Tier at $100,000, the Premier Tier at $55,000, and the Core Tier at $10,000. Each tier has corresponding Minimum Performance Standards
[
4
]
and daily stipends under the Exchange's Lead Market Maker (“LMM”) Program, as set forth in the Exchange's Fee Schedule.
[
5
]
Under the existing framework, an issuer selects the tier it considers appropriate for an ETP for the current year and may select a different tier for the following year. Rule 17.180 does not expressly address a change of listing tier during the calendar year. The Exchange proposes to add paragraph (b) to permit an issuer to elect a higher tier during the year and to specify the resulting additional fee.
Election of a Higher Listing Tier
Proposed Rule 17.180(b) would permit an issuer to elect to move an ETP to a higher listing tier during a calendar year. Accordingly, an issuer could move an ETP from the Core Tier to either the Premier Tier or the Signature Tier, or from the Premier Tier to the Signature Tier. An issuer that moves an ETP from the Core Tier to the Premier Tier could subsequently elect to move that ETP to the Signature Tier during the same year.
The proposed election would be available only for a move to a higher tier. An issuer could not use this provision to move an ETP to a lower tier during the calendar year, including to reverse an earlier change. Following a change, the higher tier would apply for the remainder of the calendar year unless the issuer elects a further change to a higher tier. The existing annual election framework would continue to permit an issuer to select any available tier, including a lower tier, for the following calendar year.
Any change would take effect on a trading day specified in the issuer's written notice to the Exchange and confirmed by the Exchange. The Exchange would coordinate the effective date with the issuer and the assigned LMM so that the applicable tier, performance standards, and stipend treatment change together. Any change would apply prospectively beginning on that date.
Incremental Listing Fee
For an ETP that moves to a higher tier during a calendar year, the issuer would pay an additional listing fee equal to the difference between the annual fee for the higher tier and the annual fee for the tier immediately preceding the change, prorated based on the number of trading days remaining in that year, including the effective date of the change, divided by the total number of trading days in that year.
For example, if an issuer moves an ETP from the Core Tier to the Premier Tier with 125 trading days remaining in the year, including the effective date, in a calendar year with 250 trading days, the additional fee would be $22,500 (($55,000−$10,000) × 125/250). A direct move from the Core Tier to the Signature Tier on the same date would result in an additional fee of $45,000 (($100,000−$10,000) × 125/250). If an ETP is upgraded more than once during the calendar year, each additional fee would be calculated using the annual fee for the tier immediately preceding that upgrade.
(
printed page 72596)
Application of the LMM Program
Beginning on the effective date of an upgrade, the Minimum Performance Standards and daily stipends applicable to the higher tier and the ETP's asset class would apply under the Fee Schedule. The upgrade would not change the standards or stipend amounts specified for any tier or create a separate stipend. An LMM would remain eligible for a daily stipend only to the extent it satisfies the applicable performance conditions.
For an ETP upgraded to the Signature Tier, the listing fee credit under Rule 17.180(a)(1)(A) would apply to qualifying instances beginning on the effective date of the upgrade. Such credits would be available for the issuer's listing fees in the following year and would expire if not used during that year. The upgrade would not create Signature Tier credits for periods before its effective date.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
6
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5)
[
7
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
8
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers as well as Section 6(b)(4)
[
9
]
as it is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members and other persons using its facilities.
The Exchange believes that the incremental fee is reasonable because it uses the existing annual fee difference between the two tiers and charges that difference only for the portion of the year during which the ETP participates in the higher tier. An issuer would not be required to pay the higher tier's full annual fee in addition to the fee already applicable to the ETP. The same calculation would apply to every issuer making the same upgrade within a calendar year, and an issuer could elect whether the additional liquidity support associated with the higher tier warrants the additional charge.
The proposal is equitably allocated and not unfairly discriminatory because each issuer would have the same opportunity to elect a higher tier for an ETP on the same terms. Differences in the additional fee would reflect the selected tiers and the remaining period of participation. The proposal would also preserve the relationship between the listing tier selected by the issuer and the corresponding LMM performance standards and stipend eligibility.
Allowing an issuer to increase liquidity support during the year would enable it to respond to changes in an ETP's trading characteristics or liquidity needs without waiting for the next year to change tiers. Applying the higher tier's standards and stipend eligibility prospectively from a common effective date would provide a clear basis for evaluating LMM performance and assessing the additional listing fee. The Exchange believes this flexibility is designed to promote liquidity and market quality for the benefit of investors, although electing a higher tier would not guarantee any particular trading outcome.
Limiting changes within a calendar year to upgrades would preserve the annual nature of an issuer's existing tier commitment while permitting the issuer to elect additional support. It would also provide greater continuity in the level of liquidity support selected for an ETP during the year. The limitation would apply equally to all issuers, and issuers would retain the ability to select a lower tier for the following year. The Exchange believes this balances additional flexibility with a predictable annual framework for issuers and LMMs.
(B) Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. Rather, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change will enhance competition among exchanges for ETP listings and among liquidity providers to participate as Lead Market Makers on the Exchange.
With respect to intramarket competition, the proposal would apply equally to all issuers. No issuer would be required to change tiers, and issuers could continue to select the tier they consider appropriate for the following year. The proposal would not change the performance standards or stipend amounts for any tier, and the existing performance conditions would continue to apply to LMMs assigned to ETPs in that tier.
With respect to intermarket competition, the proposal would provide issuers with additional flexibility to increase liquidity support for an ETP while maintaining its listing on the Exchange. Other listing exchanges could compete through their own listing fees and liquidity programs. The Exchange believes that permitting a prospective tier change at a prorated incremental fee may enhance competition for ETP listings without imposing an unnecessary or inappropriate burden on competing venues.
(C) Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received written comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
10
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(2)
[
11
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include File Number SR-TXSE-2026-043 on the subject line.
(
printed page 72597)
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File Number SR-TXSE-2026-043. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of TXSE and on its internet website at
https://www.txse.com/​regulations/​rules-filings
.
Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-TXSE-2026-043 and should be submitted on or before December 1, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

]

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106828; File No. SR-BOX-2026-22]
November 5, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 23, 2026, BOX Exchange LLC (the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to make various clean up changes and a number of technical, non-substantiative changes to its Rulebook. The text of the proposed rule change is available from the principal office of the Exchange, and also on the Exchange's internet website at
https://rules.boxexchange.com/​rulefilings
.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend IM-3120-3, IM-3120-4, Rule 5050 (Series of Options Contracts Open for Trading), IM-5050-7 (Mini-Nasdaq-100 Index Strike Prices), IM-5050-10 (Mini Option Contracts), IM-6010-1, Rule 6040 (Position Limits for Broad-Based Index Options), Rule 6090 (Terms of Index Options), Rule 7040 (Meaning of Premium Quotes and Orders), Rule 7110 (Order Entry), and Rule 7240 (Complex Orders) to remove references to Mini Options
[
3
]
and Jumbo SPY Options.
[
4
]
Additionally, the Exchange is proposing to make certain clean up changes to update outdated internal cross references, as well as various technical numbering updates to conform with the changes proposed herein. Additionally, the Exchange is proposing to make certain clean up changes to update outdated internal cross references, as well as various technical numbering updates to conform with the changes proposed herein.
Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options
The Exchange does not list Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options, and is now proposing to mark the listing rules and other ancillary trading rules related to the listing of Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options as “Reserved.” Specifically, the proposed rule change removes the contents of the following rules or subsections and mark them as reserved for future use IM-3120-3, IM-3120-4, Rule 5050(e), IM-5050-7 (Mini-Nasdaq-100 Index Strike Prices), IM-5050-10 (Mini Option Contracts), Rule 6090(c)(5), Rule 7040(c), and Rule 7240(b)(5) and (b)(6). As stated above these rules are obsolete because these products are no longer, or were never, listed on the Exchange.
[
5
]
The Exchange will also amend the following rules to remove language related to Mini Options IM-6010-1, Rule 6040(c), Rule 6090(a)(4) and (5), and Rule 7110(c)(6). As stated above the rule language within these rules are obsolete because the
(
printed page 72591)
products the rules refer to no longer, or never, traded on the Exchange.
The Exchange notes that it has no open interest in Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options respectively. In the event that the Exchange desires to list Mini Options or Jumbo SPY Options in the future, it would file a rule change with the Commission to adopt rules to list Mini Options or Jumbo SPY Options.
Technical Changes
The Exchange is also proposing to make a number of technical, non-substantive changes to the Exchange's Rulebook. The Exchange believes these changes are necessary to provide greater accuracy and clarity to the Rulebook.
The Exchange proposes to update several internal cross-references. The Exchange proposes to update internal cross-references contained in Rule 5030 (Withdrawal of Approval of Underlying). Specifically, the proposed change corrects two internal cross-references within Rule 5030(h)(1) from Rule 5020(h)(1)(i) to Rule 5020(h)(1) and the internal cross-reference from subparagraphs (b)(1),(2),(3) and (4) of Rule 5030 to subparagraphs (b)(1),(2),(3) of Rule 5030 because Rule 5020(h)(1) increases the scope of the outdated rule reference and 5030(b)(4) is currently marked as reserved.
[
6
]
The Exchange proposes to update internal cross-references contained in Rule 7130 (Execution and Price/Time Priority). Specifically, the proposed change updates the internal cross-reference within Rule 7130(b)(1) from Rule 8040(b) and (c) to Rule 8040 (c) and (d). A previous filing amended 8040(b) to be reserved, making the cross-reference in Rule 7130(b)(1) outdated and this proposed rule change would now update it.
[
7
]
Next, the proposed change updates the internal cross-references in Rules 7130(b)(2)(i) and 7130(b)(2)(ii) from subparagraph (b)(4) to (b)(3). A previous filing updated subparagraph (b)(4) to (b)(3) and the internal cross reference in 7130(b)(2)(i) and 7130(b)(2)(ii) is currently outdated.
[
8
]
The Exchange now proposes to update the aforementioned internal cross-references by updating them both to subparagraph (b)(3). The proposed change corrects another outdated internal cross-reference in Rules 7130(b)(3)(ii)(A) and 7130(b)(3)(ii)(B) from subparagraph (b)(4)(ii)(C) to (b)(3)(ii)(C). A previous filing updated subparagraph (b)(4) to (b)(3) and this proposed change will update the cross-reference in both Rules 7130(b)(3)(ii)(A) and 7130(b)(3)(ii)(B) from subparagraph (b)(4)(ii)(C) to (b)(3)(ii)(C).
[
9
]
The Exchange also proposes to update an internal cross reference contained in Rule 7620 (Complex Orders). Specifically, the proposed change updates the internal cross-reference within Rule 7620(e) from Rule 7040(a) through (c) to Rule 7040(a) and (b). This update is being made as a consequential result of marking Rule 7040(c) as reserved as previously discussed in this filing. This change will improve the accuracy of the proposed changes and rulebook.
The Exchange proposes to amend IM-15030-1(e) to update an internal rule cite. Specifically, the proposed change updates the outdated internal cross-reference within IM-15030-1 from IM-5030-1 to IM-15030-1.
The proposed technical changes are not intended to make any changes to the operation or meaning of the rules and merely seek to correct outdated internal cross references to provide greater accuracy within the Rulebook.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposal is consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
10
]
in general, and Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
11
]
in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest.
Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options
The Exchange's proposal to remove references to the listing and handling of Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options is consistent with the Act because the Exchange does not list, or has never listed, Mini Options or Jumbo SPY Options and removing the references to such products within the rules would render the Rulebook more accurate and reduce potential investor confusion. The Exchange notes that it has no open interest in Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options. In the event that the Exchange desires to list Mini Options or Jumbo SPY Options in the future, it would file a rule change with the Commission to adopt rules to list Mini Options or Jumbo Spy Options.
Technical Changes
Additionally, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and in general, will protect investors and the public interest by correcting outdated references within the rules. Specifically, by correcting inaccurate cross-references, the proposed rule change is designed to protect investors by making the rulebook more accurate thereby mitigating any potential investor confusion.
The proposed technical changes are not intended to make any changes to the operation or meaning of the rules and merely seek to correct outdated internal cross-references and make certain numbering changes to provide greater accuracy within the Rulebook.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange's proposal to remove references to the listing and handling of Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options does not impose an undue burden on competition. The Exchange does not list Mini Options or Jumbo SPY Options. Also, the Exchange notes that it has no open interest in Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options. The Exchange's proposal to correct technical changes by updating outdated internal cross-references is not intended to address competitive issues but is concerned solely with updating certain outdated references.
The proposed rule change will have no impact on trading on the Exchange, as all the rule changes are non-substantive in nature. As such, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
(
printed page 72592)
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange has neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
12
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
13
]
A proposed rule change filed pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6) under the Act
[
14
]
normally does not become operative for 30 days after the date of its filing. However, Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii)
[
15
]
permits the Commission to designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has requested that the Commission waive the 30-day operative delay because the proposed rule change merely removes obsolete rules and rule references related to Mini Options and Jumbo SPY Options, corrects outdated cross-references, and otherwise provides additional clarity in the rulebook, and does not affect the operation of any Exchange rule. The Exchange explains that therefore waiver of the 30-day operative delay would allow the changes to become promptly effective and avoid any potential confusion by providing investors with a clearer, more accurate Exchange rulebook. For this reason, and because the proposed rule change raises no new or novel legal or regulatory issues, the Commission believes that waiver of the operative delay would be consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. Accordingly, the Commission hereby waives the operative delay and designates the proposal operative upon filing.
[
16
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:

title: Self-Regulatory Organizations; Investors Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend IEX Rule 3.291 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities), To Conform to the Rules of FINRA for Purposes of an Agreement Between the Exchange and FINRA Pursuant To Rule 17d-2 Under the Act

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106827; File No. SR-IEX-2026-43]
November 5, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that, on October 29, 2026, the Investors Exchange LLC (“IEX” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II and III below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) under the Act,
[
4
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
5
]
the Exchange is filing with the Commission a proposed rule change to amend IEX Rule 3.291 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities), to conform to the rules of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) for purposes of an agreement between the Exchange and FINRA pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act.
The Exchange has designated this proposed rule change as “non-controversial” under Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
6
]
and provided the Commission with the notice required by Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
7
]
The text of the proposed rule change is available at the Exchange's website at
https://www.iexexchange.io/​resources/​regulation/​rule-filings
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend IEX Rule 3.291 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities), to make conforming changes to the Rule such that it remains substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. The Exchange notes that this filing is based on a rule change proposal recently submitted by FINRA and approved by the Commission, which amended FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others).
[
8
]
Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act,
[
9
]
the Exchange and FINRA entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the “17d-2 Agreement”).
[
10
]
The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules.
[
11
]
The 17d-2 Agreement includes a certification by the Exchange that states that the requirements contained in certain IEX Rules are identical to, or substantially similar to, certain FINRA rules that have been identified as comparable. Included among those rules is Rule 3.291, which IEX previously certified to be identical to, or substantially similar to, FINRA Rule 3220.
Currently, Rule 3.291 would not be covered under the 17d-2 Agreement because the FINRA 3220 Filing changed FINRA Rule 3220 such that the FINRA rule is no longer identical, or substantially similar to, FINRA Rule 3220. Rule 3.291 prohibits a Member
[
12
]
or person associated with a Member from, directly or indirectly, giving or permitting to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of one
(
printed page 72598)
hundred dollars per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent, or representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. By contrast, the recently amended FINRA Rule 3220 prohibits gifts in excess of $300.00, where the gift or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. The FINRA 3220 Filing also introduced provisions covering: supervision and recordkeeping requirements; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts; de minimis gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to a Member's associated persons or individual retail customers. Because of the above-described differences between Rule 3.291 and FINRA Rule 3220, Rule 3.291 currently will not be considered a common rule pursuant to the 17d-2 Agreement. To again harmonize its rules with those of FINRA, the Exchange now proposes to conform the text of Rule 3.291 to FINRA Rule 3220, so that it may be incorporated into the 17d-2 Agreement in its entirety.
The Exchange believes that these changes will help to avoid confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed changes to Rule 3.291 are designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, Rule 3.291 would apply equally to Exchange-only Members as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when a Member or person associated with a Member gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer.
First, the Exchange proposes to amend Rule 3.291 to increase the gift limit from $100 to $300 per individual per year. FINRA stated that the current gift limit of $100 has been in place since 1992.
[
13
]
FINRA increased the gift limit from $100 to $300 to account for past inflation since 1992 and to account for expected future inflation for approximately ten years, thereby reducing the frequency of future upwards adjustments to account for inflation.
[
14
]
Consistent with FINRA's determination, the Exchange believes that a $300 gift limit would continue to permit the exchange of business courtesies while helping to guard against excessiveness, and reasonably reflects changes to purchasing power due to inflation since the gift limit was last raised in 1992 as well as approximately ten years of expected future inflation.
Second, the Exchange proposes to add a new paragraph (d) to Rule 3.291 that would authorize FINRA, acting on behalf of the Exchange, to conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of 3.291 for good cause shown, provided that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. Specifically, the Exchange proposes that pursuant to Rule Series 9.600, FINRA staff, for good cause shown after taking into consideration all relevant factors, may conditionally or unconditionally grant an exemption from any provision of this Rule to the extent that such exemption is consistent with the purpose of the Rule, the protection of investors, and the public interest. This proposed provision mirrors the exemptive relief authority added by FINRA in new FINRA Rule 3220(d). Given the scope of Rule 3.291, which applies to gifts given to a wide range of recipients where the payment is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient, and given the diversity of Member sizes, structures, businesses, and distribution models, the Exchange believes it would be useful and appropriate to have the ability to provide relief from a particular provision of the Rule under specific factual circumstances.
Third, FINRA Rule 3220 incorporated published guidance interpreting FINRA Rule 3220, including NASD Notice to Members 06-69,
[
15
]
FINRA's Frequently Asked Questions on Gifts, Business Entertainment, and Non-Cash Compensation,
[
16
]
as well as an interpretive letter regarding bereavement gifts (the “Aly Letter”).
[
17
]
To maintain substantive alignment with FINRA Rule 3220, the Exchange proposes to adopt corresponding Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to Rule 3.291. Each proposed Supplementary Material section is described below.
Proposed Supplementary Material .01 (Gifts Incidental to Business Entertainment) would state that a gift given during the course of a business entertainment event is subject to Rule 3.291 unless it is consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) or .06 (De Minimis Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items) which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 Supplementary Material .04 and .06. For the purpose of the $300 limit, the cost of the business entertainment event itself would not be included in the value of the gift.
Proposed Supplementary Material .02 (Valuation of Gifts) would require Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost, exclusive of tax and delivery charges, and would require Members to value tickets for sporting or other events at the higher of cost or face value. If gifts are given to multiple recipients, Members must record the names of each recipient and calculate and record the value of the gift on a pro rata, per-recipient basis, for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 3.291. Supplementary Material .02 to FINRA Rule 3220 requires Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost rather than at the higher of cost or market value, which reduces complexity and subjectivity because market value can be difficult and burdensome to determine, while distinguishing tickets for sporting or other events accounts for the fact that such tickets are commonly purchased on secondary markets at costs that differ from face value. This proposed revision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .02 to FINRA Rule 3220.
Proposed Supplementary Material .03 (Aggregation of Gifts) would require Members to aggregate all gifts given by the Member and each associated person of the Member to a particular recipient over the course of the year for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 3.291(a), and would require each Member to state in its procedures whether it is aggregating all gifts given by the Member and its associated persons on a calendar year, fiscal year, or on a rolling basis beginning with the first gift to any particular recipient. The aggregation requirement would not apply to personal gifts under proposed
(
printed page 72599)
Supplementary Material .04 or to gifts of de minimis value or promotional or commemorative items under proposed Supplementary Material .06 as they are already not subject to the gift limit. This proposed provision, which is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .03 to FINRA Rule 3220, would help ensure that persons who give multiple gifts in a year to the same recipient do not circumvent the gift limit.
Proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) would state that gifts that are given for infrequent life events (
e.g.,
a wedding gift or a congratulatory gift for the birth of a child) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3.291(c), provided the gifts are customary and reasonable, personal in nature, and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. In determining whether a gift is “personal in nature and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient,” Members should consider a number of factors, including the nature of any pre-existing personal or family relationship between the person giving the gift and the recipient and whether the associated person paid for the gift. When the Member bears the cost of the gift, either directly or by reimbursing an associated person, FINRA will presume that such gift is not personal in nature and instead is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. This provision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .04 to FINRA Rule 3220.
Consistent with Supplementary Material .05 to FINRA Rule 3220 (Bereavement Gifts), proposed Supplementary Material .05 to Rule 3.291 separates bereavement gifts from personal gifts. Proposed Supplementary Material .05 to Rule 3.291 would state that bereavement gifts that are customary and reasonable are not considered to be in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient and, therefore, are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3.291(c). This provision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .05 to FINRA Rule 3220.
Proposed Supplementary Material .06 (De Minimis Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items), at paragraph (a), would state that gifts of a de minimis value (
e.g.,
pens, notepads, or modest desk ornaments) or promotional items of nominal value that display the Member's logo (
e.g.,
umbrellas, tote bags, or shirts) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3.291(c), provided that the value of the gift or promotional item is substantially below the $300 limit. Proposed Supplementary Material .06(b) would state that customary and reasonable solely decorative items commemorating a business transaction are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3.291(c). These provisions are substantially similar to Supplementary Material .06 to FINRA Rule 3220.
Proposed Supplementary Material .07 (Donations Due to Federally Declared Major Disasters) would state that donations by a Member or an associated person to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person to provide assistance to the individual for losses sustained in a natural event that the President of the United States has declared to be a major disaster, such as a wildfire, hurricane, tornado, earthquake, or flood, are not considered “in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient” for purposes of Rule 3.291(a) and are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3.291(a) or the recordkeeping requirements of Rule 3.291(c). This provision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .07 to FINRA Rule 3220 which recognizes that the nature of such disasters is unpredictable and catastrophic.
Proposed Supplementary Material .08 (Supervision and Recordkeeping) would state that the Exchange's supervision rules in Rule 5.110 require a Member to have a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Rule 3.291. To meet these standards, Members would be required to have systems and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that payments and gratuities in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient given by the Member and its associated persons to employees of another person are (a) reported to the Member; (b) reviewed for compliance with Rule 3.291; and (c) maintained in the Member's records. Such procedures must be reasonably designed to ensure that an associated person who is giving a payment or gratuity is not responsible for determining whether such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the recipient's employer. Members are not required to maintain records of gifts that are consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 through .07. Requiring a person other than the associated person giving the gift to assess the nature of the gift is intended to encourage objectivity in making such determinations. This proposed revision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .08 to FINRA Rule 3220.
Proposed Supplementary Material .09 (Gifts to a Member's Associated Persons or Individual Retail Customers) would state that Rule 3.291 does not apply to gifts from a Member to its own associated persons, or to gifts from a Member or an associated person to individual retail customers. The Exchange believes that proposed Supplementary Material .09 would clarify, and improve awareness and understanding of, the scope of Rule 3.291. This proposed revision is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .09 to FINRA Rule 3220.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the requirements of Rule 3.291 and FINRA Rule 3220, without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. Thus, the Exchange believes these proposed changes would help facilitate compliance with Rule 3.291 and would provide regulatory certainty to Members. Because the Exchange proposes to make conforming amendments that are substantially similar to FINRA's amendments to FINRA Rule 3220, Members that are also FINRA members would continue to be subject to a substantially similar rule when conducting business on the Exchange. In addition, Members that are not FINRA members would continue to be subject to Rule 3.291 to the extent that such Members conduct business with the public.
2. Statutory Basis
IEX believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with the provisions of Section 6(b)
[
18
]
of the Act in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act
[
19
]
in particular, in that it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
As noted above, the proposed rule change conforms Rule 3.291 to FINRA Rule 3220 so that it is substantially similar to FINRA's rule, thereby promoting uniform standards across the securities industry. The Exchange also notes the changes proposed herein align
(
printed page 72600)
Rule 3.291 with a recent filing submitted by FINRA and approved by the Commission.
[
20
]
The Exchange further believes that these changes will help to reduce and avoid potential confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed rule change is designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, Rule 3.291 would equally apply to an Exchange-only Member as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties that might arise when substantial gifts or monetary payments are given to certain persons.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to Rule 3.291 to conform to the rules of FINRA will improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the Rule's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with Rule 3.291.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
IEX does not believe that the proposed rule change will result in any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issue but to align the Exchange's rules with those of FINRA. Aligning Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220 would avoid potentially different outcomes for members of both FINRA and IEX with respect to gifts and gratuities. This change would provide greater harmonization among IEX and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance for common members and facilitating FINRA's performance of its regulatory functions under the 17d-2 Agreement. As such, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
Written comments on the proposed rule change were neither solicited nor received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has designated this rule filing as non-controversial under Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
21
]
of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
22
]
thereunder. Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
The proposal does not significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest. Further, the proposal does not impose any significant burden on competition. As discussed above, the Exchange believes that the proposed change is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest because the proposed rule change will promote greater harmonization between the Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in greater uniformity and less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance. Additionally, the proposed rule change does not raise any new policy issues not previously considered by the Commission nor impose any significant burden on competition because it would result in less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance for common members and facilitating FINRA's performance of its regulatory functions under the 17d-2 Agreement. As described above, the Exchange notes that the proposed change is directly based on proposed a rule change submitted by FINRA that was approved by the Commission.
[
23
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
24
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-IEX-2026-43 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-IEX-2026-43. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-IEX-2026-43 and should be submitted on or before December 1, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

SUMMARY:
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) proposes to
(

establish the 2027 aggregate production quotas for controlled substances in schedules I and II of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) and the assessment of annual needs for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine.
DATES:
Interested persons may file written comments on this notice in accordance with
21 CFR 1303.11(c)
and
1315.11(d)
. Electronic comments must be submitted, and written comments must be postmarked, on or before December 10, 2026. Commenters should be aware that the electronic Federal Docket Management System will not accept comments after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the last day of the comment period.

a final order establishing the 2027 aggregate production quotas for schedule I and II controlled substances, and an assessment of annual needs for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine.

Legal Authority
Section 306 of the Controlled Substances Act (
21 U.S.C. 826
) requires the Attorney General to establish production quotas for each basic class of controlled substances listed in schedules I and II, and for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine. The Attorney General has delegated this function to the Administrator of DEA pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100
.
Analysis for Proposed 2027 Aggregate Production Quotas and Assessment of Annual Needs
The proposed 2027 aggregate production quotas (APQ) and assessment of annual needs (AAN) represent those quantities of schedule I and II controlled substances, and the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine, to be manufactured in the United States in 2027 to provide for the estimated medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States, lawful export requirements, and the establishment and maintenance of reserve stocks. These quotas include imports of ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine, but do not include imports of controlled substances for use in industrial processes.
Aggregate Production Quotas
In determining the proposed 2027 APQ, the Administrator has taken into account the criteria of
21 U.S.C. 826(a)
and
21 CFR 1303.11
, including the following seven factors:
(1) Total net disposal of the class by all manufacturers during the current and two preceding years;
(2) Trends in the national rate of net disposal of the class;
(3) Total actual (or estimated) inventories of the class and of all substances manufactured from the class, and trends in inventory accumulation;
(4) Projected demand for such class as indicated by procurement quotas requested pursuant to [21 CFR] 1303.12;
(5) The extent of any diversion of the controlled substance in the class;
(6) Relevant information obtained from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), including from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Centers for Disease Control
(
printed page 72568)
and Prevention (CDC), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), and relevant information obtained from the states; and
(7) Other factors affecting medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs in the United States and lawful export requirements, as the Administrator finds relevant, including changes in the currently accepted medical use in treatment with the class or the substances manufactured from it, the economic and physical availability of raw materials for use in manufacturing and for inventory purposes, yield and stability problems, potential disruptions to production (including possible labor strikes), and recent unforeseen emergencies such as floods and fires.
21 CFR 1303.11(b)
.
DEA formally solicited data from FDA and CDC in March of 2026 and from the states in April 2026, pursuant to
21 CFR part 1303
. DEA did not solicit input from CMS for reasons discussed in previous notices.
[
1
]
DEA requested information on trends in the legitimate use of select schedule I and II controlled substances from FDA and rates of overdose deaths for covered controlled substances from CDC. DEA's request for information from the states was made directly to the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) Administrators in each state as well as through the National Association of State Controlled Substances Authorities (NASCSA).
Assessment of Annual Needs
In similar fashion, in determining the proposed 2027 AAN for the list I chemicals ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine, the Administrator has taken into account the criteria of
21 U.S.C. 826(a)
and
21 CFR 1315.11
, including the following five factors:
(1) Total net disposal of the chemical by all manufacturers and importers during the current and two preceding years;
(2) Trends in the national rate of net disposal of each chemical;
(3) Total actual (or estimated) inventories of the chemical and of all substances manufactured from the chemical, and trends in inventory accumulation;
(4) Projected demand for each chemical as indicated by procurement and import quotas requested pursuant to [21 CFR] 1315.32; and
(5) Other factors affecting medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs in the United States, lawful export requirements, and the establishment and maintenance of reserve stocks, as the Administrator finds relevant, including changes in the currently accepted medical use in treatment with the chemicals or the substances manufactured from them, the economic and physical availability of raw materials for use in manufacturing and for inventory purposes, yield and stability problems, potential disruptions to production (including possible labor strikes), and recent unforeseen emergencies such as floods and fires.
21 CFR 1315.11(b)
.
In determining the proposed 2027 AAN, DEA used the calculation methodology previously described in the 2010 and 2011 assessments of annual needs (
74 FR 60294
(Nov. 20, 2009) and
75 FR 79407
(Dec. 20, 2010), respectively).
Projected Trends for Certain Schedule II Controlled Substances
In accordance with
21 CFR part 1303
,
21 U.S.C. 826
, and
42 U.S.C. 242
, HHS continues to provide DEA with estimates of the quantities of select schedule I and II controlled substances and three list I chemicals that will be required to meet the legitimate medical needs of the United States for a given calendar year. The responsibility to provide these estimates of legitimate domestic medical needs resides with FDA. FDA provides DEA with predicted estimates of domestic medical usage for selected controlled substances based on information available to them at a specific point in time in order to meet statutory requirements. In July 2026, FDA provided DEA with the predicted estimates of domestic medical usage for selected controlled substances for 2027, which DEA considered in developing the proposed 2027 APQ.
FDA predicts that levels of medical usage for schedule II opioids in the United States in calendar year 2027 will decline on average 9.68 percent from calendar year 2026 levels. These declines are expected to occur across a variety of schedule II opioids including fentanyl, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, and oxymorphone. DEA considered the potential for diversion of schedule II opioids, as required by
21 CFR 1303.11(b)(5)
, in developing the proposed 2027 APQ. Accordingly, the APQs for fentanyl, hydrocodone (for sale), hydromorphone, oxycodone (for sale), and oxymorphone (for sale) are being proposed as reductions from their 2026 proposed revised APQ values.
FDA also provided a predicted 3.93 percent increase on average of domestic medical use of schedule II stimulants in calendar year 2027, including d-amphetamine (for sale), d,l-amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, and methylphenidate, which are prescribed to treat patients with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), from calendar year 2026 levels. FDA also raised concerns over drug shortages potentially related to the growth in telemedicine, supply chain issues, manufacturing and quality issues, and business decisions of manufacturers, which DEA considered in developing the proposed 2027 APQ. DEA recently proposed to increase the 2026 APQs for both lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate (for sale) and is proposing the same increased values for 2027 in part to address these concerns.
DEA is proposing the 2027 APQs for the schedule II stimulants d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) at higher levels than their 2026 proposed revised APQ values to address the growth in prescribing, export requirements, the global market, and to ensure sufficient inventory for domestic manufacturers of FDA-approved drug products. Medications containing one or both of these controlled substances are commonly prescribed to treat patients with ADHD. Over the past few years, dosage form manufacturers have been intermittently reporting shortages of specific ADHD medications containing amphetamine to FDA. The stated reasons for these specific shortages include increases in product demand, supply chain issues, manufacturing and quality issues, lack of active ingredients, and business decisions of manufacturers. FDA estimated a 3.90 percent increase in domestic medical usage individually for d-amphetamine (for sale) and d,l- amphetamine. DEA reviewed the most recently available domestic usage data from IQVIA and export data from DEA's internal database and Multi International Data Analysis System (MIDAS). The projection from this data estimated use for d-amphetamine (for sale) and d,l-amphetamine each increased by 6.98 percent. DEA also considered the manufacturers' reported inventories for amphetamine-based products and their drug shortage concerns when determining the proposed APQs for these substances. DEA believes the inventories, when combined with the proposed 2027 APQs, will be sufficient to support the estimated increases in
(
printed page 72569)
domestic medical use and export requirements of amphetamine products.
DEA is proposing the pentobarbital APQ at a higher level than the 2026 established APQ to support
Executive Order 14336
:
Ensuring American Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Resilience by Filling the Strategic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Reserve. The 2027 proposed pentobarbital increase is greater than the 2026 proposed revised APQ to allow for a reserve stockpile of the API for manufacturing established essential medications containing pentobarbital based on the request from Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR).
DEA Projected Trends for Certain Schedule I Controlled Substances
On August 12, 2026, DEA published in the
Federal Register
a temporary scheduling order to place O-desmethyltramadol in schedule I of the CSA until August 12, 2028, or until a permanent schedule action of this substance is complete, whichever occurs first.
[
2
]
Therefore, DEA is proposing an APQ for this basic class for the first time. DEA is also proposing the 2027 APQs for acetyl fentanyl and heroin at lower levels than their 2026 proposed revised APQ based on the decline in the amount of quota requested to support medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs. These decreases in the APQs will not affect the ability of these manufacturers to meet the estimated medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the U.S., lawful export requirements, and the establishment and maintenance of reserve stocks.
DEA is proposing higher APQs than the 2026 proposed revised APQs for the following schedule I controlled substances: 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and ibogaine to support manufacturing activities related to the increased level of research and clinical trials being conducted with these substances for potential treatment of conditions including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression. This increase in research and clinical trials aligns with two Presidential Executive Orders (E.O.). First,
E.O. 14379
:
Addressing Addiction through the Great American Recovery Initiative,
[
3
]
which prioritizes addiction treatment and recovery. Second,
E.O. 14401
:
Accelerating Medical Treatments for Serious Mental Illness,
[
4
]
which requires a pathway to be established for eligible patients to access psychedelic drugs, including ibogaine compounds, under the Right to Try Act (
21 U.S.C. 360bbb-0a
). Additionally, DEA is proposing a lower APQ than the 2026 proposed revised APQ for fentanyl-related substances based on the diminished needs of manufacturers who produce reference standards or support research.
Information Received for Consideration of the Remaining Factors
For the factors listed in
21 CFR 1303.11(b)(3)
and
(4)
, DEA registered manufacturers of controlled substances in schedules I and II provide information such as inventory, distribution, manufacturing, sales forecasts and quota requests to DEA database systems.
See,
21 CFR 1303.12
,
1303.22
, and part 1304.
The regulation at
21 CFR 1303.11(b)(5)
requires DEA to consider the extent of diversion of controlled substances.
[
5
]
Diversion is defined as all distribution, dispensing, or other use of controlled substances for other than legitimate medical purposes. In considering the extent of diversion, DEA analyzed reports of diversion of controlled substances from 2025 submitted to its Theft Loss Report database. This database is comprised of DEA registrant reports documenting diversion from the legitimate distribution chain, including employee thefts, break-ins, armed robberies, and material lost in transit. The data was categorized by basic drug class, and the amount of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) in the dosage form was delineated with an appropriate metric for use in proposing aggregate production quota values (
i.e.,
weight).
Estimates of Diversion of Covered Controlled Substances
In establishing any quota . . . , or any procurement quota established by [DEA] by regulation, for fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, oxymorphone, or hydromorphone (in this subsection referred to as a “covered controlled substance”), [DEA] shall estimate the amount of diversion of the covered controlled substance that occurs in the United States.
21 U.S.C. 826(i)(1)(A)
.
In estimating diversion under that provision, DEA:
(i) shall consider information . . . , in consultation with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, [it] determines reliable on rates of overdose deaths and abuse and overall public health impact related to the covered controlled substance in the United States; and
(ii) may take into consideration whatever other sources of information [it] determines reliable.
21 U.S.C. 826(i)(1)(B)
.
The statute further mandates that DEA “make appropriate quota reductions, as determined by [DEA], from the quota [it] would have otherwise established had such diversion not been considered.”
[
6
]
In estimating the amount of diversion of each covered controlled substance that occurs in the United States, DEA considered information from state PDMP Administrators and from legitimate distribution chain participants.
Consideration of Information From Certain State PDMPs and From National Sales Data
Pursuant to
21 CFR 1303.11(b)(6)
, DEA requested state PDMP data for the purpose of establishing its APQ. DEA believes state PDMPs to be an essential, reliable source of information for use in effectively estimating diversion of the five covered controlled substances. In April 2026, DEA sent a letter to NASCSA requesting its assistance in obtaining aggregated PDMP data for the five covered controlled substances from each state covering the years 2022-2025. The letter indicated that DEA was specifically interested in an analysis of prescription data from each state's PDMP that would assist DEA in estimating diversion and setting appropriate quotas in compliance with
21 U.S.C. 826(i)
. In its request, DEA provided specific questions, discussed in detail below, based on common indicia of potential diversion known as “red flags” by physicians, pharmacists, manufacturers, distributors, and federal and state regulatory and law enforcement agencies.
[
7
]
DEA investigators and administrative prosecutors also rely on Agency case law in which these red flags of diversion have been upheld as indicia of potential diversion.
[
8
]
Certain state regulations
(
printed page 72570)
now include red flag circumstances as potential indicators of illegitimate prescriptions, and thus of potential abuse and diversion of controlled substances.
9
See, e.g.,
The Pharmacy Place Order,
86 FR 21008
,
21012
(Apr. 21, 2021) (citing 22 Tex. Admin. Code 291.29(c)(4), specifying the geographical distance between the practitioner and the patient or between the pharmacy and the patient as a red flag).
DEA requested responses from state PDMP Administrators by June 15, 2026. NASCSA disseminated DEA's request to its PDMP Administrators and provided them with a report tool to ensure that responses to DEA's questions were extracted consistently across all responsive states. Thirty-six states and two territories provided DEA with summarized PDMP data as of July 2026, utilizing the standardized report developed by NASCSA.

Pharmacies are required by state law to enter controlled substance dispensing data into the state's PDMP database, including the prescriber's name, registered address and DEA number; prescription information (such as drug name); dispensing date; dosage dispensed; pharmacy registered address; and patient name and address. DEA considers PDMP data to be an accurate representation of dispensing activities in states. DEA received data for the following red-flag metrics:
The total number of patients who saw three or more prescribers in a 90-day period and were dispensed an opioid following each visit. For this metric, DEA requested and was provided the number of prescriptions for the five covered controlled substances dispensed to these patients, as a percentage of the total prescriptions dispensed for that particular covered controlled substance, as well as the corresponding quantity of the covered controlled substance dispensed. This metric (patients being prescribed covered controlled substances from three or more prescribers in a 90-day period) is used to identify potential doctor shopping, a common technique to obtain a high number of controlled substances, which may lead to abuse or diversion of controlled substances. DEA has long considered doctor shopping to be an indicator of potential diversion.
[
11
]
The number of patients that were dispensed prescriptions for each of the five covered controlled substances that exceeded 240 morphine milligram equivalents (MME) daily. States provided the raw number of such prescriptions dispensed, the number of prescriptions as a percentage of the total covered controlled substance prescriptions dispensed, and the corresponding quantity of the covered controlled substance dispensed. DEA believes that accounting for quantities in excess of 240 MME daily allows for consideration of oncology patients with legitimate medical needs for covered controlled substance prescriptions with high MME. Higher dosages place individuals at higher risk of overdose and death. Prescriptions involving dosages exceeding 240 MME daily may indicate diversion, such as illegal distribution of controlled substances or prescribing outside the usual course of professional practice.
The number of patients that paid cash for covered controlled substance prescriptions, without submitting for insurance reimbursement.
[
12
]
States also provided the number of prescriptions paid entirely with cash as a percentage of the total prescriptions for the five covered controlled substances dispensed, as well as the corresponding quantity of the covered controlled substances dispensed. When investigating potential diversion, cash payments are one element considered in identifying prescriptions filled for nonmedical purposes. Unusually high percentages of cash payments made to a prescriber or pharmacy for controlled substances may indicate diversion.
[
13
]
DEA received PDMP data from the states in a standardized format that allowed DEA to aggregate the data. The PDMP data sample represents a population of approximately 213.76 million people, which is approximately 62 percent of the U.S. population. DEA believes this sample is sufficient to derive a reasonable nationwide estimate.
While PDMP data is useful in estimating diversion, it is not conclusive. Further investigation would be required before concluding that any of the subject prescriptions were actually diverted. DEA continues to evaluate its methodologies in estimating diversion in an effort to set quotas more efficiently. State participation is crucial to accurate data analysis, and DEA anticipates working closely with states, as well as other federal and state entities, in future quota determinations.
To calculate a national diversion estimate for each of the covered controlled substances from the responses received from state PDMP Administrators, DEA relied upon the number of individuals who received a prescription for a covered controlled substance that met any of the three red-flag metrics for each of calendar years 2022-2025. Using the population of the states responding to DEA's request, DEA
(
printed page 72571)
then calculated the percentage of the population issued a prescription with a red flag. Using this estimated percentage for 2022-2025, DEA analyzed trends in the data to predict the estimated percentage of patients who would be expected to be included in these red-flag metrics for 2027.
DEA also reviewed aggregate sales data for each of the covered controlled substances, which it extracted from IQVIA's National Sales Perspective.
[
14
]
IQVIA sales data was selected to help quantify diversion at the national level because it reflects the best national estimate for all prescriptions written and filled, including the total quantity available for diversion or misuse. To predict the estimated national sales for 2027, DEA analyzed trends in IQVIA sales data from January 2021-April 2026.
To estimate diversion for each of the covered controlled substances, DEA multiplied the forecasted percentage of patients likely to receive a prescription for a covered controlled substance that meet any of the three red-flag metrics in 2027 by the forecasted sales data from IQVIA for 2027. Continuing Efforts to Anticipate and Prevent Drug Shortages
DEA remains committed to monitoring drug shortages, limiting their impact, and resolving them as quickly as possible. DEA continues to seek additional information that will assist in accurately forecasting domestic medical usage and export requirements of schedule I or II substances. As documented in the 2026 established APQ
Federal Register
notice DEA began utilizing IQVIA's foreign (non-U.S.) sales tracking data module in February 2024, MIDAS, which provides valuable insight into the growing export markets for schedule II stimulants. In March 2025, DEA sent a letter requesting DEA-registered manufacturers and distributors to voluntarily switch their DEA ARCOS database reporting from a quarterly to monthly basis. As of July 14, 2026, 47% of all ARCOS reporting DEA-registered manufacturers, distributors and reverse distributors report to ARCOS monthly. DEA remains committed to ensuring that all patients with legitimate medical need can access appropriately prescribed medications.
Quota Requirements for Controlled Substances in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act
On April 28, 2026, the Acting Attorney General issued
Schedules of Controlled Substances: Rescheduling of Food and Drug Administration Approved Products Containing Marijuana From Schedule I to Schedule III; Corresponding Change to Permit Requirements
as a final rule which became effective on April 28, 2026.
[
15
]
This final rule places in schedule III drug products containing marijuana that have been approved by the FDA and drug products subject to a state medical marijuana license. The final rule assigned separate drug codes for schedule III marijuana in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license, schedule III marijuana extract in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license, and schedule III naturally-derived delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinols in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license (drug codes 7362, 7353, 7386).
The final rule outlines several control measures required to satisfy the United States obligations under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961, as well as the CSA. Two related control measures of the Single Convention require: (1) manufacturers and distributors of drugs listed in Schedule I of the Convention, including marijuana, to be licensed (Articles 29 & 30); and (2) licensed manufacturers of drugs listed in Schedule I of the Convention obtain quotas specifying the amounts of such drugs they may manufacture to prevent excessive production and accumulation beyond that necessary to satisfy legitimate needs. (Articles 21 & 29). DEA is currently in the process of registering the manufacturers and distributors who will be handling the substances that have been moved to schedule III under the CSA as outlined in the final rule. Concurrently, DEA is assessing data sources and methodologies to determine the most reliable and relevant datasets for the estimation of the United States' legitimate need and production requirements for these 3 substances. Therefore, the APQ table below continues to reflect the APQs for the schedule I marijuana, marijuana extract, and delta-9-tetrahydrocananbinol (drug codes 7360, 7350, 7370) only. A separate notice will be published in the
Federal Register
once the proposed APQs for the schedule III substances
(
printed page 72572)
(drug codes 7362, 7353, 7386) are determined.
