Department of Justice
Drug Enforcement Administration
[Docket No. DEA-1568M]
AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final order.
SUMMARY:
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is adjusting the 2026 aggregate production quota for the schedule II controlled substances d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale). In making this determination, DEA has considered the factors set forth in
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
in accordance with
21 U.S.C. 826(a)
and is expediting publication of this determination to comply with the timeframes specified in
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)
.
DATES:
This final order is effective November 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration, Telephone: (571) 776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
Section 306 of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) (
21 U.S.C. 826
) requires the Attorney General to establish aggregate production quotas (APQ) for each basic class of controlled substance listed in schedule I and II. The Attorney General has delegated this function to the Administrator of DEA pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100
.
Under
21 U.S.C. 826(h)
, when a request for individual manufacturing quota is submitted by a DEA-registered manufacturer pertaining to a schedule II controlled substance on the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) list of drugs in shortage, DEA must complete review of such request no later than 30 days after receipt of the request. If, after the review is completed, DEA finds that an increase in the aggregate and individual production quotas is necessary to address a shortage of that controlled substance, DEA is to increase the aggregate and individual production quotas of that controlled substance and any ingredient therein to the level requested.
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)(B)(i)
. However, if it is determined that the level requested is not necessary to address the shortage, DEA is to provide a written response detailing the basis for the determination.
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)(B)(ii)
.
Background
DEA published the 2026 established APQ for controlled substances in schedules I and II in the
Federal Register
on January 5, 2026.
91 FR 287
. The 2026 established APQ represents those quantities of schedule I and II controlled substances that may be manufactured in the United States to provide for the estimated medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States, for lawful export requirements, and for the establishment and maintenance of reserve stocks. These quotas do not include imports of controlled substances for use in industrial processes. The final order stipulated that all APQ are subject to an adjustment, in accordance with
21 CFR 1303.15
.
[
1
]
Quotas Applicable to Drugs in Shortage Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 826(h)
Under
21 U.S.C. 356c
, manufacturers of drugs that are life-supporting, life-sustaining, or intended for use in the treatment or prevention of debilitating diseases or conditions must notify FDA of any permanent discontinuation or interruption in manufacturing likely to result in a meaningful disruption of the drug's supply in the United States. Schedule II controlled substances d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale) are drugs intended for use in the prevention or treatment of a debilitating disease or condition and therefore fall under the notification requirements of
21 U.S.C. 356c
. This provision further requires FDA to assess whether the notifications received from manufacturers concern controlled substances that are subject to production quotas in accordance with
21 U.S.C. 826
.
In conducting the review under
21 U.S.C. 826(h)
in order to determine the necessity of this adjustment, the Administrator has considered the criteria in accordance with
21 CFR 1303.13
(adjustment of APQ for controlled substances). The Administrator is authorized to increase or reduce the APQ at any time.
21 CFR 1303.13(a)
. DEA regulations state that there are five factors that shall be considered in determining whether to adjust the APQ.
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
. Accordingly, the Administrator has taken into account the following factors described below for calendar year 2026: (1) changes in the demand for that class, changes in the national rate of net disposal of the class, changes in the rate of net disposal of the class by registrants holding individual manufacturing quotas for that class, and changes in the extent of any diversion in the class; (2) whether any increased demand for that class, the national and/or individual rates of net disposal of that class are temporary, short term, or long term; (3) whether any increased demand for that class can be met through existing inventories, increased individual manufacturing quotas, or increased importation, without increasing the APQ, taking into account production delays and the probability that other individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to
21 CFR 1303.24(b)
;
(4)
whether any decreased demand for that class will result in excessive inventory accumulation by all persons registered to handle that class
(
printed page 72565)
(including manufacturers, distributors, practitioners, importers, and exporters), notwithstanding the possibility that individual manufacturing quotas may be suspended pursuant to
21 CFR 1303.24(b)
or abandoned pursuant to
21 CFR 1303.27; and (5)
other factors affecting medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs in the United States and lawful export requirements, as the Administrator finds relevant, including changes in the currently accepted medical use in treatment with the class or the substances which are manufactured from it, the economic and physical availability of raw materials for use in manufacturing and for inventory purposes, yield and stability problems, potential disruptions to production (including possible labor strikes), and recent unforeseen emergencies such as floods and fires.
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
. Based on that review, DEA is increasing the current d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale) APQs.
Analysis for the Adjustment to the 2026 d,l-Amphetamine and d-Amphetamine (for Sale) Aggregate Production Quota
On August 14 and August 24, 2026, DEA received two requests from two DEA registered manufacturers of the schedule II controlled substance d,l-amphetamine for an increase to their 2026 individual manufacturing quota pertaining to d,l-amphetamine. On August 14, 2026, DEA also received a request from a DEA registered manufacturer of the schedule II controlled substance d-amphetamine for an increase to its 2026 individual manufacturing quota pertaining to d-amphetamine (for sale). DEA reviewed the FDA drug shortage list and found multiple manufacturers reported a domestic shortage of amphetamine mixed salts tablets. Some manufacturers cited “shortage of an active ingredient” as the reason identified for the domestic shortages. Pursuant to these requests, DEA began its review under the timeframes specified by
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)
.
DEA reviewed the data provided by FDA in July 2026 on the domestic medical use of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale), as well as export data and inventory reports from both bulk and dosage manufacturers. FDA predicted the domestic medical need for d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine in 2026 will increase by 23.6 percent and 23.7 percent respectively when compared to the 2025 observed domestic medical need. DEA also reviewed the global consumption data from Multi International Data Analysis System (MIDAS). Extrapolation of the global sales of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine predicts an increase of 4.36 percent and 4.07 percent respectively in 2026 when compared to 2025. While sufficient quota was granted to meet legitimate patient needs both domestically and globally, DEA has determined that due to the increase in domestic and global medical needs, an increase to the d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) is necessary to allow for the adequate manufacturing of reserve stocks to start the next calendar year.
DEA also saw an increase in quota requests for product development activities by bulk and dosage form manufacturers of d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) to synthesize engineering and validation batches to support the filing of new drug applications for FDA review. Year-to-date amounts approved for product development by bulk and dosage manufacturers have increased 173 percent for d,l-amphetamine and 32 percent for d-amphetamine (for sale) in 2026 when compared to 2025, respectively. DEA has determined that it is necessary to increase the 2026 d,l-amphetamine and d-amphetamine (for sale) APQs to allow for the maintenance of reserve stocks and increased product development needs after considering all estimated consumption data and projected product development needs.
Analysis for the Adjustment to the 2026 Hydromorphone Aggregate Production Quota
On July 24, 2026, DEA received a request from a DEA registered manufacturer of the schedule II controlled substance hydromorphone for an increase to its 2026 individual manufacturing quota pertaining to hydromorphone. DEA reviewed the FDA drug shortage list and found multiple manufacturers reported a domestic shortage of hydromorphone hydrochloride injectable products. The manufacturers cited “demand increase for the drug or delay of manufacturing” as the reasons identified for the domestic shortages. Pursuant to this request, DEA began its review under the timeframe specified by
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)
.
DEA reviewed the most recent domestic usage data from IQVIA, as well as data provided by the FDA on the domestic medical use of hydromorphone. FDA predicted the domestic medical need for hydromorphone in 2026 will increase by 20.9 percent compared to the 2025 observed medical need. DEA also reviewed export information provided by bulk manufacturers, export data from DEA's internal database, and global consumption data from MIDAS. Export data shows that the 2026 exports of hydromorphone will increase 142 percent when compared to 2025 because one bulk manufacturer is planning to significantly increase its export of hydromorphone in 2026. DEA has determined that an increase to the hydromorphone APQ is necessary to support the estimated increase in domestic medical need and projected new export requirements.
Analysis for the Adjustment to the 2026 Methylphenidate (for Sale) Aggregate Production Quota
On July 31, August 1, and August 20, 2026, DEA received requests from DEA registered manufacturers of the schedule II controlled substance methylphenidate for an increase to their 2026 individual manufacturing quota pertaining to methylphenidate (for sale). DEA reviewed the FDA drug shortage list and found multiple manufacturers reported a domestic shortage of methylphenidate tablets and film. The manufacturers cited “demand increase for the drug” or “discontinuation of the manufacture of the drug” as the reasons identified for their portion of the domestic shortages. Pursuant to these requests, DEA began its review under the timeframes specified by
21 U.S.C. 826(h)(1)
.
Following a review of domestic and export data, as well as inventory reports from both the bulk and dosage manufacturers, DEA has determined that an increase to the APQ of methylphenidate (for sale) is necessary to address the increasing global medical demand and to allow domestic manufacturers of FDA-approved methylphenidate drug products to replenish their inventories to levels authorized by DEA regulations. FDA predicted the domestic medical need for methylphenidate in 2026 will increase by 23.4 percent compared to the 2025 observed medical need. DEA also reviewed the methylphenidate export data from DEA's internal database, as well as global consumption data from MIDAS. Extrapolation of the sales data from MIDAS predicts global consumption will increase by 8.01 percent for methylphenidate drug products in 2026 when compared to 2025.
DEA also reviewed global production and consumption data of methylphenidate published in the 2025 Psychotropic Technical Report by the International Narcotics Control Board
(
printed page 72566)
(INCB).
[
2
]
The INCB reported the United States as the leading manufacturer of methylphenidate, and although the total manufacturing of methylphenidate was reported to be at the highest level since INCB began receiving data, the global stocks of methylphenidate decreased by 11 tons, from 91.6 tons in 2023 to 80.6 tons in 2024. After considering all the domestic and global data, DEA has determined that an increase to the 2026 methylphenidate (for sale) APQ is necessary to allow for the adjustment of reserve stocks to support the increasing global medical demand.
After considering the factors set forth in
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
in accordance with
21 U.S.C. 826(a)
as well as 826(h), DEA determined that it is necessary to increase the established 2026 APQs for the schedule II controlled substances d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale) to be manufactured in the United States to provide for the estimated legitimate medical needs of the United States and export requirements to meet foreign demand. These adjustments are necessary to ensure that the United States has an adequate and uninterrupted supply of d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale) to meet legitimate patient needs both domestically and globally.
Additional Legal Considerations
The procedures previously adopted by DEA for adjustment of APQ are set forth in DEA regulations in
21 CFR 1303.13
. Under that provision, the Administrator, upon determining that an adjustment of the APQ of any basic class of controlled substance is necessary, shall publish in the
Federal Register
a general notice of an adjustment in the APQ for that class. The regulation further directs that DEA will allow any interested person to file comments or objections to the adjusted APQ within the time specified by the Administrator in the notice. Section 1303.13 further provides that, “[a]fter consideration of any comments or objections . . . the Administrator shall issue and publish in the
Federal Register
his final order determining the APQ for the basic class of controlled substance.”
The statutory timeframe applicable to actions taken under
21 U.S.C. 826(h)
was enacted by Congress after DEA established its regulations in
21 CFR 1303.13
. DEA has determined that it is not possible to increase the APQ within the Congressionally-mandated 30-day period while also complying with the procedures that DEA previously laid out in
21 CFR 1303.13
. Therefore, the Administrator has determined that, in order to comply with the 30-day timeframe in
21 U.S.C. 826(h)
, this final order must be published without opportunity for comment and made effective immediately.
Determination of 2026 d,l-Amphetamine, d-Amphetamine (for Sale), Hydromorphone, and Methylphenidate (for Sale) Aggregate Production Quota
In determining the adjustment of the 2026 d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale) APQs, DEA has taken into consideration the factors set forth in
21 CFR 1303.13(b)
in accordance with
21 U.S.C. 826(a)
as well as 826(h). Based on all of the above, the Administrator is adjusting the 2026 APQs for d,l-amphetamine, d-amphetamine (for sale), hydromorphone, and methylphenidate (for sale).
The Administrator hereby adjusts the 2026 APQ for the following schedule II-controlled substances expressed in grams of anhydrous acid or base, as follows:
Controlled substance
Current APQ (g)
Adjusted APQ (g)

d,l-amphetamine

[

]
Signing Authority
This document of the Drug Enforcement Administration was signed on November 4, 2026, by DEA Administrator Terrance C. Cole. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DEA. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of DEA. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the

.

SUMMARY:
The Deputy Secretary of War has decided to delist the entity listed in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this notice from the list of Chinese military companies operating in the United States, without prejudice to relisting the company on additional or supplementary grounds.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Kathryn Collins, (703) 697-2908.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 1260H of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (
Pub. L. 116-283
, as amended (codified at
10 U.S.C. 113
, note)) (Section 1260H) provides that the Secretary of Defense is to identify and publish a list of “Chinese military companies” annually until December 31, 2030, and to make additions or deletions to the list not less frequently than annually. Section 1260H(b)(2) requires the Secretary of Defense to publish the unclassified portion of the list in the
Federal Register
.
The Deputy Secretary of Defense has decided to delist the following entity from the list of “Chinese military companies” in accordance with section 1260H, without prejudice to relisting the entity on additional or supplementary grounds:
WuXi AppTec Co., Ltd. (WuXi AppTec)
The Deputy Secretary of War has determined that WuXi AppTec should be removed from the most recent Section 1260H List that was published in the
Federal Register
on June 10, 2026, in compliance with the order issued by the U.S. District Court of Columbia on August 7, 2026, granting WuXi AppTec's Motion for Preliminary Injunction, which enjoins the Department from enforcing, implementing, or otherwise giving effect to the Department's designation of WuXi AppTec as a Chinese military company under Section 1260H.
The entity delisted from the list of “Chinese military companies” is also identified in Mandarin and can be found in this notice's docket on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Search by the docket ID, DOD-2026-OS-2410. The Mandarin version of the delisting notice is available for public viewing at the Supporting & Related Material tab. Any correspondence related to the 1260H List must be emailed to
osd.pentagon.ousd-a-s.list.1260h-list@mail.mil
.

AGENCY:
Office of the Secretary, HUD.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice advises the public that HUD intends to make changes to its Headquarters and Field operational structure. These changes are designed to better enable HUD to address crucial workplace and mission needs by eliminating redundancies, streamlining and increasing flexibility in work processes, and consolidating administrative functions, thus allowing the Department to more efficiently deliver on its mission utilizing current resources. It does not propose any office closures or relocation of staff.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Lori Michalski, General Deputy Assistant Secretary, Office of Administration, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 Seventh Street SW, Washington, DC 20410; telephone 202-402-3921. (This is not a toll-free number.) HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech and communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit
https://www.fcc.gov/​consumers/​guides/​telecommunications-relay-service-trs
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Legal Requirements for This Notice
In accordance with section 7(p) of the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act (
42 U.S.C. 3535(p)
), a plan for the reorganization of any HUD regional, area, insuring, or other field office may take effect only upon the expiration of 90 days after publication in the
Federal Register
of a cost-benefit analysis of the effect of the plan on each HUD office involved. Such cost-benefit analysis shall include, but not be limited to (1) an estimate of cost savings supported by background information detailing the source and substantiating the amount of the savings; (2) an
(
printed page 72552)
estimate of the additional cost which will result from the reorganization; (3) a study of the impact on the local economy; and (4) an estimate of the effect of the reorganization on the availability, accessibility, and quality of services provided for recipients of those services. Where any of the factors cannot be quantified, the Secretary shall provide a statement on the nature and extent of those factors in the cost-benefit analysis. This notice is to satisfy the requirement of section 7(p). Not all changes described in this notice rise to the level legally requiring a 90-day notice period and may be implemented by the Department at its convenience. These changes are being described here to provide a full picture of the future organizational structure of the Department.
II. Required Statutory Cost-Benefit Analysis
A. Background
Since 2025, due in large part to the success of the Deferred Resignation Program, the Department experienced a significant number of voluntary departures from Federal service and a corresponding reduction in staff across all program offices. Certain offices were particularly impacted by these departures, leaving them constrained in the ability to accomplish Departmental goals and objectives. As a result, each program office undertook a thorough analysis of all operations and functional alignment in order to develop a plan to more efficiently and effectively manage the Department's programs and activities. The result of these efforts is a proposed large-scale reorganization of the Department. The proposed reorganization was communicated to Members of Congress on April 3, 2026. This notice reflects the next step in moving forward with these plans.
The proposed reorganization of the Department is expected to produce net operational efficiencies by allowing for better management of the Department's activities given its current level of staffing. On balance, the proposed reorganization of the Department from its FY 2024 organizational structure would merge smaller units with similar specializations into larger ones, reducing some of the disadvantages of a more complex hierarchy associated with the Department's previous staffing levels. In some cases, a division would be realigned under a different chain of command if doing so improves coordination with other divisions.
The goal is to begin implementing these changes by the end of fiscal year (FY) 2026, with full implementation completed during FY 2027. The reorganization is expected to significantly enhance operational efficiency, as well as improve HUD's program delivery and the service provided to HUD's customers.
B. Description of Proposed Changes
1. Departmental Management
a. Executive Secretariat
Staff levels in the Executive Secretariat (ExecSec) were drastically reduced through the voluntary departures of staff via the Deferred Resignation Program. As a result, ExecSec has already implemented cross-training and work-sharing across the office to continue to perform the duties of the office. ExecSec will consolidate these teams to more efficiently manage the work of the staff under one supervisor.
b. Office of Public Affairs
OPA will be consolidated into a single, streamlined Office of Public Affairs.
2. Office of Public and Indian Housing
The Office of Public and Indian Housing (PIH) is consolidating and realigning operations to create greater operational efficiencies and consistency in program administration and oversight. Specifically, PIH will merge all responsibilities for public housing under one Office and all voucher programs in another. This will streamline both processes and program administration. By aligning the offices along program lines, PIH expects improvements in communication and collaboration between the more interrelated units of the Office of Public and Indian Housing.
3. Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes
The Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes (OLHCHH) will reduce redundant functions performed within OLHCHH and streamline operations into three divisions, down from the current five divisions. This will create additional efficiencies of operation and better utilize OLHCHH's current staff and resources.
4. Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity
FHEO will reorganize and consolidate its office structure to adopt a more functional model designed to better fulfill FHEO's core statutory obligations under the Fair Housing Act and related authorities. FHEO will consolidate its operations under a centralized management structure designed to promote efficiencies of operation and consistency in the enforcement, compliance, and educational activities of the office. This reorganization will eliminate redundant management layers and reduce the duplication of work across FHEO. Additionally, the reorganization will reduce the variability of handling of complaints and conciliations across FHEO, bringing greater consistency to FHEO's work. The reorganization will improve workload balancing while also allowing for increased productivity through specialization, where appropriate. Finally, the centralization made possible through the reorganization will create administrative efficiencies and improve accountability and performance monitoring.
5. Office of the Chief Financial Officer
The Office of the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) will be reorganizing three divisions to ensure better administration of the Department's budget and financial management activities. CFO will establish a new division to consolidate budget assistance for program offices, reducing redundancies across the Department and assisting those program offices who experienced significant voluntary staff separations in the last year. CFO will also create new branches to focus on financial management and accountability in order to better assist the Department in managing its funds. Finally, a new division will consolidate travel management oversight and coordination in support of the Department in a more cost-effective and efficient manner.
6. Office of the Chief Information Officer
The Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) will reorganize to drive efficiency and align our work and services around a portfolio and product-based construct. This shift will optimize office organization around technical solutions management and emphasize OMB's designation of HUD as a High Impact Service Provider (HISP) and our systems and solutions that support the Government Services Delivery Improvement Act through establishment of a design and experience division. This reorganization will enable HUD to evolve into a 21st-century delivery organization that leverages best-in-class industry practices around product management and development, security, and operations (DevSecOps). It will establish a portfolio management organization construct that will enable HUD OCIO to surge and align resources around key delivery initiatives and increase standardization around delivery practices. It will establish a
(
printed page 72553)
division for data and super intelligence (SI) under the Chief Technology Officer to ensure HUD is staffing and prioritizing data and SI appropriately. Finally, core business office functions (budget, acquisition, and resourcing) will be consolidated into one office division for better synergy and standardization of processes. Additionally, OCIO will establish a customer experience division to better align responsibilities and deliver services to HUD and its customers. Additionally, contract and financial management will be realigned and consolidated to eliminate redundancies across OCIO. Overall executive operations of OCIO will also be consolidated and realigned to streamline and standardize administrative functions. OCIO will realign the management of HUD's most critical assets to improve management and the response to security threats. Finally, Divisions and branches will be renamed to better reflect the current workload and functions of each OCIO component.
7. Office of Community Planning and Development
The Office of Community Planning and Development (CPD) is modernizing operations and realigning CPD's structure to strengthen the ability of the office to meet its mission and achieve its goals. These changes will allow CPD to better deliver on its mission critical functions while maintaining strong accountability for program performance and the responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars. CPD will consolidate its Office of Grant Programs non-disaster grant programs into a single office to better integrate and synthesize existing program policy resources and reduce unnecessary barriers to affordable housing creation. CPD will also rename other offices to create better alignment with the Departmental naming conventions for consistency and clarity.
8. Government National Mortgage Association
The Government National Mortgage Association (GNMA or Ginnie Mae) is creating a new division to coordinate and address the need for greater data and market analysis to aid in data-driven decision-making. GNMA will also realign branches to bolster the work of the Office of Enterprise Risk, which will better manage Ginnie Mae's financial reporting, compliance, audit resolution, and enforcement efforts. As part of this realignment, branches will be created to allow focus on GNMA budget and economic analysis by specialized staff with unique skills in these areas. Ginnie Mae is also creating new branches to focus efforts on issuer engagement in a manner that is more tailored to the underlying assets to create efficiencies in account management and compliance. New branches will also be established to better support customer-focused information, training and support. Additional branches will be established to better focus counter party risk management and to direct and manage capital market activities. Finally, the renaming and realignment of functions relating to data and technology management will create operational efficiencies and better reflect the work of each branch.
9. Office of Policy Development and Research
The Office of Policy Development and Research will increase operational efficiencies by realigning the Chief Data Officer to the CIO as described above. Three divisions will be merged and consolidated into a single division responsible for resource management to further operational efficiencies. Finally, one division is being renamed to better reflect the functions performed in that division.
10. Office of General Counsel
The Office of General Counsel (OGC) is reorganizing its office structure to primarily breakdown artificial silos, eliminate redundancies, and streamline management responsibilities to effectively address the significant reduction in staff resulting from the voluntary separation of staff through the Deferred Resignation Program and other planned retirements. Specifically, the reorganization of OGC will eliminate the distinction between Headquarters and Regional/Field offices. Instead, OGC will have a unified structure organized based on programmatic operations. All counsel, regardless of geographic location, will report to one of three Deputy General Counsels, who will divide responsibilities loosely along the following lines: (1) general, cross-cutting legal services and administrative law, (2) grant and assistance program related legal support, and (3) housing finance legal services.
OGC's programmatic approach to legal representation will allow greater flexibility in management of the work flowing from HUD's various program offices while allowing for the development of greater expertise across the Department's grant and assistance programs as well as the Department's housing finance programs. This structure will also allow for the centralization of all administrative and general cross-cutting legal services and facilitate greater workload management across the country. With the voluntary departure of significant numbers of staff, OGC's siloed and restrictive structure made swift adaptation to the new staffing realities and shifting priorities in terms of workload extremely difficult to manage. With an emphasis on flexibility and seamless worksharing in this reorganization, OGC will be better situated to react to changing priorities and program activity levels allowing for the appropriate management of workflows without delay. Additionally, the inherent flexibilities in this reorganization mean that no staff will be relocated as a result of this reorganization and no employees will be negatively impacted in terms of grade/rates of pay.
11. Office of Field Policy and Management
The Office of Field Policy and Management (FPM) will realign the additional cross-cutting program implementation functions associated with the Build America, Buy America Act, into the office that currently oversees various cross-programmatic compliance initiatives for the Department. This shift will allow for increased efficiency in implementation as it better aligns with the existing cross-cutting implementation work and functions of FPM and is expected to enhance the stakeholder experience.
12. Office of Housing—Federal Housing Administration
a. Office of Single Family Housing
The Office of Single Family Housing is transitioning the work of its Homeownership Centers (HOCs) from a geographic-based business model to a function-based business model. Single Family will maintain three official HOC-designated offices, each with its own specialization: Philadelphia (Origination), Denver (Servicing), and Atlanta (Quality Assurance). Santa Ana will no longer be identified as a HOC, however all Single Family office locations, including Santa Ana, will continue to remain in operation, with no geographic reassignments, and minimal changes to employee position descriptions.
These changes will ensure consistency in program delivery, improved workload management across functions, centralized expertise, and streamlined collaboration between field offices and headquarters policymakers.
Additionally, the Investments Division in the Office of Multifamily Housing's Recapitalization Office was
(
printed page 72554)
originally established in 2023 to centralize the administration of the Green and Resilient Retrofit Program (GRRP) grant and loan activities, including application review, award processing, transaction closing, and ongoing portfolio monitoring. As there are no GRRP new grants/loans being funded, the GRRP functions for the existing grants/loans have been integrated into the Office of Recapitalization's existing organizational structure, with transaction-related activities assigned to the Transaction Division and closing functions assigned to the Closing Division. As a result of this functional integration, the division is no longer necessary as a separate organizational unit and is being removed from the organizational chart. All staff in the Investments Division have left the Department or taken other positions at HUD.
b. Office of Operations
To increase operational efficiency and eliminate redundancies, as other support offices across HUD provide the same services, the Office of Operations will be streamlined to support the Office of Housing's Management team with a smaller and more efficient footprint. The Office will be renamed the Office of Management Operations.
13. Office of Administration
The Office of Administration is comprised of subcomponents under the leadership of the executive front office of Administration.
a. Executive Office
The Office of the Administration executive front office (Admin) will assume the supervision of all of HUD's national security, continuity, continuity of operations, and emergency planning functions under a new Office of National Security and Continuity Programs. This realignment will elevate these functions from their current location under the CAO to report directly to the General Deputy Assistant Secretary for Admin, in recognition of the importance of these functions and the need to reduce duplicative and unnecessary layers of management in this area.
b. Office of the Chief Human Capital Officer
The Office of the Chief Human Capital Officer (OCHCO) will streamline its executive management layer by reducing its authorized Senior Executive Service (SES) allocation from six to four. Executive oversight will be consolidated under the SES positions of Chief Human Capital Officer (CHCO) and Deputy CHCO, who will oversee two balanced operational pillars led by the remaining two authorized SES directors:
1.
Workforce Accountability, Policy & Compliance:
This will unify regulatory functions, establish an independent Misconduct Inquiries & Investigations Division alongside Policy, Accountability; Personnel Security and Suitability; Reasonable Accommodation; and Performance Management and Recognition.
2.
Talent Strategy, Systems & Enterprise Intelligence:
This will consolidate Data and Human Resources (HR) Systems; house the functions of Recruitment and Staffing; Pay, Benefits and Retirement; Enterprise Training and Executive Development; Administrative Operations, Workforce Health, Wellness and EAP.
Under this realigned architecture, Employee and Labor Relations, Anti-Harassment, Executive Resources and Emergency surge hiring support will be integrated directly into the CHCO Front Office.
c. Office of the Chief Administrative Officer
The Office of the Chief Administrative Officer (OCAO) will realign staff and functions within OCAO to more efficiently use staff resources to manage the work of the office. With the realignment of the national security, continuity programs (COOP), and emergency planning functions to the executive front office of Admin, the remaining physical security functions will be managed out of the new Office of Physical Security. Additionally, the Protective Services Division, which provides protection services to the Secretary and Deputy Secretary, will be managed by a separate division reporting to OCAO. All space and project management functions will be consolidated into the Resource Management division and a division to oversee printing functions will be established within the Office of Digital Enterprise within OCAO. Finally, all FOIA, Privacy, and Electronic Records Management Functions will be aligned under OCAO into one division for efficient management.
d. Office of the Chief Procurement Officer
The Office of the Chief Procurement Officer (OCPO) will restructure its operations to establish a centralized hub for early acquisition life-cycle activities, consolidating the presently dispersed functions and allowing increased efficiency and skill development. Additional efforts to modernize the operations of OCPO will require establishment of various branches across OCPO designed to further the efficient management of procurement activities and establish greater communication and ties with the program offices across HUD.
C. Estimate of Cost Savings
Approximately 90 days following the date of publication of this notice, HUD will begin the reorganization of the Department as identified above. Each program office will separately undertake the necessary reorganization, consolidation, and realignment of functions and staff as described. Given the varying level of complexities in the reorganization plan, the full implementation of these plans is expected to occur within Fiscal Year 2026 for some offices while others will continue working towards full implementation in Fiscal Year 2027.
Because these efforts are about streamlining and consolidating organizational structures and reducing redundancies in terms of functions performed rather than any change in terms of footprint or staffing levels, nothing in these plans includes steps to relocate or reduce any staff.
[
1
]
As a result, immediate, quantifiable cost savings are not expected to be realized from anything in this reorganization plan. Instead, HUD anticipates greater efficiencies in qualitative operations and the achievement of the Department's mission and goals, including enhanced customer and stakeholder service. These efficiencies will enable the Department to continue efficient and effective management of its programs generally within the existing approved staffing levels of the Department. Current staffing levels are almost 35 percent below historic staffing levels and this reorganization will provide HUD with the ability to operate even more effectively at current staffing levels, ultimately carrying forward savings from the reduced salaries and expenses of the Department.
D. Estimate of the Additional Costs
The Department expects that there may be some minor short-term adjustment costs associated with this reorganization plan. Some managers and staff may require time and additional
(
printed page 72555)
training in order to adapt to new roles and adjust to managing a slightly different mix of workflows. These upfront costs are expected to be less than the longer-term gains from operational efficiencies generated by the reorganization. The overall goal of the reorganization of the Department's structure is to preserve the availability, access, and quality of the Department's services.
E. Study of the Impact on the Local Economy
Because there are no staff relocations or office closures required by this reorganization, there is no anticipated impact on any local economies.
F. Estimate of the Effect of the Reorganization
This reorganization is designed to better enable HUD to address crucial workplace and mission needs by eliminating redundancies, streamlining and increasing flexibility in work processes, and consolidating administrative functions, thus allowing the Department to more efficiently deliver on its mission utilizing current resources and mitigate the impact of previously realized staff reductions across the Department, primarily due to voluntary resignations through the Deferred Resignation Program (which was particularly acute for certain program offices).
The proposed reorganization advances a new alignment that will maximize the use of staffing resources to ensure flexibility and maintain quality work across all aspects of its portfolio. The intended future state of the Department will demonstrate a program-focused approach to best leverage current staff, maximize operational efficiencies, and permit better allocation of resources during periods of increased workload, all within the current footprint and geographic dispersion of HUD staff. This reorganization will also better align skillsets across the Department, modernize how offices conduct their work and address the staffing losses mentioned above. The specific shifts away from extremely siloed organizational structures with regional/field office restrictions are designed to change reporting structures, not eliminate offices or force relocation of any staff. While functions and duties of staff may change, HUD will endeavor to minimize impacts on staff and avoid to the greatest extent possible the imposition of any reduction in grade or pay because of this reorganization.
In sum, no immediately quantifiable benefits, and no significant costs or local economic impacts would arise from the reorganization, which maintains the Department's number of staff and field offices, but simply streamlines and realigns functions for optimal efficiency.
HUD will take steps to ensure that the reorganization therein complies with Title 5, applicable civil rights statutes, OPM workforce reshaping guidance, and merit systems principles. HUD's implementation of the reorganization will be phased to ensure continuity of operation. To the extent that future personnel actions may be required, HUD will ensure that they are conducted in accordance with law and regulation.
III. Environmental Impact
This notice does not direct, provide for assistance or loan and mortgage insurance for, or otherwise govern or regulate, real property acquisition, disposition, leasing (other than tenant-based rental assistance), rehabilitation, alteration, demolition, or new construction, or establish, revise or provide for standards for construction or construction materials, manufactured housing, or occupancy. Accordingly, under
24 CFR 50.19(c)(1)
, the notice is categorically excluded from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42. U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
).
Andrew Hughes,
Deputy Secretary.

This move was detailed in a separate notice published in satisfaction of the obligations under section 3535(p) and is separate and distinct from the reorganization plans discussed in this notice.

(

AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
This proposed rule would reform Medicare and Medicaid regulations deemed obsolete or excessively burdensome on healthcare providers and suppliers, with the objective of reducing costs, enhancing flexibility in delivering innovative care, and streamlining existing regulations. This reform seeks to enable healthcare professionals to devote more resources to improving patient care by eliminating or minimizing requirements that impede quality patient care or that divert resources away from furnishing high quality patient care.
DATES:
To be assured consideration, comments must be received at one of the addresses provided below, by January 11, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
In commenting, please refer to file code CMS-3484-P. Comments, including mass comment submissions, must be submitted in one of the following three ways (please choose only one of the ways listed):
1.
Electronically.
You may submit electronic comments on this regulation to
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​CMS-2026-3631
.
Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions.
2.
By regular mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-3484-P, P.O. Box 8010, Baltimore, MD 21244-8010.
Please allow sufficient time for mailed comments to be received before the close of the comment period.
3.
By express or overnight mail.
You may send written comments to the following address ONLY: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Attention: CMS-3484-P, Mail Stop C4-26-05, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21244-1850.
For information on viewing public comments, see the beginning of the “
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
” section.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
CMS Health and Safety Inquiries, 410-786-6633,
HealthandSafetyInquiries@cms.hhs.gov
,
for further information related to the following: Ongoing and public health emergency (PHE) respiratory illness data reporting for hospitals, critical access hospitals, long-term care facilities and rural emergency hospitals; obstetrical services quality assessment and performance improvement, all staff trainings, and critical access hospital co-location; long-term care facility staff COVID-19 vaccination education and Ombudsman notice; intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities staff vaccination education; and Life Safety Code, Health Care Facilities Code, and Emergency and Standby Powers Systems Code.
DCWReporting@cms.hhs.gov
,
for further information related to Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Inspection of Public Comments:
All comments received before the close of the comment period are available for viewing by the public, including any personally identifiable or confidential business information that is included in a comment. We post all comments received before the close of the comment period on the following website as soon as possible after they have been received:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the search instructions on that website to view public comments. CMS will not post on
Regulations.gov
public comments that make threats to individuals or institutions or suggest that the commenter will take actions to harm an individual. CMS continues to encourage individuals not to submit duplicative comments. We will post acceptable comments from multiple unique commenters even if the content is identical or nearly identical to other comments.
Plain Language Summary:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of this proposed rule may be found at
https://www.regulations.gov/​
.
I. Background
A. Executive Summary
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is committed to incorporating and integrating ongoing retrospective review of regulations to achieve a more streamlined and effective regulatory framework. CMS routinely reviews its regulations to identify opportunities to strengthen the patient health and safety requirements by revising the Conditions of Participation (CoPs), Conditions for Coverage (CfCs), Conditions for Certification, and Requirements for Participation, (collectively referred to as CoPs).
We conducted a comprehensive review of the CoPs for all 21 provider and supplier types with the objectives of improving the quality of existing regulations consistent with statutory requirements; streamlining procedural solutions; maximizing net benefits (including benefits that are difficult to quantify); and reducing costs and other burdens on facilities to comply with regulations. We identified obsolete and burdensome regulations that could be eliminated or reformed to enhance the effectiveness of facility operations and reduce unnecessary burden or other costs, with a particular focus on freeing up resources that health care providers could otherwise use to improve patient health and safety. We have also identified unnecessary and burdensome reporting requirements that can be eliminated to improve the efficiency of the Medicaid program.
Relationship of This Rulemaking to Future Reforms:
We are committed to working with, and welcome suggestions for future rulemaking from, interested parties to identify other reforms to the CoPs that would improve patient health and safety while reducing unnecessary burden on health care facilities and entities or improve flexibility in meeting the Federal requirements.
B. Summary of Major Provisions
We propose to reduce regulatory burden on providers and suppliers by modifying, removing, or streamlining current regulations that we now believe are excessively burdensome. We note that the appropriate term for the individual receiving care and/or services differs depending upon the facility type, such as hospital “patients” and Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICFs/IID) “clients.” When discussing each individual provider or supplier type, we use the appropriate term; however, when discussing all or multiple provider or supplier types we will use the general term “patient.” Similarly, despite the different terms used for specific entities (such as campus, center, clinic, facility, organization, or program), when we are discussing all or multiple entities, we will use the general term “facility.”
(
printed page 72635)
1. Hospitals
For hospitals, we propose to remove the recently finalized staff training requirements for transfer protocols, emergency services readiness, and obstetrics (OB) care, as well as OB-specific quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) requirements. We are also proposing policies that address informed consent requirements and policies and procedures that aim to support families' ability to request collection of birth tissues, including for cultural, religious, or personal reasons in hospitals.
2. Long Term Care (LTC) Facilities
For LTC facilities, we propose to revise the facility assessment requirement by removing the requirement for the active involvement of representatives of direct care staff in conducting the LTC facility assessment. We also propose to revise the infection control requirement to remove the ongoing (weekly) acute respiratory illness data reporting requirements and amend the reporting requirements during a Public Health Emergency (PHE) to include the data elements originally specified in the ongoing data reporting section. We are also proposing to remove requirements related to educating staff about COVID-19 vaccine and its benefits and risks, offering it to them, and documenting these actions.
Additionally, we propose to revise the physical environment requirements to exempt existing facilities from the room occupancy and bathroom facility standards when there is a change of ownership (CHOW) for the facility or a lapse in and restoration of a facility's certification. We also propose to remove the requirement for LTC facilities to provide Ombudsman notice of resident transfers related to emergent care and solicit public comment regarding additional changes to the Ombudsman notice. Finally, we solicit public comment on the role of physician assistants and nurse practitioners in delivering resident care.
3. Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals With Intellectual Disabilities (ICFs/IID)
For ICFs/IID, we propose to remove requirements related to educating staff about the COVID-19 vaccine and its benefits and risks and offering it to them.
4. Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs)
For REHs, we propose to remove expired COVID-19 requirements related to ongoing data reporting and staff vaccination regulations. We propose to remove the data reporting requirement during a PHE to reduce burden. We also propose to update the emergency preparedness requirement to revise the point of contact that REHs may use to obtain copies of standards that are incorporated by reference and to correct an inaccurate cross-reference.
5. Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs)
For CAHs, we propose revising the regulation to clarify current CMS policy that CAH distance eligibility determinations are based on proximity to hospitals that provide acute inpatient care services, including other CAHs, rather than hospitals that provide only specialty services, such as psychiatric hospitals, long-term care hospitals (LTCHs), or rehabilitation hospitals. We also propose adding a requirement that implements section 241 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (
Pub. L. 119-75
), that revised the application of the statutory distance requirement in specified circumstances as set forth in the law. In addition, we propose to remove recently finalized staff training requirements for emergency services readiness, and obstetrical (OB) care, as well as OB-specific quality assessment and improvement (QAPI) requirements. We are also proposing policies that address informed consent requirements and policies and procedures that aim to support families' ability to request collection of birth tissues, including for cultural, religious, or personal reasons in CAHs.
6. Life Safety Code (LSC) and Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) Updates for All Applicable Providers and Suppliers
We propose to update the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) LSC and HCFC editions that are incorporated into the regulations for religious nonmedical health care institutions (RNHCIs), ambulatory surgical centers (ASCs), inpatient hospices, programs of all-inclusive care for the elderly (PACE), hospitals, LTC facilities, ICFs/IID, REHs, CAHs, and dialysis facilities. The LSC and HCFC are nationally recognized fire and building safety standards published by the NFPA. We propose to adopt the most recent (2024) editions of the LSC and HCFC, with limited exceptions.
7. Emergency and Standby Power Sources
For hospitals, CAHs, REHs, and LTC facilities that are required to have emergency and standby power systems, we propose to update the current requirements to allow the use of additional sources of emergency power. We also propose to adopt the 2022 edition of the Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems (ESPS), which establishes safety and performance requirements for emergencies and standby power systems.
8. Outside Window or Door Requirement Updates
For RNHCIs, inpatient hospices, hospitals, CAHs, and LTC facilities, we propose to remove the requirement for windows and doors in every patient sleeping area and a 36-inch windowsill requirement for buildings constructed after July 5, 2016, and defer to the egress requirements within the health care occupancy chapters of the LSC. Additionally, for hospitals and CAHs, we also propose to remove the 60-inch windowsill requirement for special nursing care areas in new occupancies. We propose to remove a similar requirement for ICFs/IID related to windows in client bedrooms that are below the level of the ground outside and defer to the window requirements for resident board and care occupancies within the LSC.
9. Life Safety Code and Health Care Facility Code Waiver Authority
We propose to codify our authority to waive certain LSC and HCFC provisions in the regulatory text applicable to each affected provider type. We would permit facilities to comply with specific provisions of a newer edition of the LSC or HCFC, subsequent to CMS review. We would permit this exception after we have determined that the provision provides an equal or superior means of ensuring patient safety as compared to the provisions of the code edition currently adopted in regulation at that time.
10. Transplant Programs Request for Information (RFI)
CMS' policy on organ transplantation is to increase the number of transplants available to patients on the organ transplant waiting lists. Achieving this goal requires a sufficient number of transplant programs to provide lifesaving surgeries. There are currently over 250 Medicare-approved programs providing organ transplantation services. However, programs seeking initial Medicare approval report challenges in meeting the initial requirements for Medicare certification. We are soliciting public comments on how to reduce potential barriers for new transplant programs seeking Medicare certified transplant programs.
(
printed page 72636)
11. Supervision of Anesthesia Services RFI
We are soliciting public comments related to Medicare's physician supervision requirement for certified registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs) administering anesthesia services in hospitals, CAHs, REHs, and ASCs. Under current policy, anesthesia must be administered only by qualified practitioners. When a CRNA administers anesthesia, a physician, such as the operating practitioner or an anesthesiologist, must be immediately available to provide supervision. Since 2001, CMS has allowed a State's Governor to request an exemption from this requirement, permitting CRNAs to practice independently where consistent with State law. CMS is now requesting public input on this policy, including whether it should be retained, revised, or otherwise modified.
12. Reducing Reporting Burden for Hospital and CAH Respiratory Illness and Infectious Disease Data RFI
We are soliciting public comments on ways to reduce the reporting burden associated with respiratory illness and infectious disease data reporting requirements for hospitals, including CAHs (collectively referred to as “hospitals” for purposes of this RFI). Following the COVID-19 response, the health care community identified a need for standardized data elements and digital data collection approaches to ease this burden, particularly given the risk of overlapping or duplicative requirements across agencies for smaller or resource-constrained facilities. CMS, in partnership with CDC, has worked to reduce this burden through the development of data standards, adoption of interoperability modernization activities, and use of a single reporting system, the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN), which currently offers flexible reporting options such as Comma-Separated Values (CSV) import, Application Programming Interface (APIs), and Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based approaches. Building on these efforts, CMS is requesting public comment on how to further support hospitals' adoption of data and interoperability capabilities to reduce burden through greater automation and digital data collection.
13. Medicaid Institutional Payment Transparency
We propose to rescind requirements for States to report annually, at the facility level, on the percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services that is spent on compensation for direct care workers, the percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services that is spent on compensation for support staff, and the percentage of Medicaid payments for ICF/IID services that is spent on compensation for support staff. We also solicit public comment on approaches to address direct care worker shortages and strengthen the direct care workforce in nursing facilities and ICFs/IID.
C. Statutory and Regulatory Background
The Social Security Act (the Act) sets forth definitions for the types of providers and suppliers that may participate in Medicare and Medicaid, the requirements that each must meet to be eligible for Medicare and Medicaid participation, and the Secretary's authority to establish other requirements as necessary to protect the health and safety of patients. The following list identifies the statutory and regulatory citations for the providers and suppliers for which we are proposing to revise or remove regulations in this rule:
Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institutions (RNHCIs)—section 1821 of the Act and
42 CFR 403.700
through
403.770
.
Ambulatory Surgical Centers (ASCs)—section 1832(a)(2)(F)(i) of the Act and
42 CFR 416
.
Hospices—section 1861(dd)(1) of the Act and
42 CFR 418
.
Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)—sections 1894, 1905(a), and 1934 of the Act and
42 CFR 460
.
Hospitals—section 1861(e)(9) of the Act and
42 CFR 482
.
Long Term Care (LTC) Facilities—Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)—under section 1819 of the Act, Nursing Facilities (NFs)—under section 1919 of the Act,
42 CFR 483.1
through
483.315
,
42 CFR 438.72
, and
42 CFR 442.43
.
Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICF/IID)—section 1905(d) of the Act,
42 CFR 483.400
through
483.480
, and
42 CFR 442.43
.
Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs)—sections 1861(kkk) of the Act and
42 CFR 485.500
through
485.546
.
Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs)—sections 1820 and 1861(mm) of the Act and
42 CFR 485.601
through
485.649
.
Dialysis Facilities—sections 1881(b), 1881(c), 1881(f)(7) of the Act and
42 CFR 494
.
In addition, Title XIX of the Act established the Medicaid program as a joint Federal and State program to provide medical assistance to eligible individuals. Section 1902(a)(4) of the Act provides authority to specify “methods of administration” that are “necessary for proper and efficient” administration of the State plan.

E. Severability
We are clarifying and emphasizing our intent that if any provision of this proposed rule, if finalized, is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, or stayed pending further action, it shall be severable from the remainder of the final rule, and from rules and regulations currently in effect, and not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other, dissimilar circumstances. If any provision is held to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions which could function independently should take effect and be given the maximum effect permitted by law. In this rule, we propose several provisions that are intended to and will operate independently of each other, even if each serves the same general purpose or policy goal. Where a provision is necessarily dependent on another, the context generally makes that clear.
II. Provisions of the Proposed Regulations
A. Hospitals
Hospitals provide a range of services to treat patients with acute care needs, which may include emergency medicine, surgery, labor and delivery, cardiac care, oncology, among a wide variety of other services. Hospitals also administer general and specialty care that cannot safely be provided in other settings, under the supervision of physicians and licensed practitioners. They may operate as independent institutions or as part of a larger health care system or learning institution. As of January 2026, there are around 4,700 Medicare-certified hospitals.

11

Under sections 1866 and 1902 of the Act, hospitals seeking to participate in
(
printed page 72638)

42 CFR part 482
apply, including short-term acute care hospitals, long term care hospitals (LTCHs), rehabilitation hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, cancer hospitals, and children's hospitals), seeking to be Medicare and Medicaid providers of services must be certified as meeting Federal participation requirements. Our CoPs set out at
42 CFR part 482
establish the patient health and safety protections established by the Secretary for hospitals (except for critical access hospitals (CAHs)). The specific statutory authority for hospitals is set forth in section 1861(e) of the Act. In addition to specific terms of that subsection, the hospital provision at section 1861(e)(9) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to issue any additional regulations deemed necessary to protect the health and safety of those receiving services in the hospital.
In accordance with section 1864 of the Act, State surveyors assess hospital compliance with the conditions as part of the process of determining whether a hospital qualifies for a provider agreement under Medicare. However, under section 1865 of the Act, hospitals can elect to be reviewed instead by private accrediting organizations approved by CMS as having standards that meet or exceed the applicable Medicare standards and survey procedures comparable to those CMS requires for State survey agencies.

Hospitals must use data to identify and prioritize improvement areas (§ 482.21(b)), sustain measurable improvements (§ 482.21(c)), conduct performance improvement projects (§ 482.21(d)), and demonstrate leadership oversight over the program and that the program reflects the complexity of the facility's organization and services (§ 482.21(e)). In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule,

Commenters indicated that these requirements were overly burdensome and costly, particularly for small and rural hospitals, and expressed concern that compliance costs could contribute to the closure of labor and delivery units, which would worsen access to maternity care and potentially exacerbate maternal health disparities.
While we originally disagreed with these types of comments in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule, we have since refined our understanding of the issues that hospitals are facing in diverting resources away from direct patient care to comply with administrative standards. 2. Proposal To Remove Transfer Protocol Staff Training (§  482.43(c))
The hospital discharge planning requirements at § 482.43, “Discharge planning,” were originally published on December 13, 1994,
[
29

This includes early identification of patients at risk of adverse outcomes and timely discharge planning evaluations by qualified personnel to assess post-hospital care needs, service availability, and the patient's capacity for self-care or appropriateness of the discharge setting (§ 482.43). When needed, hospitals must document and communicate evaluation results, develop and implement discharge plans, reassess plans as patient needs change, ensure appropriate transfer or referral, and regularly review their discharge planning process.
In the September 30, 2019 final rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Revisions to Requirements for Discharge Planning for Hospitals, Critical Access Hospitals, and Home Health Agencies, and Hospital and Critical Access Hospital Changes to Promote Innovation, Flexibility, and Improvement in Patient Care,”
[
30

CMS established additional discharge planning requirements requiring hospitals to assist patients and their caregivers in selecting post-acute care providers by sharing relevant quality and resource use data that are relevant to the patient's goals of care and treatment preferences, and to document this sharing of information in the medical record (§ 482.43(a)(8)).
The discharge planning CoP was last updated in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule. Effective July 1, 2025, all hospitals must have written policies and procedures for transferring patients under their care (§ 482.43(c)). This requirement is inclusive of hospital inpatients, such as transfers from the emergency department to inpatient admission, transfers between inpatient units in the same hospital, as well as transfers between inpatient units at different hospitals. In addition, hospitals are required to provide annual training to the relevant staff (as determined by the facility) regarding the hospital policies and procedures for transferring patients under its care.
In the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule, CMS specifically agreed with commenters that supported inclusion on annual training on transfer protocols in the hospital CoPs to promote consistency in transfer processes and ensure that transfers are conducted safely by minimizing errors.
[
31
]
In light of additional public comments received through the 2025 deregulatory RFI
[
32
]
and the issuance of
E.O. 14192
and
E.O. 14219
, CMS is now reconsidering that position. CMS received comments on the 2025 deregulatory RFI stating that transfer protocols are already built into existing regulations, and that the additional formal annual staff training requirement is unnecessarily prescriptive, as staff engage with transfer processes routinely as part of daily clinical operations and maintain familiarity through regular practice, including through electronic health record systems that facilitate unit-to-unit and facility-to-facility transfer processes. CMS agrees that a separate, prescriptive annual training requirement is not necessary to ensure staff familiarity with transfer policies and procedures. CMS also recognizes that the broader existing regulatory requirements, including Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) requirements for emergency department transfers, the existing discharge planning CoP requirements (§ 482.43), and accrediting organization (AO) standards collectively support staff competency in transfer processes without the need for a separate annual training requirement.
CMS acknowledges that hospitals were required to undertake compliance efforts, including conducting initial annual training sessions and documenting staff completion in personnel records, since the July 1, 2025, effective date of § 482.43(c). However, CMS has determined that the ongoing annual compliance burden of maintaining and documenting a separate staff training requirement on transfer protocols outweighs the benefit of retaining this requirement, given that the written policies and procedures requirement remains in place and the existing operational and regulatory requirements support staff knowledge of transfer protocols.
Specifically, the compliance costs associated with the emergency services readiness staff training requirements, estimated in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule,
[
33
]
are more than $862 million and 5.1 million hours of staff time over a ten-year period, or approximately $86 million and 505,213 staff hours annually.
Removing the annual transfer protocol staff training requirement may allow clinicians to spend more time with patients and prioritize high-quality patient care, while maintaining flexibility in how hospitals ensure staff familiarity with transfer policies and reduce regulatory compliance burden. As patient transfers require coordinated clinical decision-making across settings and levels of care, maintaining written transfer policies support consistent transfer decision-making, including critical or infrequent situations. Removing this annual training requirement would not prevent hospitals, states or AOs from independently establishing and enforcing facility policies requiring annual training.

Other commenters noted that the emergency services readiness requirements at § 482.55(c) will impose large burdens on hospitals and health care professionals, particularly for small and rural hospitals with limited staffing and financial resources. CMS agrees that the combination of existing CoP requirements (including those for QAPI under § 482.21), EMTALA requirements, AO accreditation standards, specialty board certification requirements, and nationally recognized clinical resources ensure staff competency in emergency services readiness without the need for a separate, prescriptive annual training requirement. This determination is further supported by the role of state licensing boards, which require clinicians to meet continuing education and competency standards for licensure renewal, as well as private-sector patient safety organizations that advance national clinical readiness and safety practices.
CMS acknowledges that hospitals were required to undertake compliance efforts since the July 1, 2025, effective date, however, CMS has determined that the ongoing annual compliance burden outweighs the incremental benefit of retaining this requirement given the robust existing structure of other applicable regulations, AO standards, board certifications, EMTALA requirements, and QAPI requirements. a. Background on Birth Tissues Uses
Birth tissues are solely generated as a direct result of pregnancy, labor, and delivery and may be discarded, retained by the patient, stored, donated, banked for potential future medical use, and/or transferred to a third party for research or commercial purposes. These tissues can include umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord tissue, umbilical veins, placenta, amniotic membrane, chorionic membrane, amniotic fluid, and Wharton's jelly.

Cord blood is the most commonly collected birth tissue for future medical use (approximately 110,000 collections annually, or about 3 percent of births, with 75 to 80 percent stored in private banks).
