b. Need for New Hospital Standards
As discussed in section II. A. of this proposed rule, section 1861(e)(9) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish additional requirements necessary for the health and safety of patients served by Medicare-participating hospitals. Existing hospital CoPs establish the framework for protecting patient rights, promoting informed decision-making, and ensuring accurate medical and clinical record documentation. Together, the requirements safeguard patient health and safety and promote quality care for all patients in Medicare- and Medicaid-participating hospitals. Specifically, patient rights CoPs for hospitals at § 482.13(a) and (b) provide that patients or their representatives have the right to make informed decisions regarding their care, including being informed of their health status, being involved in care planning and treatment, and being able to request or refuse treatment. The hospital medical records CoP at § 482.24(c)(4)(v) requires the medical record to contain properly executed informed consent forms for procedures and treatments specified by the medical staff, or by Federal or State law if applicable. However, there are no existing CoPs related specifically to the collection of birth tissues.
We note that this differs from the regulatory framework applicable to organs and tissues collected for transplantation. For example, § 482.45 establishes specific requirements for organ, tissue, and eye procurement, including requirements related to hospitals' agreements with organ procurement organizations, tissue banks, and eye banks and policies governing the donation process. Of note, hospitals are not required to have a relationship with birth tissue procurement organizations or birth tissue banks. Organs and tissues collected for transplantation are therefore subject to an established regulatory framework and associated donation and consent process. The existing hospital CoPs do not establish comparable requirements specifically addressing the collection and disposition of birth tissues following a live birth, including circumstances in which tissues may be retained by the patient or collected, donated, transferred, stores, or used for purposes other than transplantation.
We believe that decisions involving the collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, release, or discarding of birth tissues may implicate important patient interests and rights and therefore warrant additional transparency and informed decision-making protections. Unlike many other biological materials generated during the course of medical care, birth tissues may have unique cultural, religious, personal, or familial significance to patients and their families.
[
98
]
At the same time, birth tissues may also have medical, research, or other uses that can involve their collection or transfer to entities outside of the hospital. These characteristics distinguish birth tissues from both biological materials routinely discarded in the course of medical care and organs and tissues collected through established transplantation and donation processes. Therefore, families giving birth at hospitals may reasonably wish to understand whether such tissues will be discarded, available for them to retain, used for research purposes, transferred to third parties, stored for future use, or otherwise utilized in commercial activities.
Moreover, because of the concerns discussed previously about inappropriate clinical use and profiteering, transparency is particularly important when a hospital participates in a program or arrangement through which birth tissues may be donated, transferred, banked, stored, or used by a third party and/or for commercial purposes. We believe that patients have the right to the information necessary to make an informed decision about consenting to these uses of their personal birth tissues and biological materials.
CMS understands that many hospitals may already have policies around informed consent and allow patients to request retention or release of birth tissues, subject to State law, infection prevention and control requirements, and clinical circumstances.
[
99
]
However, practices may vary, and patients may not know whether, when, or how to make such a request. Some hospitals may rely on general consent forms or medical waste policies that do not clearly inform patients about possible collection, transfer, storage, donation, commercial use, or other disposition of birth tissues. Variation in these processes can create uncertainty for patients, staff, and hospitals.
We believe that establishing new requirements to address these variations would strike the appropriate balance between improving transparency, creating consistent patient expectations and ensuring that no hospital is compelled to collect, bank, donate, or release tissues in circumstances that would be unsafe, unlawful, or inconsistent with clinical care.
c. Proposed Scope and Definition of Birth Tissues (§ 482.59(c))
Mothers who give birth in hospitals that furnish OB services should have baseline protections regarding informed decision-making, documentation, and safe handling of their birth tissues when the hospital engages in birth tissue collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release. To advance this goal, we propose to add new standards at § 482.59(c). As noted earlier in this section, we are proposing to remove the current requirements at § 482.59(c) and replace them with new standards that build on the CoPs for obstetrical services. These new standards address informed consent for birth tissue collection and patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues.
We propose to add a new standard to the OB Services CoP at § 482.59(c), titled “Birth tissue collection.” Facilities that furnish obstetrical services vary widely in their involvement with birth tissues. For example, some hospitals are deeply involved in birth tissue activities, including operating or sponsoring public cord blood donation programs, contracting with third-party collection or tissue procurement entities, or facilitating private banking arrangements. Others have more limited involvement, such as occasionally receiving requests to retain or release birth tissues to the patient for cultural, religious, or personal uses or to a private third-party for personal future medical uses, research, or donation, even where no formal relationship exists between the hospital and the third party. To account for this variation, the proposed standard would apply to only those hospitals that furnish obstetrical services and participate in one or more activities related to birth tissues including collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release to patient. For purposes of this standard, we interpret participation to include hospital-sponsored, hospital-operated, or hospital-facilitated activities, that is, any instance in which the hospital's personnel, premises, policies, or processes are used in connection with the collection, packaging, storage, transfer, banking, donation, or release
(
printed page 72647)
birth tissues. Facilities that do not engage in any of these activities would not be subject to the proposed standard.
Furthermore at § 482.59(c), we propose to define “birth tissues” to capture the materials most commonly associated with live childbirth that may be collected, retained, stored, donated, banked, transferred, or released for personal, clinical, research, and/or commercial purposes. For purposes of this proposed rule, birth tissue is limited to tissue or biological material obtained in connection with labor and delivery resulting in a live birth. This proposal does not apply to tissue or biological material obtained in other clinical circumstances. Specifically, we propose to define “birth tissue” as “human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery, (including cesarean-section delivery), such as umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord tissue, placenta, amniotic membrane, amniotic fluid,
[

and other tissues or biological materials associated with live childbirth.” This definition is intended to avoid gaps in patient protections that could arise if the rule addressed only one category of birth tissue, such as cord blood, while other tissues were collected, transferred, released, or disposed of under less transparent processes. This definition is also intended to be flexible enough to accommodate changes in collection practices and terminology over time. NIH has issued policy describing additional requirements related to research uses of such tissue.

d. Proposals for Informed Consent (§ 482.59(c)(1))
At proposed § 482.59(c)(1), we would require that the hospital ensure that it obtains informed consent from the patient or the patient's representative prior to the collection, storage, donation, transfer, banking, or release to patients of birth tissues, consistent with the hospital's scope of services and role in those activities. The consent must be documented consistent with the medical records requirements at § 482.24(c)(4)(v).
Consistent with the phrase “scope of services and role in those activities” in proposed § 482.59(c)(1), the obligations under this proposal would be tailored to the specific activities in which the hospital participates. The proposal would not require hospitals to offer new services, to purchase or provide new equipment, or initiate or sponsor a collection program, private banking arrangement, or other birth tissue collection program. Rather, it would require only that when a hospital furnishes obstetrical services and participates in a covered birth tissue activity, the hospital maintains appropriate consent, documentation, policies, procedures, and safe handling processes commensurate with its scope of services and role in that activity. For example, a hospital that operates a public cord blood collection program would be expected to ensure that its consent process includes the information and disclosures applicable to public donation. In contrast, a hospital that does not participate in a public cord blood collection program and is only collecting birth tissue in response to an individual mother's request for release of a placenta for personal or cultural reasons would be expected to document the request and release decision consistent with its policies and provide safe handling instructions.
We propose that the informed consent process include, as applicable, six categories of information: (1) a description of the birth tissues to be collected; (2) the intended use, including commercial and research uses, of the birth tissues; (3) disclosure of any third-party involvement and conflicts of interest; (4) information regarding risks, limitations, and infection prevention and quality control considerations; (5) notice that a patient's refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment; (6) and any other information required under applicable Federal or State law. These elements establish a baseline and are not intended to prescribe a single consent form or process for all hospitals or activities. Providing this information supports patient autonomy and empowers the patient to make a decision that reflects the patient's values and preferences.

Patients must receive sufficient information to understand third-party involvement and potential conflicts when they are making decisions about birth tissues from their deliveries. Depending on the activity, relevant information could include the possibility that collection may not be feasible because of maternal or neonatal clinical circumstances, that a specimen may fail to meet volume or quality criteria, that stored birth tissues may not be clinically useful in the future, or that releasing tissue for personal handling may involve infection prevention and storage considerations.
We also propose at § 482.59(c)(1)(v) that the patient be informed that refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment. Patients in labor or experiencing obstetrical emergencies may be vulnerable to time pressure or perceived pressure from clinicians, hospital staff, or third parties. Equally, the patient's decision to request collection or release of birth tissues does not obligate the hospital to provide services that are unsafe, unavailable, or inconsistent with State law or hospital policy. This is consistent with patient exercise of rights at § 482.13(b)(2).
We recognize that timing of consent in the labor and delivery context can be challenging. As previously discussed, the proposed requirements apply to birth tissue obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery resulting in live birth. The timing of the informed consent process does not alter the scope of tissues subject to this proposal. Prenatal education and consent are preferable when feasible, especially for planned donation or banking arrangements, but patients may present without prior knowledge of their options or make key requests at admission or after delivery. Under these proposals, hospitals retain flexibility to design processes that are consistent with clinical practice, patient needs, State law, and the hospital's role provided that consent is obtained before the applicable birth tissue activity occurs whenever possible, and that collection or release activities does not interfere with clinical care (for example, pathologic examination of the placenta). Patient safety takes precedence in high-acuity or emergent circumstances.
Finally, we also recognize that, in some circumstances, a patient may independently arrange with a third-party tissue bank, private bank, courier, or other entity and may ask the hospital solely to accommodate collection or release. In such cases, the hospital is not expected to become an expert in the third party's products, business practices, marketing claims, or downstream uses. The hospital should have a process, consistent with its policies, to document the patient's request; confirm, as appropriate to the hospital's role, that the patient has provided authorization or evidence of the applicable third-party consent; and document the actions taken by the hospital to accommodate, accommodate subject to reasonable conditions, delay, or deny the request based on clinical circumstances, infection prevention, and legal requirements. This approach supports patient choice while ensuring that the hospital's obligations remain proportional to the hospital's actual role and involvement. We note that FDA regulates human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products, including birth tissues.
e. Policies and Procedures for Cultural, Religious, or Personal Uses (§ 482.59(c)(2))
At § 482.59(c)(2), we propose to require the hospital to have written policies and procedures that permit patients to request retention or release of birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons, consistent with State law and the hospital's infection prevention and control program requirements under § 482.42. Such policies and procedures would not require patients to provide justification or documentation for their respective cultural, religious, or personal reasons. We propose this requirement because patient requests for retention or release may arise in routine deliveries, scheduled cesarean deliveries, emergent deliveries, or other clinical contexts, and families and staff need clear procedures for safe, consistent collection and release of birth tissues.
The proposed policies and procedures would address four core topics. First, policies must address processes for patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues. We expect hospitals to specify how and when a patient or representative may make a request, who
(
printed page 72649)
is responsible for receiving and documenting the request, what forms or authorizations must be completed, and how the hospital will communicate decisions regarding release to the patient. Hospitals should design processes that are easily understandable and accessible for their patient population and align with clinical operations.
Second, the policies and procedures must address safe handling, packaging, storage, and release practices of birth tissues. For example, we expect hospitals to identify the personnel responsible for handling birth tissues, provide appropriate containers or packaging as needed in alignment with safe handling, clearly label each tissue container or package as appropriate, accommodate tissue storage pending release as requested by the patient, establish chain-of-custody or handoff processes where needed, and implement protocols for circumstances requiring consultation with infection prevention personnel, pathology, risk management, or clinical leadership. These procedures should reflect the type of tissue, the intended use, the clinical circumstances, and the hospital's infection prevention and control program. Third, we propose that policies and procedures must address circumstances under which retention or release may be limited or denied, including infection prevention and control concerns, biohazard risks, certain clinical conditions, emergency cases, or other applicable legal requirements, as discussed below.
• Infection Prevention and Control Concerns and Biohazard Risks
Suspected or confirmed infection, contamination, or other biohazard concerns may create unacceptable risks that warrant limiting or denying retention or release. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) classifies human blood, certain body fluids, and unfixed human tissues and organs as potentially infectious materials.
[
111
]
Because placental and related birth tissues may contain blood and other biological material, hospitals would need to implement handling and packaging procedures to protect patients, staff, and others from potential exposure to bloodborne pathogens (for example, HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or other infectious agents).
[
112
]
Hospitals must have processes to address safe handling, packaging, storage, and release when patients request retention or release of birth tissues. Hospitals should also identify circumstances in which release may be limited or denied due to infection prevention and control concerns consistent with the hospital's infection prevention and control program under § 482.42.
• Certain Clinical Conditions
Retention or release may also be limited when tissue is needed for pathology review or other clinically appropriate diagnostic evaluation. Placental pathology may assist in the evaluation of adverse maternal, fetal, or neonatal outcomes, including fetal growth restriction, stillbirth,
[
113
]
infection, congenital abnormalities, preterm birth, placental insufficiency, maternal hypertensive disorders, or other complications of pregnancy and delivery. Hospitals should identify in their policies the clinical circumstances under which retention for diagnostic purposes would take precedence over patient's requests for release. To the extent possible, patient requests should take precedence over circumstances under which hospitals may want to retain the placenta or other birth tissues for elective evaluation, research, or other purposes. Unless there are circumstances such as infection prevention concerns or a need for the hospital to retain the birth tissue for appropriate diagnostic evaluation, the patient's autonomy over their biological materials related to delivery should be prioritized.
• Emergency Cases
Patient safety takes precedence in all emergency circumstances in which staff cannot safely collect, process, or release birth tissues due to emergent patient care needs. Collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release activities of birth tissues should not delay emergency care, interfere with the clinical management of labor and delivery, or alter medically appropriate obstetric or neonatal practice.
[
114 115
]
A hospital would not be expected to delay necessary clinical intervention to complete a birth tissue consent process or collection activity, and failure to collect birth tissue due to emergent clinical circumstances would not, by itself, constitute noncompliance. To the extent necessary, such consents may be obtained following resolution of the emergency and stabilization of the patient's condition.
• Other Applicable Legal Requirements
Retention, testing, handling, or disposition of birth tissue may also be limited or governed by applicable Federal, State, Tribal, territorial, or local law (See discussion of relevant State laws in section II.A.5. of this proposed rule.) By defining these criteria in advance, hospitals provide patients and staff with clear expectations and transparent and consistent processes. These proposed requirements are intended to complement, not interfere with, a hospital's existing authority to retain birth tissues when clinically appropriate or otherwise required by law.
Fourth, at § 482.59(c)(2)(i)(D), we propose that the policies and procedures must address staff education regarding the hospital's procedures for responding to patient requests. This education is intended to be focused and practical. Staff who may receive or respond to requests to know how to identify the applicable policy, document the request, process the request safely and within their scope of services, and provide safe handling instructions when tissue is released.
Lastly, we propose at § 482.59(c)(2)(ii) that the hospital provide patients who request retention or release of birth tissues with instructions for safe handling, transport, storage, and disposition of the tissues, as applicable. These instructions should be understandable, practical, and tailored to the birth tissue and release context. For example, instructions might address the need to maintain tissue in a leak-proof container, avoid exposure to other patients or staff, refrigerate or otherwise store tissue as directed, use appropriate personal protective measures, or comply with applicable local disposition requirements. The proposed requirement would not require hospitals to supervise the patient's use after release, but it does require the hospital to provide instructions that support safe decision-making at the point of release.
In summary, these proposed requirements are intended to operate alongside, not in place of, other existing Federal and State authorities. FDA regulates human cells, tissue and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps) either under Section 361 of the Public Health Service Act and 21
(
printed page 72650)
CFR part 1271 or under Section 351 of the PHS Act and relevant sections of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act and applicable regulations. FDA has issued guidance on minimal manipulation and homologous use and has stated that HCT/Ps that do not meet the criteria to be regulated solely under section 361 of the Public Health Service Act and
21 CFR part 1271
are regulated as drugs, devices, and/or biological products.
[
116
]
FDA also has taken compliance and enforcement actions addressing unapproved HCT/Ps, including products derived from birth tissues.
The proposed CoPs at § 482.59(c) occupies a narrower and distinct role, regulating the facility-patient interaction, facility policies, documentation, and processes for informed decision-making and safe release in Medicare and Medicaid participating hospitals. Nothing in this proposal determines whether any product is lawfully marketed or subject to FDA premarket review. Rather the purpose of the CoPs is to protect patient health and safety and to ensure that quality care is furnished to all patients in Medicare-participating hospitals. In accordance with section 1864 of the Act, State surveyors assess hospital compliance with the conditions as part of the process of determining whether a hospital qualifies for a provider agreement under Medicare. Alternatively, under section 1865 of the Act, hospitals can elect to be reviewed instead by private accrediting organizations approved by CMS as having standards that meet or exceed the applicable Medicare standards and survey procedures comparable to those CMS requires for State survey agencies. Examples of survey and enforcement activities include review of facility policies and procedures, auditing of patient medical records, and interviewing facility leadership and staff.
We invite public comment on proposed § 482.59(c), including the scope of hospitals and activities to which the standard should apply; the proposed definition of birth tissues; the proposed informed consent standard; and the proposed policies and procedures for cultural, religious, or personal uses.
B. Long-Term Care Facilities
LTC facilities, meaning SNFs and NFs, are institutions or distinct parts of an institution that are primarily engaged in providing skilled nursing care and related services to patients that require medical or nursing care or rehabilitation services due to an injury, disability, or illness. As of January 2026, there are around 15,000 LTC facilities caring for about 1.25 million residents daily.
[
117
]
LTC facilities seeking to be Medicare and Medicaid providers of services must be certified as meeting Federal participation requirements set forth at
42 CFR part 483
(hereafter, “LTC requirements”), which set out the resident health and safety protections established by the Secretary. The specific statutory authority for LTC facilities is set forth in section 1819 and 1919 of the Act. Sections 1819(d)(4)(B) and 1919(d)(4)(B) of the Act explicitly authorize the Secretary to issue any regulations he deems necessary to protect the health and safety of residents of LTC facilities. Under sections 1866 and 1902 of the Act, LTC facilities seeking to participate in the Medicare or Medicaid program, respectively, or both, must enter into an agreement with the Secretary or the State Medicaid agency, as appropriate.
1. Proposal To Amend Transfer Notice to Ombudsman (§ 483.15(c))
In 2016 CMS finalized revised requirements that LTC facilities must meet to participate in the Medicare and Medicaid programs.
[
118

This comprehensive update of the regulations focused on quality of healthcare furnished through Federal programs, patient safety and reducing procedural burdens on providers. Among other things, this 2016 final rule emphasized the importance of protection to residents from being inappropriately transferred or discharged, providing residents with access to an advocate who can inform them of their options and rights, and ensuring that the Office of the State LTC Ombudsman is aware of facility activities related to transfers and discharges. Specifically, as a part of ensuring resident rights at § 483.15(c), we require LTC facilities to provide notice to the resident and the resident's representative(s) before transfer or discharges. The facility must also send a copy of the notice to a representative of the Office of the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman.
In accordance with the January 30, 2017, E.O. “Reducing Regulation and Controlling Regulatory Costs” (
E.O. 13771
), on July 18, 2019, we published a proposed rule entitled, “Requirements for LTC Facilities: Provisions to Promote Efficiency and Transparency.”
[
119
]
In that rule we proposed changes to § 483.15 related to admission, transfer, and discharge rights. Specifically, we proposed to revise the requirement for facilities to send transfer and discharge notices to the State LTC ombudsman to apply only to “involuntary transfers and discharges.” In response to the proposed rule, we received comments from a wide range of individual health care professionals, various healthcare associations, LTC facilities, organizations representing providers of LTC and senior service, LTC Ombudsmen, advocacy groups for LTC consumers, and LTC consumers and their family representatives. Many commenters supported the proposed change to remove Ombudsman notifications for hospitalizations where the facility has every intention of accepting the resident back following the hospitalization. However, some commenters suggested that this should be addressed in the sub-regulatory guidance, rather than through regulatory revisions. Furthermore, these commenters indicated that the use of the terms “involuntary” or “facility-initiated” in the regulations is confusing and suggest that a notice would not be required unless a resident actively objects to the transfer or discharge. Due to circumstances surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapidly evolving needs and concerns of the LTC community at that time, we did not finalize the proposal to restrict Ombudsman notices to involuntary transfers and discharges only.
While the original intent of this requirement as finalized in the 2016 rule was to enable Ombudsman officials to intervene in cases of inappropriate resident discharges, the volume of paperwork related to notice for every transfer of care and discharge has prevented Ombudsman officials from effectively focusing their efforts on inappropriate discharges, thereby negating the purpose of the regulation. In an emergent care situation, the urgency of the transfer of a resident to an acute care hospital for emergent care must be the primary focus of LTC facility staff, with a notice of transfer provided to the resident and resident's representative(s) as soon as practicable
(
printed page 72651)
before the transfer in accordance with the requirements set forth at § 483.15(c)(4)(ii)(D). Copies of notices for emergency transfers must be sent to the Ombudsman, however the practicalities of implementing this requirement have led to the permitted practice of submitting a monthly list of residents who experienced a transfer to receive emergency care. This current practice does not meet the original intent of the regulations to prevent residents from being inappropriately transferred or discharged, as a transfer for emergency care services is inherently appropriate, nor does the practice as implemented lend itself to actionable efforts on the part of the Ombudsman officials.
We are aware that Ombudsman offices have expressed concerns about the issue of large numbers of notices and the difficulties of sorting notices in a timely manner so that problematic notices can be identified and acted upon. Responses to the 2025 deregulatory RFI
[
120
]
indicate that transfer and discharge notice requirements create administrative burden for nursing homes, particularly during emergent resident hospital transfers. Commenters indicated that while these notices may be necessary for planned discharges, they are excessive and are low priority for urgent hospital visits. Commenters recommend eliminating transfer notices for emergent care and eliminating the requirement to send a copy of the notice to the Ombudsman to reduce administrative burden and confusion for the families.
In light of the public comments and the misalignment between our original regulatory goals and the way in which LTC facilities and Ombudsman offices have complied with the regulations, we propose to modify the requirement at § 483.15(c)(3)(i) for LTC facilities to provide Ombudsman notice of resident transfers, except for transfers related to emergent care, as a way to focus Ombudsman official efforts on the reduction of inappropriate transfers and discharges and to alleviate the burdens of sending and processing these notices for both LTC facilities and Ombudsman officials.
The transfer and discharge facility requirements at § 483.15(c) would continue to require that the facility must permit each resident to remain in the facility and not transfer or discharge the resident from the facility unless certain circumstances are present. The circumstances center around the resident's welfare, whether the resident has improved sufficiently that the resident no longer needs the services provided by the facility, safety of individuals in the facility is endangered due to the clinical or behavioral status of the resident, payment issues and/or the facility ceases to operate. In addition, the resident has the right to appeal a transfer or discharge. The robust nature of the facility requirements around transfer and discharge, specifically the timing of the notice at least 30 days before the resident is transferred or discharged, would continue to assure that residents receive appropriate protection in the transfer and discharge process. The requirements would also continue to require that if the information in the notice changes prior to affecting the transfer or discharge, the facility must update the recipients of the notice as soon as practicable once the updated information becomes available. We invite comments on how to reduce burden while supporting sharing the most current, updated information related to transfer and discharge notices.

In May 2024 CMS finalized changes to the LTC facility requirements.
[

Among other things, these changes moved the existing facility assessment requirements from § 483.70(e) to their own requirement at § 483.71. As part of this revision, CMS expanded the facility assessment requirements to require the active involvement of certain categories of staff and others in the facility assessment process. One of those new categories is direct care staff, including but not limited to, RNs, LPNs/LVNs, NAs, and representatives of the direct care staff, if applicable. Most commenters at the time of the proposed rule supported the inclusion of direct care staff; however, some commenters opposed including third party representatives of direct care staff, such as union representatives.
Commenters contended that inclusion of representatives of direct care staff would be inappropriate since the facility assessment is an operational document for the facility. They also suggested that the inclusion of third parties, especially union representatives, could be disruptive, divisive, and render the facility assessment ineffective. In addition, commenters raised concerns that third parties, especially union representatives, would be primarily concerned about the well-being of the workers they represent instead of the quality of residents' care. CMS acknowledged these counter arguments to the proposal but subsequently finalized the provision, and we have continued to review and reevaluate all aspects of the facility assessment regulation. Upon review of these changes, conducted in light of recent
E.O. 14192
“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”
[
122
]
and
E.O. 14219
“Ensuring Lawful Governance and Implementing the President's `Department of Government Efficiency' Deregulatory Initiative,”
[
123
]
CMS identified the provision related to ensuring the active involvement of representatives of direct care staff as being operationally and logistically burdensome without direct benefits to resident care. LTC facilities do not have any authority over the actions or inactions of direct care staff representatives; therefore, requiring LTC facilities to be responsible for assuring their active involvement in the facility assessment process is impracticable. We have determined that holding LTC facilities responsible for the actions of those that do not have employment or contractual obligations with the facility is not an appropriate requirement for LTC facility regulations. As such, we propose to remove this provision from the requirements. We would retain the remainder of the facility assessment requirements without change.
The facility assessment is a foundational element of the LTC requirements, providing the basis for ensuring residents receive safe and appropriate care. LTC facilities are required to conduct and document a facility-wide assessment to determine what resources are necessary to competently care for their residents during both day-to-day operations and emergencies, including an evaluation of the resident population and the resources needed to serve them. The facility assessment informs several key areas of LTC facility operations, including nursing services (§ 483.35), food and nutrition services (§ 483.60), quality assurance and performance improvement (§ 483.75), infection control (§ 483.80), and training (§ 483.95). We recognize that LTC facilities serve a uniquely vulnerable population with complex, chronic, and often rapidly changing care needs. Unlike other provider types, LTC facilities serve as the permanent residence for their residents, requiring a level of individualized, continuous care planning that necessitates a structured,
(
printed page 72652)
facility-wide assessment. The facility assessment requirement reflects this distinct care environment and is intended to ensure that facilities have the resources, staffing, and systems in place to meet the needs of their specific resident population.
Although we are proposing to remove the prescriptive requirement regarding the inclusion of representatives of direct care staff in the facility assessment, we encourage LTC facilities to consider the input of any individuals the facility deems appropriate as part of a comprehensive and meaningful facility assessment. We recognize the facility assessment as an essential tool for effective LTC facility planning. While we remain committed to ensuring that facility assessments are comprehensive and meaningful, we also acknowledge the administrative burden this process may place on LTC facilities. Therefore, we invite public comments on approaches to streamline and reduce burden associated with the facility assessment process, without compromising its integrity or effectiveness. Specifically, we seek input on the following:
What process improvements or best practices have LTC facilities found effective in conducting facility assessments efficiently?
Are there existing or emerging technological tools that could assist LTC facilities in completing this process more efficiently?
How can CMS support facilities in leveraging these tools while maintaining the quality and comprehensiveness of the assessment?

The COVID-19 Public Health Emergency (PHE) placed unprecedented strain on the Nation's healthcare system, particularly LTC facilities, which faced severe staffing shortages and limited access to personal protective equipment (PPE) and critical supplies. Protecting LTC residents under these conditions required enhanced visibility into the spread and impact of infectious diseases within these settings. To address this need, CMS published a series of interim final rules with comment period (IFCs) and subsequent final rules during and after the PHE to establish and refine data reporting, testing, vaccination, and infection control requirements for LTC facilities. The data informed coordination of operations and were especially important to anticipate and prepare for surge conditions.

b. Proposal To Remove Ongoing Data Reporting Requirements (§ 483.80(g))
As part of regulatory review conducted in response to
E.O. 14219
and
E.O. 14192
, CMS solicited and received interested parties' input through the 2025 deregulatory RFI.
[
144
]
Some comments focused on the ongoing acute respiratory illness data reporting requirement. Commenters stated that this provision is duplicative of State and local requirements, noting that these requirements—including reporting clusters of respiratory symptoms and confirmed cases to local public health agencies as required under infection control regulations, as well as data reported through the CMS Minimum Data Set (MDS)—already impose excessive burden on facilities through time consumed in, data collection, verification, and submission. Moreover, the reporting creates technical challenges operating reporting software. While we received comments noting similar concerns during the CY 2025 HH PPS final rule comment period, such concerns are common when implementing new regulations and at that time we believed that facilities could overcome these challenges and the data would be used to protect the health and safety of residents. Since the implementation of this final rule, facilities have reported continuing to struggle with data reporting to the extent that they are unable to comply.
Furthermore, based on feedback on the 2025 deregulatory RFI from providers and interested parties, we have come to understand that current expenditures related to ongoing data reporting are likely diverting staff from direct resident care.
Most notably, CMS estimates that maintaining the current reporting requirement would impose approximately $61 million in average annual costs and require over 600,000 average annual staff hours. We have not identified corresponding improvements in resident health or safety that would justify this burden. In brief, the ongoing cost and administrative burden to LTC facilities outweigh any demonstrated benefit.
The burden of data reporting includes labor costs associated with developing policies and procedures to report the required information, as well as costs associated with gathering, reviewing, and organizing the data used to compile the reported information. At this time, CMS does not believe that the benefits of ongoing data reporting outweigh the costs of complying with these requirements, and interested parties have requested removal of the existing requirements.

We understand that data from healthcare providers remain a key driver to identify and respond to resident needs and public health threats.
The CDC has continued to refine data collection and promote electronic data collection directly from electronic health records, like fast healthcare interoperability resources (FHIR) enabled data reporting from hospitals. Retaining the current PHE data reporting requirements enables facilities to maintain a functional reporting capacity. This data can be used to inform and guide response efforts at the local, State, and Federal levels to protect residents and their communities, including resource allocation and load balancing within and across facilities during emergencies when system capacity is most critical.

LTC facilities must also comply with Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which prohibits discrimination based on disability in public accommodations and commercial facilities, and requires businesses and non-profit service providers to ensure equal access to their goods, services, and facilities. In addition, sections 1819(b)(1)(A) and 1919(b)(1)(A) of the Act explicitly require Medicare and Medicaid LTC facilities to care for their residents in a manner and environment that promotes the maintenance or enhancement of the safety and quality of life of each resident. During the COVID-19 PHE there was value in these requirements as we sought to protect vulnerable clients from the risks of infection with the COVID-19 virus through reduced transmission from facility staff members who dwell in the community and had the potential to contract COVID-19 and spread the infection to vulnerable ICF/IID clients. In light of the declining infection rates and deaths, declining severity, and vaccination uptake that provides a base level of protection, we find that this regulatory focus on staff vaccination for COVID-19 is no longer needed and propose to remove these requirements.
We note that while we are proposing to eliminate the staff COVID-19 education and offer requirements, we would retain the requirements related to continued education and offering of the COVID-19 vaccinations to clients and their representatives, supporting their right to make informed choices and promoting overall quality of life for clients. We would also retain the requirements related to infection control, including providing a sanitary environment, and prohibiting staff that have symptoms or signs of a communicable disease from direct contact with clients and their food. Adherence to proper infection control guidelines, including current CMS infection control requirements, continues to be an effective strategy to prevent COVID-19 cases and deaths. ICF/IID clients continue to be at increased risk of infection and complications from respiratory viruses. For example, one study found that in nursing homes with higher adherence to CDC infection prevention guidelines, including hand hygiene, disinfection, PPE use, and screenings for symptoms and elevated temperature, there were lower incidences of infection with COVID-19 compared to nursing homes with lower adherence. While the study focused on nursing homes, we find it applicable to ICFs/IID in that both share strong similarities as communal living environments with shared dining and activity spaces that facilitate person -to- person spread of infectious diseases, shared ventilation systems for spread of airborne disease, and vulnerable populations for whom the risk of disease may be magnified due to comorbidities. A broader literature review found an association between proper mask use and proper donning of PPE and a lower prevalence of COVID-19 infections. Leading organizations, including the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) and the Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology (APIC) have also recently released updated guidelines for best practices related to infection prevention and control policies in nursing homes that are an important source of information to help providers protect vulnerable residents and, by extension, vulnerable ICF/IID clients. CMS recognizes these guidelines recommend that healthcare personnel should receive recommended vaccinations or have documented evidence of immunity against vaccine-preventable diseases. Also, the guidelines recommend identifying and implementing multimodal interventions to increase vaccine acceptance by healthcare personnel.
We expect eliminating the staff COVID-19 offer and educate requirements may free up resources that ICFs/IID can use to implement best practices for infection control and prevention. Furthermore, resources will also be made available so that staff can focus more directly on clients for things like assisting with activities of daily living, engaging clients in activities, and delivering care and services in accordance with the medical care plan, if applicable.

Physical distancing and masking may be difficult for non-ambulatory clients or those with behavioral challenges, making vaccination the most effective protection. Educating clients and their representatives about vaccine benefits and safety is essential to informed decision-making. E. Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs)
A CAH is a Medicare-certified hospital that meets specified criteria required for designation as a CAH by CMS. CAHs were established as a provider-type to help ensure access to health care services in rural communities. The statutory authority for CAHs is set forth in section 1820(e) of the Act and includes statutory authority for the Secretary to issue such criteria as required at section 1820(e)(3) of the Act. Under sections 1866 and 1902 of the Act, CAHs seeking to participate in the Medicare or Medicaid program, respectively, or both, must enter into an agreement with the Secretary or the State Medicaid agency, as appropriate. CAHs seeking to be Medicare and Medicaid providers of services must be certified as meeting Federal participation requirements as set forth at
42 CFR part 485, subpart F
. Our CoPs set out the patient health and safety protections established by the Secretary for various types of providers and suppliers.
In accordance with section 1864 of the Act, State surveyors assess CAH compliance with the CoPs as part of the process of determining whether a CAH qualifies for a provider agreement under Medicare. However, under section 1865 of the Act, CAHs can elect to be reviewed instead by private accrediting organizations approved by CMS as having standards that meet or exceed the applicable Medicare standards and survey procedures comparable to those CMS requires for State survey agencies.
Under section 1820(c)(2)(B)(iii) of the Act, as implemented in our regulations at § 485.620(a), a CAH can have no more than 25 beds that may be used for acute care inpatient services or swing-bed services (post-hospital skilled nursing care), except as permitted for CAHs having distinct part units under § 485.647, in which case, beds in the distinct part unit are excluded from the 25-bed limit specified in § 485.620(a). Section 1820(c) of the Act also requires that CAHs be located in a State that has established a Medicare Rural Hospital Flexibility Program and generally must be more than a 35-mile drive on primary
(
printed page 72661)
roads (or, in the case of mountainous terrain or in areas with only secondary roads available, a 15-mile drive) from a hospital or another CAH. If prior to January 1, 2006, a facility was designated by the State as a “necessary provider” of health care services to residents in the area, the facility is exempt from the distance requirements relative to hospitals and other CAHs that are otherwise applicable to CAHs under § 485.610(c). CAHs must provide emergency care services 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and maintain an average annual length of stay of 96 hours or less. They may be granted approval to provide “swing bed” post-hospital skilled nursing care, may provide inpatient care to individuals under the care of a hospice, and may operate a psychiatric and/or rehabilitation distinct part unit of up to 10 beds each. CAHs may operate as independent institutions or as part of a larger health care system. As of January 2026, there were approximately 1,400 CAHs.

1. Proposals To Amend Certain Status and Location Requirements (§ 485.610(c) and (e))
Section 1820(c)(2)(B)(i)(I) of the Act, codified into the CoPs at § 485.610(c)(1), requires that a CAH be located more than a 35-mile drive (or a 15-mile drive on secondary roads or mountainous terrain) from a hospital or another CAH. Section 4201 of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (
Pub. L. 105-33
) established the CAH designation to help reduce the financial risks faced by rural hospitals and to improve health care access in rural areas. CAHs are acute care facilities that provide outpatient, emergency, and limited inpatient services in communities that cannot support a full-service hospital. To achieve this, Medicare reimburses CAHs a reasonable cost-based reimbursement for their services. Under section 1820(c)(2)(B) of the Act, CAHs must meet location-related requirements that aim to limit designation to facilities serving geographically isolated communities and support appropriate distribution of hospital services. In addition, 1820(c)(2)(E) of the Act authorizes CAHs to establish psychiatric and rehabilitation units as distinct parts of the CAH.
Since 2004, the Medicare program requires hospitals seeking CAH designation to be located more than 35 miles from the nearest similar hospital.

acute care

As with the proposed revision to (c)(1), psychiatric hospitals, LTCHs, rehabilitation hospitals, and REHs would not be considered acute care hospitals and therefore would not be treated as “like or similar” hospitals when evaluating compliance with the location requirements. Codifying this policy would confirm that proximity to a specialty hospital does not, by itself, affect compliance with the CAH distance requirement, and would ensure consistent location determinations, including in cases where specialty hospitals are co-located on CAH campuses. Aligning the regulations with established policy will ensure uniform application of the distance requirement nationwide, provide certainty for CAHs and survey agencies, and reduce administrative burden. Most importantly, clarifying that only acute care hospitals and CAHs are included in distance determinations will help safeguard the continued availability of essential health care services in the rural communities served by these CAHs.
In February 2026, section 241 of Division B, Title II, of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (
Pub. L. 119-75
) (“CAA 2026”), established that certain CAHs that received termination notices within a specific time frame for failure to meet distance requirements could remain CAHs or re-enroll, as applicable. Specifically, Section 241 of the CAA 2026 states that CMS may not apply the statutory distance requirement at section 1820(c)(2)(B)(i)(I) of the Act to facilities that had a CAH provider agreement and were designated and certified as CAHs as of January 1, 2024, and received a notification letter from CMS between December 1, 2024, and January 1, 2026, indicating noncompliance with the CAH distance requirement at § 485.610(c)(1) or § 485.610(e)(2). For these facilities, CMS is prohibited from enforcing the distance requirement.
Section 241 further reads that, in cases where a provider agreement for such a facility was terminated on or after December 1, 2024, but prior to the date of enactment of CAA 2026 (February 2, 2026), solely because the facility did not meet the distance requirement under section 1820(c)(2)(B)(i)(I) of the Act, the Administrator must recertify the facility as a CAH and reinstate its provider agreement. Furthermore, section 241 clarifies that this provision does not prevent the Administrator from taking other enforcement actions, including terminating a provider agreement, if a facility is found to be out of compliance with federal requirements unrelated to the distance requirement.
To implement section 241 of CAA 2026, we propose to amend the regulations at § 485.610(c)(1) and (e)(2) to add a qualifying statement to each standard stating that a CAH described in section 241 of CAA 2026 will not be subject to the distance requirements of that paragraph. For CAHs that qualify under section 241, we view the exemption from the distance requirement as not being time-limited and as applying to all future distance reviews. The statutory text does not contain a sunset clause or fiscal year limitation, and the provision's reinstatement mechanism for terminated provider agreements appears to provide an ongoing exemption for the defined affected facilities.
CMS performed a detailed analysis to identify how many CAHs would be subject to the exemption from the distance requirement, as outlined in section 241 of CAA 2026. Through this review, CMS determined that four facilities met the necessary criteria; they were designated as CAHs as of January 1, 2024, and received a notification letter from CMS during December 1, 2024 through January 1, 2026, indicating that the facility no longer met the distance requirements under section 1820(c)(2)(B)(i)(I) of the Act, or was actually terminated in that time period.
CAHs often serve as the primary, and sometimes the only source of emergency and acute inpatient care in their communities. By allowing qualifying facilities to retain or regain their CAH status despite no longer meeting the distance requirement relative to other hospitals and CAHs, section 241 of CAA 2026 supports continued access to potentially critical services. Maintaining access to these services protects patient health and safety and promotes continuity of care in underserved areas.

a. Background on Birth Tissues Uses
Birth tissues are solely generated as a direct result of pregnancy, labor, and delivery and may be discarded, retained by the patient, stored, donated, banked for potential future medical use, and/or transferred to a third party for research or commercial purposes. These tissues can include umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord tissue, umbilical veins, placenta, amniotic membrane, chorionic membrane, amniotic fluid, and Wharton's jelly.
[
222
]
Currently, the vast majority of birth tissue—approximately 96 percent- is disposed of following delivery.
[
223
]
If intended for future medical purposes, such tissue must be collected promptly and handled in a manner designed to minimize contamination.
[

]
For our analysis, it is helpful to separate our discussion of the collection of cord blood from consideration of other birth tissues.
Cord blood is the most commonly collected birth tissue for future medical use (approximately 110,000 collections annually, or about 3 percent of births, with 75 to 80 percent stored in private banks).
[

]
It is also the most researched and regulated birth tissue, at both the Federal and State level. Cord blood is unique in that families can pursue either public or private cord banking. Public cord blood banking has an established role in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for certain malignant, hematologic, immunologic, and metabolic disorders.
[
226
]
Public cord banking is free to the family as part of a national transplant registry. HRSA oversees the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program and the National Cord Blood Inventory.
[

These programs were established under the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Acts to expand donor and cord blood availability to fund and coordinate the collection, banking, and distribution of cord blood units to increase access for transplantation and research.

Conversely, private cord banks allow families to retain exclusive access to their stored cord blood for potential future personal or family use with collection and storage costs paid out of pocket by the family, which can total several thousand dollars initially, followed by annual storage costs of several hundred dollars.

b. Need for New CAH Standards
Section 1820(e)(3) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to establish additional requirements necessary for the health and safety of patients served by Medicare-and Medicaid-participating CAHs. Existing CAH CoPs establish the framework for protecting patient rights, promoting informed decision-making, and ensuring accurate medical and clinical record documentation. Together, the requirements safeguard patient health and safety and promote quality care for all patients in Medicare- and Medicaid-participating CAHs. Specifically, patient rights CoPs for CAHs at § 485.614 (a) and (b) provide that patients or their representatives have the right to make informed decisions regarding their care, including being informed of their health status, being involved in care planning and
(
printed page 72670)
treatment, and being able to request or refuse treatment. The CAH clinical records CoP at § 485.638(a)(4)(i)) requires, for each patient receiving healthcare services, a record that includes, as applicable, evidence of properly executed informed consent forms. However, there are no existing CoPs related specifically to the collection of birth tissues.
This differs from the regulatory framework applicable to organs and tissues collected for transplantation. For example, § 485.643 establishes specific requirements for organ, tissue, and eye procurement, including requirements related to CAH's agreements with organ procurement organizations, tissue banks, and eye banks and policies governing the donation process. Of note, hospitals are not required to have a relationship with birth tissue procurement organizations or birth tissue banks. Organs and tissues collected for transplantation are therefore subject to an established regulatory framework and associated donation and consent process. The existing CAH CoPs do not establish comparable requirements specifically addressing the collection and disposition of birth tissues following a live birth, including circumstances in which tissues may be retained by the patient or collected, donated, transferred, stores, or used for purposes other than transplantation.
We believe that decisions involving the collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release, or discarding of birth tissues may implicate important patient interests and rights and therefore warrant additional transparency and informed decision-making protections. Unlike many other biological materials generated during the course of medical care, birth tissues may have unique cultural, religious, personal, or familial significance to patients and their families.
[
256
]
At the same time, birth tissues may also have medical, research, or other uses that can involve their collection or transfer to entities outside of the hospital. These characteristics distinguish birth tissues from both biological materials routinely discarded in the course of medical care and organs and tissues collected through established transplantation and donation processes. Therefore, families giving birth at CAHs may reasonably wish to understand whether such tissues will be discarded, available for them to retain, used for research purposes, transferred to third parties, stored for future use, or otherwise utilized in commercial activities.
Moreover, because of the concerns discussed previously about inappropriate clinical use and profiteering, transparency is particularly important when a CAH participates in a program or arrangement through which birth tissues may be donated, transferred, banked, stored, or used by a third party and/or for commercial purposes. We believe that patients have the right to the information necessary to make an informed decision about consenting to these uses of personal birth tissues and biological materials associated with their deliveries.
CMS understands that many CAHs may already have policies around informed consent and allow patients to request retention or release of birth tissues, subject to State law, infection prevention and control requirements, and clinical circumstances.
[
257
]
However, practices may vary, and patients may not know whether, when, or how to make such a request. Some CAHs may rely on general consent forms or internal policies governing the handling and disposal of medical waste that do not clearly inform patients about possible collection, transfer, storage, donation, commercial use, or disposition of birth tissues, or about the options available to request retention. Variation in these processes can create uncertainty for patients, staff, and CAHs.
We believe that establishing new requirements to address these variations would strike the appropriate balance between improving transparency, creating consistent patient expectations and ensuring that no CAH is compelled to collect, bank, donate, or release tissues in circumstances that would be unsafe, unlawful, or inconsistent with clinical care.
c. Proposed Scope and Definition of Birth Tissues (§ 485.649(c))
Mothers who give birth in CAHs that furnish OB services should have baseline protections regarding informed decision-making, documentation, and safe handling of their birth tissues when the hospital engages in birth tissue collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release. To advance this goal, we propose to add new standards at § 485.649(c). As noted earlier in this section, we are proposing to remove the current requirements at § 485.649(c) and replace them with new standards that build on the CoPs for obstetrical services. These new standards address informed consent for birth tissue collection and patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues.
We propose to add a new standard to the OB Services CoP at § 485.649(c), titled “Birth tissue collection.” Facilities that furnish obstetrical services vary widely in their involvement with birth tissues. For example, some CAHs are deeply involved in birth tissue activities, including operating or sponsoring public cord blood donation programs, contracting with third-party collection or tissue procurement entities, or facilitating private banking arrangements. Others have more limited involvement, such as occasionally receiving requests to retain or release birth tissues to the patient for cultural, religious, or personal uses or to a private third-party for personal future medical uses, research, or donation, even where no formal relationship exists between the CAH and the third party. To account for this variation, the proposed standard would apply to only those CAHs that furnish obstetrical services and participate in one or more activities related to birth tissues including collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release to patients. For purposes of this standard, we interpret participation to include hospital-sponsored, hospital-operated, or hospital-facilitated activities, that is, any instance in which the CAH's personnel, premises, policies, or processes are used in connection with the collection, packaging, storage, transfer, banking, donation, or release birth tissues. Facilities that do not engage in any of these activities would not be subject to the proposed standard.
Furthermore at § 485.649(c), we propose to define “birth tissues” to capture the materials most commonly associated with live childbirth that may be collected, retained, stored, donated, banked, transferred, or released for personal, clinical, research, and/or commercial purposes. For purposes of this proposed rule, birth tissue is limited to tissue or biological material obtained in connection with labor and delivery resulting in a live birth. This proposal does not apply to tissue or biological material obtained in other clinical circumstances. Specifically, we propose to define “birth tissue” as “human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery, (including cesarean-section delivery), such as umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord tissue, placenta, amniotic membrane, amniotic fluid,
[

(

and other tissues or biological materials associated with live childbirth.” This definition is intended to avoid gaps in patient protections that could arise if the rule addressed only one category of birth tissue, such as cord blood, while other tissues were collected, transferred, released, or disposed of under less transparent processes. This definition is also intended to be flexible enough to accommodate changes in collection practices and terminology over time. Importantly, our definition is not intended to conflict with or alter FDA definitions or classifications of human cells, tissues, and cellular or tissue-based products (HCT/Ps) under FDA authorities or other similar FDA terminology, which remain controlling for purposes of FDA regulation.

Lastly, we note that nothing in this proposal limits or impairs a family's ability to receive their stillborn child for the purposes of holding, mourning, or making funeral arrangements. Such activities are regulated under State and local law, and hospital specific policies.

d. Proposals for Informed Consent (§ 485.649(c)(1))
At proposed § 485.649(c)(1), we would require that the CAH ensure that it obtains informed consent from the patient or the patient's representative prior to the collection, storage, donation, transfer, banking, or release to patients of birth tissues, consistent with the CAH's scope of services and role in those activities. The consent must be documented consistent with the clinical records requirements at § 485.638(a)(4)(i).
Consistent with the phrase “scope of services and role in those activities” in proposed § 485.649(c)(1), the obligations under this proposal would be tailored to the specific activities in which the hospital participates. The proposal would not require CAHs to offer new services, to purchase or provide new equipment, or initiate or sponsor a collection program, private banking arrangement, or other birth tissue collection program. Rather, it would require only that when a hospital furnishes obstetrical services and participates in a covered birth tissue activity, the hospital maintains appropriate consent, documentation, policies, procedures, and safe handling processes commensurate with its scope of services and role in that activity. For example, a hospital that operates a public cord blood collection program would be expected to ensure that its consent process includes the information and disclosures applicable to public donation. In contrast, a hospital that does not participate in a public cord blood collection program and is only collecting birth tissue in response to an individual patient's request for release of a placenta for personal or cultural reasons would be expected to document the request and release decision consistent with its policies and provide safe handling instructions.
We propose that the informed consent process include, as applicable, six categories of information: (1) a description of the birth tissues to be collected; (2) the intended use, including commercial and research uses, of the birth tissues; (3) disclosure of any third-party involvement and conflicts of interest; (4) information regarding risks, limitations, and infection prevention and quality control considerations; (5) notice that a patient's refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment; (6) and any other information required under applicable Federal or State law. These elements establish a baseline and are not intended to prescribe a single consent form or process for all CAHs or activities. Birth tissues may move through complex supply chains and may have research, clinical, manufacturing, or commercial value. We propose at § 485.649(c)(1)(i) and (ii) requirements for disclosure to ensure that patients and families fully understand how collected tissues may be transferred to a third party, processed into a product, sold, used in research, banked for future use, or discarded if quality criteria are not met. We propose at § 485.649(c)(1)(iii) to require disclosure of (both not-for-profit and for-profit) third-party involvement and conflicts of interest. ACOG and AMA both recognize the importance of conflict-of-interest disclosure in cord blood banking.

Patients must receive sufficient information to understand third-party involvement and potential conflicts when they are making decisions about birth tissues associated with their deliveries. These components of the informed consent as required at proposed § 485.649(c)(1)(i) through (vi) are consistent with general informed consent principles and with professional guidance that emphasizes disclosure of financial interests.
