We propose at § 485.649(c)(1)(iv) to require information regarding risks, limitations, infection prevention, and quality control considerations. Depending on the activity, relevant information could include the possibility that collection may not be feasible because of maternal or neonatal clinical circumstances, that a specimen may fail to meet volume or quality criteria, that stored birth tissues may not be clinically useful in the future, or that releasing tissue for personal handling may involve infection prevention and storage considerations.
We also propose at § 485.649(c)(1)(v) that the patient be informed that refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment. Patients in labor or experiencing obstetrical emergencies may be vulnerable to time pressure or perceived pressure from clinicians, hospital staff, or third parties. Equally, the patient's decision to request collection or release of birth tissues does not obligate the hospital to provide services that are unsafe, unavailable, or inconsistent with State law or hospital policy. This is consistent with patient exercise of rights at § 485.614(b)(2).
We recognize that timing of consent in the labor and delivery context can be challenging. As previously discussed, the proposed requirements apply to birth tissue obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery resulting in live birth. The timing of the informed consent process does not alter the scope of tissues subject to this proposal. Prenatal education and consent are preferable when feasible, especially for planned donation or banking arrangements, but patients in labor may present without prior knowledge of their options or make key requests at admission or after delivery. Under these proposals, CAHs retain flexibility to design processes that are consistent with clinical practice, patient needs, State law, and the CAH's role provided that consent is obtained before the applicable birth tissue activity occurs whenever possible, and that collection or release activities does not interfere with clinical care (for example, pathologic examination of the placenta). Patient safety takes precedence in high-acuity or emergent circumstances.
Finally, we also recognize that, in some circumstances, a patient may independently arrange with a third-party tissue bank, private bank, courier, or other entity and may ask the hospital solely to accommodate collection or release. In such cases, the hospital is not expected to become an expert in the third party's products, business practices, marketing claims, or downstream uses. The hospital should have a process, consistent with its policies, to document the patient's request; confirm, as appropriate to the CAH's role, that the patient has provided authorization or evidence of the applicable third-party consent; and document the actions taken by the CAH to accommodate, accommodate subject to reasonable conditions, delay, limit, or deny the request based on clinical circumstances, infection prevention, and legal requirements. This approach supports patient choice while ensuring that the CAHs obligations remain proportional to the CAH's actual role and involvement. We note that FDA regulates human cells, tissues, and cellular-tissue based products, including birth tissues.
e. Proposed Policies and Procedures for Cultural, Religious, or Personal Uses (§ 485.649(c)(2))
At § 485.649(c)(2), we propose to require the CAH to have written policies and procedures that permit patients to request retention or release of birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons, consistent with State law and the CAH's infection prevention and control program requirements under § 485.640. Such policies and procedures would not require patients to provide justification or documentation for their respective cultural, religious, or personal reasons. We propose this requirement because requests for retention or release may arise in routine deliveries, scheduled cesarean deliveries, emergent deliveries, or other clinical contexts, and families and staff need clear procedures for safe, consistent collection and release of birth tissues.
The proposed policies and procedures would address four core topics. First, policies must address processes for patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues. We expect CAHs to specify how and when a patient or representative may make a request, who is responsible for receiving and documenting the request, what forms or authorizations must be completed, and how the hospital will communicate decisions regarding release to the patient. CAHs should design processes that are easily understandable and accessible for their patient population and align with clinical operations.
Second, the policies and procedures must address safe handling, packaging, storage, and release practices of birth tissues. For example, we expect CAHs to identify the personnel responsible for handling birth tissues, provide appropriate containers or packaging as needed in alignment with safe handling, clearly label each tissue container or package as appropriate, accommodate tissue storage pending release as requested by the patient, establish chain-of-custody or handoff processes where needed, and implement protocols for any circumstances requiring consultation with infection prevention personnel, pathology, risk management, or clinical leadership. These procedures should reflect the type of tissue, the intended use, the clinical circumstances, and the CAH's infection prevention and control program. Third,
(
printed page 72673)
we propose that policies and procedures must address circumstances under which retention or release may be limited or denied, including infection prevention and control concerns, biohazard risks, certain clinical conditions, emergency cases, or other applicable legal requirements, as discussed below:
• Infection Prevention and Control Concerns and Biohazard Risks
Suspected or confirmed infection, contamination, or other biohazard concerns may create unacceptable risks that warrant limiting or denying retention or release. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) classifies human blood, certain body fluids, and unfixed human tissues and organs as potentially infectious materials.
[
268
]
Because placental and related birth tissues may contain blood and other biological material, CAHs would need to implement handling and packaging procedures to protect patients, staff, and others from potential exposure to bloodborne pathogens (for example, HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or other infectious agents).
[
269
]
CAHs must have processes to address safe handling, packaging, storage, and release when patients request retention or release of birth tissues. CAHs should also identify circumstances in which release may be limited or denied due to infection prevention and control concerns consistent with the CAH's infection prevention and control program under § 485.640.
• Certain Clinical Conditions
Retention or release may also be limited when tissue is needed for pathology review or other clinically appropriate diagnostic evaluation. Placental pathology may assist in the evaluation of adverse maternal, fetal, or neonatal outcomes, including fetal growth restriction, stillbirth,
[
270
]
infection, congenital abnormalities, preterm birth, placental insufficiency, maternal hypertensive disorders, or other complications of pregnancy and delivery. CAHs should identify in their policies the clinical circumstances under which retention for diagnostic purposes would take precedence over patient's requests for release. To the extent possible, patient requests should take precedence over circumstances under which hospitals may want to retain the placenta or other birth tissues for elective evaluation, research, or other purposes. Unless there are circumstances such as infection prevention concerns or a need for the hospital to retain the birth tissue for appropriate diagnostic evaluation, the patient's autonomy over their biological materials associated with their delivery should be prioritized.
• Emergency Cases
Patient safety takes precedence in all emergency circumstances in which staff cannot safely collect, process, or release birth tissues due to emergent patient care needs. Collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release activities of birth tissues should not delay emergency care, interfere with the clinical management of labor and delivery, or alter medically appropriate obstetric or neonatal practice.
[
271 272
]
A hospital would not be expected to delay necessary clinical intervention to complete a birth tissue consent process or collection activity, and failure to collect birth tissue due to emergent clinical circumstances would not, by itself, constitute noncompliance. To the extent necessary, such consents may be obtained following resolution of the emergency and stabilization of the patient's condition.
• Other Applicable Legal Requirements
Retention, testing, handling, or disposition of birth tissue may also be limited or governed by applicable Federal, State, Tribal, territorial, or local law (see discussion of relevant state laws in Section II. A.5.). By defining these criteria in advance, CAHs provide patients and staff with clear expectations and transparent and consistent processes. These proposed requirements are intended to complement, not interfere with, a CAH's existing authority to retain birth tissues when clinically appropriate or otherwise required by law.
Fourth, at § 485.649(c)(2)(i)(D), we propose that the policies and procedures must address staff education regarding the CAH's procedures for responding to patient requests. This education is intended to be focused and practical. Staff who may receive or respond to requests to know how to identify the applicable policy, document the request, process the request safely and within their scope of services, and provide safe handling instructions when tissue is released.
Lastly, we propose at § 485.649(c)(2)(ii) that the hospital provide patients who request retention or release of birth tissues with instructions for safe handling, transport, storage, and disposition of the tissues, as applicable. These instructions should be understandable, practical, and tailored to the birth tissue and release context. For example, instructions might address the need to maintain tissue in a leak-proof container, avoid exposure to other patients or staff, refrigerate or otherwise store tissue as directed, use appropriate personal protective measures, or comply with applicable local disposition requirements. The proposed requirement would not require CAHs to supervise the patient's use after release, but it does require the hospital to provide instructions that support safe decision-making at the point of release.
In summary, these proposed requirements are intended to operate alongside, not in place of, other existing Federal and State authorities. FDA regulates human cells, tissue and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps) either under section 361 of the Public Health Service Act and
21 CFR part 1271
or under section 351 of the PHS Act and relevant sections of the FD&C Act as well as applicable regulations. HCT/Ps that do not meet the criteria to be regulated solely under section 361 of the Public Health Service Act and
21 CFR part 1271
are regulated as drugs, devices, and/or biological products.
[
273
]
FDA has issued guidance on minimal manipulation and homologous use. FDA also has taken compliance and enforcement actions addressing unapproved HCT/Ps, including products derived from birth tissues.
The proposed CoPs at § 485.649(c) occupies a narrower and distinct role, regulating the facility-patient interaction, facility policies, documentation, and processes for informed decision-making and safe release in Medicare and Medicaid participating CAHs. Nothing in this
(
printed page 72674)
proposal determines whether any product is lawfully marketed or subject to FDA premarket review. Rather the purpose of the CoPs is to protect patient health and safety and to ensure that quality care is furnished to all patients in Medicare-participating CAHs. In accordance with section 1864 of the Act, State surveyors assess CAH compliance with the conditions as part of the process of determining whether a hospital qualifies for a provider agreement under Medicare. Alternatively, under section 1865 of the Act, CAHs can elect to be reviewed instead by private accrediting organizations approved by CMS as having standards that meet or exceed the applicable Medicare standards and survey procedures comparable to those CMS requires for State survey agencies. F. Adoption of the 2024 Edition of the Life Safety Code (National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 101) and the 2024 Edition of the Health Care Facilities Code (National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 99)
1. Background
a. Overview
CMS' oversight of Medicare and Medicaid-certified facilities includes ensuring the health and safety of patients, which involves establishing physical environment and fire safety standards. Building safety system standards are highly complex, technical, and beyond the expertise of CMS as a regulatory body. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) convenes technical experts with a vast breadth and depth of fire and building safety expertise to establish consensus-based standards, such as the Life Safety Code (LSC) (NFPA 101) and the Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) (NFPA 99), and CMS adopts these standards by following the requirements for incorporation by reference. The LSC is a compilation of fire safety requirements for new and existing buildings and establishes minimum requirements for building design, construction, operation, and maintenance necessary to protect people from fire and related hazards. It is updated and published every 3 years.
[
274
]
HCFC is a compilation of requirements for the installation, inspection, testing, maintenance, performance and safe practices for facilities, material, equipment and appliances and is updated and published every 3 years by NFPA.
CMS adopts LSC and HCFC provisions through rulemaking. The Administrative Procedure Act (
5 U.S.C. 553
) requires CMS to follow notice-and-comment rulemaking before adopting, amending, repealing regulations. Since LSC and HCFC are incorporated into Federal regulations, updating to a newer edition constitutes a regulatory change which must go through rulemaking. The process typically begins when the NFPA issues a new edition of the LSC or HCFC, reflecting updated knowledge, best practices, and safety technologies. CMS then evaluates the provisions of the new codes to determine their applicability and impact on health care facilities that participate in Medicare and Medicaid programs. The LSC and HCFC provisions adopted by CMS establish minimum requirements for fire protection and support the emergency preparedness requirements for health care facilities. The codes adopted by CMS encompass critical areas that include, but are not limited to: building construction, fire detection and suppression systems, alarm and communication systems, electrical systems, medical gas and vacuum systems, and gas and electrical equipment. Compliance with the LSC and HCFC not only supports Federal health and safety requirements but also promotes consistency across facilities, reinforces fire emergency readiness, and upholds CMS' commitment to protecting the well-being of all occupants. The LSC and HCFC codes adopted by CMS in the CoPs apply to hospitals, LTC facilities, CAHs, REHs, ASCs, ICFs/IID, hospice inpatient care facilities, PACE centers, RNHCIs and ESRD facilities.
Participation in Medicare or Medicaid requires most provider and supplier types to be certified by CMS as meeting the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs). The statutory basis for incorporating NFPA's LSC and HCFC into the regulations governing Medicare and, where applicable, Medicaid providers and suppliers rests on the authority of the Secretary general rulemaking authority as set forth at sections 1102 and 1871 of the Act, and more specifically the “health and safety” provisions applicable to each provider and supplier type, empowering the Secretary to issue regulations necessary for providing health care services, or more specifically for the health and safety of patients. In addition to these rulemaking authorities, sections 1819(d)(2)(B) and 1919(d)(2)(B) of the Act explicitly require Medicare and Medicaid LTC facilities to meet the provisions of the LSC, as specified by the Secretary in regulation.
On May 4, 2016 (
81 FR 26872
), we published a final rule, “Fire Safety Requirements for Certain Health Care Facilities”
[
275
]
that adopted the 2012 edition of the NFPA LSC and the 2012 edition of the HCFC, with the exception of chapters 7, 8, 12 and 13, which were not adopted. As such, facilities are currently required to comply with the 2012 editions of each code as part of the Medicare and Medicaid fire safety requirements. However, since the NFPA published the 2012 editions of the LSC and HCFC, there have been advances in safety and technology, and changes made to the LSC and HCFC. Newer buildings are typically built to comply with newer versions of the LSC and HCFC because State and local jurisdictions, as well as some accreditation programs, may adopt and enforce new versions of the code as they become available. This can result in confusion since, for example, a health care facility that was constructed or renovated in 2025 would likely be required by its State and local authorities to comply with a more recent edition of the LSC and HCFC, while also being required to comply with the 2012 edition of the LSC and HCFC to meet the CMS-established regulatory requirements. Additionally, in accordance with
E.O. 14192
and
E.O. 14219
, CMS solicited and received interested parties' input through the 2025 deregulatory RFI.
[
276
]
Commenters stated that complying with two different editions of the LSC and HCFC at the same time can create conflicts, duplications, and inconsistencies that increase construction and compliance costs without any fire safety or patient care benefits. They also stated that since the publication of the 2012 edition of the LSC and HCFC, there have been significant advancements in technology, improved inspection, testing, and maintenance strategies and updated
(
printed page 72675)
building design standards that have lessened the burden of managing health care facilities without compromising patient safety.
We believe that adopting the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) and 2024 edition of the HCFC (NFPA 99), would simplify and modernize the construction and renovation process for affected health care providers and suppliers, reduce compliance-related burdens, and allow for more resources to be used for patient care.
b. Waivers
Specific provisions of the adopted NFPA codes may be waived by CMS, either based on facility-specific needs and circumstances or based on widely applicable variances. First, consistent with statutory authorities, the regulations have historically included Secretarial waiver authority to grant waivers of some provisions of the LSC and HCFC in facility-specific instances. For example, section 1861(e)(9) of the Act allows CMS the authority to determine which requirements are necessary for hospitals in general, based on the discretion implicit within the “health and safety” rules. By comparison, sections 1819(d)(2)(B)(i) and 1919(d)(2)(B)(i) of the Act explicitly allow CMS to grant LSC waivers for LTC facilities if such waivers do not adversely affect health and safety. State agencies or CMS-approved accreditation organizations (AO) may recommend a waiver; however, only CMS may grant them. Accordingly, all LSC and HCFC waiver requests recommended for approval by State agencies or AOs must be forwarded to CMS for consideration. A waiver may be granted for a specific LSC or HCFC requirement if we determine that—(1) the waiver would not adversely affect patient/staff health and safety; and (2) if meeting the requirement in question would place an unreasonable hardship on the facility. In cases where a facility has been cited for a LSC or HCFC deficiency during a survey, the provider or supplier may request a waiver recommendation from its State survey agency or CMS-approved AO as part of their certification survey plan of correction. The plan of correction is a written response that a facility must submit to the surveyor after deficiencies are identified. The State survey agency or AO reviews the request and makes a recommendation to CMS. CMS reviews the waiver request and the recommendation, along with any supporting evidence and makes the final decision. CMS would not grant a waiver if patient health and safety is compromised. The LSC recognizes alternative systems, methods, or devices approved as equivalent by the authority having jurisdiction as being in compliance with the LSC. CMS, as the authority having jurisdiction over certification, will determine equivalency through the waiver approval process.

While the LSC is a set of fire protection and safety standards that addresses some aspects of accessibility in covered facilities, CMS must emphasize that the LSC is not an accessibility code, and compliance with the LSC does not ensure compliance with the requirements of section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Pub. L. 93-112, Sept. 26, 1973) or the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) (Pub. L. 101-336, July 26, 1990). Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities in programs and activities that receive Federal financial assistance, while Title II of the ADA prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities by State and local governments, requiring all public services, programs, and activities to be accessible. Title III of the ADA prohibits discrimination based on disability in public accommodations and commercial facilities, requiring businesses and nonprofit service providers to ensure equal access to their goods, services, and facilities. 2. Proposed Provisions
a. Categorical Waiver Authority
As previously noted, CMS is required to use a notice-and-comment rulemaking process to adopt new editions of the LSC and HCFC, which can be a lengthy process. The NFPA updates each of its codes every 3 years, however, each new edition of the LSC and HCFC may not contain enough significant changes to warrant undergoing the rulemaking process. In the past, CMS has issued public notices in the form of sub-regulatory memoranda related to categorical waivers that permit greater provider flexibility by proactively granting them approval to comply with specific provisions from newer editions of the LSC or HCFC. A categorical waiver is narrowly focused on a single change in a newer edition of a code and is typically a faster alternative to rulemaking, which is used to adopt a newer edition of the LSC and HCFC in their entirety.
We are proposing to codify CMS' authority to issue categorical waivers in the regulatory text of each affected provider type. CMS may evaluate specific provisions of the code, determine that a waiver would arguably apply to all similarly situated facilities, and permit the use of specific provisions of a newer edition of the LSC or HCFC only when the provision would provide an equal or superior means of ensuring patient safety as compared to the provisions of the code editions adopted in regulation at that time. A facility that wishes to use a categorical waiver would have to formally elect to do so and document their decision. Waiver approval in these instances would be subject to CMS' review of documentation maintained by the facility, verification of the applicability of the waiver, and confirmation that the terms and requirements of the waiver have been implemented by the facility. Providers and suppliers that have formally elected and documented their decision to utilize a categorical waiver and are complying with the categorical waiver conditions would not be cited for non-compliance with the specific waived provisions of the edition of the LSC or HCFC adopted by regulation. In most cases such verification of compliance occurs when an onsite survey of the facility is conducted. We would clarify that in those cases where we have issued a prior public notice providing for a categorical waiver, a State survey agency or AO (as applicable) is not required to submit an advance recommendation to CMS for such a waiver to be approved.
b. Incorporation by Reference

The 2024 edition of the HCFC (NFPA 99), issued August 25, 2023, with the exception of Chapter 7, 8, 12, and 13 (see the discussion in paragraph (h) of this section);

TIA-24-2 to NFPA 99, issued August 25, 2023 and;
The 2025 edition of the Guide on Alternative Approaches to Life Safety (NFPA 101A), issued April 22, 2024.
The materials that we propose to incorporate by reference would be reasonably available to interested parties for inspection at CMS, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21244. Copies may be obtained from the National Fire Protection Association, 1 Batterymarch Park, Quincy, MA 02169-7471,
www.nfpa.org
,

The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) provides minimum requirements, with due regard to function, for the design, operation and maintenance of buildings and structures for safety to life from fire. Its provisions also aid life safety in similar emergencies.
The 2024 edition of the HCFC (NFPA 99), (including TIAs 24-1 and 24-2), with the exception of chapters 7 (Information Technology and Communications Systems), 8 (Plumbing), 12 (Emergency Management), and 13 (Security Management) provides minimum requirements for health care facilities for the installation, inspection, testing, maintenance, performance, and safe practices for facilities, material, equipment, and appliances, including secondary hazards associated with the primary hazards (see the discussion in paragraph (h) of this section); TIA 24-1 and TIA 24-2 include targeted revisions and clarifications to health care facility requirements.
The 2025 edition of the Guide on Alternative Approaches to Life Safety (NFPA 101A) is a guide that provides alternative methods to achieve compliance with LSC (NFPA 101). It is to be used in conjunction with the LSC (NFPA 101), not as a substitute.
c. Content Overview of the 2024 Edition of the LSC (NFPA 101)
The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) includes new provisions that are vital to the health and safety of patients and staff. Our intention is to ensure that patients and staff continue to experience the highest possible degree of fire safety. As in previous sections of this proposed rule, the general term “patient(s)” refers to patient, clients, residents and all other terms used to describe the type of individuals receiving services in each facility type discussed in this section.
The following updated general requirements from the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) apply to all occupancy chapters of the code unless otherwise stated, including what the LSC terms “Health Care Occupancies (HCOs)”, “Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies” (AHCOs) and “Residential Board and Care Occupancies” (RBCOs). We propose to adopt the entirety of requirements of the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) (with one exception, addressed in section II.F.1(e)). In this section we highlight some specific requirements that represent a significant change from the 2012 edition of the LSC or additions that constitute new requirements. Each of these changes and additions is discussed in detail in the following paragraphs. This section is not intended to represent a comprehensive list of requirements.
(1) Updated Requirements for Greater Alignment With Building/Fire Codes
NFPA revised the requirements in other NFPA documents (for example, NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code) to better align with the requirements of the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) which we believe will greatly reduce conflicts between design and construction standards and operational compliance requirements. By providing a clear and unified set of standards, jurisdictions could adopt the codes without modification, which in turn would reduce conflicts that might arise between the NFPA standards and State and local fire code requirements.
(
printed page 72677)
(2) New Integrated System Testing Requirements—Section 9.11.4
NFPA 4, Standard for Integrated Fire Protection and Life Safety System Testing, is currently referenced at section 9.11.4 of the LSC for high rise HCOs and AHCOs. Section 9.11.4 requires that the system test plans be set in place to test all integrated fire and life safety systems and how they work together. Currently, they are tested individually. Integrated testing will ensure systems are working end-to-end. For example, fire alarm systems must be able to control elevators. Fire alarm testing confirms that a signal is sent to the elevator controller, but it does not verify that the elevator responds and performs its required functions. In many buildings, the fire alarm system and the elevator controller are maintained by different vendors and tested under separate standards; however, NFPA 4 requires the facility to develop and implement a plan for integrated testing to verify that these systems function together as intended. This coordination is critical in health care settings where patients often cannot self-evacuate. By confirming that all interconnected systems work in sequence, NFPA 4 helps keep evacuation routes safe, maintain a safe environment, and support staff in moving or protecting patients during a fire or other emergencies. The new provision, Integrated Fire Protection and Life Safety System Testing for high-rise buildings at section 11.8.9, requires testing to be conducted in accordance with 9.11.4.2 and NFPA 4. Both new and existing high-rise buildings will be required to adhere to NFPA 4 for integrated testing. New high-rise buildings shall be required to conduct their integrated testing prior to issuance of a certificate of occupancy. Existing high-rise buildings shall conduct their integrated testing at intervals not exceeding 10 years unless otherwise specified in an integrated system test plan in accordance with NFPA 4.
(3) New Definition of Gross Floor Area (HCOs and AHCOs)—Sections 3.3.24.2.2 and 3.3.24.2.3
The new definition of “gross floor area” no longer requires the inclusion of stairs and shafts within the boundary of smoke compartments or suites to be included in the area calculation, thus changing the way in which the size of these areas are calculated. Revisions to suite size calculations relax requirements regarding the extent of smoke detection, the use of quick-response sprinklers, and direct supervision of occupants by trained staff. Gross floor area now takes into account outside walls and fire walls of a building and walls that bound an occupancy or incidental use area. Gross floor area excludes floor openings for atriums and communicating spaces. A specific definition for HCOs and AHCOs was added to clarify smoke compartment calculations. For HCOs and AHCOs, gross floor area does not deduct stairs, elevator shafts, or service shafts but still excludes atrium and communicating space openings. We believe the changes will continue to provide safe refuge for patients in health care structures who cannot self-evacuate during a fire or emergency.
(4) New Non-Required Fire Door/Frame Does Not Require Inspections—Section 4.6.12.4
Facilities have been required to perform annual fire door inspections even when they are located in barriers that are not required to have a fire-resistance rating, as the doors were interpreted to be a life safety feature “obvious to the public.” The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), Section 4.6.12.4 states that doors and door frames located in barriers that are not required to have a fire-resistance rating under the life safety plans are also no longer required to comply with NFPA 80,
Standard for Fire Doors and Other Opening Protectives.
This change would alleviate the annual inspection and testing requirement of the door assembly and would remove the need to modify door labels to avoid the annual inspection and testing requirement. This change would reduce the burden on facilities by no longer requiring compliance with NFPA 80 for non-required fire doors and frames.
(5) New Security and Communications Systems Allowed in Stairs Requirements—Section 7.1.3.2.1(9)(c)
Section 7.1.3.2.1(9)(c), permits penetrations into an exit enclosure for security and communication systems, provided the pathways are installed in metal conduit. The new provision for means of egress at 7.1.3.2.1(9)(c) allows penetrations into
and
openings through an exit enclosure assembly for security and communication systems as long as they are installed in a metal conduit. This provision would enhance patient safety by ensuring that critical security and communication systems serving exit enclosures remain operational during an emergency.
d. New and Existing Health Care Occupancies—Chapter 18 and 19
The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) introduces several important new provisions in Chapter 18, New Health Care Occupancies, and Chapter 19, Existing Health Care Occupancies, as discussed in the sections that follow immediately in this rule. We have provided the LSC citation and a description of the updated 2024 requirements at the beginning of each section discussed.
In the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), a “Health Care Occupancy” is defined as any facility that provides inpatient care for four or more patients. However, CMS does not apply this LSC standard with respect to patient census numbers. Unless specifically noted, the requirements, conditions of participation, and conditions for coverage for all Medicare and Medicaid-participating health care providers and suppliers subject to these rules would apply on a facility basis, regardless of the size of the facility or the facility's patient census. These basic requirements are established to ensure a core level of safety and quality for all patients, regardless of where they receive health care services. We believe that patients in small facilities should be assured of the same level of fire safety as those in larger facilities. Therefore, we propose that this definition would be inapplicable to Medicare and Medicaid-certified facilities because all HCOs that provide care to one or more patients would be required to comply with the relevant requirements of the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101).
(1) New Alternate Care Sites (ACS) Requirements—Sections 18.1.1.1.10, 19.1.1.1.10
The 2024 edition of the LSC includes a new definition for “alternate care site” (ACS) (3.3.16). An ACS is defined as a building, structure, or portion thereof not currently being used for health care that is temporarily reoccupied, converted, constructed, or relocated for health care use during an urgent need in capacity to provide additional capability for an affected community. This provision permits the use of an ACS for health care during an urgent need to provide additional capability for communities. New and existing HCOs may allow an ACS to temporarily convert to an HCO with an approved fire emergency plan and comply with alternate construction, design, protection, operational, and occupancy classification requirements. The associated provisions are intended to address urgent surges in demand and ensure that affected communities have safe, code-compliant capacity during times of public health emergencies or other crises.
(
printed page 72678)
(2) New Clarity Around Suite Requirements—Sections 18/19.2.5.7.2.2 & 18/19.2.5.7.3.1and 18/19.2.5.7.2.4 & 18/19.2.5.7.3.3
Suite size and egress requirements have been clarified to make sure that requirements can be applied and enforced correctly. In both new and existing Health Care Occupancies, the requirements for means of egress from sleeping and non-sleeping suites (Sections 18/19.2.5.7.2.2 and 18/19.2.5.7.3.1) now allow additional options for providing a single exit access door in suites that would otherwise require two exit access doors. One of the exit access doors shall be permitted to be either an exit stair, exit passageway, exit door to the exterior or another suite (separated by corridor requirements in Chapters 18 and 19). The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) also provides clarified guidance for HCOs on travel distance requirements within patient care sleeping and non-sleeping suites (Sections 18/19.2.5.7.2.4 and 18/19.2.5.7.3.3).
(3) New Requirements for Hazardous Areas—Sections 18.3.2.1.3 and 19.3.2.1.5
Requirements were added for new and existing HCOs regarding hazardous areas. Rooms used as sterile core areas supporting operating rooms and anesthetizing areas shall be considered hazardous areas and be protected by smoke partitions unless provided with automatic extinguishing systems; walls that limit the transfer of smoke; and doors with self-closing or automatic-closing devices. This is a patient safety requirement to ensure that hazardous areas are protected appropriately.
(4) New Carbon Monoxide (CO) Detector Requirements—Sections 18.3.2.5.3(15)/18.3.4.6
The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) includes a new definition for CO alarms (3.3.14.1). CO alarms, whether single- or multiple-station, alert facility occupants to the presence of unsafe levels of CO within the facility. The 2024 edition of the LSC now requires facilities to have CO detection and warning equipment in accordance with NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, to enhance patient safety. Requirements for CO detection were added for cooking facilities open to the corridor, to ceilings of rooms containing fuel-burning appliances or fireplaces, and within 36 inches of the first air vent from fuel-burning heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems in new HCOs. In addition, requirements for CO detection were also added where new residential board and care facilities that have communicating garages, fuel-burning appliances, or fuel burning fireplaces. Effective with the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), new HCOs are required to have CO detection and warning equipment provided in accordance with NFPA 72 to increase patient safety. The new requirements apply to locations in facilities with fuel-burning appliances, fuel burning fireplaces, fuel burning HVAC systems, and attached garages.

Instead of fire alarm notification appliances (loud horns and strobe lights) that need to be activated, facilities are permitted to use coded announcements to staff. This should improve patient experience as the alarm notification appliances can startle patients and only signal something is wrong without providing context, while coded announcements support a patient-centered care environment. The fire alarm notification systems still need to be tested at intervals but not as frequently activated during fire drills. New and existing HCOs and new and existing AHCOs have revised the occupant notification requirements at sections 18/19.3.4.3.1 & 20/21.3.4.3.1.2 of the LSC (NFPA 101) to permit the omission of notification appliances in patient care spaces. The requirement is applicable where alarm notification would adversely affect patient care and the private operating mode (the mode in which only staff or key personnel responsible for initiating and directing emergency actions are notified) is utilized in accordance with NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code.
(6) New Requirements for Subdivision of Building Spaces—Sections 18.3.7.1 and 19.3.7.1, 20.3.7.2 and 21.3.7.2
New and existing HCOs smoke compartment maximum size has increased to 40,000 square feet where the building is protected by quick-response or listed residential sprinklers, sleeping rooms are configured for only one patient or contain no sleeping rooms, and the maximum travel distance from any point to reach a door in the required smoke barrier does not exceed 200 feet. In existing hospitals, standard-response sprinkles are permitted to continue to be used in approved existing sprinkler systems where quick-response and residential sprinklers were not listed for use at the time of installation. This requirement allows for new and existing HCOs to have more flexibility with the designs of hospital smoke compartments.
(7) New Increased Maximum Allowable Sizes for Soiled Linen and Trash Receptacles Requirements—Sections 18/19.7.5.7.1/.2
The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) states the maximum allowable size of soiled linen and trash receptacles not located in hazardous area enclosures increased from 32 gallons to 64 gallons. This modification made the requirement consistent with the threshold for a room storing soiled linen or trash to be considered a hazardous area. Additionally, the 2018 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) removed the restriction limiting the capacity of containers within any 64-square-foot area, thus improving flexibility for environmental services staff. The container density criteria requirements from Sections 18/19.7.5.7.1/.2 were removed from new and existing HCOs and AHCOs. Also, the capacity for soiled linen or trash collection receptacles increased from 32 gallons to 64 gallons and they are required to be located in a hazardous area when not attended. Two exceptions apply to receptacles used solely for the purpose of recycling of clean waste or patient records awaiting destruction, which have a maximum capacity of 96 gallons and are required to be labeled and listed in accordance with FM Approvals 6920/6921. FM (Factory Mutual) Approval is a certification system that verifies the performance and safety of products and systems.

The 2012 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), which was adopted in the CMS final rule titled,
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Fire Safety Requirements for Certain Health Care Facilities,

Considering the CMS adoption of the 2012 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), became effective on July 5, 2016, high-rise buildings containing existing HCOs (for example, hospitals, LTC facilities, inpatient hospice) must be compliant by July 5, 2028. Requiring existing HCOs in high-rise buildings to be fully sprinklered improves patient safety by providing rapid, automatic fire suppression close to the source of ignition. In health care settings, many patients cannot self-evacuate, so

e. Roller Latches—Sections 18.3.6.3.9.1 and 19.3.6.3.5
As previously stated, on January 10, 2003, we published a final rule in the
Federal Register
(
68 FR 1374
) adopting the 2000 edition of the LSC. In that final rule, we required that all affected facilities meet the provisions of the 2000 edition of the LSC, with certain exceptions. One of the exceptions to the 2000 edition of the LSC is the code's use of roller latches on corridor doors in buildings that are fully protected by a sprinkler system. A roller latch is a type of door latching mechanism to keep a door closed. Through fire investigations, roller latches have proven to be an unreliable door latching mechanism requiring extensive maintenance to operate properly. Many roller latches in fire situations failed to provide adequate protection to residents in their rooms during an emergency. Roller latches that are not properly maintained may be a danger to the health and safety of patients and staff. In addition, we found through our online survey, certification, and reporting (OSCAR) system data report that doors that include roller latches are consistently one of our most cited deficiencies. In fact, in skilled nursing facilities roller latches in corridor doors are consistently the number one cited deficiency under the life safety requirements.
The 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101) requires corridor doors to be provided with a means for keeping the door closed that is acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. The LSC permits roller latches capable of keeping the door fully closed if a force of 5 pounds is applied at the latch edge or roller latches in fully sprinklered buildings.
Regardless of its permissibility in the LSC, it was and remains our position that roller latches on corridor doors are a safety hazard under all circumstances and CMS prohibits their use on corridor doors. Therefore, we propose to continue prohibiting the use of roller latches in existing and new HCOs for corridor doors, excluding corridor doors to auxiliary spaces not classified as hazardous areas as defined by the LSC.

h. 2024 Edition of the Health Care Facilities Code (NFPA 99)
The 2024 edition of the HCFC (NFPA 99) addresses requirements for both health care occupancies and ambulatory care occupancies and serves as a
(
printed page 72681)
resource for those who are responsible for protecting health care facilities from fire and associated hazards. The purpose of this Code is to provide minimum requirements for the installation, inspection, testing, maintenance, performance, and safe practices for health care facility materials, equipment and appliances. The HCFC is a compilation of documents that have been developed over a 40-year period by NFPA and is intended to be used by those persons involved in the design, construction, inspection, and operation of health care facilities, and in the design, manufacture, and testing of appliances and equipment used in patient care areas of health care facilities. It provides information on various subjects, such as medical gas and vacuum systems, electrical systems, electrical equipment, and gas equipment. The HCFC applies specific requirements in accordance with the results of a risk-based assessment methodology. A risk-based approach allows for the application of requirements based upon the types of treatment and services being provided to patients or residents rather than the type of facility in which they are being performed.
To ensure the minimum level of protection afforded by the HCFC is applicable to all patient and resident care areas within a health care facility, CMS is proposing to incorporate by reference the 2024 edition of the NFPA 99 with the exception of chapters 7 (Information Technology and Communications Systems for Health Care Facilities); 8 (Plumbing); 12 (Emergency Management); and 13 (Security Management). We are not proposing to incorporate these chapters as we believe they are not within the scope of the CoPs and CfCs. In the following section, we describe selected provisions from the 2024 edition of the NFPA 99 that we have determined as the most significant in terms of patient health and safety. We are providing the HCFC citation and a description of the requirement at the beginning of each section discussed. The first three chapters of NFPA 99 address the administration of the HCFC, the referenced publications, and definitions.
(1) New Auxiliary Connection Requirements—Section 5.1.3.5.14
This new section of the 2024 edition of the NFPA 99 provides requirements for medical gases and vacuum systems to have auxiliary connections which allow emergency supply through a temporary source such as a truck in instances where there is an issue with the primary supply or where system maintenance requires shutdown of the source. This requirement provides additional patient safety features for health care facilities.
(2) New Oxygen Central Supply Systems Using Concentrator(s) Requirements—Section 5.1.3.9
This new section allows oxygen central supply systems to use an oxygen concentrator as one of the supply sources. Oxygen concentrators are engineered assemblies that concentrate oxygen from air to provide medical grade oxygen. This is a new form of technology allowed for health care facilities and provides additional patient safety.
(3) New Medical Gas, Vacuum, and Waste Anesthetic Gas Disposal Systems Requirements—Sections 5.1.10.1.4 and 5.1.10.2.1
This change allows for new piping corrugated medical tubing (CMT) material and is now permitted for medical gas, vacuum, and waste anesthetic gas disposal systems. CMT is flexible copper tubing that is externally coated with non-metallic fire-retardant sheath. Previously, only rigid copper tubing was allowed. Copper tubing cannot be bent and is typically brazed together, which is a specialized and labor-intensive process. CMT is typically provided in longer lengths than rigid copper tubing, is flexible requiring less cutting and fittings, and does not need to be brazed, making it more efficient and economical to install. In particular, CMT is beneficial for facilities undergoing renovations in reducing costs and time when an old system is taken out of service. This change would reduce burden, provide a new form of technology, and provide additional patient safety. This provision would enhance patient safety by lowering the risk of gas leaks, ensuring more reliable delivery of oxygen and medical gases to patients, and minimizing interruptions to critical gas and vacuum services.
(4) New Electrical Maintenance Program—Section 6.9
A new section has been added to NFPA 99 that includes requirements and prescriptive intervals for electrical system components that must undergo routine inspection, maintenance, and testing. It also consolidates existing requirements and guidance that were previously located in several sections of the code so that facilities can find a comprehensive list of minimum requirements for such a program. These requirements will reduce burden and provide patient safety by preventing electrical system failures that could disrupt patient care.
(5) New Health Care Microgrids—Section 6.10
NFPA 99 now permits normal and emergency power to be supplied by sources other than a generator or battery system, including a health care microgrid system (HCMS). HCMSs are small-scale personalized electrical networks with intelligent controls that can operate independently, or in tandem with a large-scale electric grid. The power sources for an HCMS can be provided or supplemented by a combination of alternative technologies such as fuel cells, solar panels, wind turbines, and energy storage systems. Microgrids provide a small-scale electrical network option that is tailored to each facility's needs. They are able to operate independently or with a larger electric grid. CMS issued a categorical waiver memo in March 2023 (QSO-23-11-LSC) to waive requirements in the 2012 edition of NFPA 99 that essential electric systems must be supplied by a generator or battery system, thus allowing for health care facilities to choose microgrids as a supply for essential electric systems when a microgrid best meets the needs of the facility. In proposing to adopt the 2024 edition of the NFPA 99, QSO-23-11-LSC could be rescinded as it would no longer be necessary.
(6) New Heliports Requirements—Section 16.8
A new requirement was added that references NFPA 418, Standard for Heliports, which establishes minimum fire safety requirements for the design, construction, maintenance, and operation of heliports.
i. Fire Safety Evaluation System (FSES, NFPA 101A)
On May 4, 2016, we published a final rule titled “Fire Safety Requirements for Certain Health Care Facilities,” adopting the 2012 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101). One of the references in the LSC is NFPA 101A, Guide on Alternative Approaches to Life Safety, also known as the Fire Safety Evaluation System (FSES). NFPA 101A is based on the most current LSC (NFPA 101) edition; therefore, it is published after NFPA 101.
The FSES is a scoring system in which points are scored based on predetermined criteria related to a facility's zone location, containment, extinguishment, and people movement. A facility that achieves a passing score on the FSES would be considered to meet the fire safety requirements for
(
printed page 72682)
Medicare and Medicaid certification and recertification in lieu of compliance with the LSC exactly as it is written. The FSES allow for flexibilities in the application of LSC standards to ensure equivalent fire safety protection when alternate materials, designs, or construction techniques are used in a particular facility. In 2017, CMS adopted the 2013 edition of the NFPA 101A by issuing a memo (QSO-17-15-LSC)
[
285
]
to permit the FSES option as an alternative approach to meeting the requirements of the LSC (NFPA 101) for health care occupancies and board and care occupancies. However, some LTC facilities that utilized the 2013 edition of the NFPA 101A to determine compliance with the containment, extinguishment and people movement requirements of the LSC were no longer able to achieve a passing score on the FSES due to a change in scoring methodology. To address this issue, in the August 2022 final rule (
87 FR 47502
), we finalized changes to § 483.90(a)(1)(iii) to allow LTC facilities that were Medicare or Medicaid-certified before July 5, 2016, and that had previously used the FSES to determine equivalent fire protection levels, to use the mandatory values from the 2001 edition of the FSES to meet the applicable requirements. This allowed existing LTC facilities that previously met the FSES requirements to continue to do so without incurring substantial financial burden to modify their construction type, while preserving the health and safety of residents and staff.
As we propose to adopt the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), we are also proposing to adopt the 2025 edition of NFPA 101A. We propose to offer hospitals, LTCs, CAHs, ICFs/IID, hospice inpatient care facilities, PACE centers, and RNHCIs the option to use the 2025 edition of the Guide on Alternative Approaches to Life Safety (NFPA 101A) as a method to demonstrate compliance with the provisions of the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101). Additionally, the 2024 edition of the LSC the NFPA revised the requirements in such a way that, when applying the FSES standards to achieve equivalent compliance with the LSC standards, affected LTC facilities would now achieve a passing FSES score and be considered compliant with the CMS requirements. Therefore, we propose to remove the obsolete requirements set forth at § 483.90(a)(1)(iii). We have determined that the updated mandatory point value scoring contained within the 2025 edition of the NFPA 101A would allow the appropriate degree of flexibility for LTC facilities while assuring resident and staff safety.

k. 2022 Edition of the Standard for Emergency Standby Power Systems (NFPA 110)
The 2022 edition of the Standard for Emergency Standby Power Systems (ESPS) (NFPA 110) addresses performance requirements for emergency and standby power systems. These systems provide an alternate source of electrical power in buildings when the normal electrical power source fails. Emergency power systems are made up of several components that need to work together to make sure electrical power is restored. These include power sources, transfer equipment, controls, supervisory equipment, and accessory equipment needed to supply electrical power to the selected circuits. In addition, the 2024 edition of the NFPA 101 and NFPA 99 identifies the 2022 edition of ESPS (NFPA 110) as a mandatory reference, which establishes requirements for the installation, maintenance, operation, and testing of emergency and standby power systems Therefore, CMS is proposing to replace references to the 2010 edition of the ESPS (NFPA 110), including TIAs to chapter 7, issued August 6, 2009, with an incorporation by reference of the 2022 edition of the ESPS (NFPA 110), issued April 8, 2021. In the following section, we describe selected provisions that represent a significant change from the 2010 edition of the ESPS (2010) or additions that constitute new requirements.
(1) Chapter 5 Emergency Power Supply (EPS): Energy Sources, Converters, and Accessories
This chapter establishes requirements for the selection, installation, and operating conditions of energy sources (such as generators), temperature maintenance, fuel storage, and associated accessories that together make up the EPS.
Section 5.6.9.9, Generators, Exciters, and Voltage Regulators, specifies that the generator instrument panels for Level 1 applications must provide a voltage-adjusting feature to allow ±5 percent voltage adjustment and an AC kW or kVA meter to show total generator load. This requirement ensures that operators have immediate access to critical generator performance data for safe and effective monitoring during emergency operations.
(2) Chapter 7 System Design and Environmental Considerations
This chapter introduces enhanced clarity and requirements regarding the installation environment and service accessibility for Emergency Power Supply Systems (EPSS).
Section 7.2.6.1 mandates that generator sets installed in outdoor enclosures must provide a minimum of 0.9 meters (36 inches) of working space from the outside edge of the enclosure for inspection, repair, maintenance, cleaning, or replacement, or enough space to fully open all hinged doors, whichever is greater. This codifies best practices in system accessibility and safety, ensuring that maintenance personnel have unobstructed access to critical equipment components for reliable EPSS operation.
Section 7.13.5 provides comprehensive requirements for the acceptance testing of fuel cell-based Emergency Power Supply Systems
(
printed page 72683)
(EPSS). This section mandates on-site acceptance testing protocols tailored to the unique operational characteristics of fuel cell technologies. It specifies that the EPSS must perform within the standard's limits, with compliance determined through a sequence of tests that simulate actual load conditions and system transfer responses. Key provisions include testing all fuel cell units with building load, documenting start-up timings, unit response, and all transfer switch operations. The tests also require at least 1.5 hours of continuous operation with either building or simulated loads. All voltage, frequency, amperage, and timing data must be recorded, and safeties specified to be verified on-site per manufacturer recommendations.
l. 2022 Edition of the Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems (NFPA 13)
The 2022 edition of the Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems (NFPA 13) provides the minimum requirements for the design, installation, and testing of automatic sprinkler systems to achieve a reasonable degree of protection for life and property from fire. In addition, the 2024 edition of the NFPA 101 and NFPA 99 identifies the 2022 edition of NFPA 13 as a mandatory reference. Therefore, CMS is proposing to incorporate by reference the 2022 edition of the Edition of the Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems (NFPA 13) issued April 15, 2021, to replace the currently required 1999 edition of the code.
In the following section, we describe selected provisions that represent a significant change from the 1999 edition of the NFPA 13 or additions that constitute new requirements.
(1) Chapter 19, Design Approaches
Chapter 19, Design Approaches, provides comprehensive requirements for determining water demand and design approaches for spray sprinklers, detailing both hydraulic calculation and pipe schedule methods to address occupancy hazard fire control.
Section 19.2.3, Water Demand Requirements—Hydraulic Calculation Methods, governs water demand requirements using hydraulic calculation methods for occupancy hazard fire control. This section clarified and streamlined approaches for hydraulic calculations, distinguishing it from the pipe schedule method. It now emphasizes clearer requirements and organization for determining water demand, enhancing consistency and usability for design professionals in applying the hydraulic calculation method to extra hazard occupancies and other scenarios where appropriate.
(2) Chapter 30 Existing System Modifications
Chapter 30, Existing System Modifications, consolidated all requirements related to modifications of existing sprinkler systems into a single chapter. The requirements of this chapter apply if a system is being modified, added to, or repaired. This chapter provides clear and unified guidance improving both compliance and usability for system modifications. Previously approved or existing systems shall be allowed to remain in use as installed.
m. 2023 Edition of the Standard for the Inspection, Testing, and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems (NFPA 25)
The 2023 edition of the Standard for the Inspection, Testing, and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems (NFPA 25) establishes the minimum requirements for the periodic inspection, testing, and maintenance of water-based fire protection systems to ensure their operational readiness and provide a reasonable degree of protection for life and property from fire. In addition, the 2024 edition of the NFPA 101 and NFPA 99 identifies the 2023 edition of the NFPA 25 as a mandatory reference. Therefore, CMS is proposing to incorporate by reference the 2023 Edition of the Standard for the Inspection, Testing, and Maintenance of Water-Based Fire Protection Systems (NFPA 25), issued September 1, 2022, to replace the currently required 1998 edition of the code.
In the following section, we describe selected provisions that represent a significant change from the 1998 edition of the NFPA 25 or additions that constitute new requirements.
(1) Section 8.1.1.2 Fire Pump Inspection, Testing and Maintenance
Section 8.1.1.2 requires that the minimum frequency of inspection, testing, and maintenance for fire pumps must follow both the manufacturer's recommendations and Table 8.1.1.2, which summarizes these required activities and their frequencies. Table 8.1.1.2 is more comprehensive, including new items and maintenance tasks, expanded references to specific section numbers, and consolidated maintenance tasks with clear frequencies, that is, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annually, etc. The table separates “Inspection,” “Test,” and “Maintenance” items, streamlining responsibilities and tracking requirements.
(2) Section 14.2.1 Assessment of Internal Condition of Piping
Section 14.2.1 addresses the requirements for assessing the internal condition of piping in water-based fire protection systems for the presence of foreign organic and inorganic material (for example, corrosion or obstruction). The assessment must be conducted at intervals specified in sections 14.2.1.1 (typically every 5 years) or per 14.2.1.2 (as conditions warrant). Various acceptable methods are described, including physically opening/inspecting main ends or branch lines at strategic locations most susceptible to corrosion or blockage; use of alternative non-invasive methods; assessing during major system work (for example, renovations, draining for repairs).
n. Removal of the Outside Window or Door Requirements
The 2000 edition of the LSC required that every health care occupancy patient sleeping room shall have an outside window or outside door, with new health care occupancies having an allowable sill height not to exceed 36 inches above the floor with certain exceptions. This requirement no longer existed in the 2012 edition of the LSC; however, CMS believed that outside doors and windows were necessary for the health and safety of patients and decided to retain the requirement.
On May 4, 2016, we published a final rule titled “Fire Safety Requirements for Certain Health Care Facilities,” which required hospitals, CAHs, and RNHCIs, LTCs facilities, and hospice inpatient care facilities to have outside windows and doors in every patient sleeping areas. Interested parties have expressed concerns about their ability to comply with this requirement. Additionally, the 2024 edition of the LSC does not include this requirement as an essential life safety feature; therefore, we propose to remove the outside window and door requirements for hospitals, CAHs, RNHCIs, LTC Facilities, and hospice inpatient care facilities.
We note that LTC facilities would continue to be required to provide at least one window to the outside in residents' bedrooms in accordance with the longstanding requirement at newly redesignated § 483.90(e)(1). While we are maintaining this outside window requirement, we believe it continues to impose a lower burden on providers than what was required in the outside window and door requirements at § 483.90(a)(7), which contained more
(
printed page 72684)
prescriptive specifications (for example, window sill height requirement).
Additionally, we propose to remove obsolete regulatory provisions regarding outside widows for ICFs/IID. The current requirements at § 483.470(b)(2) state that bedrooms below grade level (that is, below ground level) in an ICF/IID must have a window that can be used as a second means of escape. The window must be no more than 44 inches above the ground unless the facility is surveyed under the HCO chapter of the LSC, in which case the window must be no more than 36 inches above the floor. ICFs/IID must meet outside window requirements pursuant to the LSC; therefore, continuing to specify this requirement in our regulations is redundant and no longer necessary.

G. Transplant Programs—Request for Information (RFI)
CMS is seeking public comments related to requirements for initial approval for solid organ transplant programs, specifically the requirements concerning clinical experience (or volume) and outcome requirements for the initial approval of transplant programs, as well as the exceptions for specific type of organ(s) programs.
1. Initial Approval and Re-Approval of Transplant Programs: Background
Transplant programs, located within a hospital that has a Medicare provider agreement, provide transplant services for one or more specific organs. Transplant programs must comply with the Medicare transplant program CoPs regulations at
42 CFR 482.68
through
482.104
, and with the hospital CoPs at §§ 482.1 through 482.58. There are several types of CMS-approved transplant programs, including heart, heart-lung, lung, liver, kidney, intestine, and pancreas..
In 2005, CMS proposed CoPs for transplant programs that we believed would be necessary to: (1) protect other potential Medicare beneficiaries who are waiting for organs for transplantation; (2) establish sufficient quality and procedural standards to ensure that transplants are performed in a safe and efficient manner; and (3) reduce Medicare expenses by decreasing the likelihood that a transplant would fail (
70 FR 6140
). The regulations were intended to assess an organ transplant center's ability to perform successful transplants and deliver quality patient care as evidenced by good outcomes and sound policies and procedures. They were finalized in 2007 and set forth clear expectations for safe, high-quality transplant service delivery in Medicare-participating facilities (
72 FR 15198
).
In the 2007 final rule, CMS finalized two requirements related to the approval of transplant programs: (1) § 482.80 Data submission, clinical experience, and outcome requirements for initial approval of transplant programs and (2) § 482.82 Data submission, clinical experience, and outcome requirements for re-approval of transplant programs. After publication of the 2007 Final Rule, we continued to review how effective the transplant program requirements were, as well as the effectiveness of the sub-regulatory guidance and the data derived from the transplant program surveys.
On September 20, 2018, we published the Omnibus Burden Reduction Proposed Rule Regulatory Provisions to Promote Program Efficiency, Transparency, and Burden Reduction (
83 FR 47686
) that, among other things, proposed removing all the requirements set forth in § 482.82 for the re-approval of transplant programs. We discussed various articles that suggested that the requirements for re-approval of transplant programs had resulted in unintended negative consequences for patients on the transplant waiting lists. We were especially concerned with the findings that suggested that transplant programs that were low performing might be removing sicker patients from their transplant lists due to the outcome measures set forth in § 482.82.
[
286
]
Subsequently, on September 30, 2019, we published a final rule titled Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Regulatory Provisions to Promote Program Efficiency, Transparency, and Burden Reduction; Fire Safety Requirements for Certain Dialysis Facilities; Hospital and CAH Changes to Promote Innovation, Flexibility, and Improvement in Patient Care (
84 FR 51732
) that, among other things, finalized the removal of § 482.82. We stated that the removal of these requirements would lead to improved
(
printed page 72692)
patient outcomes, increased transplantation opportunities for patients on the waitlist, improved organ procurement for transplantation, greater organ utilization, and reduced burden on transplant programs. Most of the commenters supported the removal of the requirements in § 482.82. However, there were also commenters that were concerned about how CMS would continue to monitor transplant programs and ensure patient safety and outcomes. We indicated that the requirements set forth in § 482.80 Data submission, clinical experience, and outcome requirements for initial approval of transplant programs and § 482.96 QAPI, as well as survey processes, both routine and complaint-based, would provide the oversight needed to ensure safety and quality of care for patients and transplant recipients.
On December 3, 2021, we published, Request for Information; Health and Safety Requirements for Transplant Programs, Organ Procurement Organization, and End-Stage Renal Disease Facilities (CMS 3409-NC,
86 FR 68594
). Among the issues we solicited comments on was whether the initial approval requirements in § 482.80 created barriers to the establishment of new transplant programs (
86 FR 68594
,
68596
). We also asked about alternative requirements that could be used to ensure that new transplant programs would provide quality care for transplant recipients. Many commenters stated that the requirements in § 482.80 were a barrier due to the volume requirements and timeframe to obtain outcome requirements. However, other commenters indicated that they did not believe the initial requirements were excessive. They indicated that organ transplantation was very expensive and required complex procedures so that facilities must be ready to invest the required resources to achieve strong performance. However, since the publication of this RFI, CMS has continued to receive feedback from prospective transplant programs regarding the timeframe to obtain the 1-year outcomes data.
Initiatives Related to Kidney Health:
In 2019, the Trump Administration released Executive Order (E.O.) 13879 dedicated to advancing American kidney health citing too many at-risk patients progress to late-stage kidney failure, high mortality rates, the high cost of current treatment options, the inability of current treatment options to produce an acceptable quality of life for patients, and the lack of sufficient kidneys donated to meet the current demand for transplants.
[
287
]
In response to this E.O., CMS published a proposed rule in 2019 that was finalized in 2020, revising the outcome measures utilized to assess performance of organ procurement organizations (OPOs). The rule was specifically designed to drive OPO performance and increase the number of organs available for transplantation. There has been significant progress since the rule was finalized. Between 2019 and 2024, there was a nearly 37 percent increase in the number of organ donors and 30 percent increase in the number of organ transplants. During this same period there was a more than 26 percent increase in the number of kidneys transplanted.
In addition to this action, in 2024 the CMS Innovation Center finalized the Increasing Organ Transplant Access (IOTA) Model, which is a 6-year mandatory model for approximately half of the transplant hospitals around the country. The IOTA Model holds transplant centers accountable for the volume, efficiency, and outcomes for their patients and offers the opportunity for upside or downside payments based on performance. CMS will evaluate the results from that model as it considers future regulatory efforts and how to best increase the number of patients successfully transplanted.
Despite ongoing government initiatives, kidney disease remains a leading cause of death in the United States.
[
288
]
In 2024, approximately 35.5 million Americans were suffering from chronic kidney disease and 808,000 were living with ESRD. More than 100,000 Americans begin dialysis each year to treat ESRD with twenty percent dying within a year and 50 percent dying within 5 years.
[
289
]
Currently, nearly 90,000 Americans are on the waiting list to receive a kidney transplant, making up the vast majority of Americans waiting for organ transplantation.
[
290
]
The 2019 E.O. provided the policy framework to prevent kidney failure whenever possible through better diagnosis, treatment, and incentives for preventive care; increasing patient choice through affordable alternative treatments for ESRD (by encouraging higher value care and educating patients on treatment alternatives); and increasing access to kidney transplants by modernizing the organ recovery and transplantation systems. We seek to continue our efforts to improve the system and are therefore requesting information that may lead to improvements in certification of new transplant programs.
