H. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1-year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. This proposed rule does not mandate any requirements for State, local, or tribal governments. This proposed rule would not impose a mandate that would result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal Government, in the aggregate, of more than $193 million in any one year. Based on the cost estimates discussed in this section, we have assessed the various costs and benefits of the final updates to the conditions of participation. For the private sector facilities, the regulatory impact analysis, together with the remainder of the preamble, constitutes the analysis required under UMRA.

E.O. 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”
Executive Order 14192
, entitled “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation” was issued on January 31, 2025, and requires that “any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.” We followed the implementation guidance from OMB-M-25-20 (
https://www.whitehouse.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​2025/​02/​M-25-20-
(
printed page 72754)
Guidance-Implementing-Section-3-of-Executive-Order-14192-Titled-Unleashing-Prosperity-Through-Deregulation.pdf
) when estimating the proposed rule's impact related to the executive order. Specifically, we used a 7 percent discount rate when estimating the costs and cost savings for the purposes of the E.O 14192-The E.O 14192 looks at the long-term impact based on a 20-year window. For most of the policies we are proposing in this rule, the impacts remain the same for all years after year 1 and we assume that they will continue for years 11through 20. However, the costs and cost savings estimates for PHE reporting and OB training are influenced by several key assumptions related to the historical frequency of PHE reporting data and the annual fluctuation in staff who require OB training, respectively.
For PHE reporting, we identified a recurring pattern of significant public health emergencies occurring about once every 5 years. This pattern is central to our 20-year cost savings projection. Instead of assuming a steady annual likelihood, we modeled the projection with no PHE reporting activity in years 5 and 15, while anticipating a 32-week (7.5-month) acute infectious illness event in years 10 and 20. This approach provides a more realistic reflection of the cyclical nature of such emergencies, rather than a uniform annual occurrence.
For the OB staff training, we factored in an annual staff turnover rate of approximately 21 percent in hospitals. This, coupled with new hires, means that the number of staff requiring OB training fluctuates each year.
In summary, both the PHE reporting data and OB training requirements introduce variability to our costs and cost savings calculations.
VI. Conclusion
Eliminating unnecessary and duplicative regulatory requirements is essential to ensuring that patients will have continued access to care and allowing providers to focus on patients over paperwork. The changes that we are proposing in this rule would have significant impacts on LTC facilities, hospitals, ICFs/IID, and CAHs. As outlined in Table 25, Table 26, Table 54, Table 55, and Table 56, we expect that modifications to the current CoPs would reduce provider burden by approximately $289 million annually and more than $2.89 billion over 10 years. In addition, over 10 years it will return nearly 29.36 million hours of clinician time to providers, allowing them to prioritize patients over paperwork. As shown in Table 24, we also estimate cost savings of $687,600 over 10 years for the Federal Government, $ 687,600 over 10 years for States, and $ 304,159,413 over 10 years and more than 3.3 million hours for providers associated with the Medicaid institutional payment transparency proposals.

(d)
Standard: Fire Safety.
(1) Except as otherwise provided in this section—
(i) The hospice must meet the applicable provisions and must proceed in accordance with the 2024 edition of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101).

(ii) Establish a fire watch until the system is back in service.

(c)
Birth tissue collection.
For hospitals that furnish obstetrical services and participate in the collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release to patients of birth tissues the following standards apply. For purposes of this section, birth tissues are defined as human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery (including cesarean-section delivery), such as umbilical cord blood,
(
printed page 72760)
umbilical cord tissue, placenta, amniotic membrane, amniotic fluid, and other tissues or biological materials associated with live childbirth.
(1)
Standard: Informed consent.
The hospital must ensure informed consent is obtained from the patient or patient's representative prior to the collection, storage, donation, transfer, banking, or release to patients of birth tissues, consistent with the hospital's scope of services and role in those activities. This consent must be documented consistent with the requirements for medical records at 482.24(c)(4)(v). The informed consent process must include, as applicable:
(i) A description of the birth tissues to be collected;
(ii) The intended use (including commercial and research uses) of the birth tissues;
(iii) Disclosure of any third-party involvement and any conflicts of interest;
(iv) Information regarding risks, limitations, and infection prevention and quality control considerations;
(v) Notice that patient's or patient's representative's refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment; and
(vi) Any other information required under applicable Federal or State law.
(2)
Standard: Policies and procedures for cultural, religious, or personal uses.
The hospital must have written policies and procedures that permit patients to request retention or release of birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons, consistent with State law and the hospital's infection prevention and control program requirements under § 482.42.
(i) The policies and procedures must address:
(A) Processes for patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues;
(B) Safe handling, packaging, storage, and release practices;
(C) Circumstances under which retention or release may be limited or denied due to infection prevention and control concerns, biohazard risks, certain clinical conditions, emergency cases, or other applicable legal requirements; and
(D) Staff education regarding the hospital's procedures for responding to patient requests.
(ii) The hospital must provide patients who request retention or release of birth tissues with instructions for safe handling, transport, storage, and disposition of the tissues, as applicable.

(d) * * *
(3)
COVID-19 immunizations.
The LTC facility must develop and implement policies and procedures to ensure all the following:
(i) Before offering the COVID-19 immunization, each resident or the resident's representative receives education regarding the benefits and potential side effects of the immunization;
(
printed page 72761)
(ii) Each resident is offered a COVID-19 immunization, including all recommended doses and any applicable booster doses, unless the immunization is medically contraindicated or the resident has already been immunized;
(iii) The resident or the resident's representative has the opportunity to refuse immunization; and
(iv) The resident's medical record includes documentation that indicates, at a minimum, the following:
(A) That the resident or resident's representative was provided education regarding the benefits and potential side effects of COVID-19 immunization, including, where a multi-dose series is required, education regarding the number of doses, recommended dosing schedule, and the importance of completing the full immunization series; and
(B) That the resident either received the COVID-19 immunization (including where a multi-dose series is required, each dose administered in accordance with the recommended dosing schedule), or did not receive the COVID-19 immunization due to medical contraindication or refusal.
*

(g)
Public health emergency (PHE): Reporting of data related to acute infectious diseases
—In the event that the Secretary has declared a national, State, or local PHE for an acute infectious illness, the LTC facilities must electronically report data elements in a standardized format and frequency specified by the Secretary, including but not limited to the following:
(1) Facility census (defined as the total number of residents occupying a bed at this facility for at least 24 hours during the week of data collection).
(2) Confirmed, resident cases of a set of viral and bacterial pathogens and infectious diseases, as specified by the Secretary.
(3) Hospitalized residents with confirmed cases of a set of viral and bacterial pathogens and infectious diseases, as specified by the Secretary.
(4) Relevant confirmed infections for staff.
(5) Supply inventory shortages.
(6) Staffing shortages.
(7) Relevant medical countermeasures and therapeutic inventories, usage, or both.

Fire safety.
(1) Except as otherwise provided in this section—
(i) The LTC facility must meet the applicable provisions and must proceed in accordance with the 2024 edition of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101).
(ii) Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(1)(i) of this section, corridor doors must be provided with positive latching hardware, excluding corridor doors to auxiliary spaces not classified as hazardous areas as defined by the Life Safety Code. Roller latches and other devices capable of keeping doors closed when a 5 pound-force is applied at the latch edge are prohibited on corridor doors required to have positive latching hardware.
(iii) The LTC facility must use the 2025 edition of the Guide on Alternative Approaches to Life Safety (NFPA 101A) if the facility uses the Fire Safety Evaluation System (FSES) to show compliance with the provisions of the 2024 LSC (NFPA 101).

(3) The provisions of the Life Safety Code do not apply in a State where CMS determines, in accordance with applicable provisions of sections 1819(d)(2)(B)(ii) and 1919(d)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act, that a fire and safety code imposed by State law adequately protects patients, residents and personnel in LTC facilities.
(4) A long-term care facility may install alcohol-based hand rub dispensers in its facility if the dispensers are installed in a manner that adequately protects against inappropriate access.
(5) If CMS determines that a specific updated provision of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) provides an equal or superior means of ensuring patient safety as compared to the publications referenced in paragraph (i)(1) of this section, CMS will announce the availability of a voluntary waiver in favor of the updated provision via subregulatory guidance, provided that CMS has determined that the waiver does not adversely affect the health and safety of residents or personnel. (i) Evacuate the building or portion of the building affected by the system outage until the system is back in service, or
(ii) Establish a fire watch until the system is back in service.

(e)
Emergency and standby power systems.
The REH must install and maintain emergency and standby power systems, in accordance with the 2024 edition of the Health Care Facilities Code (NFPA 99), the 2024 edition of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), and the 2022 edition of the Emergency and Standy Power Systems (NFPA 110), based on the emergency plan set forth in paragraph (a) of this section.

Emergency power supply location.
The emergency power supply must be located in accordance with the location requirements found in the 2024 edition of the Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) (NFPA 99), the 2024 edition of the Life Safety Code (LSC) (NFPA 101), and the 2022 edition of the Emergency and Standby Power Systems (NFPA 110), when a new structure is built or when an existing structure or building is renovated.
(2)
Emergency power supply inspection and testing.
The REH must implement an emergency power supply inspection and testing requirements found in the 2024 edition of the HCFC (NFPA 99), the 2024 edition of the LSC (NFPA 101), and the 2022 edition of the Emergency and Standby Power Systems (NFPA 110).
(3)
Emergency power supply fuel.
REHs that maintain an onsite fuel source to power the emergency power supply and must have a plan for how it will keep emergency power systems operational during the emergency, unless it evacuates.

(c)
Birth tissue collection.
For CAHs that furnish obstetrical services and participate in the collection, storage, donation, banking, transfer, or release to patients of birth tissues the following standards apply. For purposes of this section, birth tissues are defined as human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products obtained during or immediately following labor and delivery (including cesarean-section delivery), such as umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord tissue, placenta, amniotic membrane, amniotic fluid, and other tissues or biological materials associated with live childbirth.
(1)
Standard: Informed consent.
The CAH must ensure informed consent is obtained from the patient or patient's representative prior to the collection, storage, donation, transfer, banking, or release to patients of birth tissues, consistent with the CAH's scope of services and role in those activities. This consent must be documented consistent with the requirements for clinical records at 485.638(a)(4)(i). The informed consent process must include, as applicable:
(i) A description of the birth tissues to be collected;
(ii) The intended use (including commercial and research uses) of the birth tissues;
(iii) Disclosure of any third-party involvement and any conflicts of interest;
(iv) Information regarding risks, limitations, and infection prevention and quality control considerations;
(v) Notice that a patient's or patient's representative's refusal to provide informed consent will not affect access to care or treatment; and
(vi) Any other information required under applicable Federal or State law.
(2)
Standard: Policies and procedures for cultural, religious, or personal uses.
The CAH must have written policies and procedures that permit patients to request retention or release of birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons, consistent with State law and the CAH's infection prevention and control program requirements under § 485.640.
(i) The policies and procedures must address:
(A) Processes for patient requests for retention or release of birth tissues;
(B) Safe handling, packaging, storage, and release practices;
(C) Circumstances under which retention or release may be limited or denied due to infection prevention and control concerns, biohazard risks, certain clinical conditions, emergency cases, or other applicable legal requirements; and
(D) Staff education regarding the CAH's procedures for responding to patient requests.
(ii) The CAH must provide patients who request retention or release of birth tissues with instructions for safe handling, transport, storage, and disposition of the tissues, as applicable.

(d)
Standard: Fire safety.
(1) Except as provided in paragraph (d)(2) of this section, dialysis facilities that do not provide one or more exits to the outside at grade level from the patient treatment area level must comply with provisions of the 2024 edition of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) applicable to Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies, regardless of the number of patients served.
(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (d)(1) of this section, dialysis facilities participating in Medicare as of October 14, 2008 that require sprinkler systems are those housed in multi-story buildings construction Types II(000), III(200), or V(000), as defined in the Life Safety Code, section 21.1.6.1, which were constructed after January 1, 2008, and those housed in high rise buildings over 75 feet in height, which were constructed after January 1, 2008.
(3) The provisions of the Life Safety Code do not apply where CMS determines that a fire and safety code imposed by State law adequately protects patients and personnel in dialysis facilities.
(4) After consideration of a recommendation by the State survey agency or approved accreditation organization, and at the discretion of the Secretary, CMS may waive for periods deemed appropriate specific provisions of the Life Safety Code which would result in unreasonable hardship upon a dialysis facility, but only if the waiver will not adversely affect the health and safety of the patients.
(5) No dialysis facility may operate in a building that is adjacent to an industrial high hazard area, as described in sections 20.1.3.7 and 21.1.3.7 of the Health Care Facilities Code (NFPA 99 and the Tentative Interim Amendments TIA 24-1 and TIA 24-2).
(6) If CMS determines that a specific updated provision of the Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) provides an equal or superior means of ensuring patient safety as compared to the publications referenced in paragraph (f)(1) of this section, CMS will announce the availability of a voluntary waiver in favor of the updated provision via subregulatory guidance. A facility that wishes to comply with the updated provision must formally elect to do so and document their decision in their records.
(e)
Standard: Building Safety.
(1) Dialysis facilities that do not provide one or more exits to the outside at grade level from the patient treatment area level must meet the applicable provisions of the 2024 edition of the Health Care Facilities Code and its Tentative Interim Amendments TIA 24-1 and TIA 24-2.
(2) Chapters 7, 8, 12, and 13 of the Health Care Facilities Code do not apply to a dialysis facility.
(3) After consideration of a recommendation by the State survey agency or approved accrediting organization, and at the discretion of the Secretary, CMS may waive for periods deemed appropriate specific provisions of the Health Care Facilities Code which would result in unreasonable hardship upon a facility, but only if the waiver does not adversely affect the health and safety of patients.
(4) If CMS determines that a specific updated provision of the Health Care Facilities Care (NFPA 99) provides an equal or superior means of ensuring patient safety as compared to the publications referenced in paragraph (f)(1) of this section, CMS will announce the availability of a voluntary waiver in favor of the updated provision via subregulatory guidance. 21 CFR 1271.3(d)
. FDA does not define or use the term “birth tissue” in
21 CFR part 1271
, its 2007 Donor Eligibility Guidance (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​eligibility-determination-donors-human-cells-tissues-and-cellular-and-tissue-based-products
), or its Minimal Manipulation/Homologous Use guidance (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​regulatory-considerations-human-cells-tissues-and-cellular-and-tissue-based-products-minimal
). In January 2025, FDA issued draft guidance entitled “Recommendations for Determining Eligibility of Donors of Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products (HCT/Ps)” (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​recommendations-determining-eligibility-donors-human-cells-tissues-and-cellular-and-tissue-based
). This document uses the term “gestational cells or tissues.” Differences may exist between FDA's definitions of HCT/Ps and “gestational cells or tissues” and CMS' definition of “birth tissues,” as CMS is not intending to incorporate FDA's definition into this rulemaking. CMS chose to define and use the term “birth tissue” because it is already familiar to tissue establishments and to hospitals that contract with them. Since this proposed CoP would regulate facility-patient interactions, as well as facility policies, documentation, and processes related to informed decision-making and the safe release of birth tissues, CMS chose terminology that is familiar to the affected industry.

21 CFR 1271.3(d)
. FDA does not define or use the term “birth tissue” in
21 CFR part 1271
, its 2007 Donor Eligibility Guidance (

), or its Minimal Manipulation/Homologous Use guidance (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​regulatory-considerations-human-cells-tissues-and-cellular-and-tissue-based-products-minimal
). In January 2025, FDA issued draft guidance entitled “Recommendations for Determining Eligibility of Donors of Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products (HCT/Ps)” (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​recommendations-determining-eligibility-donors-human-cells-tissues-and-cellular-and-tissue-based
). This document uses the term “gestational cells or tissues.” Differences may exist between FDA's definitions of HCT/Ps and “gestational cells or tissues” and CMS' definition of “birth tissues,” as CMS is not intending to incorporate FDA's definition into this rulemaking. CMS chose to define and use the term “birth tissue” because it is already familiar to tissue establishments and to hospitals that contract with them. Since this proposed CoP would regulate facility-patient interactions, as well as facility policies, documentation, and processes related to informed decision-making and the safe release of birth tissues, CMS chose terminology that is familiar to the affected industry.
